1. Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC)

Regularization
Full Citation James Kirkpatrick, Razvan Pascanu, Neil Rabinowitz, Joel Veness, Guillaume Desjardins, Andrei A. Rusu, Kieran Milan, John Quan, Tiago Ramalho, Agnieszka Grabska-Barwinska, Demis Hassabis, Claudia Clopath, Dharshan Kumaran, and Raia Hadsell. "Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 114(13):3521–3526, 2017. arXiv:1612.00796.

Core Idea

EWC frames sequential task learning as approximate Bayesian inference. After learning task A, the posterior over parameters p(θ | D_A) becomes the prior for task B. The key approximation is a Laplace approximation of this posterior: the log-posterior is expanded to second order around the MAP estimate, yielding a Gaussian whose precision is the Fisher information matrix (FIM).

The Fisher Information Penalty (Full Derivation)

Bayesian motivation log p(θ | D_A, D_B) = log p(D_B | θ) + log p(θ | D_A) − log p(D_B | D_A)

The second term is intractable, so EWC applies a Laplace approximation around the optimum θ*_A:

Laplace approximation of the prior log p(θ | D_A) ≈ log p(θ*_A | D_A) − (1/2) (θ − θ*_A)^T F_A (θ − θ*_A)
where F_A is the Fisher information matrix evaluated at θ*_A

In practice, EWC uses only the diagonal of F, yielding the per-parameter penalty:

EWC training objective L(θ) = L_B(θ) + (λ/2) ∑_i F_{A,i} (θ_i − θ*_{A,i})^2
L_B(θ) = loss on current task B
F_{A,i} = diagonal Fisher entry for parameter i, computed on task A data
θ*_{A,i} = optimal value of parameter i after training on task A
λ = hyperparameter controlling regularization strength

Computing the Diagonal Fisher

Diagonal Fisher computation F_{A,i} = E_{x ~ D_A} [ (∂ log p(y|x, θ*_A) / ∂θ_i)^2 ]
Estimated by sampling from the training data and computing squared gradients of the log-likelihood w.r.t. each parameter.

Online EWC (Schwarz et al. 2018 / Huszár 2018)

Naive EWC stores a separate quadratic penalty per past task, leading to memory linear in the number of tasks. Huszár (arXiv:1712.03847; PNAS 2018) showed this double-counts prior information. Online EWC maintains a single running Fisher and a single anchor point:

Online EWC update rule F̂^(t) = γ F̂^(t−1) + F^(t) θ* ← θ*_t (the latest optimum)
γ ∈ [0,1] controls the decay of older Fisher contributions. The penalty becomes a single term: (λ/2) ∑_i F̂^(t)_i (θ_i − θ*_i)^2

Code Repositories

PyTorch github.com/moskomule/ewc.pytorch
PyTorch github.com/pettza/EWC
TF2/Keras github.com/db434/EWC
TF2 github.com/stijani/elastic-weight-consolidation-tf2

No single "official" DeepMind release exists. The moskomule/ewc.pytorch repo is the most widely referenced community implementation.

Known Limitations Diagonal Fisher approximation. Ignores all parameter correlations. For highly correlated parameters (common in recurrent models and SSMs), this is a severe information loss. Kronecker-factored approximations (K-FAC) or rank-1 Fisher alternatives have been proposed but add significant cost.

Fisher computed at a single point. F is evaluated only at θ*_A; it says nothing about the curvature landscape between optima.

Growing penalty terms. Without online EWC, memory and computation grow linearly with tasks.

Sensitivity to λ. Too high → plasticity loss (the network cannot learn new tasks). Too low → forgetting resumes.
Applicability to RecWM EWC could protect the S5 SSM transition matrices (A, B, C, D) from drifting when the economic regime changes. The diagonal Fisher for the S5 parameterization is cheap to compute (the squared gradients of the log-likelihood are already available from backprop). However, the diagonal approximation is particularly poor for state-space models where A and B are tightly coupled through the discretization step. Recommendation: Use Online EWC as a baseline, but investigate Kronecker-factored or block-diagonal Fisher approximations that respect the (A, B) block structure.

2. Synaptic Intelligence (SI)

Regularization Online
Full Citation Friedemann Zenke, Ben Poole, and Surya Ganguli. "Continual Learning through Synaptic Intelligence." Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 70:3987–3995, 2017.

Core Idea

Like EWC, SI adds a quadratic penalty to protect important parameters. The key difference: importance is computed online during training via a path integral of each parameter's contribution to loss reduction, rather than post-hoc via the Fisher information.

The Omega Accumulation (Full Formulation)

Step 1: Online running sum during task μ

Per-parameter contribution accumulator ω̃_k^(μ) ← ω̃_k^(μ) − Δθ_k(s) · (∂L / ∂θ_k)(s)
At each optimization step s during task μ:
Δθ_k(s) = change to parameter k made by the optimizer at step s
(∂L / ∂θ_k)(s) = gradient of the task loss w.r.t. parameter k on the current minibatch
The product −Δθ · grad ≈ the parameter's contribution to loss decrease

Step 2: Normalize after task completes

Normalized importance Ω_k^(μ) = ω̃_k^(μ) / ((Δ_k^(μ))^2 + ξ)
Δ_k^(μ) = θ_k^(μ,final) − θ_k^(μ,init) (total parameter displacement during task μ)
ξ = small damping constant (e.g., 0.1) for numerical stability

Step 3: Accumulate across tasks

Cumulative importance Ω_k = ∑_{μ=1}^{T−1} Ω_k^(μ)

Step 4: Regularized objective

SI training objective L(θ) = L_T(θ) + c ∑_k Ω_k (θ_k − θ_k^*)^2
c = regularization strength hyperparameter
θ_k^* = reference point (parameter value at end of most recent task)

How SI Differs from EWC

  • Computation: SI computes importance online during training (no separate Fisher computation pass). EWC requires a post-training pass over task data to estimate the diagonal Fisher.
  • Information used: SI uses the actual optimization trajectory (path integral); EWC uses curvature at the final point only.
  • Memory: SI stores running accumulators during training (same memory as EWC at test time). No task data needs to be revisited.
  • Approximation quality: SI's path-integral importance can capture trajectory-level information that a point estimate (Fisher at θ*) misses.

Code Repositories

Official github.com/ganguli-lab/pathint

This is the official repository from Ganguli Lab accompanying the ICML 2017 paper.

Applicability to RecWM SI is attractive for the RecWM because it requires no separate Fisher computation pass—important for an online economic model that continuously receives streaming data. The path-integral importance naturally captures how much each S5 parameter contributed to fitting a particular economic regime. Recommendation: SI integrates cleanly with GateL0RD's gating mechanism: parameters that the gate keeps frozen have zero Δθ and thus accumulate no importance, correctly reflecting that they were not involved in the current task. The ξ damping term needs careful tuning for SSM parameters where Δ values can be very small due to the discretization step.

3. PackNet

Parameter Isolation Pruning
Full Citation Arun Mallya and Svetlana Lazebnik. "PackNet: Adding Multiple Tasks to a Single Network by Iterative Pruning." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), pp. 7765–7773, 2018. arXiv:1711.05769.

Core Idea

PackNet uses network pruning to create dedicated parameter subsets for each task within a single network. After training on a task, unimportant weights are pruned (freed), and the freed capacity is available for subsequent tasks. The key weights for each task are frozen and never modified again, providing zero forgetting by construction.

Algorithm (Step by Step)

  1. Train on Task 1. Fine-tune the entire network on Task 1's data to convergence.
  2. Prune. Rank all parameters by absolute magnitude. Remove a fixed percentage p% (e.g., 50–75%) of the smallest-magnitude parameters. This produces a binary mask m_1 where m_1[i] = 1 for retained parameters.
  3. Re-train with mask. Re-train the network on Task 1, but only update the retained parameters (those where m_1[i] = 1). The pruned parameters are set to zero. This recovers most of the performance lost from pruning.
  4. Freeze Task 1 parameters. The parameters in m_1 are permanently frozen. They will participate in forward passes for all future tasks but their values never change.
  5. Train on Task 2. Use the freed parameters (where m_1[i] = 0) plus any remaining unfrozen parameters. Only parameters not in any previous mask are trainable.
  6. Prune and re-train for Task 2. Repeat steps 2–4 on the Task 2 trainable set, producing mask m_2.
  7. Iterate. For Task t, the trainable parameter set is: {i : m_1[i] = 0 AND m_2[i] = 0 AND ... AND m_{t-1}[i] = 0}.
Formal mask constraint Trainable_t = {i : ∀ s < t, m_s[i] = 0} Capacity remaining after T tasks ≈ (1 − p/100)^T × |θ|
At 75% pruning, 4 tasks use: 25% + 18.75% + 14.06% + 10.55% = 68.4% of capacity

Code Repositories

Official github.com/arunmallya/packnet
Limitations Finite capacity. Each task consumes a fraction of the network; the number of tasks is bounded by network size. With 75% pruning, practical capacity for >5 tasks becomes thin.

Fixed pruning rate. The pruning percentage is a hyperparameter; optimal rates differ across tasks and are hard to set a priori.

No backward transfer. Frozen parameters for Task 1 cannot benefit from knowledge learned in Task 2.

Assumes over-parameterization. Works best with large, redundant networks (VGG, ResNet). Less effective for compact models.
Applicability to RecWM PackNet is less natural for SSMs than for CNNs, because S5 parameters are densely coupled and not obviously prunable by magnitude. However, the mask concept is useful: RecWM could maintain per-regime binary masks over latent dimensions (not individual weights), freezing subsets of the latent state that encode stable macro-economic structure while freeing other dimensions for volatile short-term dynamics. This connects to GateL0RD's native sparsity mechanism, which already produces something like a learned binary mask on latent state changes.

4. Progressive Neural Networks

Architecture Expansion
Full Citation Andrei A. Rusu, Neil C. Rabinowitz, Guillaume Desjardins, Hubert Soyer, James Kirkpatrick, Koray Kavukcuoglu, Razvan Pascanu, and Raia Hadsell. "Progressive Neural Networks." arXiv:1606.04671, 2016.

Note: This paper was not published at a peer-reviewed venue but is one of the most cited papers in continual learning (>2000 citations).

Core Idea

For each new task, a fresh "column" (a complete neural network) is instantiated and trained. Lateral connections from all previous columns feed into the new column, enabling forward transfer. Previous columns are frozen entirely, guaranteeing zero forgetting.

Lateral Connection Architecture

Layer activation for column k, layer i h_i^(k) = σ( W_i^(k) h_{i-1}^(k) + ∑_{j<k} U_{i}^(k:j) σ( V_{i}^(k:j) α_{i-1}^(j) h_{i-1}^(j) ) )
h_i^(k) ∈ R^{n_i} = activation at layer i in column k
W_i^(k) ∈ R^{n_i × n_{i-1}} = standard weight matrix within column k
U_i^(k:j) ∈ R^{n_i × n_j} = lateral connection from column j to column k at layer i
V_i^(k:j) ∈ R^{n_j × n_{i-1}} = adapter/projection matrix (dimensionality reduction)
α_{i-1}^(j) = learned scalar, initialized small (∼ 10^{-2}), ensures scale compatibility
σ = element-wise nonlinearity (ReLU in the original)

The adapter matrices V serve a dual role: they project the lateral activations into a lower-dimensional subspace (preventing parameter explosion as columns accumulate), and they allow the new column to selectively attend to the most useful features from prior tasks.

Code Repositories

PyTorch github.com/hengdashi/pnn
PyTorch github.com/CSCI-544-Group-17/progressive-neural-network
TF github.com/mhsamavatian/ProgressiveNeuralNet

No official DeepMind release found. Community implementations vary in fidelity.

Limitations Linear growth. Parameters and inference cost grow linearly with the number of tasks. For an economic model that may encounter dozens of regimes, this becomes prohibitive.

No backward transfer. Earlier columns are frozen; they cannot improve from later tasks.

Task identity required at inference. The system must know which "task" (regime) the input belongs to in order to route through the correct column.
Applicability to RecWM The full progressive architecture is too heavy for RecWM, but the lateral connection concept is directly applicable. When the world model detects a new economic regime (via the SPIB fragmentation mechanism), it could spawn a small adapter column with lateral connections to the existing S5 backbone. The adapter learns regime-specific dynamics while receiving frozen features from the shared macro model. The α-scaled adapter pattern maps naturally to GateL0RD's gating: the gate decides which lateral connections to activate, effectively learning a soft version of the column-selection mechanism.

5. Post-2023: Adapter-Based Continual Learning

LoRA Parameter-Efficient

The emergence of LoRA (Hu et al. 2022) for parameter-efficient fine-tuning has spawned a family of continual learning methods that use low-rank adapters as task-specific modules. The core insight: instead of regularizing the full parameter space, constrain task-specific updates to low-rank subspaces and manage interference between those subspaces.

5a. O-LoRA (Orthogonal Low-Rank Adaptation)

Full Citation Xiao Wang, Tianze Chen, Qiming Ge, Han Xia, Rong Bao, Rui Zheng, Qi Zhang, Tao Gui, and Xuanjing Huang. "Orthogonal Subspace Learning for Language Model Continual Learning." Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2023, pp. 10658–10671, Singapore. arXiv:2310.14152.

O-LoRA learns each task's LoRA update in a low-rank subspace that is kept orthogonal to all previous tasks' subspaces, preventing interference without replay or architectural expansion.

LoRA update per task ΔW_t = B_t A_t
B_t ∈ R^{d × r}, A_t ∈ R^{r × d}. The subspace of ΔW_t is span(B_t).
Orthogonality constraint ∀ i < t: B_i^T B_t = 0
Orthogonality regularizer L_orth(B_i, B_t) = || B_i^T B_t ||_F^2
Total training objective L(θ) = L_task(θ) + β ∑_{i=1}^{t-1} || B_i^T B_t ||_F^2
β controls the orthogonality enforcement strength
Code github.com/cmnfriend/O-LoRA

5b. InfLoRA (Interference-Free Low-Rank Adaptation)

Full Citation Yan-Shuo Liang and Wu-Jun Li. "InfLoRA: Interference-Free Low-Rank Adaptation for Continual Learning." IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), pp. 23638–23647, Seattle, WA, 2024. arXiv:2404.00228.

InfLoRA goes beyond O-LoRA by designing the LoRA subspace to be simultaneously (a) orthogonal to old task gradient spaces and (b) aligned with the new task's gradient space. This ensures that updates help the new task without hurting old ones.

Subspace design principle span(B_t) ⊥ G_old AND span(B_t) ⊂ G_new
G_old = subspace spanned by gradients of old task losses w.r.t. the input features
G_new = subspace spanned by gradients of the new task loss

InfLoRA approximates G_old using the input covariance of old tasks and constructs B_t via SVD of the projected new-task gradient matrix.

Official github.com/liangyanshuo/InfLoRA

5c. C-LoRA (Continual Low-Rank Adaptation)

Full Citation Xin Zhang, Liang Bai, Xian Yang, and Jiye Liang. "C-LoRA: Continual Low-Rank Adaptation for Pre-trained Models." arXiv:2502.17920, February 2025.

C-LoRA uses a learnable routing matrix to dynamically manage parameter updates across tasks, enabling reuse of learned subspaces while enforcing orthogonality to minimize interference. Unlike O-LoRA/InfLoRA (which use separate adapters per task), C-LoRA uses a single adapter with dynamic routing.

arXiv arxiv.org/abs/2502.17920

5d. ELLA (Efficient Lifelong Learning for Adapters)

Full Citation "ELLA: Efficient Lifelong Learning for Adapters in Large Language Models." EACL 2026. arXiv:2601.02232.

ELLA regularizes new adapters by tracking past representational subspaces. It accumulates past low-rank updates and applies an energy-based alignment penalty to discourage overlap in high-magnitude task-specific directions, enabling parameter reuse in less-used subspaces. Unlike O-LoRA's hard orthogonality, ELLA uses a soft energy-based penalty that allows partial overlap where it helps.

5e. JumpLoRA (Sparse Adapters for CL)

Full Citation "JumpLoRA: Sparse Adapters for Continual Learning in Large Language Models." arXiv:2604.16171, April 2026.

JumpLoRA introduces sparsity into LoRA blocks via JumpReLU gating. The gating function adaptively zeros out adapter entries, achieving dynamic parameter isolation without explicit orthogonality constraints. Compatible with existing LoRA-based CL methods as a drop-in improvement.

Applicability to RecWM The LoRA-based CL family is highly relevant to RecWM. The core S5 transition matrices (A, B, C, D) can be treated as the "pre-trained backbone," and per-regime LoRA adapters can capture regime-specific dynamics as low-rank perturbations: A_regime = A_base + B_r A_r. The orthogonality constraints (O-LoRA) or gradient-aware subspace design (InfLoRA) prevent regime interference. JumpLoRA's gating is particularly natural for RecWM because it mirrors GateL0RD's sparse-update mechanism at the adapter level. Concrete approach: apply InfLoRA-style subspace design to the S5 (A, B) parameter block, with JumpReLU gating tied to the GateL0RD gate signal.

6. Post-2023: Continual Learning for State-Space Models

SSM-Specific Geometry-Aware

Continual learning for SSMs is a nascent subfield. Existing CL algorithms designed for MLPs, CNNs, and Transformers treat SSM parameters as generic weights and overlook the underlying state-space geometry and temporal dynamics. Three recent papers address this gap directly.

6a. CLDSSMs (Regularization-Based CL in Deep State-Space Models)

Full Citation Yuanhang Zhang, Zhidi Lin, Yiyong Sun, Feng Yin, and Carsten Fritsche. "Regularization-Based Efficient Continual Learning in Deep State-Space Models." arXiv:2403.10123, March 2024 (revised June 2024).

This paper integrates mainstream regularization-based CL methods (EWC, SI, MAS) into deep SSM architectures, ensuring efficient updates with constant computational and memory costs for modeling multiple dynamic systems. It is the first work to systematically study how EWC/SI/MAS behave when applied to SSM parameters specifically.

Key finding Standard EWC on SSM parameters: diagonal Fisher fails to capture A-B coupling CLDSSM fix: block-structured regularization respecting (A, B, C, D) blocks

6b. Mamba-CL (Null-Space Projection for Mamba)

Full Citation D. Cheng, Y. Lu, L. He, S. Zhang, X. Yang, N. Wang, and X. Gao. "Mamba-CL: Optimizing Selective State Space Model in Null Space for Continual Learning." arXiv:2411.15469, November 2024.

Mamba-CL updates SSM parameters orthogonally to the feature subspace of previous tasks via null-space projection, providing theoretical guarantees for output consistency across tasks. It derives specific conditions for the four key Mamba parameters (Δ, A, B, C).

Null-space projection condition X_t ΔΘ = 0
X_t = feature matrix of old tasks (input representations)
ΔΘ = parameter update for the new task
Achieved by projecting the gradient onto the null space of X_t via SVD:
ΔΘ = (I − X_t^+ X_t) ∇L

6c. Inf-SSM (Grassmannian Regularization for SSMs)

Full Citation "Exemplar-Free Continual Learning for State Space Models." arXiv:2505.18604, May 2025 (revised March 2026).

Inf-SSM is a geometry-aware regularization framework that constrains state evolution via the infinite-dimensional Grassmannian of SSM observability subspaces. Unlike weight-space methods (EWC/SI) or feature-space methods (Mamba-CL), Inf-SSM regularizes the function that the SSM computes, measured by the distance between observability subspaces on the Grassmann manifold.

Observability subspace O = [C; CA; CA^2; CA^3; ...]^T (the extended observability matrix) Regularizer: d_Grass(O_old, O_new)
d_Grass is the geodesic distance on the Grassmannian, computed via principal angles between the column spaces of the old and new observability matrices.
Applicability to RecWM These three papers are the most directly relevant to RecWM's architecture. Recommended synthesis:

(1) Use Mamba-CL's null-space projection as the primary forgetting prevention mechanism for the S5 (A, B, C, D) parameters. The null-space condition X_t ΔΘ = 0 can be applied per-fragment (using SPIB's fragment boundaries to define "tasks").

(2) Layer Inf-SSM's Grassmannian regularizer on top as a functional consistency check: even if individual parameters drift, the observability subspace (and hence the model's input-output behavior) remains stable for old regimes.

(3) Use CLDSSM's block-structured approach to apply EWC or SI specifically to the (A, B) block with a block-diagonal Fisher, rather than the naive diagonal approximation.

7. Comparative Summary

Method Type Forgetting Forward Transfer Task ID Needed Memory Growth SSM-Ready
EWC Regularization Soft protection Implicit Yes O(|θ|) per task* Weak
Online EWC Regularization Soft protection Implicit Yes O(|θ|) constant Weak
SI Regularization Soft protection Implicit Yes O(|θ|) constant Moderate
PackNet Pruning/Isolation Zero (by construction) None Yes Constant (mask only) Weak
Progressive NN Architecture Zero (by construction) Via laterals Yes O(|column|) per task Moderate
O-LoRA Adapter/Subspace Soft (orthogonal) None explicit No (at inference) O(r · d) per task Moderate
InfLoRA Adapter/Subspace Designed-zero Gradient-aligned No (at inference) O(r · d) per task Good
Mamba-CL Null-space proj. Theoretical guarantee Implicit No O(feature dim) per task Native
Inf-SSM Grassmannian reg. Functional protection Implicit No O(observability dim) Native

* Naive EWC stores one Fisher + one θ* per task. Online EWC collapses to constant.

8. Synthesis: A Continual Learning Stack for RecWM

Given RecWM's architecture—S5 SSMs for state dynamics, GateL0RD for sparse latent updates, SPIB for per-fragment information bottlenecks—no single CL method is sufficient. The following layered strategy leverages the strengths of multiple approaches:

Layer 1: Null-Space Projection on SSM Parameters

Apply Mamba-CL's null-space projection to the S5 (A, B, C, D) parameter updates. When SPIB signals a new economic regime (fragment boundary), compute the feature subspace X_old from recent old-regime data and project all parameter gradients onto the null space of X_old. This provides a hard guarantee that old-regime outputs are preserved.

Layer 2: InfLoRA-Style Regime Adapters

Maintain per-regime low-rank adapters A_regime = A_base + B_r A_r using InfLoRA's gradient-aware subspace construction. The adapter B matrices are designed orthogonal to old-regime gradient spaces but aligned with the new-regime gradient space. This gives the model plasticity for new regimes without interference.

Layer 3: SI-Based Importance Tracking

Run Synaptic Intelligence accumulators on all parameters (including adapter parameters) to maintain an online importance measure. This serves as a soft fallback when the null-space projection is too restrictive (e.g., when old and new regime feature spaces partially overlap). SI's path-integral importance also provides a natural diagnostic: high-importance parameters identify which model components are regime-sensitive.

Layer 4: Grassmannian Consistency Monitor

Periodically compute the Inf-SSM Grassmannian distance between the current S5 observability subspace and stored reference subspaces for each past regime. This functional-level check catches drift that parameter-level methods miss—e.g., coordinated small changes to A and C that individually pass null-space checks but together alter the system's frequency response.

Integration with GateL0RD

GateL0RD's gating mechanism naturally partitions latent dimensions into "changing" and "stable" subsets at each timestep. This partition can drive the CL stack: dimensions that the gate keeps frozen contribute to X_old (the old-regime feature subspace), while dimensions that the gate opens are candidates for adapter updates. The L0 penalty on gate openings provides implicit regularization against unnecessary forgetting—the model must justify (via gradient signal) each dimension it chooses to update.

Research Brief

Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection

Foundations, extensions, and integration pathways for the Reflexive Constructive World Model
Prepared 2026-08-09 · For the RCE research program · Regime detection layer

Contents

  1. Adams & MacKay (2007) — The foundational BOCPD paper
  2. Fearnhead & Liu (2007) — Particle-based online changepoint inference
  3. Extensions and improvements to BOCPD
  4. BOCPD and continual learning
  5. Connection to economic regime detection
  6. Software and implementations

1. Adams & MacKay (2007) — The Foundational BOCPD Paper

Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection
Ryan Prescott Adams and David J.C. MacKay
arXiv preprint, 2007. 7 pages, 4 figures.
arXiv:0710.3742 [stat.ML], 19 Oct 2007
Cavendish Laboratory, University of Cambridge. Funded by the Gates Cambridge Trust.

1.1 Problem Setup

A sequence of observations x1, x2, ..., xT is divided into non-overlapping product partitions (Barry & Hartigan, 1992). The boundaries between partitions are changepoints. Within each partition ρ, data are i.i.d. from P(xt | ηρ). The parameters ηρ for ρ = 1, 2, ... are themselves i.i.d. (independence across segments).

Key notation:

  • rt = run length at time t (time since the last changepoint)
  • xt(r) = the set of observations associated with the current run of length r
  • xa:b = contiguous observations from time a to b inclusive
  • Pgap(g) = prior distribution over the interval between changepoints

1.2 The Recursive Algorithm

The goal is to compute the posterior distribution over the current run length P(rt | x1:t), updated online as each new datum arrives.

Marginal Predictive Distribution

Equation 1 — Predictive distribution via run-length marginalization P(x_{t+1} | x_{1:t}) = SUM_{r_t} P(x_{t+1} | r_t, x_t^{(r)}) * P(r_t | x_{1:t})

Run-Length Posterior

Equation 2 — Posterior via Bayes' rule P(r_t | x_{1:t}) = P(r_t, x_{1:t}) / P(x_{1:t})

Joint Distribution Recursion (the core equation)

Equation 3 — Recursive decomposition of the joint P(r_t, x_{1:t}) = SUM_{r_{t-1}} P(r_t | r_{t-1}) * P(x_t | r_{t-1}, x_t^{(r)}) * P(r_{t-1}, x_{1:t-1}) This decomposes into three factors: (a) P(r_t | r_{t-1}) -- the changepoint prior (Section 1.3) (b) P(x_t | r_{t-1}, x_t^{(r)}) -- the UPM predictive probability (Section 1.5) (c) P(r_{t-1}, x_{1:t-1}) -- the message from the previous time step

This is a message-passing algorithm on a trellis. At each time step, each run-length hypothesis either grows (rt = rt-1 + 1) or resets (rt = 0, indicating a changepoint).

1.3 The Changepoint Prior

The conditional prior P(rt | rt-1) has nonzero mass at exactly two outcomes:

Equation 4 — Changepoint prior (three cases) P(r_t | r_{t-1}) = { H(r_{t-1} + 1) if r_t = 0 (changepoint occurs) 1 - H(r_{t-1} + 1) if r_t = r_{t-1} + 1 (run continues to grow) 0 otherwise }

The Hazard Function

Equation 5 — Hazard function from the gap distribution H(τ) = P_gap(g = τ) / SUM_{t=τ}^{∞} P_gap(g = t)

Special case (geometric / memoryless): When Pgap(g) is a discrete exponential (geometric) distribution with timescale λ, the hazard function is constant: H(τ) = 1/λ. This is the most commonly used form. A constant hazard of 1/250, for example, encodes a prior expected segment length of 250 time steps.

1.4 Boundary Conditions

Two initialization options:

  • Fresh start (a changepoint occurred before the first datum): P(r0 = 0) = 1
  • Unknown history (observing a subset of an ongoing process): P(r0 = τ) = S(τ) / Z, where S(τ) = ∑t=τ+1∞ Pgap(g = t) is the survival function.

1.5 The Underlying Predictive Model (UPM)

The UPM provides P(xt | rt, xt(r)) — the predictive probability of the new datum given the data in the current run. For conjugate-exponential family models, this is computed analytically by marginalizing over parameters.

Exponential Family Likelihood

Equation 8 — Exponential family form P(x | η) = h(x) * exp(η^T U(x) - A(η))

Conjugate Prior on Parameters

Equation 10 — Conjugate prior P(η | χ, ν) = h~(η) * exp(η^T χ - ν A(η) - A~(χ, ν))

Sufficient Statistics Update

Equations 12-13 — Incremental sufficient statistics ν_t^{(r)} = ν_prior + r_t χ_t^{(r)} = χ_prior + SUM_{t' in r_t} u(x_{t'})

The predictive distribution conditional on run length is computed by marginalizing out the parameters:

Equation 11 — Parameter marginalization P(x_{t+1} | r_t) = INTEGRAL dη P(x_{t+1} | η) P(η_t^{(r)} = η | r_t, x_t^{(r)})

1.6 Complete Algorithm

Algorithm 1 — Online Changepoint Detection with Prediction
  1. Initialize. P(r_0) = S~(r) or P(r_0 = 0) = 1 ν_1^{(0)} = ν_prior, χ_1^{(0)} = χ_prior
  2. Observe new datum xt.
  3. Evaluate predictive probability for each run-length hypothesis r: π_t^{(r)} = P(x_t | ν_t^{(r)}, χ_t^{(r)})
  4. Calculate growth probabilities: P(r_t = r_{t-1}+1, x_{1:t}) = P(r_{t-1}, x_{1:t-1}) * π_t^{(r)} * (1 - H(r_{t-1}))
  5. Calculate changepoint probabilities: P(r_t = 0, x_{1:t}) = SUM_{r_{t-1}} P(r_{t-1}, x_{1:t-1}) * π_t^{(r)} * H(r_{t-1})
  6. Calculate evidence: P(x_{1:t}) = SUM_{r_t} P(r_t, x_{1:t})
  7. Determine run-length distribution: P(r_t | x_{1:t}) = P(r_t, x_{1:t}) / P(x_{1:t})
  8. Update sufficient statistics: ν_{t+1}^{(0)} = ν_prior, χ_{t+1}^{(0)} = χ_prior (reset for new run) ν_{t+1}^{(r+1)} = ν_t^{(r)} + 1 χ_{t+1}^{(r+1)} = χ_t^{(r)} + u(x_t)
  9. Perform prediction: P(x_{t+1} | x_{1:t}) = SUM_{r_t} P(x_{t+1} | x_t^{(r)}, r_t) * P(r_t | x_{1:t})
  10. Return to Step 2.

1.7 Computational Complexity

  • Per-step cost: O(t) at time step t — linear in the number of observations so far, because the run-length posterior vector grows by one element each step.
  • Total cost over T steps: O(T2) naive.
  • Pruning strategy: Discard run-length hypotheses whose total tail mass falls below a threshold (e.g., 10-4). This yields O(E[r]) amortized per step, where E[r] is the expected run length. Worst-case remains O(T).
  • Space: O(T) naive; O(E[r]) with pruning.

1.8 Experimental Demonstrations in the Paper

Three datasets, each using a discrete exponential prior on segment length:

  1. Well-log data (4050 measurements of nuclear magnetic response): Univariate Gaussian model on the mean (μ=1.15x105, σ=104), λgap=250.
  2. Dow Jones Industrial Average daily returns (1972-75): Zero-mean Gaussian with piecewise-constant variance. Gamma prior on inverse variance (a=1, b=10-4), λgap=250. Successfully detects Watergate, OPEC embargo, Nixon resignation.
  3. Coal mine disaster data (1851-1962): Poisson process on weekly accident counts. Gamma prior (a=b=1), λgap=1000. Detects the Coal Mines Regulations Act of 1887.
Key design insight for the RCE: The UPM is completely modular — any model that provides a predictive distribution P(xt | rt, xt(r)) can be plugged in. The changepoint detection algorithm and the observation model are cleanly separated, enabling an object-oriented "pluggable" architecture. This modularity is exactly what we need for the world model's regime-detection layer.

2. Fearnhead & Liu (2007) — Particle-Based Online Changepoint Inference

On-Line Inference for Multiple Changepoint Problems
Paul Fearnhead and Zhen Liu
Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B (Statistical Methodology), 69(4), pp. 589–605, 2007.
DOI: 10.1111/j.1467-9868.2007.00601.x · ISSN 1369-7412

2.1 Core Contribution

Published in the same year as Adams & MacKay but in a top statistics journal, Fearnhead & Liu tackle a closely related problem: online exact filtering for multiple changepoint problems, with the additional goal of enabling simulation from the true joint posterior distribution over the number and positions of all changepoints.

2.2 Algorithmic Approach

  • Exact filtering: The base algorithm provides exact posterior inference with O(n2) computational cost (quadratic in the number of observations), matching Adams & MacKay's complexity.
  • Particle-filter approximation: They show how resampling ideas from Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) reduce cost to O(n) linear time at the expense of introducing small approximation errors.

2.3 Stratified Rejection Control

The paper's main methodological innovation. Two new optimum resampling algorithms are proposed:

  1. Stratified optimal resampling: Outperforms standard multinomial resampling by reducing variance in the particle set.
  2. Rejection control: Allows the particle filter to automatically choose the number of particles required at each time step. This is a crucial practical advantage — it adapts computational effort to the difficulty of the inference problem at each moment.

2.4 Handling Multiple Changepoints with Unknown Parameters

Unlike Adams & MacKay, who focus on the most recent changepoint, Fearnhead & Liu maintain information about all past changepoints and enable sampling from the full posterior P(number of changepoints, positions | data). This is more informative but more expensive.

2.5 Comparison with Adams & MacKay

Dimension Adams & MacKay (2007) Fearnhead & Liu (2007)
Inference target P(rt | x1:t) — most recent run length Full posterior over all changepoint locations
Exact complexity O(T2) O(T2)
Approximate complexity O(E[r]) per step via tail pruning O(T) total via particle filtering
Modularity Any UPM providing predictive dist. Broader model class
Implementation simplicity Very simple (pure message passing) More complex (particle resampling)
Best for Online prediction, real-time filtering Retrospective inference with uncertainty
Implication for the RCE: For real-time economic state estimation, Adams & MacKay's formulation is the natural starting point — it gives us the current run-length posterior for predictive filtering with minimal overhead. Fearnhead & Liu becomes relevant if we need retrospective analysis of where past regime changes occurred for calibration or backtesting.

Keywords from the paper: Direct simulation, isochores, particle filtering, rejection control, sequential Monte Carlo methods, stratified sampling.

3. Extensions and Improvements to BOCPD

3.1 Learning the Hazard Rate Online

Bayesian Online Learning of the Hazard Rate in Change-Point Problems
Robert C. Wilson, Matthew R. Nassar, and Joshua I. Gold
Neural Computation, 22(9), pp. 2452–2476, 2010.
Publisher: MIT Press. Also available via PMC (NIH).

In the original Adams & MacKay formulation, the hazard rate H(τ) = 1/λ must be specified in advance. Wilson, Nassar & Gold extend this with a hierarchical model where the hazard rate is itself inferred from the data. This is critical for real-world applications where the frequency of regime changes is unknown a priori.

Key result: The hazard rate can be treated as a latent variable with its own prior. The algorithm jointly infers the run length and the hazard rate, maintaining a posterior over λ that gets updated as changepoints are observed. This means the model learns how volatile the environment is.

Why this matters for the RCE

Economic regimes do not change at a fixed rate. Crises cluster (the "volatility of volatility" phenomenon). An adaptive hazard rate allows the detector to become more sensitive during turbulent periods and less trigger-happy during stable ones.

3.2 BOCPD with Model Selection (Gaussian Processes)

Adaptive Sequential Bayesian Change Point Detection
Ryan D. Turner, Yunus Saatci, and Carl Edward Rasmussen
Temporal Segmentation Workshop at NIPS, 2009.
Available at: mlg.eng.cam.ac.uk/pub/pdf/TurSaaRas09.pdf
Gaussian Process Change Point Models
Yunus Saatci, Ryan D. Turner, and Carl Edward Rasmussen
Proceedings of the 27th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 2010.
271 citations. Available at: mlg.eng.cam.ac.uk/pub/pdf/SaaTurRas10.pdf

These two papers from the Cambridge ML group extend BOCPD in two important ways:

  1. Model selection within segments: Instead of a fixed UPM, the algorithm simultaneously selects between multiple candidate models for each segment. This enables detecting not just that a change occurred but what kind of change it was.
  2. Gaussian process UPM: Replacing the simple conjugate-exponential UPM with a Gaussian process allows the model to capture within-segment correlations and nonlinear structure. The original BOCPD assumes i.i.d. data within each segment; the GP extension relaxes this to allow temporally structured segments.
Gaussian Processes for State Space Models and Change Point Detection
Ryan D. Turner
PhD Thesis, University of Cambridge, 2012.
Comprehensive treatment unifying GPs with BOCPD. Supervisor: Carl Edward Rasmussen.

3.3 Spatio-Temporal BOCPD with Model Selection (Scalable)

Spatio-temporal Bayesian On-line Changepoint Detection with Model Selection
Jeremias Knoblauch and Theodoros Damoulas
Proceedings of the 35th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR vol. 80, pp. 2718–2727, 2018.
83 citations. proceedings.mlr.press/v80/knoblauch18a

Key advances:

  • Extends BOCPD to handle non-stationary spatio-temporal processes with online model selection.
  • Uses spatially structured Vector Autoregressions (VARs) as the UPM between changepoints.
  • Achieves linear time complexity with constant space requirements.
  • Two orders of magnitude faster than competing approaches on multivariate datasets.
  • Simultaneously performs prediction, model selection, and changepoint detection.

3.4 Robust and Scalable BOCPD

Robust and Scalable Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection
Matias Altamirano, Francois-Xavier Briol, and Jeremias Knoblauch
Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR vol. 202, pp. 642–663, 2023.
56 citations. proceedings.mlr.press/v202/altamirano23a

This paper addresses two critical weaknesses of standard BOCPD:

  1. Robustness: Leverages the generalised Bayesian perspective to achieve provable robustness to model misspecification. Standard BOCPD is sensitive to outliers and model mismatch; this approach uses scoring rules (diffusion score matching) to replace the likelihood.
  2. Scalability: Maintains conjugate posteriors with closed-form parameter updates (simple algebra, no MCMC). More than 10x faster than the closest competitor.
  3. Non-exponential family models: Breaks the restriction to exponential-family UPMs that Adams & MacKay required for tractability.
This is the state of the art for BOCPD as of 2023. The generalised Bayesian framework is especially relevant for the RCE because economic data is messy — we need robustness to outliers, fat tails, and model misspecification.

3.5 Doubly Robust BOCPD

Doubly Robust Bayesian Inference for Non-Stationary Streaming Data with φ-Divergences
Jeremias Knoblauch, Jack E. Jewson, and others
Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 2018.
110 citations.
First robust Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection with scalability improvements.

3.6 Multivariate BOCPD

Several approaches extend BOCPD to multivariate time series:

  • The bayesian_changepoint_detection Python package (Section 6) includes a MultivariateT distribution for multivariate data, following the conjugate-exponential framework.
  • Knoblauch & Damoulas (2018) use VARs within segments (Section 3.3).
  • Wendelberger, Gray & Reich (2021) apply multivariate BOCPD to near real-time deforestation monitoring, adapting the framework for outlier handling in Earth observation data. (arXiv preprint, 13 citations.)

3.7 Confirmatory BOCPD with Gaussian Processes

Confirmatory Bayesian Online Change Point Detection in the Covariance Structure of Gaussian Processes
Jiyeon Han, Kyowoon Lee, Anh Tong, and Jaesik Choi
arXiv preprint, 2019 (revised 2020).
arXiv:1905.13168

Introduces CBOCPD: statistical hypothesis tests for detecting covariance structure changes in GPs, with theoretically justified thresholds. Robust to hyperparameter tuning and provides conditions for when it outperforms standard BOCPD.

4. BOCPD and Continual Learning

4.1 Changepoint Detection as a Trigger for Model Adaptation

The core idea: when BOCPD detects a regime change (rt drops to zero with high probability), the learning system should adapt — reset, retrain, or re-weight its model. This connects BOCPD to several active research areas.

4.2 Continuous Meta-Learning Without Tasks (MOCA)

Continuous Meta-Learning Without Tasks
James Harrison, Apoorva Sharma, Chelsea Finn, and Marco Pavone
Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 2020.
122 citations. proceedings.neurips.cc

MOCA (Meta-learning via Online Changepoint Analysis) integrates a differentiable Bayesian changepoint detection scheme into meta-learning. Instead of requiring pre-segmented tasks, MOCA uses BOCPD to automatically detect task boundaries in unsegmented time series data and adapts the meta-learner accordingly. This is the most direct bridge between BOCPD and continual learning.

4.3 Distribution Shift Detection for Online Learning

Detecting and Adapting to Irregular Distribution Shifts in Bayesian Online Learning
Aodong Li, Alex Boyd, Padhraic Smyth, and Stephan Mandt
NeurIPS, 2021.
38 citations.

Addresses the problem of distribution shifts that violate stationarity assumptions in online Bayesian learning, extending BOCPD ideas to handle irregular (non-periodic) shifts.

4.4 Changepoint Detection in Neural Networks

Sequential Changepoint Detection in Neural Networks with Checkpoints
Michalis K. Titsias, Jakub Sygnowski, and Yutian Chen
Statistics and Computing, 2022.
20 citations.

Applies BOCPD-style sequential detection to neural network continual learning, using checkpoints to maintain model states that can be reverted to when regime changes are detected.

4.5 BOCPD as a Gating Mechanism for Learning Rate Adaptation

Two Determinants of Dynamic Adaptive Learning for Magnitudes and Probabilities
Cloelia Foucault and Florent Meyniel
Open Mind, 2024.

Demonstrates BOCPD as a gating mechanism combined with adaptive learning — the changepoint posterior modulates how much new observations should influence existing beliefs. When P(rt = 0 | x1:t) is high, the effective learning rate increases sharply; during stable runs, it decays.

POLA: Online Time Series Prediction by Adaptive Learning Rates
W. Zhang
IEEE ICASSP, 2021.

Explicitly uses changepoint detection to regulate learning rates in online time-series prediction.

4.6 Connection to Continual RL and Non-Stationary MDPs

Restarted Bayesian Online Change-Point Detection for Non-Stationary Markov Decision Processes
Reda Alami and Mohammed Mahfoud
Conference on Lifelong Learning Agents (CoLLAs), 2023.
BAPR: Bayesian Amnesic Piecewise-Robust Reinforcement Learning for Non-Stationary Continuous Control
Y. Zhang and L. Zheng
arXiv preprint, 2026.
Maintains a posterior distribution over run-lengths to detect environment changes in continuous RL.
A Bayesian Fast-Slow Framework to Mitigate Interference in Non-Stationary Reinforcement Learning
Y. Mao and C. Zhang
NeurIPS, 2026.
ARCADE: Adaptive Robot Control with Online Changepoint-Aware Bayesian Dynamics Learning
Rohan D. Yadav, Arundhati Das, Hyunsoo Song, Samuel Kaski, and Wenjie Pan
arXiv preprint, 2025.
Avoids full model retraining through changepoint-aware Bayesian dynamics learning.

4.7 Soft Parameter Reset (Related but Distinct)

Non-Stationary Learning of Neural Networks with Automatic Soft Parameter Reset
Alexandre Galashov, Michalis K. Titsias, Andras Gyorgy, Clare Lyle, Razvan Pascanu, Yee Whye Teh, and Maneesh Sahani
NeurIPS, 2024.
21 citations.

Rather than hard changepoint detection, this approach links parameters through an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with adaptive drift, creating a "soft reset" mechanism. Applicable to supervised learning with distributional shifts, RL, continual learning, and non-stationary contextual bandits. Not explicitly BOCPD-based, but conceptually complementary — it replaces the hard "detect-and-reset" paradigm with continuous parameter drift.

Synthesis for the RCE: The run-length posterior P(rt | x1:t) from BOCPD naturally provides a soft gating signal for adaptation. When changepoint probability is high, increase the learning rate / reduce reliance on old data. When the run is long and stable, rely on accumulated statistics. This is more principled than a hard detect-and-reset approach. The MOCA framework (Harrison et al. 2020) provides the most direct template for integrating this with the world model's meta-learning loop.

5. Connection to Economic Regime Detection

5.1 The Dominant Baseline: Markov-Switching Models

A New Approach to the Economic Analysis of Nonstationary Time Series and the Business Cycle
James D. Hamilton
Econometrica: Journal of the Econometric Society, 57(2), pp. 357–384, 1989.
14,756 citations.

Hamilton's Markov-switching model (MS) is the dominant framework for economic regime detection. It assumes the economy switches between a finite number of discrete states (e.g., expansion/recession) governed by a Markov chain with constant transition probabilities. Key differences from BOCPD:

Dimension Hamilton MS (1989) BOCPD (Adams & MacKay 2007)
Number of states Fixed, finite (usually 2-3) Unbounded (each new segment is a new state)
Recurrence States can recur (the economy returns to "expansion") Each segment has fresh parameters (no recurrence)
Transition structure Full transition matrix between states Only two transitions: continue or reset
Parameter estimation EM algorithm (offline, iterative) Online, recursive
Prior information Number of states must be specified Only hazard rate must be specified (or learned)
Online capability Not natively online (Kim filter is an approximation) Natively online, exact
Stationarity assumption Transition probabilities are time-invariant None required (adaptive with learned hazard)

V. Georgescu

12 citations.
Studies variance shifts in financial data patterns using both frequentist and BOCPD approaches.
Bayesian Changepoint and Time-Varying Parameter Learning in Regime Switching Volatility Models
M.S. Yilmaz, F.S. Gorgen, A.T. Cemgil, and N. Okay
Digital Signal Processing, 2015.
Multiple changepoint detection specifically for volatility regime switching.
Online Learning of Order Flow and Market Impact with Bayesian Change-Point Detection Methods
I.Y. Tsaknaki, F. Lillo, and P. Mazzarisi

Geometric Observables for Financial Regime Detection
W. Hammond

5.3 Comparison Studies: BOCPD vs. HMM

Drift Detection in Financial Time Series: Comparing Hidden Markov Models and Bayesian Methods
A. Hlas
2025.
Compares BOCPD with HMM approaches for portfolio construction.
A Change Dynamic Model for the Online Detection of Gradual Change
C. Browne

References both Hamilton MS and BOCPD, addresses gradual (not abrupt) changes.

5.4 NBER Recession Dating and Business Cycles

While no papers were found applying BOCPD directly to the NBER recession-dating problem, the connection is natural. The NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee identifies peaks and troughs in economic activity — precisely the changepoints that BOCPD would detect. The key advantage of BOCPD over the NBER approach is real-time detection: the NBER typically announces recessions months or quarters after they begin, while BOCPD could provide probabilistic real-time estimates. Adams & MacKay's own Dow Jones experiment (Section 1.8) demonstrates exactly this capability for financial markets.

5.5 Volatility Regime Detection

Adams & MacKay's original Dow Jones example (1972-75) is a variance-changepoint model — precisely a volatility regime detector. The BOCPD approach detects shifts in volatility without requiring a pre-specified number of volatility states (unlike GARCH with regime-switching, which requires choosing the number of regimes). Financial applications include:

  • Bull/bear market transition detection (via mean and variance changes)
  • VIX regime identification
  • Risk management: increasing hedging ratios when a high-volatility regime is detected
  • Portfolio rebalancing triggers
Integration point for the RCE: BOCPD provides the regime-detection layer that sits between raw economic data streams and the world model. When P(rt = 0 | x1:t) exceeds a threshold, the world model should: (1) increase its learning rate for the current economic state, (2) potentially reset certain sufficient statistics, and (3) update its prior on the hazard rate (via Wilson et al. 2010's extension) to reflect changing regime-change frequency. The comparison with Hamilton MS is important: BOCPD does not require pre-specifying the number of economic regimes, which is a significant advantage for a system that must adapt to genuinely novel economic conditions.

Usage Example (bayesian_changepoint_detection)

from functools import partial
from bayesian_changepoint_detection import (
    online_changepoint_detection,
    constant_hazard,
    StudentT
)

data = torch.cat([
    torch.randn(50) + 0,     # regime 1: mean=0
    torch.randn(50) + 3,     # regime 2: mean=3
])

hazard_func = partial(constant_hazard, 250)
likelihood = StudentT(alpha=0.1, beta=0.01)

run_length_probs, changepoint_probs = online_changepoint_detection(
    data, hazard_func, likelihood
)

Summary: Integration Pathway for the RCE

The recommended architecture for the Reflexive Constructive World Model's regime-detection layer:

  1. Core algorithm: Adams & MacKay (2007) BOCPD with conjugate-exponential UPMs for computational efficiency. Start with the bayesian_changepoint_detection Python package or reimplement from Algorithm 1 above for tighter integration.
  2. Hazard rate learning: Extend with Wilson, Nassar & Gold (2010) to learn the changepoint frequency from data rather than fixing it. This is essential for economic data where regime-change frequency is itself non-stationary.
  3. Robustness: Incorporate Altamirano, Briol & Knoblauch (2023) for robustness to model misspecification and outliers. Economic data is fat-tailed; the generalized Bayesian approach handles this without requiring exponential-family UPMs.
  4. Multivariate extension: Use Knoblauch & Damoulas (2018) for the spatio-temporal/multivariate case with VAR segments and model selection. Linear time, constant space.
  5. Continual learning integration: Use the run-length posterior P(rt | x1:t) as a soft gating signal for the world model's learning rate, following the MOCA paradigm (Harrison et al. 2020). When changepoint probability is high, increase plasticity; when the run is stable, increase stability.
  6. Comparison baseline: Always benchmark against Hamilton (1989) Markov-switching models, since this is what economists expect. BOCPD's advantage is online operation, no pre-specified number of states, and non-stationary hazard rates.

The key insight is that BOCPD's modularity — the clean separation between the changepoint detection algorithm and the observation model (UPM) — maps directly onto the RCE's layered architecture. The regime detector does not need to know what economic variables it is monitoring; it only needs a predictive model that says how likely each new observation is under the current regime.

§1  Hazan's Monograph & the OCO Framework

1.1  Editions & Citations

Introduction to Online Convex Optimization (1st edition)
Elad Hazan
Foundations and Trends in Optimization, Vol. 2, No. 3–4, pp. 157–325. NOW Publishers, 2016.
DOI: 10.1561/2400000013 ISBN: 978-1-68083-170-2
Introduction to Online Convex Optimization (2nd edition)
Elad Hazan
MIT Press, Adaptive Computation and Machine Learning Series. September 2022. 248 pages.
ISBN: 978-0-262-04698-5 arXiv: 1909.05207

The arXiv preprint (1909.05207) corresponds to the second edition; it was first posted 7 September 2019 and last revised 6 August 2023 (v3). The monograph grew out of Hazan's graduate course "Theoretical Machine Learning" at Princeton. The first edition, published by NOW Publishers as part of the Foundations and Trends in Optimization series, is the more commonly cited survey in the OCO literature.

1.2  The OCO Protocol

Online Convex Optimization is a sequential decision-making framework modeled as a repeated game between a learner and an adversary.

Protocol: Online Convex Optimization
for t = 1, 2, …, T:
  1. Learner selects x_t ∈ K where K ⊂ R^d is a convex compact set
  2. Adversary reveals convex loss function f_t : K → R
  3. Learner suffers loss f_t(x_t)

The adversary is oblivious (chooses the entire loss sequence in advance) or adaptive (may choose f_t based on the learner's past actions). The framework makes no statistical assumptions on the loss sequence.

1.3  Regret

Definition — Static Regret
R_T  =  ∑_{t=1}^{T} f_t(x_t)  −  min_{x ∈ K} ∑_{t=1}^{T} f_t(x)

The difference between the learner's cumulative loss and the cumulative loss of the single best fixed action in hindsight. An algorithm is no-regret if R_T / T → 0 as T → ∞.

1.4  Online Gradient Descent (OGD)

Online Convex Programming and Generalized Infinitesimal Gradient Ascent
Martin Zinkevich
ICML 2003, pp. 928–935.
Foundational OGD paper

OGD is the simplest OCO algorithm: take a gradient step and project back onto the feasible set.

Algorithm: Online Gradient Descent
Initialize: x_1 ∈ K, learning rate schedule {η_t}
for t = 1, …, T:
  Play x_t, observe f_t
  y_{t+1} = x_t − η_t ∇f_t(x_t)
  x_{t+1} = Π_K(y_{t+1})   // Euclidean projection onto K
Regret Bound — Convex Losses (Zinkevich 2003)

If each f_t is convex, ‖∇f_t‖ ≤ G, diam(K) ≤ D, and η_t = D/(G√t), then:

R_T  ≤  O(GD√T)

This is minimax optimal: there exist convex loss sequences for which any algorithm must suffer Ω(√T) regret.

Regret Bound — Strongly Convex Losses

If each f_t is λ-strongly convex and η_t = 1/(λt), then:

R_T  ≤  O((G²/λ) log T)

The logarithmic dependence on T is again minimax optimal for this function class.

1.5  Online Newton Step (ONS)

Logarithmic Regret Algorithms for Online Convex Optimization
Elad Hazan, Amit Agarwal, Satyen Kale
Machine Learning, Vol. 69, pp. 169–192, 2007. (Conference version: COLT 2006.)
DOI: 10.1007/s10994-007-5016-8
Definition — Exp-Concave Loss

A function f : K → R is α-exp-concave if the function x ↦ exp(−α f(x)) is concave. Equivalently, f is α-exp-concave if and only if:

∇²f(x)  ⪰  α ∇f(x) ∇f(x)^T    ∀ x ∈ K

Exp-concavity is strictly weaker than strong convexity but stronger than plain convexity. Key examples: squared loss (with α = 1/(2Y²) for bounded labels), log loss, and portfolio loss functions.

ONS uses second-order information to exploit the curvature of exp-concave losses. It maintains an approximation to the inverse Hessian via a running outer-product sum, updated efficiently using the Sherman–Morrison formula.

Algorithm: Online Newton Step
Initialize: x_1 ∈ K,   A_0 = ε I_d
for t = 1, …, T:
  Play x_t, observe f_t, compute g_t = ∇f_t(x_t)
  A_t = A_{t−1} + g_t g_t^T
  y_{t+1} = x_t − (1/α) A_t^{−1} g_t
  x_{t+1} = Π_K^{A_t}(y_{t+1})  // Projection w.r.t. norm induced by A_t
Regret Bound — ONS for Exp-Concave Losses (Hazan, Agarwal & Kale 2007)

For α-exp-concave losses over K ⊂ R^d:

R_T  ≤  O((d/α) log T)

The per-round cost is O(d²) for the matrix update (via Sherman–Morrison) plus O(d³) or less for projection, depending on the geometry of K.

Significance for RecWM: Economic loss functions (e.g., squared prediction error for state estimation, log-likelihood for density estimation) are typically exp-concave or strongly convex. This means logarithmic regret is achievable, making OCO regret bounds scale very favorably for economic state estimation over long horizons.

§2  Follow-the-Regularized-Leader & Mirror Descent

2.1  FTRL Framework

Definition — Follow-the-Regularized-Leader
x_{t+1}  =  argmin_{x ∈ K}   [ ∑_{s=1}^{t} f_s(x)  +  R(x) ]

where R : K → R is a strongly convex regularizer (also called a proximal function or distance-generating function). The regularizer prevents the learner from overfitting to past losses.

In the linearized variant (FTRL with linear losses), where the learner uses ⟨∇f_s(x_s), x⟩ instead of f_s(x), the update becomes:

x_{t+1}  =  argmin_{x ∈ K}   [ ⟨∑_{s=1}^{t} ∇f_s(x_s), x⟩  +  R(x) ]

2.2  Regularizer Choice Yields Specific Algorithms

Regularizer R(x) Induced Algorithm Domain
(η/2)‖x‖_2^2 Online Gradient Descent (OGD) Any convex K ⊂ R^d
η ∑_i x_i log x_i  (negative entropy) Hedge / Exponential Weights Algorithm (EWA) / Multiplicative Weights Probability simplex Δ_d
η ∑_i (x_i log x_i + (1−x_i) log(1−x_i)) Component Hedge / logistic regularization [0,1]^d hypercube
η log det(X^{−1}) Matrix Multiplicative Weights Spectrahedron
(1/α) ‖x‖_{A_t}^2  (adaptive quadratic) Online Newton Step (ONS) Any convex K ⊂ R^d

2.3  Mirror Descent

Mirror Descent (MD) generalizes projected gradient descent by replacing the Euclidean distance with a Bregman divergence.

Definition — Bregman Divergence

For a strictly convex differentiable function R:

D_R(x, y)  =  R(x) − R(y) − ⟨∇R(y), x − y⟩

Non-negative, zero iff x = y, but generally not symmetric and does not satisfy the triangle inequality.

Algorithm: Online Mirror Descent
for t = 1, …, T:
  Play x_t, observe f_t
  x_{t+1} = argmin_{x ∈ K}  [ ⟨∇f_t(x_t), x⟩ + (1/η_t) D_R(x, x_t) ]

The mirror descent update trades off following the current gradient against staying close (in Bregman divergence) to the previous iterate. When R(x) = (1/2)‖x‖_2^2, the Bregman divergence is the squared Euclidean distance and mirror descent reduces to OGD.

2.4  The FTRL–Mirror Descent Equivalence

Follow-the-Regularized-Leader and Mirror Descent: Equivalence Theorems and L1 Regularization
H. Brendan McMahan
AISTATS 2011, PMLR Vol. 15. Fort Lauderdale, FL.
PMLR: v15/mcmahan11b
Equivalence Theorem (McMahan 2011)

Lazy (a.k.a. "dual averaging") mirror descent is exactly equivalent to linearized FTRL.

Specifically, for any sequence of linear losses and any strongly convex regularizer R, the iterates produced by lazy mirror descent:

x_{t+1} = argmin_{x ∈ K}  [ ⟨∑_{s=1}^{t} g_s, x⟩ + R(x) ]

are identical to the iterates of linearized FTRL with regularizer R.

Greedy ("eager") mirror descent, which projects from the previous iterate rather than from the cumulative dual variable, is not in general equivalent to FTRL—the two diverge when the geometry of K forces non-trivial projections. However, on unconstrained problems they coincide.

The key practical consequence, established by McMahan, is that the FTRL-Proximal algorithm produces sparser solutions than FOBOS (Forward-Backward Splitting, the greedy mirror descent variant) when using L1 regularization, because FTRL applies the cumulative L1 penalty in closed form rather than incrementally.

Regret Decomposition (via Bregman Divergence)

For mirror descent / FTRL with regularizer R generating Bregman divergence D_R:

R_T(x*)  ≤  D_R(x*, x_1)  +  ∑_{t=1}^{T} D_R(x_t, y_{t+1})

The first term measures initial distance to the comparator; the second, summed "stability" of the iterates.

Further reference: Shalev-Shwartz (2012), "Online Learning and Online Convex Optimization," Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning, Vol. 4, No. 2, pp. 107–194, provides an alternative unified treatment of FTRL and mirror descent with a detailed comparison. Also see: Orabona (2023), "A Modern Introduction to Online Learning," arXiv:1912.13213, for an up-to-date textbook treatment.

§3  Adaptive & Strongly Adaptive Regret

3.1  Motivation: Why Static Regret Is Insufficient

Static regret compares against the single best fixed action over the entire horizon. When the environment changes—as it always does in economic systems, where regime shifts, structural breaks, and policy changes are the norm—the single best fixed action is a poor benchmark. An algorithm with O(√T) static regret may perform terribly on every sub-interval while still looking good on average.

3.2  Adaptive Regret (Hazan & Seshadhri 2007/2009)

Adaptive Algorithms for Online Decision Problems
Elad Hazan, C. Seshadhri
Electronic Colloquium on Computational Complexity (ECCC), 2007. Extended version: ICML 2009.
ICML 2009 paper #75
Definition — Adaptive Regret

The adaptive regret of algorithm A over time horizon T is:

AdaReg_T(A)  =  max_{[r,s] ⊆ [1,T]}   [ ∑_{t=r}^{s} f_t(x_t)  −  min_{x ∈ K} ∑_{t=r}^{s} f_t(x) ]

The maximum static regret over any contiguous time interval [r, s].

Hazan and Seshadhri proposed the Follow the Leading History (FLH) meta-algorithm. The idea is to maintain multiple copies ("experts") of a base OCO algorithm, each starting at a different time, and aggregate their predictions. Key results:

  • For exp-concave losses: O(d log² T) adaptive regret (called "weakly adaptive")
  • Efficient meta-algorithm with O(log T) computational overhead per round: O(√(s−r) · log³ T) regret on any interval [r, s]
  • Inefficient meta-algorithm with O(T) overhead per round: O(√(s−r) · log T) regret on any interval [r, s]

3.3  Strongly Adaptive Regret (Daniely, Gonen & Shalev-Shwartz 2015)

Strongly Adaptive Online Learning
Amit Daniely, Alon Gonen, Shai Shalev-Shwartz
ICML 2015, PMLR Vol. 37, pp. 1405–1411. Lille, France.
arXiv: 1502.07073 PMLR: v37/daniely15
Definition — Strongly Adaptive Regret

An algorithm A has strongly adaptive regret with rate φ(n) if for every contiguous interval I ⊆ [1, T] of length |I| = n:

SA-Reg_I(A)  =  ∑_{t ∈ I} f_t(x_t) − min_{x ∈ K} ∑_{t ∈ I} f_t(x)  ≤  φ(n)

This must hold simultaneously for all intervals, not just a worst-case one.

Main Result (Daniely, Gonen & Shalev-Shwartz 2015)

Reduction theorem: Given any base algorithm B with static regret bound R(n) on sequences of length n, there exists a meta-algorithm A that achieves strongly adaptive regret:

SA-Reg_I(A)  ≤  O(R(|I|) · log T)    for every interval I ⊆ [1, T]

Consequences for specific loss classes:

  • Convex losses: O(√(|I|) · log T) for every interval I (using OGD as base)
  • Strongly convex: O(log(|I|) · log T) for every interval I
  • Exp-concave: O(d · log(|I|) · log T) for every interval I (using ONS as base)

The meta-algorithm construction works by maintaining O(log T) "experts," each a copy of the base algorithm B, covering intervals at geometrically increasing scales. An outer sleeping-experts aggregation scheme combines their predictions. The computational overhead is O(log T) times the cost of the base algorithm.

3.4  Improved Strongly Adaptive via Coin Betting (Jun et al. 2017)

Improved Strongly Adaptive Online Learning using Coin Betting
Kwang-Sung Jun, Francesco Orabona, Rebecca Willett, Stephen Wright
AISTATS 2017 (also arXiv: 1610.04578).
arXiv: 1610.04578 Submitted: Oct 2016, revised Aug 2017
Key Improvement (Jun, Orabona, Willett & Wright 2017)

Using a coin-betting reduction, the authors obtain a parameter-free strongly adaptive algorithm that, compared to algorithms with the same per-round time complexity as Daniely et al., achieves a strongly adaptive regret improved by a factor of at least √(log T). Specifically:

SA-Reg_I  ≤  O(√(|I| · log(T/|I|)))    for every interval I

The coin-betting framework (Orabona & Pál 2016) provides a principled way to avoid learning-rate tuning: the wealth of a gambler in a coin-betting game translates directly into regret bounds for online learning.

3.5  Parameter-Free Online Learning (Orabona & collaborators)

Coin Betting and Parameter-Free Online Learning
Francesco Orabona, Dávid Pál
NeurIPS 2016.
Foundational coin-betting framework
A Modern Introduction to Online Learning
Francesco Orabona
arXiv: 1912.13213 (monograph, continuously updated).
arXiv: 1912.13213

The broader research program on parameter-free learning aims to design algorithms whose regret bounds hold without requiring knowledge of problem parameters (gradient bounds G, domain diameter D, strong convexity constant λ, time horizon T). This is essential for deployment in real-world economic systems where these parameters are unknown.

ICML 2020 Tutorial: "Parameter-free Learning and Optimization Algorithms" by Francesco Orabona (Boston University) and Ashok Cutkosky (Google Research / Stanford). Slides and a 4-part video playlist available at parameterfree.com/icml-tutorial/.

3.6  Dynamic Regret and Its Connection to Adaptive Regret

Dynamic Regret of Strongly Adaptive Methods
Lijun Zhang, Tianbao Yang, Rong Jin, Zhi-Hua Zhou
ICML 2018 (arXiv: 1701.07570).
arXiv: 1701.07570
Definition — Dynamic Regret

Given a comparator sequence x_1*, x_2*, …, x_T* ∈ K:

DynReg_T  =  ∑_{t=1}^{T} f_t(x_t) − ∑_{t=1}^{T} f_t(x_t*)

When x_t* = argmin_{x} f_t(x) (pointwise minimizers), this is the strongest form. The path length P_T = ∑_{t=2}^{T} ‖x_t* − x_{t−1}*‖ measures how much the comparator changes.

Key Connection (Zhang, Yang, Jin & Zhou 2018)

Dynamic regret can be decomposed using adaptive regret plus a measure of functional variation:

DynReg_T  ≤  SA-Reg +  functional variation terms

This enables leveraging strongly adaptive algorithms to automatically achieve low dynamic regret without knowing the path length P_T or functional variation in advance. For convex functions, this yields O(√T(1 + P_T)) dynamic regret. For strongly convex and exp-concave functions, even tighter bounds are obtained.

§4  Connections to Nonstationary Time Series Prediction

4.1  Why Adaptive Regret Matters for Regime Changes

Economic time series are characterized by structural breaks: regime changes in monetary policy, financial crises, technology shocks, pandemic disruptions. A forecasting algorithm with good static regret may perform well "on average" over a decade while being catastrophically wrong during every crisis—precisely when accurate prediction matters most.

Strongly adaptive regret bounds address this directly: an algorithm with O(√|I|) SA-regret on every interval I guarantees that on any contiguous period—including a 6-month crisis regime—the algorithm's cumulative loss is at most O(√|I|) worse than the best fixed predictor for that period. This means:

  • Automatic regime detection: The algorithm does not need to know when regimes change. It adapts at the rate implied by the length of the current regime.
  • No stationarity assumption: Unlike statistical methods that assume (weak) stationarity or ergodicity, OCO makes no distributional assumptions on the data.
  • Graceful degradation: If the environment happens to be stationary, SA-regret reduces to standard static regret. If it is highly nonstationary, the algorithm's performance degrades gracefully, governed by the interval length rather than the total horizon.

4.2  Key Papers on Nonstationary Prediction via OCO

NonSTOP: A NonSTationary Online Prediction Method for Time Series
Christopher Xie, Avleen Bijral, Juan Lavista Ferres
arXiv: 1611.02365 (2016).
arXiv: 1611.02365

NonSTOP explicitly handles nonstationary artifacts (trend, seasonality) in time series by applying learned transformations before prediction in a "learning with experts" framework. It provides sub-linear regret bounds and a data-dependent regret analysis of Follow-the-Leader under nonstationarity, including results for cointegrated multivariate series.

A Stability Principle for Learning under Non-Stationarity
Chengpiao Huang, Kaizheng Wang
arXiv: 2310.18304, 2023 (revised May 2025).
arXiv: 2310.18304

This paper proposes a look-back window selection principle that maximizes historical data utilization while keeping cumulative bias within an acceptable range relative to stochastic error. They achieve minimax optimal regret bounds under strongly convex and Lipschitz loss conditions, with experiments on electricity demand prediction.

Discounted Adaptive Online Learning: Towards Better Regularization
Zhiyu Zhang, David Bombara, Heng Yang
arXiv: 2402.02720, 2024.
arXiv: 2402.02720

This work revisits discounted regret—a metric that downweights older losses—as a way to handle changing environments. The core insight is that FTRL-based algorithms with appropriate discounting achieve instance-optimal performance, improving upon constant learning rate baselines. Results extend to online conformal prediction.

Mixture of Online and Offline Experts for Non-stationary Time Series
Zhilin Zhao, Longbing Cao, Yuanyu Wan
arXiv: 2202.05996, 2022.
arXiv: 2202.05996

MOOE combines static "offline" experts trained on historical regimes with a dynamic online expert for the current distribution. A meta-expert adaptively reweights these components—recognizing when the current data distribution matches a previously observed regime. Directly relevant to economic forecasting where historical regimes may recur.

4.3  The Argument for OCO in Economic State Estimation

The following chain of reasoning connects OCO theory to the RecWM program:

  1. Economic state estimation as sequential prediction. At each period t, the world model outputs a state estimate x_t; the economy then reveals data that defines a loss f_t(x_t) (e.g., squared prediction error on macro indicators). This is exactly the OCO protocol.
  2. Exp-concavity of natural loss functions. Squared error loss with bounded outcomes is exp-concave with α = 1/(2Y²). Log-likelihood losses for well-specified exponential family models are exp-concave. This means ONS-type algorithms can achieve O(d log T) regret on economic prediction tasks.
  3. Regime changes require adaptive regret. Static regret is meaningless when the best fixed predictor changes. Strongly adaptive algorithms guarantee O(√|I| · polylog T) on every interval I, providing simultaneous near-optimality across all regimes.
  4. Dynamic regret bounds path length. If regime changes are infrequent (small P_T), strongly adaptive algorithms automatically achieve near-static-regret performance. If changes are frequent, the bounds degrade proportionally to the "difficulty" of the sequence as measured by path length or functional variation.
  5. No distributional assumptions. Unlike ARIMA, GARCH, or state-space models, OCO algorithms guarantee performance against adversarial sequences. This is crucial for economic systems where "black swan" events violate any parametric distributional assumption.
