Curiosity-Driven Continual World Model Expansion

A technical survey of exploration objectives, intrinsic motivation, and self-supervised world model learning — with implications for structured economic state estimation

Compiled 2026-08-09 · 16 papers surveyed

1. Plan2Explore — Planning to Explore via Self-Supervised World Models

Planning to Explore via Self-Supervised World Models
Ramanan Sekar, Oleh Rybkin, Kostas Daniilidis, Pieter Abbeel, Danijar Hafner, Deepak Pathak
ICML 2020 · arXiv:2005.05960
arXiv GitHub Project Page

Core Idea

Plan2Explore is a self-supervised reinforcement learning agent that learns a world model entirely without task-specific rewards, then rapidly adapts to downstream tasks in zero-shot or few-shot fashion. The key innovation is prospective exploration: rather than computing novelty retrospectively (as in count-based or prediction-error methods), Plan2Explore plans to seek out expected future novelty by imagining trajectories through its learned world model and selecting actions that maximize anticipated model uncertainty.

Architecture: RSSM World Model

The method builds on the Dreamer framework, using a Recurrent State-Space Model (RSSM) as the learned world model. The RSSM maintains a latent state s_t composed of a deterministic recurrent component h_t and a stochastic component z_t:

RSSM Dynamics Deterministic: h_t = f_θ(h_{t-1}, z_{t-1}, a_{t-1})
Stochastic prior: p_θ(z_t | h_t)
Stochastic posterior: q_θ(z_t | h_t, o_t)
Observation: p_θ(o_t | h_t, z_t)
Reward: p_θ(r_t | h_t, z_t)

Exploration Objective: Ensemble Disagreement

The exploration signal is the disagreement among an ensemble of K one-step predictive models in the latent space. Each ensemble member q_k predicts the next latent state. The intrinsic reward at each imagined step is the variance across ensemble predictions:

Exploration Bonus r_t^explore = Var({q_k(z_{t+1} | s_t, a_t)})_{k=1}^{K}

Concretely, given K ensemble members each predicting &hat;z_{t+1}^{(k)}:
r_t^explore = (1/K) ∑_{k=1}^{K} || &hat;z_{t+1}^{(k)} − &bar;z_{t+1} ||²
where &bar;z_{t+1} = (1/K) ∑_{k=1}^{K} &hat;z_{t+1}^{(k)}

This formulation captures epistemic uncertainty — regions where the model has not yet gathered sufficient data to converge. Unlike prediction error against ground truth (which conflates epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty), ensemble disagreement isolates the reducible component of uncertainty.

Planning for Future Novelty

The critical advance over prior work is that Plan2Explore does not merely react to novel states after visiting them. Instead, it uses the world model to imagine future trajectories and selects actions that maximize the cumulative expected disagreement along those imagined rollouts. The exploration policy π_explore is optimized via actor-critic learning in imagination:

Objective max_{π_explore} E_{π_explore, p_θ} [ ∑_{t=0}^{H} γ^t r_t^explore ]

This amounts to planning to visit states where the world model is most uncertain, making exploration directed rather than random.

One-Shot / Few-Shot Adaptation

After the unsupervised exploration phase, the world model has been trained on diverse experience. For a new downstream task with reward function r_task, Plan2Explore:

  1. Freezes the world model (or continues training it with new data)
  2. Trains a new reward predictor from the world model's latent states
  3. Optimizes a task-specific policy entirely in imagination using the learned world model

Because the world model already captures the environment dynamics, this adaptation requires zero or minimal real-world interaction — the agent can learn the task policy purely by dreaming through the pre-trained model.

Key Implementation Details

  • Built on TensorFlow (1.14 and 2.x versions available)
  • Key hyperparameters: intrinsic_scale, ensemble_model_type, model_size, state_size, ensemble_loss_scale
  • Ensemble size K is typically 5-10 models
Relevance to Economic World Models Plan2Explore's architecture maps directly to economic state estimation. The RSSM's factored latent state (deterministic + stochastic) mirrors the separation between structural economic dynamics (trend, institutional regime) and stochastic shocks (demand shocks, policy surprises). Ensemble disagreement as the exploration signal identifies regions of the economic state space where the model's understanding is weakest — precisely the states where additional data collection or scenario analysis would be most informative. The few-shot adaptation mechanism is analogous to rapid policy transfer when a new economic objective (e.g., a new KPI or regulatory constraint) is introduced.

2. LEXA — Discovering and Achieving Goals via World Models

Discovering and Achieving Goals via World Models
Russell Mendonca, Oleh Rybkin, Kostas Daniilidis, Danijar Hafner, Deepak Pathak
NeurIPS 2021 · arXiv:2110.09514
arXiv GitHub (Training) GitHub (Benchmark) Project Page

How LEXA Extends Plan2Explore

LEXA (Latent Explorer Achiever) builds directly on Plan2Explore's world-model-based exploration but adds a crucial component: goal-conditioned achievement. Where Plan2Explore explores to build a general world model and then adapts with reward functions, LEXA decomposes unsupervised learning into two complementary agents operating within a shared world model:

  1. Explorer (π_e) — Plans to discover novel states using the world model, similar to Plan2Explore's disagreement-driven exploration. Uses foresight: queries the model for the most novel states rather than retrospectively searching replay buffers.
  2. Achiever (π_a) — A goal-conditioned policy trained to reliably reach states discovered by the explorer. Goals are specified as latent state targets.

Architecture

Both policies are trained from imagined trajectories within the shared RSSM world model. The explorer's discovered states become training goals for the achiever, creating a curriculum of increasingly diverse and challenging targets:

Explorer Objective max_{π_e} E_{π_e, p_θ} [ ∑_{t} r_t^{novelty} ]
where r_t^{novelty} = ensemble disagreement (as in Plan2Explore)
Achiever Objective max_{π_a} E_{π_a, p_θ} [ −d(z_T, z_g) ]
where z_g is a goal latent state discovered by the explorer,
d(·, ·) is a distance metric in latent space (temporal or cosine variants)

Zero-Shot Goal Achievement

At test time, a user-specified goal image is encoded into the latent space, and the achiever policy directly pursues it — no additional learning required. LEXA solves challenging locomotion and manipulation tasks provided as goal images zero-shot.

Training Variants

The codebase supports multiple distance metrics: lexa_temporal (temporal distance in latent space), lexa_cosine (cosine similarity), and comparisons with DIAYN, DDL, and GCSL.

Relevance to Economic World Models LEXA's explorer-achiever decomposition maps to a natural economic workflow: the explorer identifies underexplored economic regimes (e.g., rare market conditions, untested policy configurations), while the achiever learns to navigate toward specified economic targets (desired inflation rates, employment levels, growth trajectories). The goal-conditioned architecture enables "what-if" scenario planning: specify a desired economic state as a goal, and the achiever computes the policy trajectory to reach it. The zero-shot capability is particularly relevant for responding to novel economic objectives without retraining.

3. RND — Random Network Distillation

Exploration by Random Network Distillation
Yuri Burda, Harrison Edwards, Amos Storkey, Oleg Klimov
ICLR 2019 · arXiv:1810.12894
arXiv DI-engine Docs

Core Mechanism

RND introduces a strikingly simple exploration bonus based on the prediction error between two neural networks. The key insight: a predictor network trained on visited states will have low error on familiar observations and high error on novel ones, providing a novelty signal without explicit state counting.

Mathematical Formulation

Two networks are maintained:

  • Target network f : O → R^k — a fixed, randomly initialized network that maps observations to embeddings. Parameters ψ are set at initialization and never updated.
  • Predictor network &hat;f} : O → R^k — a trainable network with identical architecture. Parameters θ are learned via gradient descent.
Training Loss L(θ) = E_s [ || f_ψ(s) − &hat;f}_θ(s) ||² ]
Intrinsic Reward r_t^{int} = || f_ψ(s_t) − &hat;f}_θ(s_t) ||²

The predictor is trained to match the target's outputs on states the agent has visited. On novel states, the predictor has not been trained, so the prediction error (= intrinsic reward) is high. As the agent revisits states, the predictor improves and the bonus decays.

Two Sources of Prediction Error

Burda et al. carefully analyze the sources of prediction error:

  1. Epistemic uncertainty — Error due to insufficient training data. This is the desirable novelty signal that decays with more visits.
  2. Aleatoric uncertainty — Irreducible error from stochastic environment dynamics. This is undesirable as it creates the "noisy TV problem" where the agent fixates on inherently unpredictable stimuli.

RND's deterministic target network avoids most aleatoric noise, but the distinction remains important. The combined reward is:

Combined Reward r_t = r_t^{ext} + w · r_t^{int}
where w controls exploration-exploitation tradeoff

Observation Normalization

RND normalizes observations using a running mean and standard deviation, then clips to [-5, 5]. The intrinsic reward is also normalized (mean 0, std 1) or min-max scaled to [0, 1] for stable training.

Relevance to Economic World Models RND can serve as a computationally cheap novelty detector for economic state spaces. The target network provides a fixed random projection of economic observations; the predictor's error on new data points indicates whether an economic state is genuinely novel (a new regime) or familiar. The epistemic/aleatoric decomposition is critical for economics: stochastic market noise is aleatoric and should not drive exploration, while genuinely novel structural states (e.g., an unprecedented policy configuration) represent epistemic uncertainty that the model should actively investigate. RND's simplicity makes it suitable as a lightweight anomaly detector layered on top of a structured economic world model.

4. ICM — Intrinsic Curiosity Module

Curiosity-driven Exploration by Self-supervised Prediction
Deepak Pathak, Pulkit Agrawal, Alexei A. Efros, Trevor Darrell
ICML 2017 · arXiv:1705.05363
arXiv

Architecture: Three Coupled Models

ICM formulates curiosity as the error in predicting the consequence of the agent's own actions, computed in a learned feature space rather than raw observation space. The system comprises three jointly-trained components:

  1. Feature encoder φ — Maps high-dimensional observations o_t to compact features φ(o_t)
  2. Inverse dynamics model — Predicts the action a_t taken between states φ(o_t) and φ(o_{t+1}). This shapes the feature space to encode only action-relevant information, filtering out distractors.
  3. Forward dynamics model — Predicts the next feature &hat;φ(o_{t+1}) given current features φ(o_t) and action a_t
Inverse Model Loss L_inverse = CrossEntropy(&hat;a}_t, a_t)
where &hat;a}_t = g(φ(o_t), φ(o_{t+1}))
Forward Model Loss (= Intrinsic Reward) r_t^{int} = ½ || &hat;φ(o_{t+1}) − φ(o_{t+1}) ||²
where &hat;φ(o_{t+1}) = f(φ(o_t), a_t)
Total Loss L = (1 − β) L_inverse + β L_forward

Why the Inverse Model Matters

The inverse model constrains the feature space to encode only aspects of the environment that are influenced by the agent's actions. Without it, the forward model would need to predict everything — including irrelevant stochastic dynamics (weather, background motion) — leading to permanently high prediction error on uncontrollable elements (the "noisy TV" problem). By learning features through the inverse model, ICM focuses curiosity on controllable aspects of the environment.

Relevance to Economic World Models ICM's inverse model offers a principled approach to identifying policy-relevant economic features. In economic modeling, many observable variables are driven by exogenous noise (commodity price fluctuations, weather shocks) that a policymaker cannot control. The inverse model architecture would learn to encode only those economic features that respond to policy actions, making curiosity about model errors focus on the controllable portion of the economic state space. The forward model then captures the causal dynamics of how policy actions propagate through these controllable features.

5. Self-Supervised Exploration via Disagreement

Self-Supervised Exploration via Disagreement
Deepak Pathak, Dhiraj Gandhi, Abhinav Gupta
ICML 2019 · arXiv:1906.04161
arXiv GitHub (TensorFlow)

Ensemble Disagreement as Exploration

This paper provides the theoretical and empirical foundation for the disagreement-based exploration signal later used in Plan2Explore. The core idea, drawn from active learning: train an ensemble of K forward dynamics models and use their disagreement as intrinsic motivation.

Ensemble Disagreement Reward r_t^{int} = Var_{k=1}^{K} [ f_k(s_t, a_t) ]

= (1/K) ∑_{k=1}^{K} || f_k(s_t, a_t) − &bar;f}(s_t, a_t) ||²
where &bar;f} = (1/K) ∑_{k} f_k

Differentiable Optimization

A key contribution: the disagreement objective can be optimized differentiably without reinforcement learning. Rather than using the disagreement as a reward signal in an RL loop, the policy gradient can be computed directly through the ensemble, yielding more sample-efficient exploration. This is possible because the ensemble predictions are differentiable functions of the policy parameters.

Advantages Over Prediction Error

Ensemble disagreement has a crucial advantage over single-model prediction error (as in ICM): it better separates epistemic from aleatoric uncertainty. In stochastic environments, a single model will always have high prediction error on inherently unpredictable transitions. An ensemble, however, will agree on the distribution of stochastic outcomes while disagreeing on outcomes it has insufficient data to characterize — isolating genuine novelty.

Relevance to Economic World Models The differentiable optimization pathway is particularly relevant for economic models where sample efficiency matters (real economic data is expensive and slow to collect). Building an ensemble of economic dynamics models and using their disagreement to identify underexplored regions of the economic state space provides a principled way to direct data collection, scenario generation, or sensitivity analysis toward the most informationally valuable regions. The stochastic environment results are directly applicable: economic systems are inherently stochastic, so the ensemble disagreement's ability to separate structural uncertainty from noise is essential.

6. BYOL-Explore — Exploration by Bootstrapped Prediction

BYOL-Explore: Exploration by Bootstrapped Prediction
Zhaohan Daniel Guo, Shantanu Thakoor, Miruna Pislar, Bernardo Avila Pires, Florent Altché, Corentin Tallec, Alaa Saade, Daniele Calandriello, Jean-Bastien Grill, Yunhao Tang, Michal Valko, Rémi Munos, Mohammad Gheshlaghi Azar, Bilal Piot
NeurIPS 2022 · arXiv:2206.08332
arXiv

Unified Prediction Loss

BYOL-Explore extends the Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL) self-supervised learning framework to exploration. The key simplification: it learns a world representation, world dynamics, and an exploration policy all together by optimizing a single prediction loss in latent space, with no additional auxiliary objectives.

Architecture

Following BYOL's asymmetric architecture:

  • An online network (encoder + predictor) that processes current observations and predicts future latent representations
  • A target network (encoder only) that provides prediction targets, updated as an exponential moving average (EMA) of the online network

The prediction error between the online predictor's output and the target network's encoding of the actual next state serves as the intrinsic reward. The EMA update prevents representation collapse without requiring negative pairs, contrastive losses, or ensembles.

Intrinsic Reward (BYOL-Explore) r_t^{int} = || q_θ(z_t, a_t) − sg(&bar{z}_{t+1}) ||²
where q_θ is the online predictor, &bar{z}_{t+1} is the target encoding,
and sg(·) denotes stop-gradient

Results

Achieves superhuman performance on the 10 hardest Atari exploration games and solves the majority of DM-HARD-8 tasks (a partially-observable 3D benchmark) purely through intrinsic reward — without requiring human demonstrations, unlike prior methods.

Relevance to Economic World Models BYOL-Explore's single-loss simplicity is architecturally attractive for economic settings where maintaining multiple auxiliary losses creates optimization complexity. The EMA target network provides a stable prediction target that adapts gradually, mirroring how economic baselines shift slowly while the online model tracks current dynamics. The bootstrapped approach naturally handles partial observability, a defining feature of economic environments where key variables (e.g., aggregate demand, household expectations) are never fully observed.

7. Curiosity-Driven Exploration and Continual Learning

The intersection of intrinsic motivation and continual learning is an active research frontier. The central challenge: curiosity signals based on prediction error degrade as the model learns (which is the intended behavior for exploration), but in continual learning settings, catastrophic forgetting can cause prediction error to increase on previously mastered states, creating pathological revisitation of old territory.

FARCuriosity — Fragmentation and Recall

Neuro-Inspired Fragmentation and Recall to Overcome Catastrophic Forgetting in Curiosity
Jaedong Hwang, Zhang-Wei Hong, Eric Chen, Akhilan Boopathy, Pulkit Agrawal, Ila Fiete
NeurIPS 2023 Workshop (IMOL) · arXiv:2310.17537
arXiv

FARCuriosity addresses the specific problem that prediction-based intrinsic rewards suffer from catastrophic forgetting — the curiosity module forgets previously visited states, causing their novelty signal to spike again and trapping the agent in revisitation loops. The solution is biologically inspired:

  1. Fragmentation — When surprisal exceeds a threshold, the agent fragments the environment into regions and assigns a separate local curiosity module to each fragment.
  2. Storage — On fragmentation, the current module is stored in long-term memory (LTM).
  3. Recall — When re-entering a previously explored fragment, the agent retrieves the matching module from LTM, restoring its learned prediction model and maintaining appropriate (low) novelty estimates.

This prevents any single prediction module from being trained on the full environment, limiting the scope of forgetting.

Information Gain as Exploration Bonus in World Models

Information gain provides a Bayesian perspective on exploration. The information gain from observing state s_{t+1} after taking action a_t in state s_t is the reduction in uncertainty about the world model parameters:

Information Gain IG(a_t, s_t) = H[p(θ | D_t)] − E_{s_{t+1}} [H[p(θ | D_t, s_{t+1})]]

= E_{s_{t+1}} [D_KL( p(θ | D_t, s_{t+1}) || p(θ | D_t) )]

= I(θ; s_{t+1} | D_t, a_t)

This is the mutual information between the model parameters and the next observation. Maximizing information gain directs exploration toward states that would maximally reduce model uncertainty — the Bayesian counterpart to ensemble disagreement. In practice, information gain is approximated via ensemble methods, variational inference, or dropout-based uncertainty.

Epistemic Uncertainty for World Model Expansion

Several approaches use epistemic uncertainty to guide world model growth:

  • Ensemble variance (Plan2Explore, Pathak et al. 2019) — Variance of ensemble predictions approximates epistemic uncertainty
  • Bayesian neural networks — Posterior uncertainty over weights directly quantifies epistemic uncertainty, but is computationally expensive
  • Dropout as approximate inference (Gal & Ghahramani, 2016) — MC Dropout provides cheap epistemic uncertainty estimates
  • Prediction error decomposition (RND) — Uses the gap between a trainable predictor and a fixed random target to measure novelty

Continual Learning and Catastrophic Forgetting

Continual Learning and Catastrophic Forgetting
Gido M. van de Ven, Nicholas Soures, Dhireesha Kudithipudi
Learning and Memory: A Comprehensive Reference, 3rd Ed., 2025 · arXiv:2403.05175
arXiv

The three main families of continual learning methods — all relevant to maintaining world models over non-stationary economic distributions:

  • Regularization-based (EWC, SI) — Penalize changes to parameters important for previous tasks. Directly applicable to world models that must retain knowledge of past economic regimes.
  • Replay-based (experience replay, generative replay) — Maintain or generate examples from previous data distributions. Analogous to maintaining a representative sample of historical economic states.
  • Architecture-based (progressive networks, PackNet) — Allocate new model capacity for new tasks. Maps to expanding world model modules for newly encountered economic regimes.
Relevance to Economic World Models Economic world models face continual learning by necessity: the data-generating process is non-stationary (regimes change, institutions evolve, shocks arrive). FARCuriosity's fragmentation approach maps to maintaining separate sub-models for distinct economic regimes (e.g., expansion vs. recession, pre- and post-policy-change). Information gain as the exploration objective provides a principled criterion for when to collect new economic data or run new simulations: direct resources toward observations that maximally reduce model uncertainty. The replay-based continual learning approach is natural for economic models that must remember how to predict behavior during past regimes while adapting to current conditions.

8. Active Inference and Expected Free Energy

Active inference, developed by Karl Friston and colleagues, provides a unified Bayesian framework in which perception, learning, and action are all driven by minimizing free energy (a variational bound on surprisal). The exploration-exploitation tradeoff emerges naturally from the decomposition of expected free energy (EFE).

Expected Free Energy Decomposition

Expected Free Energy (EFE) G(π) = E_{q(o_τ, s_τ | π)} [ ln q(s_τ | π) − ln p(o_τ, s_τ) ]

Decomposes as:
G(π) = − E_q [ ln p(o_τ) ] − E_q [ D_KL( q(s_τ | o_τ, π) || q(s_τ | π) ) ]

= pragmatic value (exploitation) + epistemic value (exploration)

The first term (pragmatic value / extrinsic value) drives the agent toward preferred observations (goal-directed behavior). The second term (epistemic value / intrinsic value) is the expected information gain about hidden states — it drives the agent to seek observations that maximally resolve uncertainty about the world. Exploration thus emerges as an intrinsic consequence of free energy minimization, not an add-on bonus.

Key Papers in Active Inference for World Models

  • Friston, K. (2010). The free-energy principle: a unified brain theory? Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 11(2), 127-138. The foundational paper establishing free energy minimization as a unifying principle.
  • Friston, K., et al. (2015). Active inference and epistemic value. Cognitive Neuroscience, 6(4), 187-214. Formalizes the expected free energy decomposition and epistemic drive.
  • Friston, K., et al. (2017). Active inference: a process theory. Neural Computation, 29(1), 1-49. Full process theory connecting perception, learning, and action under free energy minimization.
  • Fountas, Z., et al. (2020). Deep active inference agents using Monte-Carlo methods. NeurIPS 2020. arXiv:2006.04176. Scales active inference to deep neural network world models using Monte Carlo tree search for planning.
  • Millidge, B., Tschantz, A., & Buckley, C. L. (2021). Whence the expected free energy? Neural Computation, 33(2). Provides rigorous derivation of EFE and its relationship to information gain.

Connection to Curiosity-Driven Exploration

Active inference subsumes the curiosity-driven methods described above as special cases:

  • Information gain (epistemic value in EFE) ≈ Bayesian information gain used in ensemble disagreement methods
  • Prediction error minimization (free energy minimization) ≈ ICM's forward model error, but computed as a proper variational bound
  • Expected novelty planning (EFE over future trajectories) ≈ Plan2Explore's imagined rollouts with disagreement reward
Relevance to Economic World Models Active inference is particularly natural for economic world models because it treats the agent as both a modeler and an actor within the system — precisely the situation of an economic agent or policymaker. The EFE decomposition provides a principled way to balance exploitation (pursuing known-good economic policies) against exploration (gathering information about uncertain economic dynamics). The epistemic value term provides a Bayesian criterion for when model expansion is warranted: allocate resources to reduce uncertainty about economic state variables where the expected information gain is highest. This connects directly to the Reflexive Constructive Economics framework's concern with endogenous model uncertainty under intervention.

9. Recent Work (2024–2026)

Dr. Strategy — Strategic Dreaming (2024)

Dr. Strategy: Model-Based Generalist Agents with Strategic Dreaming
Hany Hamed, Subin Kim, Dongyeong Kim, Jaesik Yoon, Sungjin Ahn
arXiv:2402.18866 · 2024
arXiv

Extends LEXA with a divide-and-conquer strategy using latent landmarks as structural waypoints. Three-policy architecture:

  • Highway policy πl — navigates between landmarks
  • Explorer πe — explores from selected landmarks
  • Achiever πm — reaches goal states from nearby positions
Landmark Quantization (VQ-VAE) L_l = ||s − dec_φ(l_k)||² + β ||sg(l_k) − enc_φ(s)||²

Results: 94% success on 9-room navigation (vs. 19-28% for baselines), 87% on 3D mazes (vs. 40-51% for LEXA). The landmark structure enables long-horizon planning by decomposing exploration into local and global components.

SENSEI — Semantic Exploration via Foundation Models (2025)

SENSEI: Semantic Exploration Guided by Foundation Models to Learn Versatile World Models
Cansu Sancaktar, Christian Gumbsch, Andrii Zadaianchuk, Pavel Kolev, Georg Martius
arXiv:2503.01584 · 2025
arXiv

Combines vision-language model guidance with ensemble disagreement for world model exploration. Three-stage process:

  1. Reward distillation — GPT-4 compares image pairs by "interestingness," training a semantic reward function
  2. World model learning — RSSM learns dynamics while predicting semantic rewards and epistemic uncertainty
  3. Adaptive exploration — Combines semantic rewards and ensemble disagreement with dynamic weighting

The adaptive weighting shifts from seeking "interesting" states (semantic reward) to exploring novel behaviors (disagreement) once interesting regions are found — preventing the agent from fixating on states the VLM finds interesting but the world model already understands well.

InDRiVE — Latent Disagreement for Autonomous Driving (2025)

InDRiVE: Reward-Free World-Model Pretraining for Autonomous Driving via Latent Disagreement
Feeza Khan Khanzada, Jaerock Kwon
arXiv:2512.18850 · 2025
arXiv

Applies the Plan2Explore paradigm (DreamerV3 + latent ensemble disagreement) to autonomous driving in CARLA. Two-phase approach: reward-free intrinsic pretraining followed by zero-shot/few-shot transfer. Demonstrates that curiosity-driven world model pretraining generalizes to unseen driving environments.

DISDAIN — Optimistic Exploration via Discriminator Disagreement (2022)

Learning More Skills Through Optimistic Exploration
DJ Strouse, Kate Baumli, David Warde-Farley, Vlad Mnih, Steven Hansen
ICLR 2022 (Spotlight) · arXiv:2107.14226
arXiv

Uses ensemble of discriminators to measure epistemic uncertainty in unsupervised skill learning, rewarding agents for visiting states where discriminators disagree most — indicating under-explored skill regions.

MoReFree — Reset-Free RL with World Models (2025)

Reset-Free Reinforcement Learning with World Models
Zhecheng Yang, Thomas M. Moerland, Mike Preuss, Aske Plaat, Eric S. Hu
arXiv:2408.09807 · 2025
arXiv

Demonstrates that model-based approaches substantially outperform model-free methods in reset-free (continual) settings. The world model enables the agent to plan without costly real-world resets, achieving superior data efficiency across continual tasks.

General Intelligence Requires Rethinking Exploration (2022)

General Intelligence Requires Rethinking Exploration
Minqi Jiang, Tim Rocktäschel, Edward Grefenstette
arXiv:2211.07819 · 2022
arXiv

Argues that exploration is essential to all learning systems (not just RL), and that open-ended learning — continuously discovering and solving new problems — is a path to general intelligence. Proposes "generalized exploration" bridging supervised and reinforcement learning.

Relevance to Economic World Models Dr. Strategy's landmark-based decomposition maps to hierarchical economic structure: landmarks correspond to macroeconomic regimes, the highway policy navigates between regimes, and local exploration/achievement operate within regime-specific dynamics. SENSEI's use of foundation models to define "interestingness" parallels using domain expertise or economic theory to guide exploration toward economically meaningful states rather than merely uncertain ones. InDRiVE validates that curiosity-driven pretraining transfers to new environments, supporting the case for building general economic world models that transfer across policy contexts. MoReFree's reset-free result is directly relevant: economic systems cannot be "reset" for experimentation, so world model-based planning is essential.

10. Synthesis: Architecture for Curiosity-Driven Economic World Models

Drawing together the surveyed methods, a curiosity-driven continual economic world model would integrate the following components:

Proposed Architecture Stack

Layer Method Source Economic Function
World Model Core RSSM (deterministic + stochastic latent state) Dreamer / Plan2Explore Separates structural dynamics from stochastic shocks
Exploration Signal Ensemble disagreement in latent space Pathak 2019 / Plan2Explore Identifies under-explored economic regimes
Novelty Filter RND for fast anomaly detection Burda 2018 Lightweight regime-change detector
Feature Learning Inverse model for policy-relevant features ICM (Pathak 2017) Filters exogenous noise from controllable state
Goal Conditioning Explorer-Achiever with latent goals LEXA Scenario planning: specify target economic state
Hierarchical Planning Landmark-based decomposition Dr. Strategy Navigate between macro regimes, explore locally
Continual Learning Fragmented local modules + LTM recall FARCuriosity Maintain regime-specific sub-models
Bayesian Foundation Expected free energy (EFE) Active Inference Principled explore-exploit under reflexivity
Semantic Guidance Foundation model reward distillation SENSEI Theory-guided exploration of meaningful states

Key Design Principles

  1. Epistemic over aleatoric. Ensemble disagreement and information gain separate reducible uncertainty (what the model hasn't learned) from irreducible noise (inherent economic stochasticity). Exploration should target the former.
  2. Prospective, not retrospective. Plan to explore (Plan2Explore's core insight) rather than react to past novelty. In economics, this means using the world model to simulate which data collection or policy experiments would be most informative before committing resources.
  3. Fragmented continual learning. Economic regimes are discrete modes with distinct dynamics. Maintaining separate model modules per regime (FARCuriosity) prevents catastrophic forgetting when the economy transitions between regimes.
  4. Goal-conditioned planning. The LEXA architecture enables counterfactual reasoning: "what policy sequence would reach this target economic state?" This is the computational core of reflexive economic modeling.
  5. Hierarchical state space. Economic state spaces are naturally hierarchical (macro regime > sectoral dynamics > firm-level behavior). Dr. Strategy's landmark decomposition provides the planning architecture for this hierarchy.

Open Problems

  • Reflexivity. In economic systems, the model's predictions change the system being modeled. None of the surveyed methods account for this feedback loop. The exploration signal must be adjusted for the fact that model-guided interventions alter the data-generating process.
  • Causal structure. Current methods learn correlational dynamics. Economic world models require causal structure (interventional distributions, counterfactuals) to support policy analysis. Integrating causal discovery with curiosity-driven exploration is an open frontier.
  • Multi-agent interaction. Economic systems involve strategic agents. The world model must capture equilibrium dynamics, not just single-agent MDP transitions.
  • Scale of latent space. Economic state spaces are vastly higher-dimensional than robotic control. The ensemble size and disagreement computation must scale accordingly.

Status: Research Architecture — Nothing Described Below Exists Yet

No running code. No trained model. No deployed system. No backtest results. No customers. This document describes what we intend to build, not what we have. Every capability described is a design specification, not a feature announcement.

Product Vision

RecWM: A Continually-Learning World Model for Financial Markets

An architecture designed to model market dynamics with native online learning, typed multi-timescale fragments, and endogenous reflexivity estimation.

1. What We Propose to Build

RecWM is a research architecture for a continually-learning world model of financial markets. The core thesis: financial markets are non-stationary systems where predictions themselves change the data distribution (performativity), and existing models handle neither of these properties natively.

The design decomposes market state into typed fragments operating at different timescales, uses sparse gating to control which fragments update at each step, and estimates its own reflexive impact on the market.

The thesis in one sentence: A world model with native continual learning and endogenous performativity estimation would outperform frozen models on regime-transition prediction and tail-risk estimation. This is an empirical claim that has not yet been tested.

Design Principles

Continual Learning

No frozen weights. Five CL mechanisms (GateL0RD implicit, O(N) RTRL, per-fragment EWC, BOCPD regime detection, slow-fast weights) prevent catastrophic forgetting while enabling adaptation.

Multi-Timescale

Seven fragment types from tick-level liquidity (τ=1–5 days) to structural trends (τ=250–1000 days). The same τk parameter governs discretization, gate penalty, prediction horizon, and EWC strength.

Reflexivity-Aware

Estimates its own performative impact via ε(t). When predictions become self-fulfilling, the model detects this and adjusts its update rate. Novel — no existing system does this.

Traceable

Every output traces to specific fragments, data sources, and mathematical pathways. Designed for regulatory compliance (EU DORA, AI Act, SR 11-7).

2. The Problem

Three properties of financial markets make existing ML models fundamentally inadequate:

Non-Stationarity

The relationship between interest rates and investment behaves differently in 2007 (pre-crisis) vs. 2009 (zero-lower-bound) vs. 2022 (fastest hiking cycle in 40 years). A model trained on one regime degrades when the regime changes. No existing time-series foundation model — Chronos-2, TimesFM, Moirai — supports native online learning. They are offline-only.

Performativity

A model that predicts a crisis and is acted upon changes the probability of that crisis. The distribution shift is endogenous, caused by the model itself. Perdomo et al. (ICML 2020) formalized this as "performative prediction," but nobody has applied it to financial markets. We aim to be the first.

Multi-Timescale Structure

Markets operate across timescales from microseconds to decades. Liquidity shifts in hours; credit cycles turn over years. Existing models either pick one timescale or treat all data at a single resolution, losing critical cross-timescale interactions.

3. Proposed Architecture

The design has two regions: a four-layer world model (WM) that encodes and predicts market state, and five continual learning (CL) mechanisms that keep the world model current without catastrophic forgetting.

Each fragment operates at a characteristic timescale τk. The same parameter τk governs four things: S5 discretization step, GateL0RD sparsity penalty, SPIB prediction horizon, and EWC consolidation strength. This is the typed-Δ principle — one hyperparameter, four roles.

5. Target Outputs (Design Specification)

If built and validated, RecWM would produce four derived signals that no existing system provides:

Reflexive Instability Index

Formula: ε̂(t) / (γ/β), where ε̂ is the estimated performative sensitivity and γ/β is the convergence threshold (Perdomo et al. ICML 2020, Thm 3.5).

What it means: How close the market is to a self-reinforcing feedback loop. Near 1.0 = predictions becoming self-fulfilling.

Novel. Depends on making ε(t) learnable — our hardest open problem.

Fragment Coherence

Formula: Smallest eigenvalue of the sheaf Laplacian LF across fragment types (Hansen & Ghrist 2019).

What it means: When fragments tell contradictory stories (liquidity says calm, risk says crisis), coherence drops. Detects brewing dislocations.

Novel application. Sheaf Laplacian has zero finance applications for signal fusion.

Regime Transition Probability

Formula: BOCPD posterior P(rt=0 | x1:t) computed on fragment latent states.

What it means: Real-time probability that the current market regime is ending. Standard method (Adams & MacKay 2007), applied to learned representations.

Standard method, novel input (fragment latents instead of raw data).

Latent Scenario Distribution

Formula: Forward rollout in latent space (Dreamer-style imagination): z(t+h) = f(z(t), ..., z(t+h-1)).

What it means: Generate plausible future market states in representation space, not observation space. Non-Gaussian tails emerge naturally.

Novel for finance. Zero Dreamer/RSSM papers applied to trading.

7. Compute Requirements (Estimated)

Training

~84M parameters total (7 fragment S5 blocks × ~12M each). Estimated ~200–400 GPU-hours on A100 for full training on 5 years of daily data. Cost: ~$400–800 at cloud spot prices. This is NOT a foundation model — it is a structured latent model.

Inference

Forward pass through 7 fragment encoders + S5 core: target <100ms latency. Likely achievable on a single A10G or even CPU for daily-frequency updates. Real-time intraday would need GPU.

CL Overhead

EWC Fisher diagonal: O(N) per fragment. BOCPD run-length update: O(rmax) per step. Slow-fast EMA: negligible. Total CL overhead estimated at <10% of forward pass.

Imagination

Latent rollouts are ~100× cheaper than observation-space generation. 1,000 scenarios at 20-step horizon: estimated ~1 second on A10G. This is a design estimate, not a benchmark.

10. Build Order (Proposed)

PhaseWeeksWhatKill Criterion
0. Data Pipeline 1–2 FRED + Yahoo Finance + GDELT ingestion. Temporal alignment (publication-time, not reference-period). Fragment-typed schema. If data quality is too low for any fragment type, reduce to 5 fragments.
1. Single Fragment S5 3–4 Liquidity fragment only. S5 backbone with typed-Δ. Train on FRED liquidity series. Measure prediction accuracy vs. AR(1) and GARCH baselines. If single-fragment S5 does not beat AR(1) by >5% RMSFE on held-out data, stop. The typed-Δ hypothesis is wrong.
2. GateL0RD + SPIB 5–6 Add gating layer and information bottleneck to single fragment. Verify gate-open rates match τ typing. Measure compression quality. If gate statistics don't correlate with market events, the sparse-update thesis is wrong.
3. Two Fragments 7–8 Add Risk fragment. Cross-fragment coupling. Sheaf consistency check. First test of whether multi-fragment outperforms single. If cross-fragment adds <2% improvement over independent fragments, the composition thesis is weak.
4. Continual Learning 9–12 EWC + BOCPD + Slow-Fast. Train on 2000–2007, test on 2008 (GFC), continue to 2010–2019, test on 2020 (COVID). Measure BWT and FWT. If BWT < −0.10 (severe forgetting despite CL), the CL stack needs fundamental rethinking.
5. Full System 13–16 Scale to 7 fragments. ε(t) estimator. Imagination engine. Full prequential evaluation on 2000–2026 data. If ε(t) proxy doesn't correlate with known reflexive episodes (Feb 2018, Mar 2020), the performativity bridge is unvalidated.

11. From Architecture to P&L

A world model that doesn't help make money is an academic exercise. Here is how each novel component connects to hedge fund economics:

ComponentP&L MechanismEstimated EdgePrerequisite
ε(t) Reflexive Instability Size positions inversely to ε. When ε is high, reduce exposure (reflexive markets are unpredictable). When ε is low, increase (standard models are reliable). 50–200bps drawdown reduction per reflexive episode Must demonstrate ε correlation with realized tail events
BOCPD Regime Detection Earlier regime detection = earlier reallocation. Each day of earlier detection in a regime transition is worth ~5–20bps in a macro portfolio. 1–3 day earlier detection vs. threshold methods Must beat standard CUSUM/threshold on historical regime changes
Fragment Coherence (Sheaf) When fragments disagree, reduce conviction. When they agree, increase size. Coherence-weighted sizing avoids whipsaw. Improved Sharpe from conviction-weighted sizing Must demonstrate coherence drops precede dislocations
Latent Imagination Generate 1,000 forward scenarios in latent space. Compute optimal allocation across scenario distribution. Non-Gaussian tails captured naturally. Better tail-risk estimation vs. Gaussian VaR Must demonstrate latent rollouts produce calibrated quantiles

13. What RecWM Is Not

  • Not a language model. It does not generate text. It is a structured latent model with mathematical pathways.
  • Not a trading bot. It produces signals and scenarios. Trading decisions remain with the human.
  • Not a competitor to Bloomberg. Bloomberg is a data terminal. RecWM would supplement a Bloomberg terminal, not replace it.
  • Not a foundation model. ~84M parameters, not 50B. The intelligence comes from architecture (typed multi-timescale + CL + reflexivity), not from scale.
  • Not built yet. Everything above is a design specification. The kill criteria in Section 10 define when we should stop if the thesis is wrong.
The one thing that matters. All of the above is worthless if the core hypothesis fails: that making ε(t) state-dependent and learnable produces a meaningfully better model than treating reflexivity as a constant or ignoring it entirely. Week 4 of the build plan tests this directly. If single-fragment S5 with typed-Δ doesn't outperform AR(1) on held-out data, everything downstream collapses. That's not a risk to manage — it's the fundamental bet.
Status: Theoretical Design — Not Implemented

The mathematics below specifies what RecWM would compute if built. No code exists. No experiments have been run. All building blocks are credited to their original authors. The "Five Fundamental Objects" are theoretical constructs from Reflexive Constructive Economics (RCE), not software modules.

Theoretical Foundations

Reflexive Constructive World Model (RecWM) — the mathematical substrate for modelling financial markets as continuously constructed realities under reflexive dynamics and hard constraints.

1The Core Equation

Every financial model implicitly answers the question: given the current state of the world, what happens next? Traditional approaches—DSGE, VAR, GARCH—treat the state as exogenous to the agents observing it. RecWM rejects this. The world is constructed by agent actions that are themselves driven by beliefs about that world. The master equation is:

W(t+1) = C( W(t), A(B(t)), Φ(t) )

where:

  • W(t) — the world state at time t, a structured collection of typed world fragments (prices, order books, institutional states, macro aggregates, narratives).
  • B(t) — the belief field, a joint distribution over all constructive units’ beliefs about W(t), each other, and themselves.
  • A(·) — the action map, transforming beliefs into concrete market actions (orders, speeches, regulation, portfolio rebalancing).
  • C(·) — the construction operator, the mechanism by which actions, filtered through hard constraints, produce the next world state.
  • Φ(t) — the constraint field, encoding regulatory limits, liquidity floors, accounting identities, and physical resource bounds that no agent can violate.
Why this is different. Classical models separate the “model” from the “system.” RecWM embeds the model’s own predictions inside the system: beliefs drive actions that construct the world that updates beliefs. The loop B → A → ΔW → ΔB is not a bug to be linearized away—it is the fundamental mechanism of financial markets.

The equation is deliberately constructive: we do not assert the existence of an equilibrium and study perturbations around it. Instead, we compute the next state from typed primitives, in finite time, with checkable constraints. This is closer to algebraic topology (pushout diagrams, colimits over typed data) than to equilibrium economics.

2Five Fundamental Objects

The core equation is instantiated through five formally defined objects. Together they span the ontology of RecWM.

Figure 6. Five fundamental objects of RecWM. Constructive Units, Constraint Fields, and World Fragments feed into C(·). Reflexive Loops and Composition Operators complete the ontology.

2.1 Constructive Units (CU)

Definition 2.1 (Constructive Unit)

A constructive unit is a 4-tuple CU_i = (s_i, b_i, A_i, κ_i) where:

  • s_i ∈ S — internal state (capital, positions, mandate parameters)
  • b_i : W → Δ(W) — belief map (current world → distribution over world states)
  • A_i : S × Δ(W) → Actions — action policy (state × beliefs → market actions)
  • κ_i ∈ {central_bank, fund, corporate, retail, government} — unit type, determining the action space, constraint set, and characteristic timescale

The type κ_i is not a label—it determines structural properties:

TypeAction SpaceTimescaleConstraint Set
central_bankRate decisions, QE/QT, forward guidanceWeeks–quartersMandate, credibility
fundPortfolio trades, leverage adjustmentMilliseconds–monthsRisk limits, margin, redemptions
corporateIssuance, buyback, capex, M&AQuarters–yearsCovenants, cash flow, rating
retailBuy/sell, deposit/withdrawDays–monthsCapital, attention, sentiment
governmentFiscal policy, regulation, sanctionsMonths–yearsLegislative process, political

2.2 World Fragments (WF)

Definition 2.2 (World Fragment)

A world fragment is a 4-tuple WF_j = (v_j, σ_j, τ_j, ρ_j) where:

  • v_j ∈ R^{d_j} — value vector of dimensionality d_j
  • σ_j — schema defining the fragment’s internal structure and valid operations
  • τ_j ∈ R+ — characteristic timescale (the natural rate of change)
  • ρ_j : WF × WF → R — coupling function measuring interaction strength with other fragments
Fragment TypeDimensionalityTimescale τExample
Tick1–51ms–1sIndividual trade, quote update
Microstructure10–501s–5minOrder book shape, spread dynamics
Price5–201min–1dayOHLCV bar, implied vol surface
Flow20–1001hr–1weekFund flows, positioning data
Macro50–2001week–1quarterGDP, CPI, employment, PMI
Institutional100–3001month–1yearRegulatory state, credit conditions
Narrative128–5121week–yearsDominant market story, regime label

2.3 Constraint Fields (Φ)

Definition 2.3 (Constraint Field)

The constraint field Φ(t) = (Φ_reg(t), Φ_liq(t), Φ_phy(t), Φ_acc(t)) is a 4-layer structure:

  • Φ_reg — Regulatory constraints: capital requirements (Basel III/IV), position limits, short-sale bans, circuit breakers. Formalized via IG 2.0 / ADICO grammar (Crawford & Ostrom 1995).
  • Φ_liq — Liquidity constraints: margin requirements, funding availability, collateral haircuts, market depth. These are endogenous—they tighten under stress.
  • Φ_phy — Physical constraints: settlement cycles (T+1/T+2), network latency, computational limits, storage capacity for commodities.
  • Φ_acc — Accounting constraints: double-entry identities, balance sheet mechanics (assets = liabilities + equity), flow-of-funds consistency. These are inviolable—they hold by definition.

Constraint fields interact with the construction operator C by projection: any proposed next state W'(t+1) is projected onto the feasible set F(Φ(t)) = {W : Φ_reg(W) ≤ 0 ∧ Φ_liq(W) ≤ 0 ∧ Φ_phy(W) ≤ 0 ∧ Φ_acc(W) = 0}. The projection is not optional—it is load-bearing. Violations of accounting identities are not “small errors”; they are incoherent states.

2.4 Reflexive Loops (RL)

Definition 2.4 (Reflexive Loop)

A reflexive loop is the cyclic dependency B → A → ΔW → ΔB where beliefs drive actions, actions change the world, and the changed world updates beliefs. The reflexivity coefficient ε measures the sensitivity:

ε = sup_(θ, θ') || D(θ) - D(θ') ||_W / || θ - θ' ||

where D(θ) is the data distribution induced when agents act on model parameters θ, and ||·||_W is the Wasserstein-1 distance. This is exactly the “ε-sensitivity” of Perdomo et al. (ICML 2020, Def. 3.1). When ε is large, the model strongly affects the data it learns from—the hallmark of financial markets where published forecasts, algorithmic strategies, and central bank guidance all reshape the very quantities they predict.

2.5 Composition Operators

Definition 2.5 (Fragment Composition)

The tensor product WF_a ⊗ WF_b → WF_{ab} composes two world fragments into a joint fragment, satisfying three axioms:

  1. Associativity: (WF_a ⊗ WF_b) ⊗ WF_c = WF_a ⊗ (WF_b ⊗ WF_c)
  2. Constraint preservation: Φ(WF_a ⊗ WF_b) ⊆ Φ(WF_a) ∩ Φ(WF_b) (composition cannot relax constraints)
  3. Scale consistency: τ_{ab} = min(τ_a, τ_b) (the composite updates at the faster timescale)

Composition operators enable hierarchical world construction. A “market microstructure” fragment composes tick-level and order-book fragments. A “credit conditions” fragment composes institutional-state and flow fragments. The composition is not concatenation—it creates genuine interaction terms through the coupling functions ρ.

3Belief Fields

Beliefs are not static parameters—they form a field over the space of constructive units, evolving through a combination of private updating and social contagion.

b_i(t+1) = (1 - α) · U(b_i(t), o_i(t)) + α · Σ_j w_{ij} · b_j(t)

where:

  • U(b, o) — private Bayesian update of belief b given observation o (or an approximate update via a learned recognition model)
  • α ∈ [0,1] — social influence weight (how much agent i is swayed by others’ beliefs)
  • w_{ij} — influence weight from agent j to agent i, typically sparse (most agents don’t directly observe each other)
  • o_i(t) — agent i’s observation at time t, which depends on W(t) and the agent’s observation function

Definition 3.1 (Belief Coherence)

The coherence measure χ(t) = 1 - (1/N(N-1)) Σ_{i≠j} D_KL(b_i(t) || b_j(t)) ranges from 0 (complete disagreement) to 1 (consensus). Low coherence signals fragile markets; high coherence signals herding risk.

The social influence term connects to Morris and Shin’s global games framework (AER 2002): when agents share a strong common signal, coherence spikes, and actions correlate—producing the coordination cascades observed in currency crises, bank runs, and liquidity spirals. The weight matrix w_{ij} can be learned from observed co-movement patterns using DCC-GARCH (Engle 2002) or network inference methods.

4Reflexive Fixed Points

A reflexive fixed point is a pair (B*, W*) satisfying:

B* = U(B*, W*)     and     W* = C(W*, A(B*), Φ)

This is the performative stable point (Perdomo et al. 2020, Def. 3.2): the model parameters at which retraining on the distribution they induce produces the same parameters. Existence requires the composed map F = U ˆ C ˆ A to be a contraction.

Stability Analysis

Linearize around the fixed point. Let δB = B - B* and δW = W - W*. The Jacobian of the coupled system is:

J = ∂(B(t+1), W(t+1)) / ∂(B(t), W(t)) =
[ (1-α) · ∂U/∂b + αW , (1-α) · ∂U/∂o · ∂o/∂W ]
[ ∂C/∂A · ∂A/∂B , ∂C/∂W ]

Stability requires ρ(J) < 1 where ρ denotes spectral radius. The off-diagonal blocks encode reflexivity: ∂C/∂A · ∂A/∂B is the “beliefs shape the world” channel; ∂U/∂o · ∂o/∂W is the “world shapes beliefs” channel. Their product controls stability.

Perdomo, Zrnic, Mendler-Dünner & Hardt (ICML 2020). “Performative Prediction.” Theorem 3.5: Repeated Risk Minimization converges to a performative stable point if ε < γ/β, where ε is sensitivity, γ is strong convexity, and β is smoothness of the loss. Proposition 3.6 proves the bound is tight.
Attribution warning. The convergence condition ε < γ/β is Theorem 3.5 of Perdomo et al. ICML 2020, not the survey by Hardt & Mendler-Dünner (Statistical Science 2025). The survey cites this result but does not originate it. A referee would catch this.

5World Models: Theoretical Lineage

RecWM inherits ideas from four lines of research in deep learning-based world models, while extending each in fundamental ways.

Ha & Schmidhuber (2018) — “World Models”

Introduced the V-M-C architecture: a Vision model (VAE) compresses observations, a Memory model (MDN-RNN) predicts future latent states, and a Controller selects actions. Key insight: you can train the controller entirely inside the learned dream. Limitation: untyped latent space, no constraint enforcement, no reflexivity. (NeurIPS 2018)

Dreamer / DreamerV2 / DreamerV3 (Hafner et al. 2020–2023)

Replaced the MDN-RNN with a Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM): a deterministic path plus a stochastic branch, enabling long-horizon imagination. DreamerV3 introduced symlog predictions, free bits for KL balancing, and showed a single architecture could master 150+ tasks without tuning. Limitation: single homogeneous latent state; no multi-timescale fragments. (ICLR 2020, NeurIPS 2021, arXiv 2023)

JEPA — LeCun (2022)

Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture: instead of predicting raw observations (pixel-level), predict in latent space. Avoids the generative model’s curse of modelling irrelevant detail. Limitation: no notion of actions or interventions; static architecture. (Position paper, Meta AI)

State Space Models: S4, S5, Mamba

Gu et al. (2022) S4 showed structured state spaces can model long-range dependencies with O(N log N) complexity. S5 (Smith et al. 2023) simplified to parallel scan over diagonal A, enabling O(N) training. Mamba (Gu & Dao 2024) added input-dependent selection. Limitation: untyped, single timescale, no constraint awareness. (ICLR 2022, ICLR 2023, arXiv 2024)

How RecWM extends these. (1) Typed fragments replace the homogeneous latent state, each with its own timescale and schema. (2) Constraint fields are first-class objects, not post-hoc projections. (3) Reflexivity is modelled explicitly: the loop B → A → ΔW → ΔB is the architecture, not a nuisance. (4) Continual learning is native: financial regimes change, so the model must update without catastrophic forgetting.

6State Space Models: S5 Typed-Delta Backbone

RecWM uses S5 (Smith et al. 2023) as the backbone dynamics model, but with a critical extension: typed discretization step sizes matched to fragment timescales.

Continuous Form

dh/dt = A · h(t) + B · u(t)
y(t) = Re(C · h(t)) + D · u(t)

where h(t) ∈ C^N is the hidden state, u(t) is the input, y(t) is the output, and A is diagonal (the key S5 simplification from S4’s DPLR parameterization).

ZOH Discretization with Typed Step Sizes

The standard zero-order hold (ZOH) discretization uses a uniform step size Δ. RecWM replaces this with fragment-typed step sizes:

A_k = exp(A · Δ_k),    B_k = A^{-1}(A_k - I) · B

where Δ_k = τ_k / τ_max is the normalized timescale for fragment type k. This means tick-level fragments update with fine temporal resolution while narrative fragments use coarse steps—matching the natural dynamics of each.

Fragment Typeτ (seconds)Δ_k (normalized)Effective Horizon
Tick0.001–1~10^{-8}Next milliseconds
Microstructure1–300~10^{-5}Next minutes
Price60–86400~10^{-3}Next hours–day
Flow3600–604800~10^{-2}Next days–week
Macro604800–7.9×10^6~10^{-1}Next weeks–quarter
Institutional2.6×10^6–3.15×10^7~0.5Next months–year
Narrative604800–3.15×10^71.0Next weeks–years
Why diagonal A enables O(N) RTRL. With diagonal A, the Jacobian ∂h(t)/∂h(t-1) = diag(A_k) is diagonal, so real-time recurrent learning (RTRL) requires only O(N) per step instead of O(N^3). This is critical for continual learning (Section 11): the model can update online without ever unrolling through time.

7GateL0RD Fragment Updates

Not every fragment should update at every timestep. The GateL0RD mechanism (Gumbsch, Butz & Martius, NeurIPS 2021) provides a principled way to learn when to update each fragment, using hard-concrete gates with L0 regularization.

Hard-Concrete Sampling

The gate variable g(t) ∈ {0, 1} is sampled from a stretched hard-concrete distribution:

u ~ Uniform(0, 1)
s = sigmoid((log(u/(1-u)) + log(α)) / β)
s_bar = s · (ζ - γ) + γ
g = min(1, max(0, s_bar))

where α is a learned location parameter (per fragment), β is a temperature, and γ < 0, ζ > 1 are the stretch parameters ensuring exact zeros and ones.

State Update Rule

z(t) = g(t) · z̃(t) + (1 - g(t)) · z(t-1)

When g(t) = 0, the fragment is perfectly preserved (not approximately—exactly copied). When g(t) = 1, the fragment updates to the new candidate z̃(t). The L0 penalty encourages sparsity:

L_gate = Σ_k λ_k · P(g_k ≠ 0)

where λ_k ∝ τ_k / τ_max: slow fragments (narrative, institutional) are penalized more heavily for updating, naturally encoding the prior that slow things should change rarely.

Gumbsch, Butz & Martius (NeurIPS 2021). “Sparsely Changing Latent States for Prediction and Planning in Partially Observable Domains.” Introduced GateL0RD: L0-gated RNNs that naturally segment temporal sequences into events, with the gate providing interpretable “event boundaries.”

The connection to continual learning is immediate: when a gate is closed, the effective learning rate for that fragment is zero, providing natural protection against catastrophic forgetting without any explicit memory mechanism.

8Information-Theoretic Foundations

Stochastic Predictive Information Bottleneck (SPIB)

The representation for each fragment is trained via the SPIB objective (Wang et al. 2021):

max I(z; state_{t+Δ}) - β · I(z; X_t)

This is a stochastic extension of the Information Bottleneck (Tishby et al. 1999): compress the input X_t into a latent z that is maximally predictive of the future state at horizon Δ, while discarding information about the present that is not predictive. The trade-off parameter β controls compression.

Rate-Distortion Theory

SPIB is a special case of rate-distortion theory (Shannon 1948, Berger 1971). The rate-distortion function R(D) = min_{p(z|x): E[d(x,z)] ≤ D} I(X; Z) gives the minimum number of bits needed to represent the source at distortion level D. In RecWM, “distortion” is prediction error at the fragment’s characteristic horizon.

Why Δ_k = τ_k

A critical design choice: the prediction horizon for each fragment equals its characteristic timescale. This ensures that:

  • Tick fragments predict the next milliseconds (where they have signal)
  • Macro fragments predict the next quarter (where they have signal)
  • No fragment is asked to predict faster or slower than its natural dynamics

VampPrior for the Marginal

The marginal p(z) = (1/K) Σ_k q(z | x_k) is approximated via the Variational Mixture of Posteriors (VampPrior, Tomczak & Welling, AISTATS 2018). This avoids the over-regularization that a standard Gaussian prior causes in VAEs, and naturally clusters the latent space by regime.

9Identifiability and Causal Structure

A world model is only useful if its latent variables correspond to real quantities. RecWM achieves identifiability through four complementary mechanisms.

9.1 Independent Decoders with Sparse Jacobians

Each fragment type k has its own decoder g_k : z_k → x_k. The Jacobian ∂g_k / ∂z is constrained to be sparse: fragment k’s reconstruction depends only on its own latents and a small set of coupling terms. This is the multi-decoder approach of Locatello et al. (ICML 2020), extended with typing.

9.2 SlowVAE Laplace Prior

The SlowVAE (Klindt et al., ICML 2021) imposes a Laplace prior on temporal differences: p(z_t | z_{t-1}) ∝ exp(-|z_t - z_{t-1}| / λ). This biases latent variables toward slow features (Wiskott & Sejnowski 2002), which are identifiable up to component-wise transformations under mild conditions.

Klindt, Schott, Sharma, Ustyuzhaninov, Brendel, Bethge & Paiton (ICML 2021). “Towards Nonlinear Disentanglement in Natural Data with Temporal Sparse Coding.” Proved that slow features in nonlinear ICA are identifiable with Laplace transition priors.

9.3 Structural Sparsity

The causal structure among latent fragments is recovered via structural sparsity constraints. Zheng, Ng & Zhang (NeurIPS 2022) showed that with sparse mixing functions and sufficient diversity in the data, latent causal variables are identifiable from observational data alone. RecWM applies this at the fragment level: the coupling functions ρ_j are regularized toward sparsity.

9.4 Mechanism Sparsity and Causal Emergence

Lachapelle et al. (CLeaR 2022) formalized mechanism sparsity: each causal mechanism depends on few parents. Combined with the independent mechanism principle (Schölkopf et al. 2012), this gives identification of the causal graph from distribution shifts—exactly what regime changes provide in financial data.

Causal emergence is detected via SVD of the fragment interaction matrix: when a set of micro-level fragments can be compressed into a macro-fragment with higher effective information (Liu, Yuan & Zhang, Entropy 2024), the macro-fragment is “more causal” than its components. This provides a principled criterion for fragment hierarchy.

Liu, Yuan & Zhang (Entropy 26(8):618, 2024). “Exact Causal Emergence for Linear Stochastic Iteration Systems.” Closed-form optimal coarse-graining from principal eigenvectors of the transition matrix. Complexity O(n^3) in the number of variables. A “linear stochastic iteration system” is a VAR model.

10The Unified Loss Function

RecWM is trained end-to-end with a composite loss that balances reconstruction, prediction, sparsity, gating, martingale consistency, and cross-fragment coupling:

L = L_recon + Σ_k L_SPIB^{(k)} + α · L_sparsity + Σ_k L_gate^{(k)} + μ · L_MZ + ν · L_coupling

Each term:

TermDefinitionRole
L_recon Σ_k || x_k - g_k(z_k) ||^2 Reconstruction accuracy per fragment type
L_SPIB^{(k)} -I(z_k; state_{t+τ_k}) + β_k · I(z_k; X_t) Predictive compression at fragment timescale
L_sparsity Σ_{j≠k} |∂g_k / ∂z_j| Cross-fragment Jacobian sparsity (identifiability)
L_gate^{(k)} λ_k · P(g_k ≠ 0) GateL0RD L0 penalty, stronger for slow fragments
L_MZ E[(r_t - r_f) · z_t]^2 Martingale / no-arbitrage consistency
L_coupling Σ_{j,k} |ρ_{jk} - ρ̂_{jk}(z)|^2 Cross-fragment coupling accuracy
The martingale term L_MZ is unique to RecWM. It enforces the no-arbitrage principle directly in the loss: under the risk-neutral measure, discounted price processes must be martingales. This is not a soft preference—violations indicate the model has learned a spurious arbitrage that cannot exist in liquid markets.

11Continual Learning Theory

Financial markets are non-stationary by nature. Regimes change, regulations evolve, new instruments appear. RecWM addresses this through a five-layer continual learning stack, each layer providing progressively stronger protection against catastrophic forgetting.

Figure 7. Five-layer continual learning stack. Each layer adds progressively stronger forgetting protection at increasing computational cost. All layers are active simultaneously.

CL-0: GateL0RD Natural Continual Learning

The simplest and cheapest layer. When a gate g_k(t) = 0, the state z_k(t) = z_k(t-1) exactly. Gradients with respect to the parameters of fragment k are multiplied by the gate opening probability p, giving an effective learning rate η_eff = p · η. For slow fragments (narrative, institutional), p is typically 0.01–0.05, providing ~20–100x natural forgetting protection.

CL-1: O(N) RTRL Streaming

Because the S5 backbone has diagonal A, the sensitivity matrix dh(t)/dθ can be maintained in O(N) per timestep via Real-Time Recurrent Learning (Williams & Zipser 1989). This enables true streaming: the model processes each timestep once, updates parameters, and discards the observation. No truncated BPTT, no replay buffer, no epoch.

CL-2: Per-Fragment EWC

Elastic Weight Consolidation (Kirkpatrick et al., PNAS 2017) penalizes movement away from previously important parameters. RecWM applies EWC per fragment, using the online Fisher approximation of Schwarz et al. (2018). The regularization strength λ_k scales with the fragment timescale: slow fragments resist change more.

CL-3: BOCPD + DER++

Bayesian Online Change Point Detection (Adams & MacKay, arXiv 2007) monitors the fragment prediction errors for structural breaks. When a change point is detected with posterior probability > 0.8, the system triggers Dark Experience Replay++ (Buzzega et al. 2020): stored logits from the previous regime are replayed alongside new data, enabling graceful transition without destroying old knowledge.

CL-4: Slow-Fast Weights

A Polyak-averaged “slow” copy of the parameters tracks the long-term structure. The averaging rate adapts: during stable regimes, η_slow → 0 (the slow copy barely moves); at regime transitions, η_slow → 0.01 (the slow copy absorbs the new regime quickly). Inference uses the slow weights for stability, with fast weights contributing residual corrections.

12Financial Mathematics

RecWM is grounded in five pillars of modern financial mathematics, each contributing specific structural constraints or modelling techniques.

12.1 Rough Volatility

Gatheral, Jaisson & Rosenbaum (Quantitative Finance 2018) showed that log-volatility behaves as fractional Brownian motion with Hurst exponent H ≈ 0.1, far rougher than the H = 0.5 of standard Brownian motion. This implies:

log σ(t) ~ fBM_H,    H ≈ 0.1

RecWM’s state-space backbone naturally captures rough dynamics because the diagonal A matrix can represent arbitrary spectral densities, including the power-law spectrum S(f) ∝ f^{-(2H+1)} characteristic of rough processes. The fragment type “microstructure” is specifically designed for this timescale.

Gatheral, Jaisson & Rosenbaum (Quantitative Finance 18(6):933–949, 2018). “Volatility is Rough.” Demonstrated that H ≈ 0.1 across virtually all equity option markets, rendering classical stochastic volatility models (Heston H=0.5) misspecified.

12.2 Regime-Switching Models

Hamilton (Econometrica 1989) introduced Markov-switching models where the economy transitions between discrete regimes (expansion/recession) with state-dependent dynamics. RecWM generalizes this in two ways: (1) regimes are continuous (the narrative fragment, not a discrete label); (2) regime transitions are endogenous (driven by belief field dynamics, not an exogenous Markov chain).

12.3 BOCPD

Adams & MacKay (arXiv 0710.3742, 2007) provided a Bayesian framework for online change point detection with O(E[r]) amortised per-timestep updates, where r is the run length (with pruning to cap worst-case cost; without pruning the naive algorithm is O(t) per step). RecWM uses BOCPD at CL-3 to detect regime transitions in fragment prediction errors, triggering replay and adaptation.

12.4 Online Convex Optimization

Hazan (Foundations and Trends in Optimization 2016) provides the regret framework for online learning. RecWM’s streaming updates achieve sublinear regret R_T = O(sqrt(T)) under the assumption that the loss sequence has bounded variation. The constraint field Φ ensures the decision set is convex at each step.

12.5 Adaptive Kalman Filtering

The S5 backbone can be interpreted as a nonlinear Kalman filter with learned dynamics. The fragment-typed step sizes correspond to different process noise covariances per fragment, and the GateL0RD gates implement an adaptive measurement selection (only incorporating observations when the gate opens).

12.6 Cross-Asset Contagion

RecWM models contagion through the coupling functions ρ_{jk}. Three classical frameworks inform this:

  • DCC-GARCH (Engle 2002): dynamic conditional correlations as time-varying coupling strengths
  • Copulas (Joe 1997, Nelsen 2006): tail dependence beyond linear correlation, especially Clayton/Gumbel for asymmetric crash dependence
  • Network models (Acemoglu et al. 2015): contagion through interconnected balance sheets, where the adjacency matrix is learned from the fragment coupling structure

13Reflexivity and Performativity

Reflexivity is the central intellectual contribution of RecWM. We synthesize three traditions.

13.1 Soros Reflexivity Theory

George Soros (1987, 2013) argued that financial markets are fundamentally reflexive: participants’ biased views influence events, and events influence views, creating a two-way feedback. This was a philosophical claim, not a formal theory. RecWM provides the formalization.

13.2 MacKenzie: An Engine, Not a Camera

Donald MacKenzie (2006) documented how the Black-Scholes model did not merely describe options markets—it created them. Option prices converged toward Black-Scholes predictions as traders adopted the formula, a phenomenon MacKenzie called “Barnesian performativity.” RecWM generalizes this: every model deployed in a market is potentially performative; the reflexivity coefficient ε quantifies how strongly.

MacKenzie (2006). An Engine, Not a Camera: How Financial Models Shape Markets. MIT Press. The foundational sociological account of financial model performativity, documenting how Black-Scholes changed the very markets it claimed to describe.

13.3 Performative Prediction

Perdomo et al. (ICML 2020) formalized performativity in machine learning: when predictions influence the data-generating process, standard ERM assumptions break. Their framework defines:

  • ε-sensitivity (Def. 3.1): the distribution shift per unit parameter change
  • Performative stability (Def. 3.2): the fixed point where retraining reproduces the same model
  • Performative optimality (Def. 3.3): the parameters minimizing true performative risk

13.4 The ε < γ/β Condition

ε < γ / β

This is Theorem 3.5 of Perdomo et al. (ICML 2020): Repeated Risk Minimization converges to a performative stable point if the sensitivity ε is less than the ratio of strong convexity γ to smoothness β. Proposition 3.6 shows the bound is tight. Three distinct thresholds emerge:

ConditionGuaranteeSource
ε < γ/β RRM converges to performative stable point Perdomo et al. 2020, Thm 3.5
ε < γ/[(β+γ)(1+1.5ηβ)] Repeated Gradient Descent converges Perdomo et al. 2020, Thm 3.8
ε ≤ γ/(2β) Performative risk is convex (optimum findable) Miller, Perdomo & Zrnic, ICML 2021, Thm 3.1
The unnamed gap. The region γ/(2β) < ε < γ/β is stable but not optimizable: the system converges to a fixed point, but that fixed point may not minimize performative risk. This gap is unnamed in the literature. We conjecture that real financial markets live in this gap: stable enough to trade, but not optimizable enough for convergence to a social optimum.

13.5 How EWC Reduces Effective Reflexivity

EWC (CL-2) has an unexpected benefit for reflexivity. By penalizing large parameter changes, EWC reduces ||θ_{t+1} - θ_t||, which in turn reduces the distribution shift ||D(θ_{t+1}) - D(θ_t)||_W. The effective reflexivity becomes:

ε_eff = ε / (1 + λ_EWC · F_max)

where F_max is the largest Fisher diagonal entry. Strong EWC regularization can push ε_eff below γ/β even when bare ε exceeds it, stabilizing a system that would otherwise oscillate.

14Active Inference and Free Energy

14.1 Friston’s Free Energy Principle

The Free Energy Principle (Friston 2010) states that any system that persists in a changing environment must minimize a free energy functional:

F = E_q [log q(θ) - log p(o, θ)] = D_KL(q(θ) || p(θ | o)) + const

where q(θ) is the agent’s approximate posterior over world parameters, and p(o, θ) is the generative model. Minimizing F is equivalent to maximizing model evidence log p(o) while keeping the posterior close to the prior.

14.2 Active Inference for Decision-Making

Active inference (Friston et al. 2017) extends this to action selection: agents select actions that minimize expected free energy (EFE):

G(π) = E_{p(o,s|π)} [log q(s|π) - log p(o, s)] = -I(o; s | π) + D_KL(p(o|π) || p̃(o))

The first term drives epistemic behavior (explore to reduce uncertainty); the second drives pragmatic behavior (act to achieve preferred outcomes p̃(o)). In financial markets, this naturally decomposes into information-gathering (research, monitoring) and position-taking (trading).

14.3 Connection to Portfolio Optimization

The niche construction formulation (Constant & Friston): the environment (“niche”) infers the agent back, via dη/dt = -∇F(η | a). In financial markets, this is literal: a large fund’s trades move prices, changing the environment, which changes the optimal portfolio, which changes the trades. The dual flow dμ/dt = -∇F(μ | s) and dη/dt = -∇F(η | a) is the active inference formulation of reflexivity.

Planning as inference. Under active inference, planning reduces to inference over policies (sequences of actions). Combined with the S5 backbone for fast imagined rollouts, this provides a principled framework for multi-step portfolio planning that naturally trades off exploration and exploitation.

15Convergence Guarantees

RecWM’s convergence theory rests on showing that the master equation defines a contraction mapping.

Theorem 15.1 (Contraction)

Define F(W) = C(W, A(B(W)), Φ). If:

  1. C is L_C-Lipschitz in its first argument
  2. The composed map A ˆ B is ε-sensitive (Perdomo Def. 3.1)
  3. L_C · (1 + ε) < 1

then F is a contraction mapping with rate r = L_C · (1 + ε) < 1, and by the Banach fixed-point theorem, iteration W_{n+1} = F(W_n) converges to a unique fixed point W*.

Exponential Convergence Rate

|| W_n - W* || ≤ r^n · || W_0 - W* ||,     r = L_C(1 + ε)

The convergence is exponential with rate -log(r) = -log(L_C(1+ε)). Faster convergence requires either reducing L_C (tighter constraint fields, smoother construction) or reducing ε (less reflexive markets, stronger EWC regularization).

Role of Constraint Field Tightness

Constraint fields reduce L_C by projecting the construction operator onto a smaller feasible set. Tighter constraints (higher capital requirements, position limits, circuit breakers) directly shrink the Lipschitz constant of C, making convergence easier. This formalizes the intuition that regulation stabilizes markets—not by eliminating reflexivity, but by reducing the amplification of the reflexive loop.

Conversely, relaxing constraints (deregulation, shadow banking, regulatory arbitrage) increases L_C. If L_C(1+ε) exceeds 1, the system loses its contraction property and can enter unstable oscillations—a formal description of financial crises as loss of contractivity.

The crisis condition: L_C(1+ε) ≥ 1. This is our formal criterion for systemic instability. RecWM monitors both L_C (estimated from the Jacobian of the construction operator) and ε (estimated from the sensitivity of predictions to parameter perturbation) in real time. A rising product signals approaching instability before it manifests in prices.

1 Executive Summary

RecWM has a strong theoretical core—the typed fragment architecture (S5 backbone + GateL0RD + SPIB), the constraint field formalism, and the five-layer continual learning stack are genuine differentiators. But comparing against a well-specified competitor and an exhaustive ideal-spec reveals significant gaps across 9 tiers that must be addressed before the product can compete in institutional markets.

The hard truth: RecWM currently exists as a theoretical architecture with zero production code. The competitor already has working implementations of HAR-RV volatility forecasting (11× better than GARCH), conformal prediction intervals, NOTEARS causal DAGs, differentiable portfolio optimization, sheaf neural networks for cross-asset contagion, and persistent homology for topological early warning. The ideal spec adds 14 full tiers of capability including fixed income, derivatives, compliance, execution analytics, and operational infrastructure. RecWM needs to close these gaps or it ships as an academic paper, not a product.
What RecWM has that others don’t:
• Constraint fields Φ — No competitor formalizes regulatory/liquidity/physical/accounting constraints as first-class mathematical objects that filter the action space. This is genuinely novel.
• Typed world fragments with characteristic timescales — The τk-driven discretization (different Δ for Liquidity vs Structure) is architecturally elegant and well-motivated.
• Reflexive loop formalism — The ε coefficient tracking Perdomo Thm 3.5 convergence is theoretically rigorous. No competitor has this level of performativity awareness.
• EWC reducing effective reflexivity — The result εeff ≤ ε/(1+Ω·λmin(F)) connecting continual learning to market stability is original theory.

Below: a tier-by-tier gap analysis with research-backed assessments of what to build, what papers to cite, what libraries to use, and what order to build in.
