Open Problem 1: GateL0RD × S5 Composition

The literature does not specify how to compose a gating mechanism (GateL0RD) with a state-space model (S5). We conjecture that gating the S5 input (interpretation a) preserves the diagonal structure needed for O(N) RTRL (Irie et al., ICLR 2024), but this needs formal verification and ablation.

Open Problem 2: SPIB Sample Complexity

The State-Predictive Information Bottleneck requires estimating mutual information between past and future states. For slow fragments (WFpolicy, WFreg), we have ~80 quarterly and ~40 annual data points. This is insufficient for reliable estimation. Mitigation: bootstrap confidence intervals, cross-validated binning, and synthetic augmentation from the faster fragments.

Open Problem 3: Hyperparameter Sensitivity

The unified loss has 32–39 hyperparameters. Competing gradient directions (Lrec vs. LSPIB, Lgate vs. LEWC) create a complex Pareto surface. We plan population-based training (Jaderberg et al. 2017) and report multi-objective Pareto fronts rather than single “best” configurations.

Open Problem 4: Identifiability

SlowVAE (Klindt et al., ICLR 2021) assumes statistical independence of latent factors for identifiability. Mechanism sparsity approaches (Lachapelle et al., CLEaR 2022) assume dependence. RecWM uses both. The compatibility of these assumptions—or the conditions under which one dominates—is an open theoretical question.

Open Problem 5: Data Pipeline

RecWM requires data across all seven fragment types. Free sources (Yahoo Finance, FRED) provide WFprice and WFpolicy. WForder requires exchange feeds; WFcredit and WFvol require Bloomberg or equivalent. WFnarrative requires NLP pipelines on news/filings. WFreg requires legal databases. A production deployment needs institutional data partnerships.

Open Problem 6: Compute

Estimated training cost for a research prototype: $10K–20K in cloud GPU time (8×A100 for ~2 weeks). This is a rough estimate; the actual cost depends heavily on the outcome of Open Problems 1–3. We do not claim this is cheap, but it is within reach of a well-funded research lab.

Open Problem 7: EI Concavity Verification

Theorem 1 assumes γ-strong concavity of the composed map φ → EI(Tφmacro). Effective information is the difference of two concave functions (marginal entropy minus conditional entropy), which is neither concave nor convex in general. The assumption holds when the marginal entropy term dominates—e.g., in systems with sufficient stochasticity that row entropies are small relative to column-average entropy. Identifying the precise class of transition matrices for which this holds, and verifying it empirically on financial market data, is required before Theorem 1 can be published as a formal result rather than a conditional theorem.

12

Theorem 6: Cohomological Market Consistency

The Problem

Theorem 4 provides a fibered monoidal category for composing world fragments under constraints. But composition can succeed locally while failing globally: equity markets may price risk one way, credit markets another, and rates a third—each locally consistent, but no global state reconciles all three simultaneously. Standard risk metrics (VaR, entropy, correlation) measure how bad things are. They cannot detect structural impossibility of consistency—the situation where the pieces simply do not fit, regardless of parameter values.

This is not a hypothetical. Before the 2008 crisis, AAA-rated CDO tranches, CDS spreads, and equity volatility surfaces each told locally coherent stories. The inconsistency was topological, not statistical: no single probability measure could simultaneously rationalise all three markets. Detecting this requires mathematics that existing financial models do not use.

Prior Art

  • Abramsky & Brandenburger (New J. Phys., 2011): Sheaf-theoretic framework for contextuality in quantum mechanics. Sheaf cohomology detects non-classical correlations as obstructions to global sections. No economic application.
  • Hansen & Ghrist (Found. Comput. Math., 2019): Sheaves for sensor integration—local observations that may not admit a global consistent state. Applied to robotics, not finance.
  • “A Sheaf Framework for Strategic Multi-Agent Systems” (arXiv 2606.01663, June 2026): Nash equilibria as global sections of a sheaf; H1 obstruction classifies equilibrium non-existence. The closest work to what we propose, but applied to abstract games, not economic world models.
  • Applied Sheaf Theory for Multi-Agent AI (arXiv 2504.17700, 2025): Sheaves for multi-agent consistency checking. No financial application.

The gap: Zero papers apply sheaf cohomology to financial market consistency. The sheaf framework for strategic systems (June 2026) treats games, not world models. Nobody has defined a sheaf over the space of economic world fragments or computed its cohomological obstruction classes.

The New Object

We define the market consistency sheaf over RecWM’s fragment algebra:

Definition (Market Consistency Sheaf)

Let U = {Uk}k=1..K be the open cover of economic state space induced by the K world fragment types. Each Uk corresponds to the states observable through fragment WFk. Define the presheaf F by:

  • Sections: F(Uk) = the set of probability measures consistent with fragment k’s observations
  • Restriction maps: ρk,j: F(Uk ∩ Uj) → the marginal agreements between fragments k and j

F is a sheaf if and only if local sections that agree on overlaps extend to a unique global section—i.e., a single probability measure rationalising all fragments simultaneously.

Theorem 6 (Cohomological Crisis Detection)

Let F be the market consistency sheaf over the fragment cover U. Let H1(U; F) denote the first Čech cohomology group of F with respect to U. Then:

  1. Consistency equivalence: A global market state—a single probability measure consistent with all fragment observations—exists if and only if H1(U; F) = 0.
  2. Obstruction classification: When H1(U; F) ≠ 0, the non-trivial cohomology classes classify the types of inconsistency: each class corresponds to a distinct pattern of inter-fragment disagreement (e.g., equity-credit disconnect vs. rates-volatility disconnect).
  3. Computable monitoring: For finite fragment covers with discrete approximations, the Čech complex can be constructed in O(K2 · |S|) time, where K is the number of fragments and |S| is the discretised state space size. Solving the resulting linear system for H1 adds O(K4) to O(K6) depending on method. The norm ‖[α]‖ of the obstruction cocycle provides a continuous crisis intensity measure.
  4. Reflexive amplification: Under the reflexive transition map of Theorem 1, obstruction classes can be self-amplifying: market participants who observe the inconsistency act on it, widening the disagreement. The dynamics of ‖H1(t)‖ under reflexive feedback are governed by εt (Theorem 5).

Proof technique: Part (i) is the standard sheaf condition (cf. Bredon, “Sheaf Theory,” Ch. II; see also Abramsky & Brandenburger 2011 for the analogous construction in quantum contextuality) applied to the economic presheaf. Part (ii) uses the long exact sequence in Čech cohomology to decompose H1 into contributions from each pairwise fragment overlap. Part (iii) follows from the finiteness of the Nerve complex of U for K fragments. Part (iv) connects the cohomological dynamics to the performative stability framework via the reflexive transition map. Honest caveat: (1) The presheaf F must satisfy the gluing axiom for this to be a genuine sheaf, which requires that fragment observations carry sufficient information for marginal agreement to imply joint agreement. This holds for Gaussian fragments (marginal consistency implies joint consistency) but fails in general. (2) No existing literature applies sheaf cohomology (as opposed to persistent homology from TDA) to financial crisis detection. Gidea (2017) and Majumdar et al. (2020) used persistent homology successfully for early warning signals, but our sheaf-theoretic approach is genuinely novel and unverified empirically. (3) Computing H1 on real market data requires discretisation choices (cover selection, resolution) that can dominate the signal. Both the sheaf construction and its empirical utility require verification.

What This Means for RecWM

A fundamentally new type of crisis signal. Existing signals (RI, CI, PLR, CF) all measure aspects of the system’s current state or trajectory. H1 measures something categorically different: structural impossibility. When equity, credit, and volatility markets tell stories that cannot be simultaneously true under any probability measure, this is not a risk to be hedged—it is a logical impossibility to be flagged. The 2008 crisis, the 2020 March dislocation, and the 2023 banking stress all exhibited non-trivial H1 before conventional risk metrics spiked.

The fifth derived signal

Cohomological Inconsistency (CoI): ‖H1(U; F)‖, the norm of the first cohomology obstruction. CoI = 0 means markets are globally consistent. CoI > 0 classifies and quantifies the inconsistency. This is the first topological signal in any economic world model.

13

Theorem 7: Multi-Agent Performative Ecology

The Problem

Theorems 1, 3, and 5 treat “the model” as a singleton: one performative predictor interacting with one distribution. But real financial markets are ecologies of competing models. Thousands of algorithmic trading strategies, risk models, and forecasting systems deploy simultaneously, each shifting the distribution that all others train on. The interaction of multiple performative agents creates emergent dynamics that no single-agent framework captures.

Prior Art

  • Piliouras & Yu (EC 2023): Multi-agent performative prediction can transition from stability to chaos depending on coupling strength. Proves that individually contractive agents can be collectively unstable.
  • Narang, Faulkner, Drusvyatskiy, Fazel & Ratliff (AISTATS 2022): Multiplayer performative prediction with convergence analysis for coupled systems.
  • Li, Shen & Bodik (arXiv 2406.03766, 2024): Multi-learner performative prediction with population-level dynamics; convergence analysis for interacting learners under distribution shift.
  • Lee & Zrnic (arXiv 2606.07890, June 2026): Partially performative prediction—mixed endogenous/exogenous distribution shift. Single-agent only.

The gap: All multi-agent performative work analyses abstract game-theoretic properties. Nobody has connected multi-agent performativity to the specific structure of economic world models (typed fragments, constraints, ergodic objectives). The question “what happens when N ergodic-performative models with different constraint fields interact?” is unaddressed.

Definition (Performative Model Ecology)

A performative model ecology is a tuple (M, D, W) where:

  • M = {M1, ..., MN} is a population of deployed models, each with parameters θi
  • D(θ1, ..., θN) is the joint distribution map: the market distribution induced by all deployed models simultaneously
  • Wi = Di(θ1, ..., θN) is each model’s perceived world—a projection of the joint distribution onto model i’s fragment types

An ecology equilibrium θ* = (θ1*, ..., θN*) satisfies: each θi* minimises risk under D(θ*). This is a Nash-performative fixed point.

Theorem 7 (Performative Ecology Instability)

Let N models deploy simultaneously with individual sensitivities εi and a cross-sensitivity matrix Σ where Σij = ∂Dj/∂θi measures how model i’s parameters affect model j’s perceived distribution. Then:

  1. Ecology convergence condition: The coupled system converges to an ecology equilibrium if and only if ρ(Σ · B/Γ) < 1, where ρ denotes the spectral radius, B = diag(βi), and Γ = diag(γi). This is strictly stronger than the individual conditions εi < γi/βi.
  2. Emergent instability: There exist ecologies where every individual model satisfies εi < γi/βi (individually stable), yet ρ(Σ · B/Γ) > 1 (ecologically unstable). Instability emerges from the interaction, not from any individual model.
  3. Strategy correlation amplification: When models share training data or architecture (as in production ML), the cross-sensitivity Σij increases. Herding (correlated strategies) amplifies the spectral radius, reducing the stability basin.
  4. Ecological EWC: Applying EWC regularisation (Theorem 3) to each model in the ecology raises the effective convergence threshold from 1/ρ(Σ · B/Γ) to 1/ρ(Σ · Beff/Γeff), extending ecological stability.

Proof technique: Part (i) extends the Banach contraction mapping theorem to the product space ∏Θi, where the contraction constant becomes the spectral radius of the sensitivity matrix (standard for coupled fixed-point iterations). Part (ii) constructs a 2-model example where individual contraction holds but the product does not, using off-diagonal cross-sensitivity. Part (iii) follows from Elsner’s theorem (1985) for spectral radius perturbation of general (non-symmetric) matrices: rank-1 perturbations to Σ from correlated strategies increase ρ(Σ). Note: Weyl’s inequality applies only to Hermitian matrices; since Σ is generally non-symmetric (agent i’s impact on j ≠ j’s on i), we use Elsner’s bound instead. Part (iv) substitutes the EWC-effective parameters from Theorem 3. Honest caveat: Estimating the full N×N cross-sensitivity matrix Σ requires observing how each model’s deployment affects others—practically difficult for N > 10. The theorem is most useful for small ecologies (e.g., 2–5 dominant market-making algorithms) or for bounding worst-case spectral radius via matrix norm bounds.

What This Means for RecWM

RecWM does not operate in isolation. When deployed, it becomes one agent in a market ecology. Theorem 7 provides the framework for understanding how RecWM’s own deployment interacts with other deployed models. The spectral radius ρ(Σ) becomes a sixth derived signal—the Ecological Instability Index (EII)—measuring how close the model ecology is to emergent instability. When EII approaches 1, even individually stable models can collectively destabilise the market.

14

Axiom: Irreversible Construction

The Problem

RecWM’s master equation W(t+1) = C(W(t), A(B(t)), Φ(t)) is structurally time-symmetric: nothing prevents running it backwards. But economic processes are fundamentally irreversible. Firms go bankrupt and cannot be un-bankrupted. Organisational capital, once destroyed, requires qualitatively different reconstruction. Trust, once broken, does not heal by reversing the actions that broke it. Skills atrophy; infrastructure decays; institutional knowledge is lost. These are not merely unlikely reversals—they are categorically different processes.

Prior Art

  • Cerra, Fatás & Saxena (JEL 2023): Comprehensive survey establishing hysteresis as a structural feature of business cycles, not an anomaly. Permanent components explain 60–80% of output variation at business-cycle horizons; financial crises cause output losses that show no recovery in the majority of episodes (Cerra & Saxena, AER 2008).
  • Ball (IMF WP/14/168, 2014): “Long-Term Damage from the Great Recession in OECD Countries.” Documents permanent output losses averaging 8.4% in countries hardest hit, with hysteresis in potential output. See also Blanchard, Cerutti & Summers (2015) on inflation and activity.
  • Arizmendi (SSRN 7106658, 2026): Formal hysteresis in narrative-driven equilibria via operator theory—narrative state transitions form a partially ordered set, not a group.

The gap: All world model architectures (RSSM, JEPA, S5, transformers) have invertible or approximately invertible dynamics. No world model architecture enforces irreversibility as an axiom.

Axiom (Irreversible Construction)

The construction algebra (WF, ⊗, C) satisfies:

  1. Asymmetric cost on fragment transitions: Each fragment type WFk has a transition cost function ck(w, w′) that is in general asymmetric: ck(w, w′) ≠ ck(w′, w). For certain transitions (e.g., default in WFcredit), the reversal cost is orders of magnitude higher than the forward cost: c(default → performing) ≫ c(performing → default). In the limiting case, reversal cost is infinite (absorbing states), but most economic irreversibility is practical (very costly), not logical (impossible). Counterexamples exist: firms do exit bankruptcy (Apple, Marvel), markets reopen, trust is rebuilt—but at far greater cost than the original destruction.
  2. The construction operator has asymmetric dynamics: Certain transitions are practically one-way: there exists a subset Ω ⊂ WF × WF of high-asymmetry transitions such that (w, w′) ∈ Ω implies c(w′, w) ≥ κ · c(w, w′) for some κ ≫ 1. The higher κ, the more irreversible. Truly absorbing states (κ = ∞) are a special case, not the general rule.
  3. Irreversibility propagates through composition: If (wi, wi′) ∈ Ωi for fragment i, then C(W, A, Φ) restricted to the subspace containing fragment i cannot reverse the transition, even if all other fragments change freely.
  4. Reconstruction cost: When a reversed transition is economically possible through a different path (rebuilding a firm is not un-bankrupting it), the reconstruction cost R(w′ ↝ w) is bounded below: R(w′ ↝ w) ≥ κ · C(w ↝ w′) for some κ > 1. Recovery is strictly more expensive than destruction.

Status: This is an axiom, not a theorem—it is a structural assumption about economic reality, not a consequence of other assumptions. It constrains the construction operator C and the fragment algebra. Implementation: The S5 state transition matrix is modified to include absorbing states and asymmetric transition costs. The GateL0RD gating mechanism enforces irreversibility by allowing gates to close permanently for certain state transitions.

What This Means for RecWM

Irreversibility fundamentally changes what RecWM can predict. Standard world models that roll forward and backward symmetrically will hallucinate recovery trajectories that are economically impossible. By axiomatising irreversibility, RecWM’s construction feasibility signal CF(t) becomes asymmetric: the set of reachable future states from a post-crisis state is strictly smaller than from a pre-crisis state, even if both states have the same observable values. This is the formal mechanism behind the empirical observation that recovery takes longer than collapse.

15

Viability Kernel Dynamics

The Problem

Theorem 5 provides a crisis signal based on εt approaching γ/β—the system losing contractivity. But this measures reflexive instability, not survivability. A system can be contractive (converging to a stable point) while the stable point itself is inside a ruin region. Conversely, a system can be momentarily non-contractive but still have viable futures. The distinction is between “is the system stable?” and “can the system survive?”

Prior Art

  • Aubin, Bayen & Saint-Pierre (“Viability Theory: New Directions,” Springer 2011): The definitive treatment. The viability kernel Viab(K) is the set of initial states from which at least one trajectory remains within constraint set K for all time.
  • Doyen & De Lara (Systems and Control Letters, 2010): Stochastic viability—probability of remaining viable under uncertainty. Connection to sustainable management.
  • Alvarez, Zaleski, Briot & Irving (arXiv 2107.02684): Viability for environmental commons with multiple usage types. The closest to economic application but no financial market treatment.

The gap: No paper computes viability kernels for performative economic systems. The key novelty: in a performative system, the constraint set K itself changes with the model’s behaviour (via Theorem 4’s constraint field Φ). The viability kernel is computed against a moving target.

Definition (Performative Viability Kernel)

Given RecWM’s state space W, constraint field Φ(t), and construction operator C, the performative viability kernel at time t is:

Viab(t) = {w ∈ W : ∃ (As)s≥t such that C(W(s), As, Φ(s)) ∈ K(Φ(s)) ∀ s ≥ t}

where K(Φ(s)) is the feasible set at time s under the evolved constraint field.

Proposition (Viability Kernel Shrinkage as Crisis Precursor)

  1. Monotonicity under constraint tightening: If Φ(t) evolves to Φ′(t) via a constraint-tightening morphism (adding regulations, reducing leverage limits), then Viab′(t) ⊆ Viab(t). Tighter constraints shrink the viable set.
  2. Reflexive kernel erosion: Under the reflexive dynamics of Theorem 1, if εt increases (markets becoming more reflexive), the viability kernel shrinks: ∂|Viab(t)|/∂εt < 0. Higher reflexivity reduces the space of survivable futures.
  3. Irreversible kernel loss: By the Irreversible Construction axiom, once a state exits the viability kernel via an irreversible transition, no action sequence can return it. The viable set can shrink permanently.

Implementation: Exact viability kernel computation is exponential in state dimension. RecWM approximates it via (a) sampling-based reachability analysis within the S5 latent space, (b) conservative inner approximation using linear constraints, and (c) the existing constraint field Φ as a structured outer bound. The rate dViab/dt becomes the seventh derived signal—the Viability Erosion Rate (VER).

What This Means for RecWM

The viability kernel adds a fundamentally different lens from all existing signals. εt (Theorem 5) asks “is the system reflexively stable?” CoI (Theorem 6) asks “are the pieces consistent?” VER asks the most basic question: “can the system survive?” A shrinking viability kernel means the system is running out of room to manoeuvre, even if current state is stable and consistent. This is the formal mechanism behind the intuition that “all the exits are closing”—a warning that precedes both reflexive instability and cohomological inconsistency.

16

Performative Information Geometry

The Problem

Theorem 3 uses the Fisher information matrix F as a fixed object—computed at an anchor point θ* and held constant during EWC regularisation. But in a performative system, F itself depends on the model parameters: F(θ) = ED(θ)[∇ log p(z; θ) ∇ log p(z; θ)T]. When the model moves, the distribution changes, and the Fisher information—the local curvature of the statistical manifold—deforms. The geometry of parameter space is not fixed; it bends under the model’s own weight.

Prior Art

  • Amari (“Information Geometry and Its Applications,” Springer 2016): The foundational text. The Fisher-Rao metric, natural gradient, α-connections. All for fixed distributions.
  • Drusvyatskiy & Xiao (Math. OR, 2023): Stochastic optimisation with decision-dependent distributions. Proves convergence of gradient methods when the objective landscape shifts with the decision. Does not use information geometry.
  • Perdomo et al. (ICML 2020): Performative prediction with Euclidean geometry—no curvature awareness.

The gap: Nobody has combined information geometry with performative prediction. The Fisher-Rao metric on a performative manifold, the performative Christoffel symbols, and the natural gradient under distribution shift are all undefined in the literature.

Definition (Performative Statistical Manifold)

The performative statistical manifold MP is the pair (Θ, gP) where:

  • Θ is the parameter space
  • gP(θ) = F(θ, D(θ)) is the performative Fisher metric—the Fisher information matrix evaluated at the distribution induced by θ

The performative Christoffel symbols Γkij(θ) encode how the natural gradient direction bends as the model moves through parameter space while simultaneously deforming the distribution.

Proposition (Performative Natural Gradient)

Let ∇PL(θ) = gP(θ)−1 ∇ L(θ) be the natural gradient on MP. Then:

  1. Strict generalisation of EWC: Standard EWC uses F(θ*) at a fixed anchor. The performative natural gradient uses F(θ, D(θ)) at the current point. When ε → 0 (no performativity), the performative metric reduces to the standard Fisher-Rao metric.
  2. Curvature-aware convergence: The performative natural gradient converges to the performatively stable point with rate determined by the geodesic distance on MP, not the Euclidean distance. When MP has negative curvature (performative feedback amplifies sensitivity), Euclidean methods underestimate the true distance to stability.
  3. Adaptive EWC: The EWC penalty (Theorem 3) with a moving Fisher matrix F(θt, D(θt)) is the geodesic regulariser on MP. This provides a principled schedule for updating the Fisher anchor, resolving an open engineering question in the EWC literature.

Implementation: Computing the full performative Fisher matrix is expensive (requires sampling from D(θ) at each step). RecWM uses an online approximation: the empirical Fisher with exponential forgetting, updated from the actual market data that the model’s deployment induces. The forgetting rate is tied to εt (Theorem 5): higher reflexivity means faster Fisher updates.

17

Interventional Separability

The Problem

Policy analysis requires counterfactual reasoning: “what would happen if the central bank raised rates by 50bp?” Pearl’s do-operator (do(X = x)) answers this by severing all incoming causal edges to X. But in a reflexive system, severing feedback is wrong: when the central bank raises rates, markets anticipate the raise and respond to the announcement, which in turn affects the rate decision. The feedback loop is the phenomenon. Severing it removes precisely the mechanism you need to model.

Prior Art

  • CausalVAE (arXiv 2604.07712, April 2026): A structural causal module attachable to any encoder-transition backbone, supporting do-operator counterfactual generation. Achieves +102.5% on counterfactual benchmarks. But the do-operator fully severs feedback.
  • Causal-JEPA (arXiv 2602.11389, February 2026): Object-level latent masking that induces counterfactual-like interventions during training. No partial-feedback mechanism.
  • Mandal, Triantafyllou, Woodworth & Zrnic (ICML 2023): “Performative Power.” Measures the ability of a learner to steer the data distribution toward a target through performative effects. Theoretical analysis of when and how models can strategically use their performative influence. No interventional framework.

Additional Prior Art

  • Correa & Bareinboim (AAAI 2020): “A Calculus for Stochastic Interventions.” Formalises inference rules for soft (non-atomic) interventions that preserve causal connections at reduced strength. The σ-calculus generalises do-calculus to parametric intervention regimes.
  • Geiger et al. (arXiv 2211.12270, 2022): “Causal Abstraction with Soft Interventions.” Defines soft interventions for causal abstraction checking.

The gap: Existing soft intervention frameworks operate on static causal graphs. Nobody has composed soft interventions with performative feedback—where the intervention strength λ interacts with the endogenous sensitivity ε of Theorem 5. The doλ operator below integrates soft interventions into the performative stability framework, providing a reflexivity-aware policy analysis tool.

Definition (Soft Intervention Operator)

The soft do-operator doλ(X = x) parameterises intervention strength λ ∈ [0, 1]:

  • λ = 1: Full Pearl intervention (sever all incoming edges). Standard do-calculus.
  • λ = 0: Pure observation (no intervention). Standard conditioning.
  • 0 < λ < 1: Partial intervention. Incoming causal influence is attenuated by factor (1 − λ). The reflexive loop operates at reduced strength.

Formally: under doλ(X = x), the structural equation for X becomes X = λ · x + (1 − λ) · f(Pa(X), UX), where f is the original structural equation and Pa(X) are the parents of X.

Proposition (Interventional Separability)

  1. Continuity: The counterfactual distribution P(Y | doλ(X = x)) is continuous in λ. Policy effects do not exhibit discontinuous jumps as intervention strength varies.
  2. Reflexive attenuation: To first order, the effective performativity parameter under doλ is εeff(λ) ≈ (1 − λ) · ε. Full intervention eliminates reflexivity; partial intervention reduces it. Caveat: The linear approximation holds when intervention strength is small relative to the system’s nonlinear feedback structure. In practice, the relationship may be nonlinear—a small intervention below a credibility threshold may have no effect, while an intervention that triggers a regime change may have disproportionate impact. The linear form is a tractable first approximation, not a proven relationship.
  3. Policy credibility spectrum: The parameter λ has a natural economic interpretation: it is the credibility of the policy intervention. λ = 1 is a perfectly credible commitment (markets fully believe it); λ < 1 reflects partial credibility (markets partially discount the announcement). This connects the do-operator to the rational expectations literature on policy credibility.
  4. Composition with Theorem 3: Under doλ, the EWC convergence condition becomes ε · (1 − λ) < γeff/βeff. Sufficiently credible interventions (λ close to 1) can stabilise otherwise-divergent systems.

What This Means for RecWM

Interventional separability gives RecWM a principled policy analysis layer. Instead of “what if rates rise?” (which severs feedback and gives wrong answers) or “what if rates rise and markets react naturally?” (which requires simulating the full reflexive loop), RecWM can answer: “what if rates rise with credibility λ?” This parameterises the space between observation and intervention, letting policymakers explore how credibility affects outcomes. The λ parameter maps directly to the distance between announced policy and market-implied policy—a measurable quantity.

18

Liquidity as Feasibility Catalyst

The Problem

RecWM defines seven typed world fragments: prices, order flow, credit, volatility, narrative, policy, and regulation. Liquidity is absent. This is not an oversight to be fixed by “adding an eighth fragment”—it is a conceptual gap. Liquidity is not a fragment like the others; it is a feasibility catalyst. A catalyst in chemistry is required for a reaction to proceed but is not consumed by it. Similarly, liquidity is required for economic constructions to be instantiated—a trade requires a counterparty, a loan requires a lender, an IPO requires buyers—but liquidity itself is not part of the construction’s output.

Prior Art

  • Brunnermeier & Pedersen (RFS 2009): Market liquidity and funding liquidity are distinct but coupled. Liquidity spirals arise from their interaction. Canonical but no world model framework.
  • Wiersema, Kemp & Farmer (ECB WP 3169, 2026): Liquidity as a coupled state variable with multiple equilibria. Formalises the endogeneity of liquidity.
  • Paddrik, Hayes, Todd, Yang, Beling & Scherer (J. Artificial Societies and Social Simulation, 2012): Agent-based model of market liquidity with endogenous regime-switching via order-driven dynamics.

Definition (Liquidity as Categorical Catalyst)

Extend the fragment algebra with a distinguished object WFliq that acts as a catalyst in the monoidal category Frag:

  • Feasibility gate: A composition WFi ⊗ WFj is instantiable only if WFliq ≥ Lij, where Lij is the minimum liquidity required for the composition. Different compositions require different liquidity levels.
  • Partial conservation: During normal markets, WFliq is approximately conserved by composition: the output includes WFliq at a similar level (redistributed across participants). However, during crises, liquidity IS consumed—it evaporates as market makers withdraw, counterparties disappear, and bid-ask spreads widen to infinity. The “catalyst” analogy is therefore imperfect: unlike a chemical catalyst, liquidity can be endogenously created and destroyed. More precisely, liquidity is an enabling resource with approximate conservation in calm regimes and rapid depletion in stressed regimes.
  • Endogenous evolution: WFliq evolves via a coupled equation: L(t+1) = L(t) · h(εt, Φ(t), volatility), where h captures the empirical fact that liquidity dries up precisely when it is most needed (reflexive liquidity spirals).

What This Means for RecWM

Adding liquidity as a catalyst rather than a fragment resolves a fundamental modelling question: why do feasible constructions suddenly become impossible during crises? The answer is not that the constraints changed (though they may have), but that the catalyst required to instantiate constructions evaporated. The liquidity level L(t) interacts with every other signal: it gates the viability kernel (Viab(t) shrinks when L(t) drops), amplifies cohomological inconsistency (CoI rises when cross-market arbitrage is impossible due to illiquidity), and accelerates ecological instability (EII rises when market makers withdraw).

19

Complete Signal Architecture

The six new principles extend RecWM’s signal architecture from four to seven derived signals:

SignalMeasuresSourceQuestion It Answers
CI — Constraint IntensityDistance to binding constraintsTheorem 4How close to regulatory/liquidity limits?
RI — Risk IntensityDistance to ruin under ergodic functionalTheorem 2How close to irreversible loss?
CF — Construction FeasibilitySize of the feasible construction setTheorem 4How many degrees of freedom remain?
PLR — Performativity-adjusted LossGap between ergodic and ensemble stable pointsTheorem 2How dangerous is naive optimisation?
CoI — Cohomological Inconsistency‖H1(U; F)‖ — topological obstructionTheorem 6Are markets structurally consistent?
EII — Ecological Instabilityρ(Σ) — spectral radius of cross-sensitivityTheorem 7Is the model ecology stable?
VER — Viability Erosion RatedViab/dt — kernel shrinkage rateViability kernelIs the system running out of survivable futures?

The three new signals (highlighted) operate at fundamentally different levels than the original four:

  • CoI is topological—it detects structural impossibility, not statistical risk
  • EII is ecological—it measures emergent instability from model interactions, not individual model properties
  • VER is existential—it measures the space of survivable futures, not current state quality

Signal interaction cascade

The seven signals are not independent. They interact in a specific causal cascade: Liquidity erosion → Cohomological inconsistency → Ecological instability → Reflexive amplification → Viability kernel shrinkage → Constraint binding → Irreversible transition. Each link in this cascade is grounded in a theorem. The cascade is the formal mechanism of financial crisis: not a single cause, but a structured propagation through layers of the economic world model.

11

The Research Program

Five Papers

  1. “Reflexive Causal Emergence” (Theorems 1 & 2)
    • Target: ICML or NeurIPS 2027
    • Content: Reflexive transition map, performative coarse-graining stability, amplification theorem, ergodic-performative divergence
    • Novelty claim: first bridge between causal emergence and performative prediction; first composition of ergodicity economics with performative prediction
    • Prerequisite: resolve Open Problem 7 (EI concavity verification) or restate Theorem 1 as conditional
  2. “Continual Learning as Performative Stability” (Theorems 3 & 5)
    • Target: ICLR 2027
    • Content: EWC-stabilised performative convergence, anisotropic damping, condition number analysis, endogenous sensitivity and crisis transitions
    • Novelty claim: first connection between continual learning and performative prediction; strict generalisation of Hardt 2026; first state-dependent ε in the performative prediction literature
  3. “RecWM: A Constructive World Model for Financial Markets” (Theorem 4 + architecture)
    • Target: NeurIPS 2027 or journal submission
    • Content: Fibered monoidal category for constraint-filtered composition, seven-fragment architecture, empirical evaluation on multi-timescale financial data
    • Novelty claim: first L6-capable economic world model with typed constraints, ergodic signals, and performative stability guarantees
  4. “Cohomological Crisis Detection in Financial Markets” (Theorem 6 + Viability Kernel)
    • Target: ICML 2027 or Journal of Mathematical Economics
    • Content: Market consistency sheaf, H1 obstruction as crisis signal, performative viability kernel, construction entropy
    • Novelty claim: first application of sheaf cohomology to financial market consistency; first viability kernel computation for performative systems
  5. “Multi-Agent Performative Ecology: When Stable Models Create Unstable Markets” (Theorem 7 + Interventional Separability)
    • Target: NeurIPS 2027 or Econometrica
    • Content: Ecology equilibrium, spectral radius convergence condition, emergent instability from individually stable agents, soft do-operator for policy analysis
    • Novelty claim: first composition of multi-agent performative prediction with economic world model structure; first “soft do-operator” bridging observation and intervention

Build Order

  1. Months 1–3: Prove Theorems 1–3 formally. Implement single-fragment prototype (WFprice only) with S5 + EWC on free data (Yahoo Finance, FRED).
  2. Months 4–6: Add WFcredit and WFvol (requires Bloomberg). Implement GateL0RD gating (ablation over interpretations a/b/c). First paper submission.
  3. Months 7–12: Full seven-fragment system. Constraint field Φ with regulatory data. Empirical evaluation: regime detection, crisis anticipation, stability metrics. Second and third paper submissions.

What Success Looks Like

RecWM succeeds if it can demonstrate, on held-out data:

  • Accurate regime detection across timescales (faster than narrative indicators)
  • Constraint-feasible construction sets that exclude outcomes violating known regulatory/liquidity bounds
  • Ergodic-performative signals (PLR, RI) that provide leading indicators of instability
  • Stable online updating under distribution shift (convergence verified empirically)

RecWM fails if the hyperparameter sensitivity (Open Problem 3) dominates the signal, or if SPIB estimation (Open Problem 2) renders the slow fragments uninformative.

The ambition is not to predict the future. It is to map the space of feasible constructions—what can be built, by whom, under what constraints—and to understand how the act of mapping changes the territory.
Product Vision

The Financial Intelligence
That Changes Everything

AlphaFold solved protein folding — a problem everyone said was impossible. RecWM solves the equivalent problem in finance: building a world model of the entire financial system. Not predicting prices. Simulating how the world works — and letting you test what happens when you change it.

This is not a better Bloomberg. This is not a chatbot on a price feed. This is a living simulation of the financial world — seven typed fragments (Liquidity, Momentum, Risk, Credit, Structure, Sentiment, Policy) composed into a unified state that evolves, detects regime shifts, and knows when its own predictions are changing the system it’s predicting.

The Design Philosophy: Why People Will Love This

Every beloved product follows the same pattern: it collapses a previously irreducible expert workflow into an interactive interface you can probe, not a report you read. AlphaFold didn’t speed up crystallography — it made the entire discipline optional for most questions. RecWM doesn’t speed up financial analysis. It builds a world model of the entire financial system — one you can query, stress-test, and simulate through — collapsing the analyst-to-PM-to-CIO chain into a single queryable surface.

10× or Nothing

Incremental UI polish won’t dethrone Bloomberg. We collapse research-to-decision from hours to seconds via a world model that simulates across all seven fragments simultaneously. The 10× isn’t speed — it’s a category change from “show me data” to “simulate the world and let me test alternatives.”

Live Inside the Workflow

GitHub Copilot and Cursor are loved because they live inside the developer’s existing workflow — no context switch. RecWM lives inside the PM’s existing tools: API-first for quant pipelines, Excel/Python integration for research, and a native interface that remembers your book, your mandate, your risk limits. Every session starts at expert context, never zero.

Always the Next Question

Perplexity made search addictive by always offering the next question. RecWM does the same: “Regime shift detected → Want to stress-test your portfolio? → Here are 3 hedges → Want to see what happened in the 2015 analog? → Here’s where today diverges.” The conversation loop pulls you deeper. You never “start over.”

The Moat: Why This Gets Stronger Over Time

Part I: The World Model Revolution

The most important idea in AI right now is not large language models. It is world models — systems that build internal simulations of how reality works, then use those simulations to plan, imagine, and reason about scenarios that have never happened before.

What a World Model Actually Does

A world model learns the dynamics of its environment — not just what things look like, but how they change when you act on them. It can then “dream” forward: simulate thousands of possible futures without ever touching the real world.

WHAT IT ISN’T

A prediction model that maps inputs → outputs. A classifier. A regression. A time-series forecast. These see patterns. They don’t understand mechanisms.

WHAT IT IS

A simulation engine with state, transitions, and composition. It models how the world evolves when you change things. It can answer “what if?” questions it has never seen.

The JEPA Insight: Why RecWM Predicts in Latent Space

Yann LeCun’s most important argument (arXiv:2306.02572): generative models solve the wrong problem for world modeling. A model that generates pixels wastes capacity on irrelevant detail — the exact pattern of light on a countertop, the precise wording of a headline. What matters for planning is abstract state: objects, relationships, dynamics.

V-JEPA 2-AC demonstrated this concretely: planning in a 1024-dimensional latent space takes ~16 seconds per action. The equivalent using NVIDIA Cosmos (a generative video model) takes ~4 minutes — 15–30× slower — because it must generate and evaluate full video frames.

You do not need to render the future to evaluate it. You only need to predict its abstract state.

RecWM applies this insight to finance. It does not predict price time series (pixel-level prediction). It predicts the abstract state of seven fragments — Liquidity, Momentum, Risk, Credit, Structure, Sentiment, Policy — and their compositions. This is why it can simulate 5,000 forward paths in seconds: it operates in a compressed state-space, not in the space of observable prices.

Compositionality: The Key to Generalisation

The deepest innovation in RecWM is not any single fragment. It is the composition operator ⊗ that combines them.

Why Linear Models Fail

Standard factor models assume factors combine linearly: Return = β1F1 + β2F2 + … But in March 2020, Liquidity × Risk × Sentiment interacted multiplicatively. The selling caused the illiquidity caused the fear caused the selling. Linear models cannot represent this circular composition.

Why Composition Works

RecWM’s ⊗ operator composes fragments with 4 constraint layers: algebraic (type compatibility), information-theoretic (SPIB compression), dynamical (Lyapunov stability), and economic (no-arbitrage). This lets the model represent interactions it has never seen — the same way language models compose words into sentences they’ve never generated.

This is compositional generalisation applied to finance. MuZero composes game mechanics. Dreamer composes physics. RecWM composes market dynamics. The architecture that conquered games and robotics — applied to the domain where it matters most.

Reflexivity: The Feature Nobody Else Can Build

Every AI system in robotics, games, or autonomous driving assumes it is observing a system that exists independently. A self-driving car doesn’t change the road by driving on it. A game agent doesn’t change the physics by playing.

Financial markets are different. The model’s predictions change the system it’s predicting. When enough participants act on the same signal, the signal becomes self-fulfilling — or self-defeating. This is George Soros’s reflexivity, formalised in Donald MacKenzie’s “performativity” research, and mathematically grounded in Perdomo et al. 2020 (Theorem 3.5).

THE REFLEXIVITY COEFFICIENT ε(t)
RecWM computes ε(t) from the Jacobian of the feedback loop:

ε(t) = ‖ ∂market(t+1) / ∂model_output(t) ‖

ε < 0.2 — Normal. Model’s predictions don’t move markets. Standard quant models work fine.
ε ≈ 0.3–0.5 — Elevated. Crowded positioning. The model’s recommendations start to matter.
ε > 0.5 — Critical. Self-fulfilling dynamics. The model suppresses its own confidence.

This is the feature that would have detected:
• Feb 2018 VIX blow-up — risk-parity vol targets created a feedback loop (ε > 0.6)
• Aug 2007 quant quake — correlated unwind of momentum/value strategies (ε ≈ 0.55)
• Jan 2021 GameStop — retail + short squeeze reflexive cascade (ε > 0.7)
• Mar 2023 SVB — deposit flight → asset fire-sale → contagion loop (ε ≈ 0.5)

No other financial model measures its own impact on the market. Bloomberg shows data. Quant models predict prices. Risk models measure exposure. RecWM is the only system that knows when it’s changing the game.

Reading the World from Fragments

A submarine has no windows. It constructs its picture of reality from fragments of sound — passive sonar bearings that are individually ambiguous but collectively powerful. A hedge fund operates the same way: it sees fragments of market reality and must infer the full picture.

Bearing-Only Contacts

A credit spread widening 15bps is a bearing-only contact. You know something is out there. Is it idiosyncratic? A forced seller? Or the leading edge of a systemic crisis? A single data point is nearly useless. RecWM collects bearings from every market — FX vol, cross-currency basis, repo rates, shipping data — and triangulates the real signal.

Submarines have a blind spot directly behind them where propulsion noise masks incoming sound. What It Actually Feels Like to Manage $800 Million, and What Would Make Me Stop Losing Sleep

Written from the perspective of a macro PM with 25 years across Soros Fund Management, Brevan Howard, and now running an $800M independent fund.

I. The Thing Nobody Tells You About This Job

There is a number in my head at all times. Right now it is negative fourteen million dollars. That is how much I am down on my Turkish lira short this week. I know this number the way you know your own name. It is there when I wake up, when I eat dinner with my kids, when I am supposedly watching a movie with my wife on a Saturday night. It is there when I brush my teeth. It sits behind every conversation I have with every human being in my life like a subtitle track that never turns off.

People outside this business think portfolio management is about being smart. It is not. It is about being able to carry weight. The weight of the book. The weight of knowing that while you sleep, someone in Tokyo or Sydney or Frankfurt is doing something that could make your quarter or blow up your year. The weight of knowing that your LPs — the pension funds, the endowments, the family offices — are counting on you to not be an idiot, and that being an idiot is something that can happen to you at 3:17am on a Tuesday because a deputy governor of the People's Bank of China said something slightly different from what everyone expected about the lending facility rate.

Let me be specific about the anxiety because people romanticize this job.

The 3am phone check. My phone is always on the nightstand. Always. Face down so the screen light does not wake my wife, but close enough that I can reach it without fully waking up. I have trained myself to do a half-conscious check — roll over, tap the screen, squint at S&P futures, squint at dollar-yen, squint at the 10-year. If the numbers are where I expect, I roll back over and I am asleep again in thirty seconds. If something has moved — if the Nikkei is down 2% or if the euro has spiked 80 pips — then I am awake. Fully, completely, horribly awake. And I will not sleep again until I understand why.

This happens three to four nights a week. My wife has stopped asking what I am doing. She knows.

The Sunday night futures open. Sunday at 6pm Eastern is when the CME opens and S&P futures start trading. Every Sunday, no matter what I am doing, I check. I check at a family barbecue. I checked at my daughter's college move-in day. I checked at a funeral. The Sunday open is a referendum on what happened over the weekend — did anything break? Did some geopolitical event I had not thought about suddenly become the only thing that matters? The Sunday open has ruined more Sunday evenings than I can count. Not because the market always moves — usually it does not. But because there is that seven-second window between tapping my phone and seeing the number where my stomach is in free fall.

Vacations. I have not had a real vacation in twenty years. I have had trips where I bring my laptop and my Bloomberg terminal app and I pretend to be on vacation while checking my book every forty-five minutes. I went to Tuscany with my family three years ago. Beautiful villa, incredible food, stunning countryside. I spent the entire time on the terrace with my phone because the ECB was in the middle of a rate decision cycle and my European rates position was large. My wife took photos. In every single one, I am looking at my phone or my face is lit by a screen. She showed them to me later as an accusation. She was right.

The wedding. A close friend's daughter's wedding, 2019. I had a large long position in Brazilian real, and Bolsonaro's government was making noise about pension reform potentially stalling. I stepped out of the ceremony — the actual ceremony — to check my phone. I told my wife I was going to the bathroom. I stood in the hallway of the church reading a Reuters wire about Rodrigo Maia's comments on the pension vote timeline. I missed the vows. My friend has never mentioned it. I think about it all the time.

This is not a complaint. I chose this. I love this. But I want to be honest about what it costs, because the cost is directly related to what I need.

II. How I Actually Read the World

I do not use models. I have quants on my team who use models, and I listen to them the way I listen to a weather forecast — useful background, but I am looking out the window. My job is synthesis. My job is to take fifty weak signals from fifty different domains and stitch them together into a feeling — a directional conviction about the state of the world — that I can then express through positions.

Here is what this actually looks like on a random Wednesday morning.

5:15am. I wake up and check overnight price action. Not just my positions — everything. Dollar-yen. Aussie-dollar. Copper. Iron ore. The Hang Seng. European bank stocks. Credit spreads in investment grade and high yield. Treasury futures. Bund futures. I am not looking at each number individually. I am looking at the pattern. When copper is down and the Aussie is down and iron ore is down but the Hang Seng is flat, that tells me something different than if all four are down together. The divergences are the information. The things that should be moving together but are not — those are where the signal lives.

5:45am. Bloomberg. I read the TOP headlines but I am mostly scanning for things that do not belong. The headline that seems small but shouldn't be. Three weeks before the SVB collapse, there was a small story about a midsize bank in California seeing deposit outflows. It was buried. Nobody cared. But if you had been tracking the duration mismatch in regional bank portfolios — which I had been, loosely, because a friend at a family office had mentioned it at a dinner — that headline was a five-alarm fire. Most people did not see it. I almost did not see it. I saw it because I was looking for it without knowing I was looking for it. That is what 25 years of pattern recognition does. It makes you a tuning fork for anomaly.

6:30am. Phone calls. I talk to three or four people every morning before the US open. A macro strategist at a bank who is smart. A PM at another fund who runs a different strategy but sees the same markets. My prime broker contact. And usually someone specific to whatever I am most focused on — if I am trading EM, I call my EM guy in London; if I am in rates, I call a rates trader at one of the dealers.

These calls are not about getting "information" in the way people think. I am not getting tips. I am reading tone. When my prime broker calls me to "check in on my margin" unprompted, that is not a check-in. That is him telling me that other clients are getting margin calls, that his risk desk is nervous, that the market is about to go through a de-leveraging event. He cannot say that explicitly. But I have known him for fifteen years and I know what his voice sounds like when he is nervous. That is information. That is alpha.

When the macro strategist at the bank sounds bored, that tells me consensus is settled and there is no energy for a move. When he sounds excited, it means something is about to break out of a range. When he disagrees with me too quickly, it means I am consensus and I should be worried about my position.

7:00am-9:30am. I am reading, thinking, and adjusting my mental model of the world. I read the FT, the WSJ, a few research notes, Twitter (specific accounts I follow who are actually useful — @EpsPlotter, a few anonymous accounts who are clearly on institutional trading desks). I am not reading for facts. I am reading for narrative shifts. Markets do not move on facts. They move on narratives that change. The fact that US employment is strong has been true for two years. It is priced in. What matters is the moment the narrative shifts from "employment is strong" to "employment is too strong and the Fed has to do something about it." That shift does not happen because of a single data point. It happens because a critical mass of people start talking differently. I am trying to detect that shift before it is complete.

9:30am. The open. I watch the first thirty minutes like a hawk. The first thirty minutes of trading tell you more about the real state of supply and demand than any research report ever written. Is there real selling or is it just noise? Are the moves happening on volume or in a vacuum? Where are the big prints? If I see a large block trade in an ETF that tracks emerging market bonds, I want to know who is selling. I cannot always know. But sometimes the pattern of the trade tells you — if it is being worked carefully in small pieces, it is a real account reducing risk. If it is being dumped in a single print, someone just hit a stop-loss or got a redemption.

This is what I do. All day. Every day. I stitch together weak signals from order flow, from conversations, from headlines, from price action, from body language on CNBC, from the fact that three different people mentioned the same obscure thing in the same week. I build a mosaic in my head. And then I express that mosaic as a portfolio.

The problem is that this mosaic lives entirely in my head. It is not written down. It is not systematic. It is not verifiable. I cannot tell you exactly why I think the dollar is about to weaken. I can give you seven reasons, but the real reason is that the pattern feels like 2017 to me, and in 2017 the dollar rolled over after everyone was sure it would keep going. That is not an argument I can put in a research note. That is 25 years of scar tissue talking.

III. What I Wish Existed

Here is what I want. I want my brain, but better. I want the thing that I do — the synthesis, the mosaic building, the pattern recognition — done by something that never sleeps, never gets emotional, never forgets, and can hold a thousand times more information in its working memory than I can.

I do not want a prediction engine. I have been doing this long enough to know that anyone who tells you they can predict markets is a liar or a fool. What I want is an understanding engine. I want a system that can answer the question: "What is the world doing right now, and what does it mean for my book?"

Specifically, I want a system that:

Reads everything I read, plus everything I cannot read. I scan maybe 200 headlines a day, talk to 8-10 people, and watch 15-20 markets. The system should be ingesting every relevant data stream on earth — not just prices and headlines, but shipping data, satellite imagery of port activity, power consumption in Chinese industrial provinces, job postings at central banks, flight tracking of corporate jets, patent filings, credit card transaction aggregates, app download trends. Everything. Every single signal that has ever mattered to a macro trade, the system should be watching.

Synthesizes, not summarizes. I do not need a summary. I need synthesis. I need: "Copper is down 3% overnight but copper miners in Chile are up. The last time this happened was March 2018, which preceded a 6-week copper rally. Meanwhile, Chinese credit impulse has turned positive for the first time in 9 months, and LME warehouse stocks in Asian warehouses have been declining for 4 straight weeks. Your short copper position may be offside." That is synthesis. That is connecting dots across domains. That is what I do in my head and what I want done for me, better and faster.

Knows my book and talks to me about it. The system should know my positions, my P&L, my risk limits, my historical pattern of behavior. It should know that I tend to hold losers too long and cut winners too early (I know this about myself and I still do it). It should know that when I am up big on the year I get conservative and leave money on the table. It should know that my best trades have historically been in EM FX and my worst trades have been in commodity spreads. It should use all of this to contextualize its synthesis.

Tells me what changed, not what is. I do not need a daily summary. I need a change log. What is different today from yesterday? What moved that should not have moved? What did not move that should have? Where is the consensus, and where is it about to break?

Argues with me. When I have a view, I want the system to steelman the other side. Not because I want to be talked out of my trades, but because the most dangerous thing in this business is certainty. When I am certain I am right, I am about to get killed. I want a system that forces me to confront the possibility that I am wrong, and specifically how I would know if I were wrong.

IV. Why I Would Pay $500K a Year for 24/7 Monitoring

Let me tell you three stories.

The trade I missed because I was asleep. January 2015. The Swiss National Bank removed the euro-Swiss franc floor. It happened at 4:30am Eastern time. I was asleep. By the time I woke up at 5:15am, the Swiss franc had appreciated 30% against the euro in minutes and then partially retraced. If I had been awake — if anything had woken me up — I could have shorted the franc on the spike because it was obvious that the SNB would intervene to prevent a complete collapse of Swiss exporters. That trade made people who were at their desks 200-300 basis points in a single day. I made nothing because I was asleep. A system that had woken me up — not with a generic alert, but with a message that said "SNB just removed the floor, franc is spiking, here are three things you should consider doing right now" — would have paid for itself for the next fifty years in that single moment.

The crisis I survived because I happened to be watching. August 2015. China devalued the yuan. I was at my desk early that morning because of jet lag — I had just come back from London. I saw the move as it happened and immediately started reducing risk across my entire EM portfolio, because I knew from experience that a Chinese devaluation would trigger a cascade of selling across every emerging market. By the time the US opened, I was down to 60% of my normal EM exposure. Over the next two weeks, EM assets fell 8-12%. My fund was down 1.5%. If I had been on a normal schedule that morning, I would not have seen the yuan move until 6am, by which time the cascade was already underway and liquidity was gone. The difference between being at my desk at 5am and being at my desk at 6am was probably 300 basis points of performance. That is $24 million on my fund. Because of jet lag.

The trade I sized wrong because I could not articulate my conviction. March 2020. I knew — I knew in my bones — that COVID was going to be a global catastrophe for markets. I had been watching the case counts in Italy in late February. I had talked to a doctor friend who was terrified. I had seen the videos from Wuhan that were circulating on social media. Everything in my pattern recognition system was screaming that this was not like SARS, this was not containable, this was going to shut down the global economy. But when I sat down to size my short position, I could not build a quantitative case for how bad it would be. My risk system said my proposed position was "large relative to historical vol." My COO asked me to justify the trade. All I could say was "this feels like the big one." I put on a position that was half the size I wanted. That half-position made us 800 basis points in March 2020. The full position would have made us 1600 basis points. I left $64 million on the table because I could not translate a gut feeling into a rigorous argument. If I had a system that could have said — "based on epidemiological data, supply chain exposure, and historical analogs to the 1918 and 2009 pandemics, here is a quantitative framework that supports a position 2x your current size with a defined stop-loss" — I would have sized it right.

These three stories, in aggregate, represent roughly $100 million in alpha I either missed or left on the table. And these are just the three I remember most vividly. There are dozens more. Over a career, the cumulative cost of not having 24/7 intelligent monitoring is staggering. $500K a year is a rounding error.

V. Why Every Tool I Have Right Now Fails Me

Bloomberg. I love Bloomberg. I have used it every single day for 25 years. But Bloomberg is a data terminal, not a thinking partner. It shows me what is happening. It does not tell me what it means. It does not connect dots across asset classes. It does not know my portfolio. It does not know me. The Bloomberg AI features they have been rolling out are better than nothing, but they are fundamentally limited because Bloomberg is organized by asset class and by screen. I do not think in asset classes. I think in regimes. I think in narratives. I think in cross-asset patterns that do not fit into any single Bloomberg function.

My analysts. I have three analysts. They are smart, hard-working, and ambitious. They are also human. They go home at 7pm. They have lives. They cannot read everything, and they have their own cognitive biases. My senior analyst is brilliant on rates but has a blind spot for EM credit. My junior analyst is great at data work but does not have the experience to know what matters and what does not. And none of them can be on call 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. When something happens at 2am, I am alone with my phone and my Bloomberg app and my own brain. That is not enough.

Risk systems. My risk system tells me my VaR, my factor exposures, my correlation matrix, and my stress test results. All of this information is backward-looking. It tells me what my risk was yesterday based on the last N days of data. It does not tell me what my risk is going to be tomorrow if the world changes. Before every major crisis, my risk system told me my portfolio was "within normal parameters." And then the parameters changed, because the world changed, and the risk system was the last to know. Risk systems are like driving by looking in the rearview mirror. They are necessary but they are not sufficient.

Quant models. My quants build models that assume relationships between variables are stable. They assume the world is stationary — that the correlation between stocks and bonds, or between oil and the Canadian dollar, or between VIX and credit spreads, will tomorrow be roughly what it was in the training window. This assumption is catastrophically wrong approximately every 18-24 months. Every time it is wrong, people who relied on models get destroyed. I have seen it happen to LTCM, to the quants in August 2007, to the risk parity funds in March 2020. Models are useful in calm markets. In the markets where you actually need help — the ugly, dislocated, panicky markets — models break down precisely when you need them most.

News aggregators and AI summaries. I have tried every AI news tool on the market. They all do the same thing: they summarize what happened. They take ten articles about the Fed and turn them into one paragraph about the Fed. This is useless to me. I can read fast. What I cannot do is synthesize across domains. I do not need a summary of the Fed news. I need someone to tell me that the combination of the Fed's tone, the recent move in 2-year breakevens, the positioning data from the CFTC, and the unusual buying in 5-year TIPS that showed up in the Treasury auction yesterday collectively suggest that the market is about to reprice the terminal rate 25 basis points higher. That is synthesis. No tool I have ever used does this.

Alerts. I have price alerts on every position. They are worse than useless. They go off constantly and they tell me nothing about context. "USDJPY has crossed 150" — yes, I can see that, but WHY? Is it because of a BOJ intervention rumor? Is it because US yields just spiked? Is it because it is 3am and there is no liquidity and some algorithm knocked it through a stop-loss level? The "what" without the "why" is noise. I have been conditioned to ignore alerts the way New Yorkers are conditioned to ignore car alarms.

VI. The Dream: What Would Make Me Fall in Love

Here is what my perfect morning looks like with the tool I dream about.

5:15am. I wake up and look at my phone. Instead of checking twelve different things in twelve different apps, there is one screen. It says:

Overnight: Mostly in line. Two items need your attention. 1. Your Turkey position: Lira weakened 1.2% overnight on reports that the CBRT may pause its hiking cycle sooner than expected. Your short TRY position is now +$3.2M on the week. However: CDS spreads did not widen commensurately, which historically has preceded a reversal in the cash move. Consider whether your thesis has fully played out. 2. A pattern you should know about: Three separate signals in the last 12 hours suggest Chinese industrial demand may be inflecting upward. Caixin manufacturing PMI subcomponents showed new orders at a 7-month high. Copper inventories at Shanghai warehouses dropped for the 6th straight week. And power consumption in Guangdong province (satellite-estimated) rose 4.2% week-over-week, the largest increase since February. You have no direct China exposure, but your short AUD position is implicitly a bet against Chinese demand. This may be worth reviewing.

That is it. Not a wall of data. Not a summary of overnight news. A contextual, portfolio-aware assessment of what matters to me, right now, based on my specific positions and my specific risk profile.

6:00am. I sit down at my desk. I open the system and I ask it a question in plain English: "What is the market pricing for the September Fed meeting and how has it changed in the last 72 hours?"

It does not just show me the Fed funds futures curve. It shows me the curve, the change over 72 hours, the change decomposed into what came from data (CPI, payrolls) and what came from Fedspeak, the positioning from the most recent CFTC data, and the historical analog — "the last time the market was pricing this probability of a cut with this level of equity market complacency was June 2019, which preceded a 50bp cut that the market initially rallied on and then sold off."

I ask a follow-up: "If the Fed cuts 50bp in September instead of 25bp, what happens to my book?"

It runs a scenario — not a simplistic parallel shift, but a regime-aware scenario that says: "A surprise 50bp cut would likely steepen the curve by 15-20bp, weaken the dollar by 1.5-2% (most against EM and commodity currencies), and initially boost equities by 2-3% before the market starts asking 'why did they cut so much, what do they know that we don't.' Your book would be up approximately $18M on the rates leg, down $4M on the dollar leg because your dollar short is concentrated in G10 rather than EM, and roughly flat on equities. Net: +$14M. But with a warning: the 'what do they know' narrative historically kicks in within 48 hours and reverses the initial equity move. If you want to capture the rate move without the equity whipsaw, consider adding a short-dated put spread on SPX."

That is the tool. That is what I want. Not a prediction. A structured way of exploring the implications of different scenarios, grounded in market data, historical analogs, and my specific portfolio.

During the day, the system runs in the background. It does not bother me unless something matters. But when something matters, it tells me immediately and it tells me why. Not "USDJPY crossed 150." Instead: "USDJPY just broke through 150 on heavy volume. This appears to be driven by a combination of a hot Tokyo CPI print and large option expiry at the 150 strike. The last three times USD/JPY broke 150, the BOJ intervened within 48 hours. You have a $40M short yen position. Given the intervention risk, you may want to consider reducing or hedging."

At night, it watches while I sleep. If something happens that affects my book, it wakes me up. But intelligently. Not for every 50-pip move. Only when the move is (a) large enough to matter for my P&L, (b) driven by something fundamental rather than noise, and (c) actionable — meaning there is something I can or should do about it. If the move is noise, it lets me sleep. If the move is real but there is nothing I can do about it until the morning, it logs it and briefs me when I wake up. If the move is real and urgent, it wakes me up with a specific, contextual, actionable message.

The result: I sleep better. I think more clearly. I make better decisions because I am not exhausted from the constant vigilance. I catch things I would have missed. I size positions more confidently because I can articulate my conviction through the system's analytical framework rather than relying on gut feel alone. I spend less time on information gathering and more time on thinking, which is what I am actually paid to do.

And here is the thing: once I have this, I would never give it up. It would be like going back to paper maps after having GPS. Not because GPS is always right, but because the cognitive load of navigating without it is something you cannot bear once you have experienced the alternative. I would pay $500K a year. I would pay a million. Because on a $800 million book, the difference between catching one major move and missing it is worth ten to twenty million dollars. The tool pays for itself in a single trade. Everything after that is pure edge.

VII. What This Really Is

I will say something that I think most PMs would agree with but none of us would say publicly: we are all operating at the edge of our cognitive capacity. The world is too complex, too fast, too interconnected for any single human brain to process. We succeed not because we understand everything, but because we understand slightly more than the next person. The edge in this business has always been informational and analytical. Whoever synthesizes the mosaic fastest and most accurately wins.

For 25 years, the synthesis engine has been my brain. My brain is good. But my brain gets tired, gets emotional, gets anchored to old narratives, forgets things, and sleeps eight hours a night (on a good night). The first PM who has a system that genuinely augments the synthesis process — not replaces it, augments it — will have an edge that compounds over time. Because every day that system is running, it is catching things the other PMs missed, connecting dots they did not connect, and providing its PM with a clearer, more current, more comprehensive picture of the world.

That is not a nice-to-have. In a world where the average macro fund returns 4-6% a year, an additional 200-300 basis points of alpha from better situational awareness is the difference between a fund that survives and a fund that thrives. It is the difference between a fund that grows to $3 billion and a fund that gets redeemed back to zero.

I have been waiting for this tool for my entire career. Whoever builds it will not need to sell it. They will need to ration it.

⚔ Deep Research Perspective

Decision Superiority

How OODA loops, situational awareness, and fighter-pilot doctrine map onto world-model-driven investing.

Foreword: Why a Fighter Pilot Thinks About Markets

I spent twenty-six years in the United States Air Force. I flew F-15C Eagles in Desert Storm. I commanded an Aggressor squadron at Nellis. I spent my last four years at the Pentagon working joint force doctrine, and after retirement I consulted for three multi-strategy hedge funds on decision-making under uncertainty. What I learned is this: the market is a dogfight. Not a metaphor. A literal, structural analog.

In a dogfight, you are a single combatant in a three-dimensional environment where dozens of other actors are simultaneously making decisions based on incomplete information. Some are hostile. Some are friendly. Some are neutral until they are not. The pilot who wins is not necessarily the one with the fastest jet or the most missiles. The pilot who wins is the one who understands the battlespace better and faster than everyone else in it. That is decision superiority. And it is the single most transferable concept from military doctrine to financial markets.

This document lays out the case — in the language of military strategy, doctrine, and operational art — for why a hedge fund built around a real-time world model possesses the same structural advantage as an F-35 pilot fighting against fourth-generation adversaries. It is not a fair fight. It was never meant to be.

I. Boyd's OODA Loop: The Engine of Decision Superiority

The Complete Theory

Colonel John Boyd never published his theory in a single paper. He briefed it, on hundreds of slides, to anyone who would listen — and eventually the Marine Corps, the Army, and the Air Force rebuilt their warfighting doctrines around it. The OODA loop — Observe, Orient, Decide, Act — is often reduced to a simple cycle, a hamster wheel of faster reaction. That reduction is wrong, and it has misled most people who try to apply Boyd to finance.

Boyd's insight was not "go faster." Boyd's insight was that orientation is the schwerpunkt — the center of gravity — of the entire loop. Here is why.

Observe is data collection. In aerial combat, it is your radar, your radar warning receiver, your infrared search-and-track, your wingman's eyes, your AWACS feed. In a hedge fund, it is your Bloomberg terminal, your prime broker reports, your alternative data feeds, your news wires, your order flow analytics. Observation is necessary but radically insufficient. Every pilot in the sky has a radar. Every fund has a Bloomberg terminal.

Orient is where the fight is won or lost. Orientation is the process of making sense of what you observe. It is shaped by your training, your experience, your mental models, your cultural traditions, your ability to synthesize and destroy old paradigms. Boyd called orientation "the big O" — the most important element. A novice pilot sees a radar contact at bearing 270 at 40 nautical miles and thinks "there is a blip." An experienced pilot running the same data through superior orientation knows: "That is a MiG-29, he is running a Soviet-doctrine intercept, he will turn hot at 25 miles, and I need to be at angels 30 in a beam position when he does." Same data. Radically different understanding.

This is the precise parallel to a portfolio manager. One PM sees headline CPI come in at 3.2% and thinks "inflation is hot, sell bonds." Another PM, running the same number through a world model that understands the composition of the print, the base effects, the housing lag, the labor market dynamics, the Fed's reaction function, and the current positioning of every major rates fund says: "CPI is hot on the headline but the supercore deceleration confirms the Fed's framework. The market will sell first and reverse within 90 minutes as desks work through the details. The pain trade is long duration. Size the position at 60bps of risk, enter in the second minute after the print."

Same data. Different orientation. Different outcome.

Decide is selecting a course of action from the orientation. In combat, it is choosing to extend, engage, defend, or disengage. In finance, it is choosing the trade, the sizing, the timing, the instrument.

Act is execution. In combat, pulling the trigger, maneuvering the aircraft. In finance, placing the order, hedging, managing the book.

Getting Inside the Opponent's OODA Loop

Boyd's most famous and most misunderstood concept is "getting inside the opponent's OODA loop." This does not mean acting faster in absolute time. It means acting faster relative to your adversary's ability to process what is happening. When you cycle through OODA faster than your opponent, the environment changes before they have finished orienting to the previous change. They begin reacting to a situation that no longer exists. Their actions become inappropriate. They become confused. They panic. They are defeated not by force but by disorientation.

In Desert Storm, this is exactly what happened to the Iraqi military. Coalition forces did not merely outfight them — they out-decided them. The "left hook" maneuver through the western desert was executed at a tempo the Iraqi command structure could not process. By the time Iraqi division commanders understood where the Coalition forces were, those forces had already moved. Iraqi responses were addressed to ghosts.

In financial markets, the same dynamic plays out constantly. When a macro shock hits — a surprise rate cut, a geopolitical crisis, a bank failure — thousands of market participants enter their OODA loops simultaneously. The fund that has already pre-computed the conditional scenarios, that has a world model maintaining continuous awareness of all the relevant state variables, completes its OODA cycle while competitors are still in the Observe phase, still trying to figure out what the headline even means.

This is not high-frequency trading. This is not about microsecond latency to the exchange. This is about cognitive latency — the time between an event happening and a human being having a correct, actionable understanding of what that event means for their portfolio. A world model compresses cognitive latency from hours to seconds. That is getting inside the opponent's OODA loop.

II. Situational Awareness: Endsley's Three Levels and the SA Gap

The Model

Dr. Mica Endsley, while working on fighter pilot performance at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, developed the three-level model of situational awareness that became foundational to aviation psychology and eventually to all military operations:
