Competitive Positioning & Differentiation
Key takeaways for investor positioning of an on-premise continual-learning risk AI platform.

The market is large and growing fast. AI in finance is a $38B+ market growing at 30%+ CAGR. Even the narrower financial risk management software segment ($4.2B) is growing at 13.6%. Risk analytics broadly ($43B) provides a massive addressable market.

No one owns the intersection. The competitive landscape fragments into three camps, none of which occupies the on-premise + continual learning + world model intersection:

  • Risk incumbents (Moody's, Murex, Calypso): deep domain expertise and regulatory trust, but static models, legacy architecture, and no ML/AI capabilities. They recalibrate annually, not continuously.
  • AI platforms (Palantir, C3.ai, DataRobot, H2O.ai): modern ML infrastructure and some on-premise support, but generic (not finance-specific), no continual learning, and no causal modeling. They are AutoML commodities.
  • Data/NLP players (Kensho, FactSet, SymphonyAI): strong data assets or niche capabilities (AML, NLP), but cloud-only, narrow scope, and no risk modeling depth.

Banks are spending aggressively. JPMorgan alone spends $20B on technology and $2B specifically on AI. The top 10 global banks collectively spend $80-100B+ on technology annually. Risk technology is a $25-30B sub-segment. And 85%+ of banks plan to increase AI budgets by 20%+ in the next two years.

Regulatory tailwinds favor on-premise. DORA (EU), SS1/23 (UK PRA), OCC Heightened Standards (US), and GDPR all push banks toward solutions where they control data residency and model governance. The 29% on-premise share of financial risk management software is not shrinking — it is being reinforced by regulation.

Continual learning is the unsolved problem. Every competitor retrains models in batch (quarterly or annually). In a world where market regimes shift in days (COVID, SVB, tariff shocks), static models are structurally fragile. Continual learning that adapts to distribution shift in real-time — while maintaining explainability for SR 11-7 compliance — is a genuine technical moat.

Causal world models are the frontier. The move from correlation-based ML to causal/structural models that can answer counterfactual and interventional queries ("what happens to our portfolio if the Fed cuts 100bps and oil spikes 30%?") is where risk analytics must go. No commercial vendor has this. The closest academic work (causal inference in econometrics, agent-based models, active inference) has not been productized.

Released
March 30, 2023 (arXiv: 2303.17564, last revised December 21, 2023)
Parameters
50.6 billion (70 transformer decoder layers, 40 attention heads, hidden dim 7,680)
Context length
2,048 tokens; vocabulary size 131,072

Training Data

708B
total training tokens
363B
financial tokens (FinPile)
345B
general-purpose tokens

FinPile is Bloomberg's proprietary dataset spanning 2007–2023, comprising earnings reports, SEC filings, market analyses, Bloomberg News, and financial social media. Training ran for 53 days on 512 NVIDIA A100 40 GB GPUs, completing 139,200 steps.

Performance

On public financial benchmarks, BloombergGPT achieved 62.5% average accuracy versus 51.9–54.4% for comparably sized general-purpose models, while matching or exceeding those models on standard NLP benchmarks (reading comprehension, NER, etc.).

Current Status (2025–2026)

BloombergGPT is integrated into the Bloomberg Terminal ecosystem, serving over 325,000 subscribers (each paying roughly $30,000/year). The model has not been open-sourced or made available outside Bloomberg's products.

Competitive erosion. While BloombergGPT was groundbreaking when released, the rapid improvement of general-purpose models (GPT-4, Claude, Gemini) has narrowed its domain advantage. Industry discussion has shifted toward whether fine-tuning frontier models is more cost-effective than training domain-specific LLMs from scratch. Bloomberg has not publicly announced a successor model, but the sub-100B parameter category still captured 69.2% of the financial AI market in 2025.

CEO Jamie Dimon stated that the firm spends $2B/year on AI and generates an equal amount in cost savings. AI has already reduced headcount by 30–40% in discrete areas, though most displaced employees were offered other internal roles. JPMorgan employs the largest AI workforce among financial institutions—more AI researchers than the next seven largest competitors combined.

LLM Suite

Released in summer 2024, LLM Suite is JPMorgan's internal generative AI platform. It went from zero to 200,000 onboarded users within eight months, eventually reaching 230,000+ employees. Named 2025 "Innovation of the Year" by American Banker. The tool supports research summarization, document drafting, data analysis, and code generation across all business lines.

IndexGPT

Trademark filed with the USPTO on May 11, 2023, for a ChatGPT-like service that would select investments for customers using generative AI. Intended for use across advertising, business consulting, and finance-focused software. JPMorgan must launch the product within roughly three years of trademark approval to retain the mark. As of mid-2026, no public launch has been confirmed—the product appears to remain in development or may have been absorbed into broader AI initiatives.

COiN (Contract Intelligence)

Launched in 2017, COiN uses NLP, machine learning, and image recognition to automate analysis of complex legal and financial contracts. It reduced annual processing time from 360,000 person-hours to seconds, primarily in commercial lending and M&A. The system uses unsupervised learning to identify and categorize repeated clauses across the bank's contract corpus.

DocLLM

Paper
"DocLLM: A layout-aware generative language model for multimodal document understanding" (arXiv: 2401.00908, December 31, 2023)
Authors
Dongsheng Wang, Natraj Raman, Mathieu Sibue, Zhiqiang Ma, Petr Babkin, Simerjot Kaur, Yulong Pei, Armineh Nourbakhsh, Xiaomo Liu (JPMorgan AI Research)
Architecture
Extends traditional LLMs with a lightweight layout-awareness mechanism using bounding box spatial information instead of expensive image encoders. Decomposes attention into disentangled matrices to align textual and spatial modalities. Pre-training objective: infilling text segments to handle irregular layouts.
Results
Outperformed state-of-the-art LLMs (including GPT-4 + OCR) on 14 of 16 document intelligence datasets. Generalized to 4 of 5 previously unseen datasets. Tasks: forms, invoices, receipts, reports, contracts.

DocLLM is the technological successor to COiN and powers solutions for automated invoice processing, key-information extraction from legal documents, and client onboarding paperwork.

AI Research Lab

JPMorgan AI Research is headquartered in New York with offices in London, Madrid, Paris, and the Bay Area. The group pursues primary research in NLP, explainable AI, reinforcement learning, and graph neural networks, with over 450 use cases deployed in production (target: 1,000 by end of 2026). The bank also operates an Explainable AI Center of Excellence.

Regulatory Research Brief — August 2026

AI Deployment in Financial Services: Regulatory Landscape 2024–2026

Specific regulations, article references, compliance timelines, and enforcement actions governing the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning by banks, insurers, and investment firms across major jurisdictions.

Contents
  1. EU DORA
  2. EU AI Act — Financial Services
  3. SEC AI Rules & Enforcement
  4. MAS Singapore
  5. Bank of England / PRA / FCA

  7. Why Banks Prefer On-Premise AI
1

EU DORA — Digital Operational Resilience Act

Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 In force
  • Enacted: 14 December 2022 (published OJ 27 December 2022)
  • Entered into force: 16 January 2023
  • Date of application: 17 January 2025

Scope

Applies to nearly all EU financial entities: banks, investment firms, insurance and reinsurance undertakings, payment institutions, electronic money institutions, crypto-asset service providers, central securities depositories, trade repositories, and their critical ICT third-party service providers (including cloud providers and AI vendors).

Key Pillars and Article References

Pillar Articles Requirements
ICT Risk Management Arts. 5–16 Establish governance frameworks for identifying, protecting, detecting, responding to, and recovering from ICT risks. Maintain asset inventories, cybersecurity policies, business continuity plans, and information security policies.
Incident Reporting Arts. 17–23 Classify and report major ICT-related incidents to competent authorities within specified timeframes. Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS) on classification criteria and reporting formats adopted by the ESAs.
Resilience Testing Arts. 24–27 Conduct regular digital operational resilience testing. Significant entities must perform threat-led penetration testing (TLPT) at least every three years.
Third-Party Risk Arts. 28–44 Due diligence, contractual provisions (Art. 30(2) mandatory provisions; Art. 30(3) additional requirements for "critical or important" functions), and register of all ICT third-party contractual arrangements.
Information Sharing Art. 45 Voluntary sharing of cyber-threat intelligence among financial entities.

Impact on Cloud AI Deployments

DORA does not single out AI systems by name, but its requirements apply to all ICT services, including cloud-hosted AI/ML platforms. Key implications:

  • Art. 30(2)–(3): Contracts with cloud AI vendors must include mandatory provisions on data location, service levels, audit rights, and exit strategies. Providers supporting "critical or important" functions face additional requirements.
  • Arts. 28–29: Financial entities must maintain a register of all ICT third-party contracts (including AI-as-a-service) and conduct risk assessments before onboarding.
  • Arts. 5–16: AI models hosted externally must be covered by the firm's ICT risk management framework, including asset inventories, incident response plans, and business continuity procedures.
  • Critical Third-Party Provider (CTPP) designation: The ESAs can designate major cloud/AI providers as CTPPs, subjecting them to direct oversight by EU Lead Overseers (Arts. 31–44).

Enforcement Status

As of mid-2026, no public DORA enforcement actions have been reported. The ESAs (EBA, ESMA, EIOPA) finalized the Regulatory Technical Standards and Implementing Technical Standards in 2024. Supervisory authorities across the EU began compliance assessments in the first half of 2025.

2

EU AI Act — Application to Financial Services

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Phased implementation
  • Published: 12 July 2024 (OJ L series)
  • Entered into force: 1 August 2024
  • Full high-risk obligations: 2 August 2026 (see note on Digital Omnibus deferral below)

Compliance Timeline

Date Milestone
2 Feb 2025 Prohibited AI practices must cease (Art. 5)
2 Aug 2025 Governance provisions and obligations for general-purpose AI (GPAI) models apply
2 Aug 2026 High-risk AI system requirements enforceable (Annex III systems)
2 Aug 2027 Remaining provisions fully applicable

Digital Omnibus deferral: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 deferred the Chapter III, Sections 1–3 obligations for high-risk AI systems to 2 December 2027. However, organizations should treat August 2026 as the planning deadline, as the deferral may not cover all high-risk obligations and enforcement bodies may act earlier.

Financial Services AI Systems Classified as High-Risk (Annex III)

  • Credit scoring and creditworthiness assessment (Annex III, point 5(b)): AI systems intended to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score, with the exception of systems detecting financial fraud. This covers LLM-based credit analysis, automated loan officer recommendations, and applicant risk classification.
  • Insurance risk assessment and pricing (Annex III, point 5(c)): AI used for risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance for natural persons.
  • AML individual risk profiling: AI-driven profiling of individuals for anti-money laundering purposes.

Trading AI: Algorithmic trading systems are not explicitly listed in Annex III as high-risk. They remain subject to MiFID II requirements (Directive 2014/65/EU, Art. 17 on algorithmic trading) but are not automatically captured by the AI Act's high-risk framework unless they fall under another Annex III category.

Fraud detection: Standalone fraud detection tools receive an exception under Annex III but may still trigger obligations under other provisions depending on personal data processing.

Obligations for High-Risk Financial AI (Key Articles)

Requirement Article Summary
Risk management system Art. 9 Establish and maintain a risk management system throughout the AI system's lifecycle
Data governance Art. 10 Training, validation, and testing datasets must meet quality criteria; examine for biases
Technical documentation Art. 11 Comprehensive documentation before placing on market
Record-keeping Art. 12 Automatic logging of events during system operation
Transparency Arts. 13–14 Instructions for deployers; sufficient transparency for users to understand output
Human oversight Art. 14 Designed to allow effective human oversight during use
Accuracy & robustness Art. 15 Appropriate levels of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity

Enforcement

Financial regulators (EBA, ESMA, EIOPA) enforce compliance for financial services. Maximum penalties: up to 35 million EUR or 7% of global annual turnover for prohibited practices; up to 15 million EUR or 3% of turnover for other infringements.

3

SEC AI Rules, Proposals, and Enforcement

Predictive Data Analytics (PDA) Rule — Withdrawn

Release No. 34-97990 / IA-6353 (S7-12-23) Withdrawn
  • Proposed: July 2023, under Gensler-led SEC
  • Withdrawn: 17 June 2025
  • No substitute rule followed

The proposed rules would have required registered investment advisers and broker-dealers to identify and "eliminate or neutralize the effect of" conflicts of interest arising from the use of predictive data analytics, AI, and similar technologies in investor interactions. Following public comment and a change in SEC leadership, the proposal was formally withdrawn with no replacement.

Current Regulatory Approach

The SEC applies existing securities laws rather than creating standalone AI regulations. As stated by enforcement officials, "technology does not change the underlying obligation." Oversight operates through:

  • Anti-fraud provisions (Securities Exchange Act Section 10(b), Investment Advisers Act Section 206)
  • The Marketing Rule (accuracy of AI capability claims)
  • Fiduciary duty and Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI) obligations
  • Supervision and recordkeeping requirements
  • Regulation S-P (data protection for customer information)

Gensler vs. Atkins

Gary Gensler (Chair, 2021–Jan 2025): Pursued expansive AI-specific rulemaking; championed the PDA rule to address AI conflicts proactively; described AI as potentially "the most transformative technology of our time" and a systemic risk requiring new regulation.

Paul Atkins (Chair, Apr 2025–present): Adopted a "return to basics" approach. Withdrew the PDA proposal. Favors technology-neutral enforcement using existing securities law rather than prescriptive AI-specific rules. Maintains active enforcement against AI fraud and misrepresentation.

AI Washing Enforcement Actions

The SEC established the Cybersecurity and Emerging Technologies Unit (CETU) in February 2025 to focus on AI-related misconduct, fraud, and cybersecurity issues.

Date Target Allegation Outcome
Mar 2024 Delphia (USA) Inc. False claims about AI use in investment processes Settled; combined $400K civil penalties (with Global Predictions)
Mar 2024 Global Predictions Inc. Misleading statements about AI-driven investment capabilities Settled; cease-and-desist, censure
Jan 2025 Presto Automation Inc. Overstated AI capabilities of Presto Voice; undisclosed human intervention and third-party technology reliance First AI washing action against a public company
Apr 2025 Nate Inc. (founder/CEO) Fraudulently raised $42M+ by falsely claiming AI processed shopping transactions (actual: manual workers) SEC + DOJ parallel charges
4

Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)

FEAT Principles

Principles on Fairness, Ethics, Accountability and Transparency Active since 2018

Published in 2018 as a principles-based framework for responsible AI/data analytics in the financial sector:

Principle Core Requirements
Fairness Avoid unfairly biased outcomes. Define fairness metrics per application, monitor for demographic bias, take corrective action, maintain documentation.
Ethics AI must serve legitimate purposes without creating disproportionate harm. Institutions need proactive ethical review, not reactive damage control.
Accountability Clear responsibility structures from board to development teams. Designated governance functions and incident escalation procedures.
Transparency Customers understand how AI influences decisions affecting them. Regulators can review processes. Internal audit has full access to documentation.

Veritas Initiative (2019–present)

Industry-led collaborative translating FEAT principles into practice. Provides assessment methodologies, fairness metrics libraries, and assessment templates that financial institutions can use to test and validate the fairness of their AI systems.

Project MindForge

Phase 2 launched November 2024. Mission: enable financial institutions at different levels of AI maturity to scale AI responsibly. Published the AI Risk Management Operationalisation Handbook (January 2026), drawing on FEAT Principles, Veritas work, and Phase 1 risk identification.

AI Risk Management Guidelines (AIRG)

Consultation Paper on Guidelines on AI Risk Management Finalizing 2026
  • Released for consultation: 13 November 2025
  • Consultation closed: 31 January 2026
  • Final guidelines: Expected 2026; will be treated as supervisory expectations

Key requirements in the consultation draft:

  • Board-level AI oversight and designated governance function
  • Comprehensive AI system inventory classified by materiality
  • Full lifecycle controls: development, deployment, monitoring, retirement
  • Materiality assessment: customer outcomes, financial risk, reputational damage, operational criticality
  • Third-party AI vendor management: due diligence, contractual protections, performance monitoring, exit strategies
  • GenAI-specific controls (via MindForge): hallucination management, prompt injection prevention, data leakage safeguards

Applies to all MAS-regulated financial institutions (banks, insurers, fintechs, capital markets firms, payment service providers) with proportionality based on scale and AI deployment maturity.

AI Verify

Open-source testing toolkit developed by Singapore's IMDA. Provides fairness, transparency, and robustness testing capabilities that complement the MAS framework.

5

Bank of England / PRA / FCA

SS1/23 — Model Risk Management Principles for Banks

Supervisory Statement SS1/23 (PS6/23) Effective 17 May 2024

The PRA's first dedicated model risk management supervisory statement. Effective 17 May 2024 for PRA-regulated UK-incorporated banks, building societies, and designated investment firms. Even institutions not directly in scope are encouraged to adopt SS1/23 as industry best practice.

Five Guiding Principles

Principle Summary
1. Identification & Classification Maintain centralized model inventories. LLMs and foundation models must be inventoried alongside their applications, with documented links and use cases.
2. Governance Board-level accountability for model risk. Metrics addressing interpretability, complexity, and ethical risk.
3. Development, Implementation & Use Controls across the model lifecycle. AI models embedded in customer service, fraud detection, or HR analytics fall in scope.
4. Independent Validation Techniques like generation testing, override tracking, and parallel outcome analysis for AI (rather than traditional backtesting).
5. Risk Mitigants Fallback mechanisms, escalation paths, and real-time monitoring for AI models, especially in customer-facing applications.

FS2/23 — AI and Machine Learning Feedback Statement

Published October 2023 by PRA/FCA. Concluded that the principles in SS1/23 are "sufficient to cover AI model risk" but identified areas for strengthening, particularly around models with AI characteristics. Key findings:

  • AI/ML models present heightened risks in interpretability, data quality, and speed of deployment
  • Existing model risk management frameworks need adaptation, not wholesale replacement, for AI
  • The PRA would monitor developments and consider further guidance as needed

October 2025 AI/ML Roundtable

The PRA held CRO roundtable sessions on 20 and 22 October 2025 with 21 PRA-regulated firms to discuss AI/ML adoption in the context of SS1/23 implementation. Topics included LLM governance, foundation model risk, and practical challenges in model inventory for AI systems.

LLM-Specific Guidance

No standalone LLM guidance has been issued as of mid-2026. The PRA's position is that SS1/23 principles apply to foundation models and LLMs, with particular emphasis on:

  • Inventorying LLMs and their downstream applications
  • Documenting the chain from foundation model to deployed use case
  • Validation approaches adapted for generative outputs

FCA Position

The FCA published Discussion Paper DP5/22 on AI in financial services (October 2022) and has participated jointly with the PRA in the FS2/23 feedback statement. The FCA focuses on consumer protection, market integrity, and fairness outcomes from AI deployment, relying on existing regulatory perimeter rather than AI-specific rules.

6

Data Residency Requirements Affecting Financial AI

The number of jurisdictions with some form of data localization requirement has grown from 35 in 2017 to 62 in 2026. The following have the most direct impact on cloud AI deployments in financial services.

Jurisdiction Regulation Financial Data Requirements
China Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL), Art. 38; Cybersecurity Law; Data Security Law Critical Information Infrastructure Operators must localize all data within China. No transfer pathway available for sensitive/critical systems. Cross-border transfers require CAC security assessment, certification, or standard contract filing. First administrative penalty for unlawful cross-border transfer issued by Shanghai authorities May 2025.
India RBI Directive (Apr 2018); DPDP Act 2023; SEBI, IRDAI requirements RBI: All payment system data must be stored exclusively in India. SEBI: Critical governance, risk, and compliance data must remain in-country. IRDAI: Policy and claims data stored locally. DPDP Act enables government to blacklist countries for data transfers; rules being implemented 2025-2026.
Russia Federal Law No. 242-FZ Primary databases of Russian citizens' personal data must reside on Russian servers. Applies broadly to any operator collecting financial data from Russian residents.
Indonesia OJK Directives; Gov. Regulation No. 71/2019 Banks and financial institutions must maintain primary data centers domestically. Offshore storage permitted only if government supervision effectiveness is not diminished.
Saudi Arabia SAMA Regulations Financial institutions must maintain primary data storage within Saudi Arabia. Certain cross-border transfers require prior SAMA approval.
Nigeria CBN Directives Financial institutions must maintain local data storage and obtain approval for specific cross-border transfers of financial data.
EU / EEA GDPR; DORA (Art. 28–44) Not strict localization, but GDPR restricts transfers to countries without adequacy decisions. DORA requires contractual provisions on data location for ICT third-party services. Schrems II invalidated Privacy Shield; Standard Contractual Clauses or binding corporate rules required for US transfers.
Brazil LGPD; new Standard Contractual Clauses (Aug 2025) New SCCs effective August 2025. 48-hour breach notification mandate. Penalties up to 2% of revenue or R$50 million.

Impact on Cloud AI Deployments

  • AI models trained on customer financial data cannot simply be sent to a cloud provider in another jurisdiction without navigating transfer mechanisms
  • Inference data (inputs/outputs) often classified as personal or sensitive data, triggering localization rules
  • Model training data residency is increasingly scrutinized — even if inference runs locally, training data provenance matters
  • Multi-jurisdiction operations require either regional cloud deployments or on-premise solutions to satisfy conflicting requirements
7

Why Banks Prefer On-Premise AI

While the industry trend is toward hybrid infrastructure (over 80% of enterprises blend on-premises and cloud, with 63% using more than one cloud provider), several structural forces push banks toward on-premise or private-cloud AI deployments.

Regulatory Drivers

  • Supervisory approval requirements: Many jurisdictions require banks to obtain supervisory authority approval before adopting cloud services or outsourcing arrangements. This creates friction for cloud AI adoption.
  • Control mandates: When approving outsourcing, supervisory authorities typically require banks to retain "full control over their business activities," including the ability to audit, access, and terminate arrangements.
  • DORA (Arts. 28–44): The third-party risk management requirements impose extensive contractual and oversight obligations on cloud AI providers, making on-premise deployment operationally simpler in many cases.
  • Data localization (Section 6 above): Where financial data must stay onshore, using a foreign cloud provider's AI services becomes legally complex or impossible.
  • Model risk management: Both PRA SS1/23 and MAS AIRG require model inventories, validation, and oversight that are easier to demonstrate with on-premise systems under the bank's direct control.

Data Sensitivity Concerns

  • More than half of cloud-based data is classified as sensitive, yet fewer than one in ten organizations encrypt all of it
  • 34% of organizations running AI workloads in the cloud have experienced breaches linked to those deployments
  • Financial data (transaction histories, credit profiles, trading strategies) is among the most sensitive data categories; exposure creates both regulatory liability and competitive risk
  • LLMs and generative AI raise additional concerns about training data leakage and prompt injection exposing customer data

Operational and Strategic Factors

  • Absolute control: On-premise gives banks direct control over infrastructure, data flows, and model updates without dependency on a third party's operational decisions
  • Vendor lock-in avoidance: Banks increasingly demand open ecosystems and portable AI models to avoid dependency on a single cloud provider
  • Latency and performance: Trading and risk models often require sub-millisecond latency that cloud deployments cannot guarantee
  • Audit and compliance: Supervisory bodies demand explicit contractual provisions covering security standards, compliance audits, and clear data control agreements — on-premise simplifies this chain

The Hybrid Reality

In practice, most large banks operate hybrid architectures: on-premise for the most sensitive and latency-critical AI workloads (trading models, core credit decisioning, AML systems), cloud for less sensitive workloads (document processing, customer analytics, internal productivity tools). The trend is toward cloud-agnostic deployment with consistent governance across environments, rather than a binary on-prem-vs-cloud choice.

2. Detailed Competitor Profiles

Bloomberg Terminal

What they do well
  • 325,000 subscribers. $31,980/year. $12B+ annual revenue.
  • BPIPE: real-time data feeds for virtually every asset class globally
  • BQL: programmable query language over financial data
  • PORT: portfolio analytics used by thousands of institutional investors
  • ASKB (Feb 2026): agentic AI interface over terminal data
  • BloombergGPT: 50.6B params, 709B tokens including proprietary FinPile
  • Workflow integration: OMS, EMS, compliance, messaging — the entire PM workflow
What they don't do
  • No simulation engine — retrieves and summarizes, doesn't project
  • PORT uses linear factor models — no regime dynamics
  • ASKB is RAG over existing data, not forward modeling
  • No counterfactual reasoning ("what if Fed hikes 50bps")

Honest assessment: Bloomberg could build this. They have the data, the distribution, and the engineering talent. If they decide financial world models matter, they will be the most dangerous competitor. The fact that they haven't built it yet doesn't mean they can't.

Microsoft MarS (ICLR 2025)

What they do well
  • Published at ICLR 2025 — peer-reviewed, not just a preprint
  • Market simulation engine with agent-based dynamics
  • Realistic order-book simulation with stylized facts preservation
  • Microsoft Research backing — virtually unlimited compute and talent
  • Open-source components available
What they don't do
  • Microstructure-level only — no macro-financial composition
  • Single-asset simulation, not multi-timescale economic dynamics
  • No continual learning (static model, offline training)
  • No reflexivity measurement (simulates agents, doesn't measure feedback)

Honest assessment: MarS is a real, working market simulator with peer review. RecWM proposes to work at a higher level of abstraction (macro-economic composition rather than order-book dynamics). These are complementary levels, not direct competitors — but MarS exists and RecWM doesn't.

Bridgewater Associates

What they do well
  • $160B AUM — the largest hedge fund in the world
  • The "Economic Machine" maps cause-and-effect across economic cycles
  • Processes 100M+ data points per trading decision
  • 40+ years of live performance data
  • Closest existing thing to a financial world model
What they don't do
  • Rules-based, not learned — human researchers code the causal graph
  • Cannot update its own ontology when new forces emerge
  • Internal infrastructure — not a product, not for sale
  • No formal reflexivity measurement

Honest assessment: Bridgewater's Economic Machine is what RecWM aspires to be — but learned rather than coded. They have 40 years of institutional knowledge about which economic forces compose and how. RecWM has equations. If Bridgewater decided to ML-ify their machine, they would start from a position of vastly superior domain knowledge.

Sooth Labs

What they do well
  • ~$50M raised at ~$335M valuation (April 2026)
  • Founded by Yaser Sheikh (ex-Meta VP) and Ruslan Salakhutdinov (ex-Apple AI)
  • Backed by Yann LeCun, Jeff Dean — top-tier ML credibility

What they don't do

Honest assessment: Sooth is orthogonal, not competitive. Their output ("probability of CPI > 4%") could be an input signal to RecWM. But they have $50M, a star team, and institutional credibility. We have zero of those things. Their existence validates the "world model for X" framing but also shows what "funded and staffed" looks like.

TradeFM / Time-Series Foundation Models

What they do well
  • TradeFM: 524M parameters, trained on massive financial time-series corpora
  • Chronos-2 (Amazon): probabilistic forecasting, zero-shot transfer
  • TimesFM (Google): 200M params, generalist time-series model
  • Moirai (Salesforce): multi-variate, any-frequency, any-horizon
  • Scale, compute, and engineering resources we cannot match
What they don't do
  • All offline-only — train once, deploy statically
  • No native continual learning (ELF and TS-Memory are post-hoc adapters)
  • No typed fragment structure — treat all series identically
  • No compositional reasoning about how series interact

Honest assessment: These models have massive scale advantages. If any of them adds native CL (which is technically straightforward for SSM-based architectures), they could subsume RecWM's core technical contribution. The gap is real today but fragile.

Macrocosm (J. Doyne Farmer)

What they do well
  • Founded by J. Doyne Farmer — pioneer of complexity economics, Santa Fe Institute
  • Agent-based economic simulation grounded in decades of academic work
  • Production-grade macro simulation for policy institutions
  • Real economic theory, not just ML pattern matching
What they don't do
  • Agent-based, not SSM-based — different computational paradigm
  • Macro-level focus, less granularity at portfolio level
  • Simulation requires explicit agent specification

Honest assessment: Farmer has spent 30+ years thinking about exactly this problem. His approach (agent-based complexity models) is theoretically more principled than RecWM's (learned latent dynamics). If Macrocosm produces good macro forecasts, it invalidates the need for a learned world model.

Quant Funds (Two Sigma, Citadel, DE Shaw, Man AHL, WorldQuant)

What they do well
  • Combined AUM ~$185B+ with decades of live performance
  • Massive ML infrastructure (thousands of GPUs, petabytes of data)
  • Top-tier talent — PhD researchers in ML, physics, math
  • Proven ability to extract alpha from statistical patterns
  • WorldQuant BRAIN: 375K users, crowdsourced alpha research
What they don't do
  • Correlation machines — find patterns, don't model why they exist
  • No compositional structure across economic forces
  • When regimes shift, patterns break (no explicit regime modeling)

Honest assessment: Any of these firms could build RecWM internally if they wanted to. They haven't — possibly because the approach doesn't work, or because they have approaches that work better. Their continued success using "simple" ML is evidence against the hypothesis that compositional world models are necessary.

5. The Actual Gap (If One Exists)

After honestly assessing what competitors do well, here is what remains as a potential gap:

The CL gap is real but fragile

No existing time-series foundation model supports native online learning. Chronos-2, TimesFM, Moirai, TradeFM are all offline-only. ELF (ICML 2025) and TS-Memory (KDD 2026) are post-hoc adapters bolted onto frozen backbones. Building CL into the architecture — not bolting it on — is a genuine vacancy in the literature.

Why it's fragile: SSM architectures (S4, S5, Mamba) have diagonal state matrices that make O(N) RTRL straightforward. Any team with SSM expertise could add native CL. The gap exists because nobody has prioritized it for financial applications, not because it's technically hard. Google, Amazon, or Salesforce could close this gap in a quarter.

The composition gap is speculative

No existing system treats economic signals as typed fragments with different timescales and explicit compositional structure. Standard approaches either treat all inputs identically (foundation models) or compose them manually (Bridgewater).

Why it's speculative: There is no empirical evidence that typed-fragment composition outperforms standard multi-variate time-series modeling. It's an aesthetic preference backed by economic intuition, not demonstrated results. The hypothesis needs testing (Bet 1 in the build plan).

The reflexivity gap is the most novel and most questionable

No deployed system explicitly measures and accounts for its own performative impact on markets. Perdomo et al. (ICML 2020) formalized the theory but nobody has operationalized it for financial world models.

Why it's questionable: For a model to have measurable performative impact, it must be deployed at sufficient scale to move markets. A research prototype has ε ≈ 0. The reflexivity story only becomes relevant if RecWM is widely adopted — a chicken-and-egg problem. The theoretical contribution (state-dependent ε(t)) is interesting regardless, but the practical value is distant.

6. Risks to the Thesis

The competitive thesis — that there is a real gap for compositional financial world models with native CL — faces several risks:

RiskProbabilityImpactWhat Would Happen
Foundation models add CLHighFatalIf Chronos-3 or TimesFM-2 ships with native online learning, RecWM's core technical differentiator disappears. Their scale advantage is insurmountable.
Typed composition doesn't helpMediumFatalIf treating series as typed fragments produces no measurable improvement over standard multi-variate modeling, the entire architecture is unnecessary complexity.
Bloomberg builds a simulation layerMediumSevereBloomberg has the data, distribution, and engineering to build this in 12 months. If they decide "financial world model" is a feature, they own the market.
Macrocosm succeedsMediumSevereIf agent-based macro simulation produces better forecasts than learned latent dynamics, RecWM's approach is the wrong paradigm.
Reflexivity is unmeasurableMedium-HighModerateIf ε(t) turns out to be noisy, constant, or unlearnable, the most novel contribution collapses. The rest of the system (typed CL) still works but loses its theoretical distinction.
Markets stay predictable enoughLow-MediumFatalIf simple models (ARIMA + regime switching) continue to perform "well enough" for institutional needs, there is no demand for compositional world models.
Bottom line. The competitive landscape is crowded with well-funded, well-staffed, battle-tested systems. RecWM's thesis — that a specific combination of typed fragments, native CL, and reflexivity measurement creates something meaningfully new — is plausible but unproven. Every competitor listed above has something RecWM doesn't: deployed code, paying customers, or both. The honest framing is not "this category is empty" but "there may be a gap at the intersection of CL + composition + reflexivity, and we'd like to test whether filling it produces useful results."
Caveat on "Economic World Models" as a Field

"EWM" is not an established research field. The term was coined by a single survey paper (Han et al., arXiv 2608.06020, August 2026) that retrospectively labeled existing work. The L1-L6 capability ladder is a useful organizing framework from that one paper, not an accepted community standard. The research threads below are real and well-cited; the framing that unifies them as "Economic World Models" is one survey's interpretation.

01

Han et al. — "From Economic Agents to Agentic Economies"

arXiv 2608.06020 · August 6, 2026 · Han, Li, Qian, Gu, Gao, Luo, Zha, Tao, Wang, Cong
Survey Field-naming (single paper)

This paper formally names the field of Economic World Models and defines an EWM as "a generative engine for economic environments: it predicts how an economy moves by modeling how agents inside observe, reason, act, interact, and adapt under economic institutions and constraints." The critical distinction from physical world models: economic state transitions are generated endogenously by agents themselves through beliefs, expectations, and strategic interactions.

The survey screened 7,836 candidate papers (6,008 from arXiv, 1,828 from UTD-24 business/economics journals, 1950–April 2026), validating 737 as genuine EWM papers through three-stage LLM-assisted classification.

The L1–L6 Capability Ladder

LevelNameAgent CapabilityEconomic WorldReal-World Link
L1Fixed Rule-Based Agent WorldsFixed rule-based agentsFixed rules; endogenous outcomesOffline
L2Adaptive Rule-Based Agent WorldsAdaptive symbolic/algorithmic agents (RL, evolutionary)Fixed rulesOffline
L3LLM-Based Autonomous Agent WorldsLLM-based with beliefs, memory, reasoningFixed rulesOffline
L4Self-Evolving Agent WorldsAgents acquire new strategies, skills, toolsFixed rulesOffline
L5Evolving Economic WorldsAdaptive, autonomous, self-evolvingInstitutions & rules evolve endogenouslyOffline
L6Sim-to-Real Economic TwinsAll adaptive componentsInternally evolving worldOnline correction against real observations

The stark finding: "Higher-level EWMs remain rare. L4 systems appear only recently. L5 systems are even rarer. L6 sim-to-real economic twins are nearly absent." Most literature clusters at L1–L3. The arXiv vs. journals split is telling: arXiv pushes AI agent capabilities (L1–L3); business/economics journals concentrate on L1–L2 with stronger economic discipline but less AI sophistication.

The formal state is defined as s_t = (x_t, {z_t^i}, {b_t^i}, I_t) with five operators: belief update, action selection, individual state update, aggregation, and institutional/rule evolution. L6 maintains a two-loop architecture: an inner loop generates endogenous dynamics, an outer loop performs real-time correction against observed data.

RecWM Relevance

RecWM's design targets L6. The survey identifies this rung as empty, and the formal framework aligns with RecWM's architecture (typed world fragments = state representation, constraint fields = the institutional layer I_t, reflexive loops = the belief-update operator B^i feeding back through aggregation G). The paper references interventions in state transitions but does not develop counterfactual/interventional benchmarks — confirming the identified opportunity to build the field's missing interventional evaluation benchmark.

02

World Model Architectures (2025–2026)

JEPA, Genie 2, World Labs, Sooth Labs

JEPA — Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture

V-JEPA 2 (June 2025) scaled to 1.2B parameters trained on 1M+ hours of video, achieving 30x faster physical reasoning than NVIDIA Cosmos. The action-conditioned variant (V-JEPA 2-AC) enables zero-shot robotic manipulation. LeCun left Meta in November 2025 to start a company pursuing this vision. Extensions already exist: VL-JEPA (language), Audio-JEPA, MTS-JEPA (time-series), LeWorldModel (RL).

The core principle — predict in a learned abstract space, ignore stochastic noise, learn dynamics — is directly importable to economics. An economic JEPA would learn latent representations of economic states and predict transitions in that space, sidestepping the intractable problem of modeling every transaction. The challenge: financial data is sparse, irregular, and multimodal (unlike dense video frames), requiring different encoder architectures.

Genie 2/3 (DeepMind)

Genie 2 (Dec 2024) generates playable 3D worlds from a single image. Genie 3 (August 2025) reached 720p/24fps with one-minute consistency. Architecture: video autoencoder + transformer dynamics model + classifier-free guidance. The encode-predict-decode-conditioned-on-actions pattern is the right skeleton for an economic simulator — the actions are interventions, the decoded output is the counterfactual world state.

World Labs (Fei-Fei Li)

Raised $1.23B total, valued at $5B. Product "Marble" (launched February 2026) generates persistent, editable 3D worlds. Most important contribution is Li's June 2026 taxonomy: Renderer (generates output), Simulator (maintains state under actions), Planner (maps observations to actions). An economic world model is fundamentally a Simulator in this framework.

Sooth Labs (April 2026)

~$50M from Felicis at ~$335M valuation. Backed by LeCun and Jeff Dean. Describes itself as "a world model for global foresight" — calibrated, auditable forecasting of geopolitical, economic, and real-world events. Founded by Yaser Sheikh (ex-Meta VP) and Russ Salakhutdinov (Hinton student, Apple's first AI research head).

Other Finance-Adjacent World Models

  • EconAgent: LLM-powered macro simulation with heterogeneous agents
  • Bank of Japan experiment: 1,000 GPT-4o-mini agents simulating consumption/competition. Results matched theory but BoJ flagged LLMs fail in novel scenarios
  • "Three-in-One" World Model (May 2026): Frozen DBM beliefs + intervention adapter for counterfactual marketing analysis
Field-Wide Gap

A major April 2026 survey (400+ papers) proposes L1 Predictor / L2 Simulator / L3 Evolver, where L3 Evolver (self-revising) remains aspirational across all domains — not just economics. No world model in any field is self-correcting against real-world observations. The L6/L3-Evolver capability is empty everywhere.

RecWM Relevance

All current world model companies build for physical/visual worlds or exogenous event forecasting. None model endogenous economic dynamics with reflexive feedback. Sooth is the closest vocabulary competitor but architecturally orthogonal: it forecasts what the world will do (exogenous), while RecWM models what happens when you act (endogenous, interventional). Sooth's output is plausibly an input signal to RecWM. JEPA's latent-space prediction is the most transferable architectural idea. Li's Renderer/Simulator/Planner taxonomy correctly categorizes RecWM as a Simulator, which is the hardest of the three to build.

03

Microsoft MarS — Market Simulation Engine

arXiv 2409.07486 · ICLR 2025 · Microsoft Research
ICLR 2025

MarS is an autoregressive Transformer-based foundation model that generates order-level market data. The core insight: treat order flow as a language and apply GPT-style next-token prediction. This is a genuine engineering advance over price-series or return-distribution simulators.

Architecture: The Large Market Model

  • Order Model: Causal Transformer on individual orders. Each order tokenized with its LOB state. Scaled to 1.02B parameters, trained on 32B tokens.
  • Order-Batch Model: Autoregressive Transformer on time-bucketed order batches. Scaled to 3B parameters, trained on 10B tokens.
  • Ensemble: Batch model generates candidate distributions; order model fills in individual orders. Balances microstructure fidelity with macro realism.

Supports controlled generation via natural language descriptions ("flash crash," "circuit breaker"), interactive order injection, and historical conditioning. The model reproduces the empirical Square-Root Law of market impact and discovers three additional impact factors (resiliency, LOB pressure, LOB depth).

Performance: The 1.02B order model outperforms DeepLOB by ~13.5% at 1-minute and ~22.4% at 5-minute horizons for price trend prediction.

What MarS Does Not Handle

DimensionMarSCausal / Reflexive Approach
CausalityCorrelational (next-token prediction)Interventional (do-calculus, counterfactuals)
ReflexivityMechanical feedback via clearing house onlyEndogenous: predictions alter the system
Agent modelImplicit (single learned distribution)Explicit heterogeneous agents with beliefs
Regime changesAssumes stationarityStructural break detection in causal graph
PerformativityNot modeledCore feature

MarS treats the market as a natural phenomenon to be replicated. It can tell you "what order flow looks like given this history," but cannot answer "what happens to order flow when everyone starts using this model's predictions." Follow-up work: DiffLOB (2026, diffusion models for counterfactual LOB) and TradeFM (2026, 524M-param generative Transformer for trade-flow).

RecWM Relevance

MarS proves foundation-model scaling laws hold on order-level market data — an important existence proof. But it is architecturally incapable of modeling the most important feature of financial markets: that the models people use to understand markets change the markets themselves. RecWM's reflexive loop and constraint field are precisely the missing layers. MarS-generated order flow could serve as a realistic environment substrate underneath RecWM's causal/reflexive architecture.

04

Kronos — Foundation Model for the Language of Financial Markets

arXiv 2508.02739 · AAAI 2026 · Shi, Fu, Chen, Zhao, Xu, Zhang, Li
AAAI 2026 Finance-specific FM

Kronos is a decoder-only autoregressive Transformer built in two stages. First, a K-line Tokenizer (Transformer autoencoder with Binary Spherical Quantization) converts continuous OHLCV(A) candlestick bars into discrete tokens. Each bar produces two hierarchical subtokens: a coarse subtoken encoding market direction, regime, and bar magnitude, and a fine subtoken encoding wick structure, intra-bar volatility, and volume. Vocabulary size is 220, factorized. Second, standard causal Transformer pre-training with RoPE and RMSNorm, predicting coarse then fine subtokens. Model sizes from 4.1M (Mini) to 499.2M (Large). Code open-source (MIT) at github.com/shiyu-coder/Kronos.

The "12B K-lines" are 12 billion candlestick records from 45 global exchanges (equities, futures, FX, crypto) across 7 time granularities (1-min through weekly). This is domain-specific financial pre-training, not general time series data.

Results (benchmarked against 25 baselines including TimesFM, Chronos, Moirai)

  • Price forecasting: 93% higher RankIC over the leading TSFM baseline
  • Volatility forecasting: 9% lower MAE than alternatives
  • Synthetic K-line generation: 22% improvement in generative fidelity
  • Investment simulation: highest annualized excess return and information ratio
  • Test-time scaling via Monte Carlo averaging of stochastic samples further improves forecasts

The critical distinction from general TSFMs: Kronos does not compete on standard general forecasting benchmarks (M4, Monash). Its gains are measured on financial tasks specifically. The hierarchical tokenization — separating regime/direction from fine-grained volatility — suggests economic state variables can be factored into macro-regime and micro-dynamics layers.

Competitors: TimesFM (Google, 200M params, 100B time points), Chronos (Amazon, T5 architecture), Moirai (Salesforce, any-variate attention), Timer, Lag-Llama, MOMENT, UniTS.

RecWM Relevance

Kronos validates that financial-domain foundation models dramatically outperform general-purpose TSFMs on financial tasks. For RecWM, it could serve as the perception backbone — encoding raw market data into latent states that feed the causal/reflexive layers. The hierarchical coarse/fine tokenization maps naturally to RecWM's multi-scale architecture. But the limitation is fundamental: Kronos is purely autoregressive with no causal structure, no intervention semantics, and no mechanism for structural breaks. It predicts what comes next, not what would happen under intervention.

05

FANTOM — Regime-Switching Temporal Causal Discovery

arXiv 2506.17065 · NeurIPS 2025 · Rahmani & Frossard (EPFL)
NeurIPS 2025

Full title: "Flow based approach for Dynamic Temporal Causal models with non-Gaussian or Heteroscedastic Noises." FANTOM addresses a fundamental problem: the causal structure itself changes across regimes, and noise distributions are non-Gaussian and heteroscedastic — exactly the conditions in economic data.

Architecture

FANTOM jointly infers three things: (i) the number of regimes K, (ii) regime boundaries/indices, and (iii) each regime's causal DAG. Two main components:

  • Conditional normalizing flows (CNFs) — spline flows handle heteroscedastic noise. A hypernetwork predicts spline parameters respecting the causal graph structure (only parents influence each variable's noise distribution).
  • Bayesian Expectation Maximization — E-step updates posterior regime assignments via Bayes rule; M-step maximizes observational likelihood with Bernoulli-distributed edges, Gumbel-softmax gradient estimation, and augmented Lagrangian for acyclicity enforcement.

Regime number discovery: starts with more windows than expected, progressively merges regimes with insufficient samples. Regimes can reoccur non-consecutively.

Identifiability Results

  • Theorem 4.2 (stationary): temporal heteroscedastic causal models are identifiable under acyclicity and mild noise assumptions.
  • Theorem 4.3 (non-stationary): the number of regimes K, their indices, and their DAGs are identifiable up to permutation.

Results

Synthetic data (5 nodes, 2 regimes): ~95% regime detection accuracy, outperforms CASTOR by 15–20% in structural Hamming distance. Robust under t-distributed and mixture noise. 30–40% improvement over stationary baselines on the Causal Chambers real-world benchmark when heteroscedasticity is present.

Related: "Systems with Switching Causal Relations: A Meta-Causal Perspective" (Willig et al., ICLR 2025 spotlight) introduces meta-causal states grouping models by equivalent qualitative behavior. "On the Identifiability of Regime-Switching Models with Multi-Lag Dependencies" (Balsells-Rodas et al., arXiv 2601.03325) proves identifiability for multi-lag switching models.

RecWM Relevance

FANTOM maps directly to RecWM's constraint field layer. When the economy shifts regimes (the Greif-Laitin quasi-parameter mechanism), the underlying causal graph changes — FANTOM provides the inference machinery for this. The identifiability guarantees (Theorems 4.2, 4.3) ensure the discovered causal structure is the true one, not an artifact. The flow-based noise model handles heavy-tailed financial distributions. A natural architecture: FANTOM discovers regime-specific causal skeletons, Kronos-style autoregressive models forecast within each regime, and RecWM's reflexive loop wraps both in a performative feedback mechanism. This is "crisis as lattice descent" from the World Fragment Algebra, grounded in actual causal discovery with formal identifiability.

06

Decision-Focused Learning

SPO+ (Elmachtoub & Grigas) · Online DFL · ICLR 2026 search ongoing
ICLR 2026 Active frontier

Decision-focused learning (DFL) inverts the standard ML pipeline. Instead of training a prediction model to minimize forecast error (MSE) and then feeding predictions to an optimizer, DFL trains the prediction model end-to-end to minimize downstream decision loss — the regret of the decisions made using those predictions.

Key Foundational Results

  • SPO+ (Elmachtoub & Grigas, 2022): A convex surrogate loss for predict-then-optimize problems. Shows that optimizing for decision quality rather than prediction accuracy leads to better decisions, especially when the prediction-to-decision mapping is nonlinear.
  • Donti et al. (2017): Task-based end-to-end learning through differentiable optimization layers (OptNet). Differentiate through the optimizer to backpropagate decision loss to the predictor.
  • Wilder et al. (2019): Decision-focused learning for combinatorial optimization on graphs.

Online DFL (Capitaine et al., ICLR 2026)

"Online Decision-Focused Learning" extends DFL from the batch setting to online non-stationary environments where data distribution and optimization objectives evolve. Two algorithms: DF-FTPL (Follow-The-Perturbed-Leader) and DF-OGD (Online Gradient Descent), using regularization to restore differentiability and perturbation with near-optimal oracles for non-convexity. These provide the first provable regret guarantees for online decision-focused learning, including both static and dynamic regret bounds.

Key Results from 2025–2026

  • Prediction inflation: Lee et al. (May 2025) show SPO training systematically overestimates returns for assets in the optimal portfolio and underestimates excluded assets. These biases improve decision quality despite increasing raw MSE. DFL's gradient tilts errors by the inverse covariance matrix.
  • Regret = Covariance (arXiv 2605.14019): For linear-quadratic problems, decision regret equals a specific covariance structure — closed-form link between prediction quality and decision quality.
  • Solver-free approaches (June–Aug 2026): Multiple papers eliminate the need to differentiate through solvers entirely, using surrogate optimization layers and affine-parametric QPs with warm-starting.
  • Portfolio applications: Wang & Hasuike (Jan 2026) apply SPO to US ETF data with transaction costs; strong robustness during COVID-regime. "Decision-Focused Learning for Goal-Based Investing" (Quantitative Finance 26(1), 2026) enhances portfolio feasibility under uncertainty.
Critical Insight

As DFL optimization strengthens, MSE can increase exponentially while regret decreases. A DFL-trained economic world model will look "wrong" by traditional forecasting metrics while making better decisions. This has deep implications for model validation: you cannot evaluate a decision-focused world model by prediction accuracy alone. The model learns the decision-relevant covariance structure of uncertain parameters, not their point forecasts.

RecWM Relevance

DFL is the training objective RecWM should use. Train the world model to minimize decision regret, not forecast MSE. This aligns with RCE's emphasis on construction over prediction: quality is measured by whether it enables better actions, not by prediction accuracy. The DPO component in the formal core is essentially DFL applied to the world model's belief-action loop. The critical open frontier: Online DFL under performativity — where decisions change the distribution that generates future data. This maps exactly onto RecWM's reflexive loop and has no prior art combining both frameworks.

07

Structured State Spaces (S4 / Mamba) in Finance

CMDMamba · CryptoMamba-SSM · StockMamba · Various 2025–2026
Emerging

SSMs (S4, S5, Mamba, Mamba-2) are gaining significant traction in financial time series. Their core advantage: O(n) complexity versus O(n²) for Transformers, with Mamba's selective state mechanism learning which inputs matter contextually — ignoring noise in calm markets, attending to everything during volatility spikes.

Key Finance-Specific Results

  • CMDMamba (Frontiers in AI, 2025): Dual-layer Mamba architecture with dual convolutional feed-forward networks. Captures price fluctuations at both micro and macro levels. Near-linear time complexity enables real-time processing for risk management.
  • CryptoMamba-SSM (IEEE, 2026): Linear-complexity volatility prediction for cryptocurrency. Demonstrates effective capture of long-range dependencies in highly non-stationary crypto markets.
  • StockMamba (Mathematics, 2026): Replaces static market gating with a Mamba-2 state-space model that scans market regime dynamics in linear time. Uses a RegimeClassifier that assigns one of six regimes (Normal, Stressed, Noisy, Informed, Trending, Mean-Reverting).
  • Attention-Mamba (ACM, 2025): Hybrid architecture integrating Mamba with attention mechanisms for stock prediction. Captures both long-range dependencies (via Mamba) and local salient patterns (via attention).

Can Mamba Replace Transformers in Finance?

The emerging consensus: no, but it complements them strategically. SSMs excel at efficient session-level state maintenance (processing millions of tick events), while specialized Transformers retain advantages for precise limit-order-book analysis. Hybrid systems combining both are the emerging pattern. Practitioners report 1–3ms inference for Mamba versus 10–50ms for comparable Transformers — material for strategies with tight latency budgets.

Critical gaps: lack of head-to-head comparisons on identical datasets, limited interpretability tooling, and absence of stress-testing through actual market crises.

RecWM Relevance

SSMs are a strong candidate for RecWM's temporal backbone. Their linear complexity allows processing the long sequences needed for economic modeling (months/years of data, not just minutes). StockMamba's regime classification is particularly interesting — it shows SSMs can learn to detect regime changes, which could feed into RecWM's constraint field layer. The continuous-time formulation of S4 (via HiPPO initialization) also connects naturally to the continuous-time dynamics in active inference's belief update equations. Hybrid Mamba-Transformer architecture is likely the right engineering choice for RecWM's perception layer.

08

Performative Prediction — Latest Results

Perdomo et al. 2020 · Hardt & Mendler-Dünner 2025 · Lee & Zrnic 2026 · Rodemann et al. ICML 2026
Stat. Science 2025 ICML 2026

The Foundation: Perdomo et al. (ICML 2020)

Introduced performative prediction — the framework where deploying a predictive model changes the distribution it aims to predict. The convergence condition ε < γ/β (Theorem 3.5) guarantees repeated risk minimization converges to a performatively stable point at linear rate, where ε is distribution sensitivity, γ is strong convexity, and β is smoothness. This is proven tight by Proposition 3.6.

Three distinct thresholds on the same parameters:

  • ε < γ/β — RRM contraction (Perdomo Thm 3.5)
  • ε < γ/[(β+γ)(1+1.5ηβ)] — RGD convergence (Thm 3.8)
  • ε ≤ γ/(2β) — performative risk convex, optimum findable (Miller, Perdomo & Zrnic ICML 2021, Thm 3.1)

Hardt & Mendler-Dünner: "Performative Prediction: Past and Future" (Statistical Science, Aug 2025)

The definitive survey. Traces the intellectual history of performativity from economics and social science to ML. Key contribution: distinguishing between learning (adapting to changed distributions) and steering (influencing behavior through predictions), and introducing the concept of performative power — a platform's capacity to shape participant behavior. Notes that performativity has been fundamental to economics and finance but absent from ML development.

Lee & Zrnic: "Partially Performative Prediction" (June 2026)

Extends the framework to the realistic case where distribution shift is both endogenous and exogenous simultaneously. Key insight: in practice, shift is rarely purely one or the other — models influence future data through decisions they support, while the world drifts for reasons beyond the learner's control. Defines online analogues of performative stability and optimality that track evolving partially performative environments. Analyzes when repeated retraining successfully adapts.

Rodemann et al.: "Performative Learning Theory" (ICML 2026)

Embeds performative prediction into statistical learning theory. Proves generalization bounds under performative effects on samples, populations, or both. Key finding: increased model influence on data generation correlates with reduced learning capacity. A fundamental trade-off: predictors face a choice between significantly affecting outcomes and extracting insights from data. Counterintuitively, retraining on performatively distorted samples can improve generalization guarantees. Uses min-max and min-min risk functionals in Wasserstein space. Validated on German labor market data (1975–2017).

Adjacent: Reflexivity as Prompt (Park, May 2026)

Tests whether making LLMs aware of Soros's reflexivity theory improves financial forecasting. Evaluates GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Pro on the dot-com bubble and GFC. Finding: reflexivity awareness improves directional accuracy for some models but higher directional accuracy does not guarantee better risk-adjusted returns. The prediction-to-profit gap is itself evidence for performativity.

Open Gaps

Endogenous ε: In all existing work, the sensitivity parameter ε is a fixed constant. Making ε_t learned and state-dependent — so the system dynamically crosses γ/β — turns a static condition into a crisis mechanism. Nobody has done this.

The unnamed gap: The region γ/(2β) < ε < γ/β is performatively stable but not optimizable. This may be where real economies live. Unnamed in the literature.

Counterperformativity: MacKenzie & Bamford (2018) named it. The performative prediction survey explicitly lists it as out of scope. No mathematics exist.

Proper scoring under performativity: Boeken, Zoeter & Mooij (arXiv 2510.21335) proved classical proper scoring rules fail under performativity. Fix: divergence-based scoring.

RecWM Relevance

Performative prediction is the mathematical foundation for RecWM's reflexive loop. The convergence condition ε < γ/β is exactly the invertibility requirement for implicit differentiation in a differentiable performative-equilibrium (DEQ) layer. The invention surface is clear: (1) endogenous ε as a crisis mechanism, (2) DEQ layer over a learned market-response map, (3) formal counterperformativity theory. Lee & Zrnic's partially performative framework is directly applicable: real economic data contains both endogenous and exogenous shift, and RecWM needs to handle both.

09

Active Inference in Economics

Friston (FEP) · Factorised AI for Multi-Agent (AAMAS 2025) · Agentic Finance (Entropy, March 2026)
Embryonic for econ

The Framework

Active inference, rooted in Karl Friston's Free Energy Principle, posits that agents perceive and act to minimize variational free energy with respect to a generative model of their environment. It unifies perception, action, and learning under a single objective. The key distinction from reinforcement learning: agents don't maximize reward but minimize surprise (free energy), which naturally balances exploitation (pursuing preferences) with exploration (reducing uncertainty).

Multi-Agent Strategic Interactions (AAMAS 2025)

"Factorised Active Inference for Strategic Multi-Agent Interactions" integrates active inference with game theory. Each agent maintains explicit, individual-level beliefs about the internal states of other agents. The ensemble-level expected free energy (EFE) characterizes basins of attraction of games with multiple Nash Equilibria — and reveals that EFE is not necessarily minimised at the aggregate level. This is a dynamical systems approach to equilibrium selection rather than a static one.

Agentic Finance (Entropy, March 2026)

A portfolio management framework extending active inference to non-stationary financial environments. Integrates inference, control, and execution under endogenous uncertainty. Key finding: the Passivity Paradox — frozen belief transfer outperforms naive adaptive learning. A Professional Agent achieves a Sharpe ratio of 0.39 while its adaptive counterpart degrades to −0.28. The paper shows that classical valuation models emerge as limiting cases when epistemic components vanish.

Niche Construction (Constant & Friston)

The dual-flow formulation dμ/dt = −∇F(μ|s), dη/dt = −∇F(η|a) — the niche infers the organism back. Applied to economics: markets adapt to participants, and participants adapt to markets, simultaneously. This is the formal machinery for modeling reflexive co-evolution.

Industry: VERSES AI / Genius

VERSES AI is developing the Genius THINK module using active inference for finance — understanding, modeling, and driving higher returns without high volatility. They claim active inference is "much more efficient than current deep learning methods" due to its ability to decide where to focus, improving sample efficiency.

RecWM Relevance

Active inference is one of RecWM's three formal substrates. The Passivity Paradox result is particularly interesting: it suggests that in non-stationary environments, not updating beliefs can outperform naive adaptation — exactly the kind of counterintuitive result a reflexive world model should predict (aggressive adaptation creates performative feedback that destabilizes the system). The dual-flow niche construction formulation maps directly to RecWM's reflexive loop. The AAMAS 2025 result on EFE not minimizing at the aggregate level suggests that individual rationality under active inference does not imply collective optimality — a formal version of the performativity problem.

10

Causal Representation Learning

iVAE (Khemakhem et al.) · Hyvärinen nonlinear ICA · CHiLD (NeurIPS 2025) · CLeaR 2026
NeurIPS 2025 CLeaR 2026

The Central Question

When can you recover the true latent causal variables from high-dimensional observations? Standard representation learning (autoencoders, VAEs) can learn some representation, but without additional structure, the learned variables are unidentifiable — infinitely many representations explain the data equally well.

Key Identifiability Results

  • iVAE (Khemakhem, Kingma, Monti & Hyvärinen, 2020): Shows that nonlinear ICA becomes identifiable when you have access to auxiliary variables (e.g., time indices, domain labels). The conditional independence structure in the latent space, given the auxiliary variable, is sufficient for identifiability up to permutation and element-wise transformation.
  • Hyvärinen et al. (Annals ISM, 2024): "Identifiability of latent-variable and structural-equation models: from linear to nonlinear." Comprehensive treatment connecting nonlinear ICA to structural equation models.
  • Li et al. (2024): Relaxed the number of auxiliary variables needed to n+1 for subspace identifiability.
  • Sparse mixing: Recent work shows that sparsity in the generation process can substitute for auxiliary variables as an identifiability condition.

Temporal Causal Representations

  • CHiLD (NeurIPS 2025): Causally Hierarchical Latent Dynamics framework. Shows the joint distribution of hierarchical latent variables can be uniquely determined using three conditionally independent observations. Exploits natural sparsity of hierarchical structure. Implements via variational inference with normalizing flow-based hierarchical prior networks.
  • Temporal CRL with instantaneous dependence (ICLR 2025): Extends identifiability to settings where causal effects can be instantaneous — critical for financial markets.
  • Latent SDEs (June 2026): "Disentangling Continuous-Time Latent Dynamics: Identifiability of Latent SDEs via Diffusion Shifts." Tackles identifiability in continuous-time, connecting to the SDE formulations used in finance.

The JASA 2026 Perspective

"Toward Interpretable Deep Generative Models via Causal Representation Learning" (Journal of the American Statistical Association, April 2026) frames CRL as the path to interpretable deep generative models, arguing that causal structure provides the missing constraint that makes deep models both identifiable and interpretable.

RecWM Relevance

CRL provides the formal foundation for RecWM's perception layer: given raw economic data (prices, flows, text, filings), can you recover the latent causal variables (sentiment regimes, credit conditions, liquidity states) that drive the economy? The identifiability results say yes, under conditions: you need either auxiliary variables (which time indices provide naturally in economic data), sparsity in the causal mechanism, or interventional data. CHiLD's hierarchical structure maps to RecWM's multi-scale architecture (micro transactions, meso sectors, macro economy). The latent SDE identifiability work connects directly to the continuous-time formulation in active inference. CLeaR 2026 (April 2026, Cambridge MA) is the venue for this community.

Synthesis: Where RecWM Would Sit (If Built)

The field of Economic World Models was formally named in August 2026, and the territory is almost entirely unmapped above L3. The existing work clusters into three camps that do not talk to each other:

  1. Foundation model camp (MarS, Kronos, time series FMs): Scale and statistical fidelity, no causality, no reflexivity. Treats markets as weather.
  2. Causal/structural camp (FANTOM, CRL, performative prediction): Theoretical depth, identifiability results, but no systems at scale. Treats markets as mechanisms.
  3. Agent camp (LLM agents, active inference, multi-agent games): Models beliefs and strategic interaction, but in toy environments. Treats markets as games.

RecWM's hypothesis is that you need all three simultaneously: the perception fidelity of foundation models, the causal structure of the mechanism camp, and the reflexive agency of the game camp. No existing system combines them. The L6 rung is empty.

Three potential research gaps (untested):

  1. Interventional evaluation benchmark — the field has no way to score whether a world model answers "what if" questions correctly. Building this would be a genuine contribution regardless of RecWM's success.
  2. Endogenous ε in performative prediction — making the sensitivity parameter learned and state-dependent turns a static convergence condition into a dynamic crisis mechanism. Mathematically clean, no prior art.
  3. DEQ layer for performative equilibrium — the contraction condition ε < γ/β is exactly the invertibility requirement for implicit differentiation. A differentiable equilibrium layer over a learned market-response map is a novel construction that borrows a proven condition.
