Product Architecture Research

Making RecWM the Most Loved Financial Product Ever Built

Seven psychological dimensions of product addiction, mapped to specific design recommendations for the Reflexive Constructive World Model. Each mechanism is grounded in behavioral research; each recommendation connects to a concrete RecWM capability.

Treasury4 · August 2026 · 7 Fragments · 42 Recommendations
01

The Bloomberg Addiction: Keyboard Speed, Social Lock-in, and the Single Pane of Glass

Core Mechanism

Bloomberg's 325,000+ subscribers at ~$25K/year stay because of compound switching costs: muscle memory (keyboard shortcuts faster than any GUI), social network lock-in (IB Chat processes 200M+ messages/day), data monopoly (fixed-income datasets that exist nowhere else), and the sunk cost of a brutal learning curve that, once conquered, becomes a moat against competitors.

Why Bloomberg Users Refuse to Leave

A power user can check 11 data points on a bond, message a trade idea to hundreds of counterparties, pull 3 research pieces, and forward 5 news items—all in 60 seconds, never touching the mouse. The command-line grammar (AAPL Equity GO, TOP GO) is faster than any modern GUI because it eliminates the parse-scan-click loop entirely. After 2–3 years, this becomes involuntary motor memory. Switching to Refinitiv doesn't just feel slower; the user's fingers literally don't know how to work there.

IB Chat is the hidden fortress. With 200 million messages per day and binding trade execution within the chat window, Bloomberg is Wall Street's social network. Leaving Bloomberg means leaving the network—cutting yourself off from counterparties, research desks, and deal flow. Quotes in IB Chat are legally binding. Compliance systems are built on top of it. The messaging layer is the moat, not the data.

Bloomberg's 24/7 helpdesk answers in seconds—not minutes, seconds. This creates an experience unlike any other enterprise software: you are never stuck. The learning curve is brutal, but the safety net is always there, creating a paradox of difficulty and support that accelerates skill acquisition.

"The Bloomberg keyboard is ugly, the interface is from 1990, and the price is obscene. But after 10 years of using it, asking me to switch is like asking me to write with my left hand."

— Senior PM, multi-strategy hedge fund

RecWM Design Recommendations

R1 Build a command grammar, not just a chat interface

RecWM must support a terse command language alongside natural language. SIM liquidity-drain EM 30d should instantly spawn a scenario. STRESS portfolio tail-risk -2sigma should run a stress test. Power users need to be faster in RecWM than in any alternative. The command language should be learnable in layers: natural language first, then progressively shorter aliases as the user develops proficiency.

Mechanism: Motor memory lock-in + progressive skill mastery

R2 Make the world model query faster than looking at Bloomberg

When a PM wonders "what's driving EM credit spreads today?"—the answer should appear in <2 seconds with causal attribution across all 7 fragments. Bloomberg shows you data; RecWM should show you the mechanism. The speed advantage must be visceral and immediate.

Mechanism: Speed superiority creates preference; preference creates habit

R3 Embed messaging into simulation

When a PM creates a stress-test scenario, they should be able to share it with their team in one action—not as a screenshot, but as a live, interactive simulation that colleagues can fork, modify, and run against their own books. This is IB Chat for world models: the social layer isn't separate from the analytical layer.

Mechanism: Social network lock-in via shared analytical objects

R4 Invest in a support model that answers in seconds, not tickets

RecWM's AI itself should serve as the "helpdesk"—context-aware, able to explain any output, teach any feature, and guide any workflow. A PM should never feel stuck. "Why did the world model predict this?" should always have an answer. This is Bloomberg's helpdesk, automated and omnipresent.

Mechanism: Difficulty + instant support = accelerated mastery + loyalty

R5 Own proprietary data that exists nowhere else

RecWM's world-model state itself is proprietary data. The causal graph connecting Liquidity, Momentum, Risk, Credit, Structure, Sentiment, and Policy doesn't exist in Bloomberg, Refinitiv, or any feed. The world model's beliefs—its probability distributions over regime states, its causal attributions, its scenario forecasts—are a dataset that only RecWM can provide. Make this explicit: "This insight is derived from 7-fragment causal inference. No other system produces this."

Mechanism: Data monopoly creates irreplaceability

R6 Build the single pane of glass for portfolio intelligence

Bloomberg's power is that everything is in one place. RecWM must unify: world-model state, portfolio exposure, scenario simulation, risk analytics, historical analogs, and team communication. Every context switch to another tool is a failure. The PM should be able to go from "what's happening in the world?" to "what does it mean for my book?" to "what should I do?" to "here's the trade" without leaving RecWM.

Mechanism: Context-switch elimination creates dependency

02

Developer Tool Love: In-Flow, Progressive Disclosure, and the Autocomplete Dopamine Hit

Core Mechanism

Tools like Copilot, Cursor, and VS Code earn fanatical devotion through flow-state preservation: they work inline (no alt-tab), anticipate intent (autocomplete dopamine), disclose complexity progressively (simple start, infinite depth), and provide safety nets (undo everything) that encourage bold experimentation.

Why Developers Become Evangelists

Research consistently shows context switching costs ~23 minutes to refocus. Copilot and Cursor eliminated this by embedding intelligence directly in the editor. The user never leaves their workflow. The cognitive cost of "let me look that up" drops to zero. This is why inline tools beat dashboard tools every time.

The autocomplete dopamine hit is neurologically real. Variable ratio reinforcement—the same mechanism that makes slot machines addictive—operates when Copilot sometimes predicts exactly what you wanted. The brain releases more dopamine in anticipation of a reward than in receiving it. When the prediction is unpredictably excellent, the user enters a state of heightened engagement, watching for the next good suggestion.

VS Code's progressive disclosure is a masterclass: a new user sees a text editor; a power user sees a programmable development environment. Every feature is discoverable but none is forced. The user always feels "I'm learning more" without ever feeling "I'm overwhelmed." This creates a perpetual sense of growing mastery.

Git's version control gives developers courage. When you can always revert, you take risks you'd never take otherwise. This is why developers experiment more in version-controlled environments—the safety net doesn't just prevent loss, it changes behavior.

RecWM Design Recommendations

R7 Build world-model intelligence inline, not in a separate dashboard

RecWM should surface insights inside the PM's existing workflow—next to their positions, inside their risk reports, alongside their trade blotter. The world model's opinion should appear as an annotation on reality, not a separate app to visit. Consider: a sidebar that shows the world-model state for whatever the PM is looking at, updating in real time.

Mechanism: Flow-state preservation via zero context switching

R8 Autocomplete for scenarios

When a PM starts typing a scenario hypothesis ("What if China..."), RecWM should autocomplete with world-model-informed suggestions: "...devalues by 5%?", "...restricts capital outflows?", "...accelerates treasury liquidation?" Each suggestion should be grounded in the current world-model state, not generic. The Tab-to-accept pattern from Copilot should work here. Some suggestions will be surprisingly prescient; this variable reward drives engagement.

Mechanism: Variable ratio reinforcement via autocomplete + anticipation dopamine

R9 Progressive disclosure: simple surface, infinite depth

Layer 1: A single view showing "World Model State: Normal / Stressed / Crisis" with the dominant driver. Layer 2: Click to see all 7 fragments and their interactions. Layer 3: Click any fragment to see the causal graph, historical analogs, and probability distributions. Layer 4: Query the model directly in natural language or command grammar. Layer 5: Write custom simulations. Each layer is discoverable from the previous one but never forced.

Mechanism: Perpetual mastery curve prevents boredom and overwhelm

R10 Version control for scenarios and simulations

Every scenario the PM creates should be versioned. They should be able to fork a scenario, modify assumptions, compare branches, and revert to any previous state. "What did I assume last Tuesday when I ran this stress test?" should be instantly answerable. This safety net encourages experimental thinking: the PM can simulate wild scenarios without fear of losing their careful analysis.

Mechanism: Safety nets increase risk-taking and engagement

R11 Let users customize and extend the world model

Power users should be able to add custom fragments, define custom risk factors, create custom scenario templates, and build custom dashboards. Like VS Code extensions, this transforms RecWM from "their tool" to "my tool." The customization effort creates IKEA-effect attachment, and the resulting configuration becomes part of the PM's professional identity.

Mechanism: Customization creates identity + IKEA-effect attachment

R12 Show the "ghost suggestion"

Like Copilot's grayed-out code suggestion, RecWM should show faint "ghost" insights at the edge of the PM's current view. "The world model sees elevated correlation between your top 3 positions..." appears as a ghost suggestion that the PM can accept (expand) or dismiss. This creates the "it reads my mind" feeling without being intrusive.

Mechanism: Anticipation of intent builds trust and dependency

03

The Next-Question Loop: Curiosity Gaps, Zeigarnik Effect, and Escalating Stakes

Core Mechanism

Perplexity and ChatGPT created addictive loops through curiosity gaps (partial information that demands completion), the Zeigarnik effect (incomplete tasks that occupy the mind), and variable ratio reinforcement (unpredictably valuable discoveries). A world model that detects regime shifts and offers branching simulations creates even stronger loops because the stakes are real money.

The Psychology of "One More Question"

George Loewenstein's information gap theory explains why partial information is irresistible: when we perceive a gap between what we know and what we want to know, curiosity becomes almost painful. Perplexity exploits this by always showing "Related Questions"—each one a new gap. A world model that says "Liquidity fragment is signaling stress—but it hasn't propagated to Credit yet" creates a curiosity gap with real financial consequences.

The Zeigarnik effect (1927) demonstrates that incomplete tasks occupy mental resources more than completed ones. This is why restaurant servers remember open orders but forget closed ones. In product design: progress bars, notification badges, and "continue watching" sections all exploit this. A running simulation that hasn't resolved, a stress test that's still processing, a regime-shift alert that hasn't been fully investigated—these create persistent cognitive pull.

TikTok's recommendation engine creates infinite engagement through content variety, surprise, and escalating relevance. Each video is a micro-discovery; the algorithm rapidly learns what holds attention. A world-model insight feed that mixes macro regime signals, portfolio-specific alerts, historical analogs, and counterparty intelligence—with increasing personalization—creates the same dynamic, but for professional insight.

RecWM Design Recommendations

R13 Design the "cascade chain" interaction

Every insight should naturally lead to the next question. Pattern: "The world model detected a regime shift in EM liquidity" → "Want to see which of your positions are exposed?" → "Here are 3 scenario branches" → "Want to stress-test against the worst one?" → "Here's a hedge that reduces tail risk by 40%" → "Want to see the historical analog?" Each step is one click. Each click reveals a new curiosity gap.

Mechanism: Chained curiosity gaps + Loewenstein information gap theory

R14 Create persistent "unfinished" states

When a PM starts investigating a signal but doesn't finish, RecWM should show a subtle indicator: "You have 2 unresolved signals" or "Your EM stress test is still running." These are not notifications—they're cognitive hooks. The Zeigarnik effect ensures the PM thinks about them even when away from the terminal. When they return, the unfinished investigation is exactly where they left it.

Mechanism: Zeigarnik effect creates involuntary mental engagement

R15 Build the "For You" insight feed

A personalized feed of world-model insights, ordered by relevance to the PM's book. Mix: (1) fragment state changes that affect their positions, (2) historical analogs to current conditions, (3) scenarios other PMs at their firm are exploring, (4) regime-shift early warnings, (5) cross-fragment causal chains. Like TikTok, the feed learns rapidly from what the PM engages with and what they skip.

Mechanism: Variable ratio reinforcement via unpredictably valuable discoveries

R16 Escalate stakes naturally

"This pattern has preceded 3 of the last 5 drawdowns exceeding 10%" is not an insight—it's a cliffhanger. RecWM should calibrate the urgency of its language to the actual risk level. When the world model detects conditions that historically preceded major losses, the framing should make the stakes unmistakable without being alarmist. The PM should feel they cannot look away.

Mechanism: Escalating stakes via real financial consequences

R17 Show "what others are simulating" (anonymized)

"12 PMs at your firm ran stress tests on China scenarios this week." This creates social curiosity ("What do they know that I don't?") and FOMO. The specifics are anonymized; the signal is that smart people are worried about something. This combines informational curiosity with social pressure.

Mechanism: Social curiosity gap + fear of missing information

R18 The "morning briefing" ritual

Every morning: "Here's what changed in the world model overnight." A personalized 60-second summary of fragment state changes, new causal links, updated scenario probabilities, and portfolio-specific implications. This creates a daily habit loop (cue: morning; routine: check briefing; reward: feel prepared). The briefing always ends with a question: "The Sentiment fragment shifted—want to see why?"

Mechanism: Habit loop formation + daily curiosity gap

04

Zero-Friction Personalization: The World Model That Knows Your Book

Core Mechanism

Spotify's Discover Weekly creates emotional loyalty by "knowing the user better than they know themselves." Netflix's personalized thumbnails, Amazon's "customers also bought"—all exploit the same dynamic: context-aware intelligence beats context-free intelligence so overwhelmingly that users anthropomorphize the algorithm and develop emotional attachment. A world model that knows your portfolio, mandate, risk limits, and trading history can deliver personalization that makes Spotify look generic.

How Personalization Creates Loyalty

Spotify's Discover Weekly delivers 30 personalized song recommendations every Monday. It combines collaborative filtering ("users like you also listened to...") with content analysis (audio features, lyrical themes, blog mentions). The result feels "magical"—users regularly describe it as "Spotify knows me better than I know myself." This anthropomorphization is the marker of deep personalization: the algorithm becomes a trusted advisor.

The key insight from Spotify's product design team: they reframed algorithmic curation as "aggregation of millions of human curatorial decisions" to resolve "algorithm anxiety"—the feeling that machine-generated recommendations are cold or manipulative. By framing personalization as collective human intelligence, Spotify made it feel warm.

Data gravity is the lock-in mechanism. Once Spotify has 5 years of listening history, leaving feels like losing a part of yourself. Netflix's taste profiles, Amazon's purchase history—each creates a switching cost that grows with time. The longer you use the personalized system, the worse any alternative feels, because the alternative doesn't know you.

RecWM Design Recommendations

R19 Portfolio-aware everything

Every single output of RecWM should be filtered through the PM's current book. "EM liquidity is draining" becomes "EM liquidity is draining—your BRAZ10 position has 2.3x more exposure to this than your average book." The world model never speaks in the abstract when it can speak in the specific. Every insight is personalized to the PM's actual risk.

Mechanism: Context-aware intelligence creates irreplaceability

R20 Learn trading style, not just positions

Over time, RecWM should learn the PM's decision patterns: Do they tend to hedge early or late? Do they prefer macro or micro catalysts? Do they size positions based on conviction or volatility? This behavioral model should inform how RecWM presents information: a PM who likes to hedge early gets earlier warnings; a PM who trades macro themes gets fragment-level summaries first. Frame this as: "RecWM adapts to your investment process."

Mechanism: Behavioral personalization creates "it thinks like I think" attachment

R21 The "PMs like you" signal

Anonymized collaborative intelligence: "PMs with similar mandates are increasing duration hedges this week." Like Amazon's "customers also bought," this leverages social proof while respecting information barriers. The PM gets the benefit of collective intelligence without seeing anyone's specific positions. RecWM becomes the medium through which the collective wisdom of the firm flows.

Mechanism: Collaborative filtering + social proof

R22 Solve cold start with mandate-based initialization

New users shouldn't face a blank screen. On day one, RecWM should ask: "What's your mandate?" and immediately configure itself. A long/short equity PM gets different default views than a macro PM. The world model pre-loads relevant fragments, sets appropriate alert thresholds, and presents a "Here's what the world model thinks matters most for a book like yours" onboarding. Value in minutes, not weeks.

Mechanism: Immediate value creation reduces time-to-attachment

R23 Make personalization transparent, not creepy

Every personalized insight should be explainable: "We're showing you this because your book has elevated exposure to EM credit, and the Liquidity fragment is signaling stress in that sector." Like Spotify framing its algorithm as "human curatorial decisions," RecWM should frame its personalization as "world-model reasoning about your specific situation." Transparency turns "it's watching me" into "it understands my situation."

Mechanism: Explainability resolves algorithm anxiety

R24 The "decision journal" that remembers everything

RecWM should automatically log every scenario explored, every stress test run, every alert acted on or dismissed. Over time, this becomes an irreplaceable institutional memory: "Show me every time I investigated EM liquidity stress and what I did." This creates data gravity that grows monthly. After 2 years, the switching cost is not just learning a new tool—it's losing your analytical history.

Mechanism: Data gravity via accumulated decision history

05

Emotional Design: Crisis Bonding, Peak Moments, and the "It Saved My Ass" Story

Core Mechanism

Kahneman's peak-end rule says people judge experiences by their most intense moment and the ending. In finance, the "peak" is almost always a crisis. A tool that performs brilliantly during a PM's worst day creates an emotional bond that no feature comparison can overcome. The "it saved my ass" story becomes the most powerful marketing the product will ever have.

Designing for the Moments That Define Loyalty

Don Norman's three levels of emotional design provide the framework. Visceral: RecWM must look and feel like a precision instrument—information-dense but never chaotic, like a well-designed cockpit. Behavioral: every interaction must be fast, predictable, and rewarding. Reflective: using RecWM must make the PM feel like a better, more sophisticated investor. The reflective level creates brand advocates and justifies premium pricing.

High-stress professionals—surgeons, pilots, special forces operators—develop intense attachment to the tools that performed under pressure. Military units develop bonds through shared stress that persist for decades. The same psychology applies to traders during market crises: the tool that was there during March 2020, that showed them the risk before it hit, that gave them clarity when everything was chaos—that tool becomes emotionally irreplaceable.

The word-of-mouth mechanism in finance is the war story. Trading floors, PM dinners, conference hallways—the stories that spread are always crisis stories. "I was about to get margin-called, but the system flagged the concentration risk 2 hours before the move." These stories are the highest-converting marketing channel in institutional finance.

RecWM Design Recommendations

R25 Design "Crisis Mode" as a first-class experience

When market volatility exceeds a threshold, RecWM should automatically shift to crisis mode: simplified interface, larger fonts, clear action items, no decorative elements. The world model should communicate like a flight computer during an emergency: calm, specific, actionable. "Your portfolio VaR has breached your limit. The primary driver is [X]. Here are 3 immediate actions ranked by effectiveness." This is the moment that creates emotional bonding.

Mechanism: Peak-end rule + trauma bonding to tools under stress

R26 Be the early warning system that creates "it saved me" stories

RecWM's causal architecture gives it a structural advantage: it can detect stress propagating through fragments before it reaches the PM's positions. Design specific "early warning" alerts that are rare (no alert fatigue), specific (not "markets are volatile"), and actionable ("Liquidity fragment stress is propagating toward EM credit. Your CEMBI exposure may be affected within 24–48 hours. Here's the historical analog."). Every true positive creates a war story.

Mechanism: Rare, accurate warnings create "it saved my ass" narratives

R27 Post-crisis attribution: "Here's what happened and why you survived"

After a market event, RecWM should generate a personalized post-mortem: "During last week's selloff, your portfolio was exposed to [X]. The world model alerted you on [date]. You [acted/didn't act]. Here's how your P&L compared to peers who had similar exposure." This reinforces the PM's good decisions (building confidence and tool reliance) and gently shows where the tool's advice would have helped.

Mechanism: Success attribution creates "tool made me better" belief

R28 The "confidence builder" feedback loop

Track the PM's decision quality over time: "When you followed world-model signals, your Sharpe improved by X. When you went against them, your drawdowns were Y% deeper." This isn't about making the PM dependent—it's about making them more confident. Better decisions → more confidence → more reliance on the tool → deeper usage → even better decisions. The virtuous cycle is the product.

Mechanism: Confidence-competence spiral via performance feedback

R29 Visceral design: the instrument panel aesthetic

RecWM's visual language should evoke a surgical instrument or aircraft cockpit: precise, information-dense, authoritative. Use monospaced numerals for all data. Color-code fragment states with semantic meaning (not decoration). Subtle animation should indicate live model computation—the world model is alive, always running, always watching. The interface should feel like it's working for you even when you're not actively querying it.

Mechanism: Visceral-level emotional design creates "this is a serious tool" feeling

R30 Celebrate wins, not just prevent losses

When a PM's thesis plays out exactly as the world model predicted, acknowledge it: "Your scenario from March 12 played out. The Momentum fragment shifted as you predicted. Your positioning captured 85% of the move." This is the positive peak in the peak-end rule. Losses are where the tool proves its value through warnings; wins are where it proves its value through validation. Both create emotional attachment.

Mechanism: Peak-end rule applied to positive experiences

06

Community and Status: The Multiplayer World Model

Core Mechanism

Bloomberg IB Chat processes 200M+ messages per day because it's where deals happen. TradingView has millions of idea-sharing users because analytical status is intoxicating. GitHub's contribution graph became a developer identity marker. The product that controls the social graph of professional interaction controls the profession. A shared world model creates network effects that no individual tool can replicate.

How Professional Communities Create Lock-in

Bloomberg's messaging moat is the canonical example. When every counterparty, research analyst, and salesperson is on IB Chat, leaving Bloomberg means leaving the network. Trades executed in chat are binding. Compliance is built on top. The messaging layer is more defensible than the data layer because data can be replicated; a social network cannot.

TradingView created status hierarchies through published ideas, reputation scores, follower counts, and "Community Awards" that recognize consistent, high-quality analysis. The platform posts over 600 comments daily on ideas. Status in analytical communities is earned through demonstrated accuracy and insight quality—a more meritocratic status game than follower counts on social media.

GitHub's contribution graph demonstrates the power of visible activity. The psychology is complex: initially motivating through streak maintenance, it eventually traps users through loss aversion—they become more afraid of losing a long streak than motivated by the achievement itself. This is a design to learn from carefully: status mechanics should reward quality, not just quantity.

RecWM Design Recommendations

R31 Shared scenarios as social objects

Scenarios and stress tests should be shareable, forkable, and commentable. A PM should be able to publish a scenario to their team: "Here's my base case for Q4. Fork it and show me yours." The scenario becomes a social object around which discussion, debate, and collective intelligence form. The team's shared scenario library becomes institutional capital that lives inside RecWM.

Mechanism: Social objects create conversation and network effects

R32 The "analytical leaderboard" (internal only)

Within a firm: track which PMs' scenarios were most predictive, whose stress tests identified real risks, who used the world model most effectively. This isn't a competition for competition's sake—it's a quality signal. "The 3 most prescient scenario analyses this quarter came from [PM names]. Here's what they saw." Status earned through demonstrated analytical rigor, not volume.

Mechanism: Status hierarchies via demonstrated skill + meritocratic competition

R33 Collective intelligence indicators

"42 PMs across 8 firms are currently stress-testing tail scenarios in EM credit." This aggregate, anonymized intelligence makes the world model more valuable with every user. No individual PM produces this signal; only the network does. This is the pure network effect: the product becomes more valuable as more people use it, and this value is impossible to replicate outside the network.

Mechanism: Direct network effect via collective intelligence

R34 The research-sharing layer

PMs should be able to publish world-model-grounded research internally: "My analysis of how the Liquidity and Credit fragments interact during EM stress, with simulation evidence." This creates a TradingView-like community within the firm, where analytical status is earned through world-model-backed arguments. The research lives inside RecWM, making it the intellectual hub of the firm.

Mechanism: Content creation creates platform value + professional identity

R35 "Scenario convergence" alerts

When multiple PMs independently arrive at similar scenarios, that's a signal: "3 PMs on your desk independently simulated a US Treasury liquidity shock this week. The world model's base case assigns this a 12% probability." Convergence of independent analysis is powerful social proof. Divergence is equally interesting: "Your scenario contradicts 4 of your colleagues—want to see where the assumptions differ?"

Mechanism: Social proof + intellectual curiosity via agreement/disagreement signals

R36 The "world model community" across firms (opt-in)

An anonymized, cross-firm layer where aggregate scenario activity is visible. No firm's positions or specific analyses are exposed, but the collective behavior of the network—what risks are being investigated, what scenarios are trending, what fragments are under stress across the user base—creates a meta-intelligence that no individual firm can produce. This is the ultimate network effect: RecWM as the nervous system of the financial markets.

Mechanism: Cross-network effects create irreplaceability at the industry level

07

The "I Can't Go Back" Moment: Switching Costs, Data Gravity, and Institutional Embedding

Core Mechanism

The "I can't go back" moment occurs when the accumulated switching cost exceeds the perceived benefit of any alternative. This cost compounds across four dimensions: procedural (re-learning workflows), relational (losing integrations), data (losing history), and psychological (the IKEA effect and competence trap). The goal is to make each dimension grow independently so that the total switching cost becomes overwhelming.

The Anatomy of Irreversible Adoption

Palantir's lock-in illustrates data gravity at scale: customers build proprietary ontologies, custom pipelines, and business logic on top of the platform. Migrating would cost millions and disrupt operations for months. Salesforce compounds this with AI-layer switching costs (Agentforce) that sit on top of already-massive CRM switching costs. Each new layer makes the foundation harder to remove.

The IKEA effect (Norton, Mochon, Ariely, 2012) shows that people overvalue things they helped build. Effort justification creates cognitive dissonance: "I spent 6 months configuring this system; it must be valuable." This psychological attachment is separate from, and additional to, the rational assessment of the tool's quality. A PM who has spent months tuning their world-model views, building custom scenarios, and calibrating alert thresholds has made RecWM theirs—and values it disproportionately.

The competence trap completes the lock-in: expertise in one system creates resistance to learning alternatives. Bloomberg users who have spent years mastering the terminal literally cannot use Refinitiv efficiently. Their expertise is Bloomberg-specific. The sunk cost of that learning, combined with the diminished productivity during any transition, makes switching feel not just costly but incompetent.

RecWM Design Recommendations

R37 Make the world model learn from the PM's decisions

RecWM should develop a "PM model" that captures the individual's investment process: their risk tolerance, their typical position sizing, their preferred hedging strategies, their historical accuracy on different fragment types. This model improves with every interaction. After 12 months, switching to another tool means starting from scratch—the new tool doesn't know how you think. After 24 months, the PM model is a genuine competitive advantage that lives inside RecWM.

Mechanism: Data gravity via behavioral model that improves with time

R38 Integration into the investment workflow stack

RecWM should feed into order management systems, risk platforms, compliance systems, and reporting tools. When the world model's signals flow into the PM's execution infrastructure, removing RecWM doesn't just remove an analytical tool—it breaks the pipeline. This is the "load-bearing infrastructure" strategy: the product becomes structural, not supplementary.

Mechanism: Workflow integration creates structural dependency

R39 The accumulating scenario library

Every scenario, stress test, simulation, and analysis ever run should be searchable, replayable, and referenceable. "Show me every tail-risk scenario I ran in the last 18 months and which ones actually materialized." This library becomes irreplaceable institutional knowledge. When a PM leaves a firm and their successor inherits their RecWM workspace, the analytical history transfers. The tool outlasts the individual; it becomes the firm's memory.

Mechanism: Institutional knowledge capture creates firm-level lock-in

R40 Custom fragment definitions and risk factors

Let firms define custom fragments: "Regulatory Risk (our sector)," "China Policy (our exposure)," "Counterparty Credit (our prime brokers)." These custom fragments, calibrated with proprietary data and institutional expertise, represent the firm's intellectual capital embedded in the world model. Removing RecWM means losing these bespoke models. The more customized the world model becomes, the higher the switching cost.

Mechanism: IKEA effect + institutional IP embedding

R41 Progressive mastery badges (private)

Track the PM's growing expertise: first scenario created, first accurate prediction, first shared analysis, first custom fragment. These are private milestones, not public gamification—they reinforce the PM's sense of investment in the tool. "You've run 847 simulations and your scenario accuracy is in the top quartile of RecWM users." The sunk cost of this expertise makes switching feel like professional regression.

Mechanism: Competence trap via demonstrated expertise investment

R42 The "time machine" feature

RecWM should let users rewind the world model to any historical date and see what it would have shown. "Show me the world-model state on March 1, 2020." This creates a unique analytical capability that exists only within RecWM's historical simulation data. The longer the system runs, the richer the historical dataset, and the more valuable the time machine becomes. This is data gravity that literally grows every day.

Mechanism: Accumulating proprietary data creates escalating switching costs

++

Synthesis: The Addiction Stack

The 42 recommendations above are not independent features—they form an interlocking addiction stack where each layer reinforces the others. The stack has a specific sequence:

Phase Timeframe Primary Mechanism Key Recommendations User State
Hook Day 1–7 Immediate value via mandate-based initialization + "For You" feed R9, R15, R22 "This is actually useful"
Habit Week 2–8 Morning briefing ritual + cascade chains + autocomplete dopamine R8, R13, R18 "I check this every morning"
Mastery Month 2–6 Command grammar + progressive disclosure + customization R1, R9, R11 "I'm faster in RecWM than anywhere else"
Identity Month 3–12 IKEA effect + custom fragments + shared scenarios + status R31, R32, R34, R40 "This is MY tool, MY setup"
Bond First crisis Crisis mode + early warnings + "it saved me" story R25, R26, R27 "It saved my ass"
Lock-in Year 1+ Data gravity + PM model + workflow integration + institutional embedding R24, R37, R38, R39 "I literally cannot do my job without this"

The Critical Insight

Bloomberg's addiction is primarily negative: users stay because leaving is too costly. RecWM's addiction must be primarily positive: users stay because the tool makes them measurably better at their job, and they know it. The confidence-competence spiral (R28), the decision journal (R24), and the post-crisis attribution (R27) create evidence that the PM performs better with RecWM. This transforms the product from a tool they use into a capability they possess.

The world model's unique structural advantage is that it provides causal explanations, not just correlations or predictions. When a PM understands why something is happening—which fragment is driving it, how the causal chain propagates, what the historical analogs suggest—they develop genuine insight. The tool doesn't just save them time; it makes them smarter. And a tool that makes you smarter is one you never leave.

The Single Most Important Design Principle

Every interaction with RecWM should end with the PM feeling one of three things:

  • "I understand something I didn't before." The world model explained a causal mechanism that no other tool surfaces.
  • "I'm prepared for something I wasn't before." A scenario or stress test revealed a risk or opportunity the PM hadn't considered.
  • "I'm more confident in my position." The world model validated or challenged the PM's thesis with evidence, either way increasing decision quality.

If every session delivers at least one of these feelings, the PM will return tomorrow. And the day after. And every day for the rest of their career.

RecWM Product Architecture Research · Treasury4 · August 2026

Product Vision Research

Simulation as Product

How six industries built products that let users enter alternative realities, explore counterfactuals, and make better decisions before committing to the irreversible.

August 2026 · Internal Research Document
I
Aviation
Flight Simulators: The Original "Simulate Before You Commit"

The Link Trainer and the birth of embodied simulation

In 1929, Edwin Link built a device that would create an entirely new product category. The Link Trainer was a stubby blue box with a cockpit, mounted on pneumatic bellows connected to a vacuum pump. The controls were real. The instruments were real. And when a student pilot pulled back on the stick, the box pitched up. When they banked, it rolled. The bellows created just enough motion that the pilot's vestibular system bought the illusion.

The military rejected it initially. Link spent years selling his trainers to amusement parks. Then, in 1934, the US Army Air Corps lost twelve pilots in 78 days trying to fly airmail routes in bad weather. The Army bought six Link Trainers the same week. By the end of World War II, over 10,000 units had been produced, training an estimated 500,000 Allied pilots. The product insight was simple and devastating: you cannot practice dying. You can only simulate it.

10,000+
Units Built (WWII)
500K
Pilots Trained
$10-25M
Modern Level D Cost
6-DOF
Motion Axes

The evolution to total fidelity

The arc from Link Trainer to modern Level D full-flight simulator traces a relentless pursuit of perceptual completeness. In the 1960s, Evans & Sutherland pioneered computer-generated imagery for visual systems. By the 1980s, hydraulic motion platforms could produce six degrees of freedom. Today, a Level D simulator from CAE, L3Harris, or FlightSafety International costs $10-25 million installed. It must replicate characteristic buffet motions, precise ground handling, atmospheric turbulence, and present at least 150 degrees of horizontal visual field at distant focus. The FAA certifies each unit under 14 CFR Part 60 with an active Statement of Qualification.

The economics that made simulation mandatory

The cost differential is stark. Operating a commercial jet for training runs $5,000-15,000 per hour in fuel, wear, crew, and airspace costs. A Level D simulator session costs $200-500 per hour to operate. But the economics go deeper: you cannot practice an engine fire on a real 737 full of passengers. You cannot practice windshear on final approach. You cannot deliberately stall a widebody at 2,000 feet. Simulation made it possible to train for the scenarios that matter most precisely because they are the ones you cannot rehearse in reality.

The Colgan Air Flight 3407 crash in 2009 killed 50 people and exposed how little stick-and-rudder training pilots were actually getting. Congress responded with the 1,500-hour rule and mandated that all Part 121 first officers hold an Airline Transport Pilot certificate. The simulation industry expanded dramatically as the only way to deliver the required training volume safely.

The UX that creates presence

What makes a flight simulator work as a product is not any single fidelity dimension but the coherence of the illusion. The visual system fills peripheral vision. The motion platform provides onset cues that trick the otolith organs. The sound system reproduces engine harmonics, gear extension, rain on the windscreen. The controls offer force feedback calibrated to the actual hydraulic feel of the aircraft type. When these channels agree, the pilot's brain stops processing "simulator" and starts processing "flight." This is the product lesson: coherence beats resolution. A perfectly coherent low-fidelity simulation is more useful than a high-resolution simulation with mismatched cues.

The concept of "negative training" reinforces this: when simulation teaches the wrong habits, when the motion is slightly off or the visual latency creates false vestibular cues, pilots learn reflexes that are dangerous in real aircraft. The product must be right, or it must not exist.

The aha moment

Aviation's aha moment came in two stages. First: simulation is cheaper than crashing. Second, and more profound: simulation is better than reality for learning. You can pause an engine failure. You can replay the last 30 seconds of an approach. You can freeze the world at the moment of decision and ask, "What did you see? What did you miss?" You can inject a windshear on short final that no sane training captain would ever create in a real aircraft. The simulator became not a substitute for flying but a superior instrument for a specific cognitive task: building the decision-making reflexes that keep people alive.

Product pattern: Embodied counterfactual rehearsal

The flight simulator established that the killer product is not "a model you look at" but "a world you enter." The user's body must be engaged. The scenario must be consequential. And the simulation must allow exploration of the precise situations that are too dangerous, too expensive, or too rare to encounter in reality. The product value is in the counterfactual: what happens if I do X instead of Y, in a world where getting it wrong costs nothing?

II
Defense
Military War Games: Red Teams and the Doctrine of Simulated Failure

The simulation stack

The US military operates the most sophisticated simulation ecosystem on earth. At the tactical level, JCATS (Joint Conflict and Tactical Simulation) models entity-level operations: individual vehicles, squads, weapons systems, each with realistic sensor ranges, movement rates, and lethality curves. Human operators on networked workstations role-play both friendly and enemy forces, controlling their entities through a graphical interface while results flow to higher-level commanders through actual command-and-control systems. JCATS is installed in hundreds of US military organizations, across NATO, and in more than 30 countries.

OneSAF (One Semi-Automated Forces) provides a comprehensive modeling and simulation environment supporting both constructive and virtual simulations, with detailed terrain, environmental conditions, and modeling from individual entities up to brigade-level forces. Command: Modern Air/Naval Operations (originally CMANO) covers air and naval operations from post-WWII to the near future, and has been adopted by professional military organizations for its operational fidelity.

Millennium Challenge 2002: When the simulation told an unwelcome truth

The most instructive military simulation story is one of failure and institutional denial. In the summer of 2002, the Pentagon ran Millennium Challenge, the largest and most expensive war game in US history, designed to validate a new concept called "Rapid Decisive Operations." Retired Marine Lieutenant General Paul Van Riper commanded the Red Force (enemy).

Van Riper recognized that fighting on Blue Team's terms meant losing. American forces possessed overwhelming advantages in networked sensors, precision weapons, and information systems. Any adversary that engaged conventionally would be detected, tracked, and destroyed. So Van Riper went asymmetric. He used motorcycle couriers instead of radio communications (invisible to signals intelligence). He launched swarms of small boats and cruise missiles in a coordinated attack.

In the opening hours, Van Riper's Red Force sank sixteen US Navy warships, including an aircraft carrier. Had it occurred in reality, it would have been the largest American naval defeat since Pearl Harbor.
Task & Purpose, reporting on MC 2002

The Pentagon's response was revealing: they reset the exercise, refloated the fleet, constrained Red Force tactics, and guided the war game to a predetermined Blue Force victory. Van Riper was told he could not shoot down V-22 Ospreys, could not use chemical weapons against paratroopers, and had to expose his offensive weapons to be destroyed. He wrote a detailed report on the exercise's shortcomings and delivered six hard copies to senior leadership. He never received feedback.

Red teaming as product principle

The military's simulation ecosystem embodies a product principle that most commercial software ignores: the simulation is only valuable if it can tell you things you do not want to hear. Van Riper's Red Team was the simulation working correctly. The institutional failure was in overriding the output. NATO's Computer Assisted Exercise (CAX) systems now integrate JCATS, OneSAF, and JTLS-GO to provide scalable simulation for multinational training, mission rehearsal, and interoperability testing. The best of these exercises deliberately empower the red team to find the breaks.

Adversarial exploration

The simulation must contain an intelligent adversary. In military terms, "red teaming." The user explores not just scenarios but opposition strategies.

Fog of war as UX

Real military simulations deliberately limit information. The user does not see the whole board. Uncertainty is a feature, not a bug.

After-action review

Every military simulation ends with structured debrief: what happened, why, what decisions led to what outcomes. The replay is as valuable as the play.

Product pattern: Adversarial counterfactual with honest output

Military simulation teaches that the product must be willing to embarrass the user. A simulation that only confirms priors is a PowerPoint deck with extra steps. The value is in the surprise: the scenario you did not anticipate, the adversary move you did not model, the cascade failure you did not think possible. And the product must include a structured mechanism for learning from the surprise, not just experiencing it.

III
Epidemiology
Pandemic Models: When Simulation Became the Decision

The model that moved governments

On March 16, 2020, Neil Ferguson's team at Imperial College London published Report 9. It was the output of CovidSim, an agent-based microsimulation model that had been in development since 2005, originally built for H5N1 influenza pandemic planning. The model simulated individual people, their movements, their contacts in households, schools, workplaces, and communities. It modeled viral transmission as a stochastic process across these contact networks.

The headline finding: without intervention, COVID-19 would cause approximately 510,000 deaths in Great Britain and 2.2 million in the United States. Within days, both the UK and US governments reversed course from mitigation to suppression strategies. The simulation did not just inform policy; for a critical period, the simulation was the policy.

2.2M
Projected US Deaths (No Action)
137
Countries Modeled
2005
Model First Developed

The scenario planning interface

What made CovidSim a product rather than a paper was its scenario interface. The covidsim.org tool allowed policymakers to explore combinations of interventions: school closures, workplace distancing, home isolation, household quarantine. Each combination produced a different epidemic curve. The user could see not just "what happens" but "what happens if we close schools but keep workplaces open" versus "what happens if we close everything for six weeks then relax." The counterfactual was the product.

IHME (Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation) at the University of Washington took a different approach, using statistical curve-fitting rather than agent-based modeling. Their projections were more accessible, with a clean web interface showing projected deaths, hospital beds needed, and ventilator demand. The IHME dashboard became the default reference for US state governors making reopening decisions.

What went right and wrong

The pandemic models demonstrated both the power and the peril of simulation as product. What went right: the models forced decision-makers to confront exponential growth before it was visible in the data. They made the consequences of inaction vivid and specific. They provided a framework for comparing intervention strategies.

What went wrong: the models were treated as predictions rather than scenarios. The 2.2 million number was not a forecast; it was the output of a specific (and extreme) assumption set. But it was communicated as a prediction, and when reality diverged (because interventions were implemented), the models were criticized for being "wrong" rather than credited for being useful. The IHME model's tight confidence intervals gave false precision. And the opacity of complex agent-based models made it difficult for non-specialists to interrogate assumptions.

The fundamental product failure was a UX failure: the models did not clearly communicate that they were explorable scenarios, not crystal balls. The interface should have forced users to confront their own assumptions before seeing outputs.

Product pattern: Assumption-explicit scenario exploration

Pandemic modeling teaches that simulation products must make assumptions visible and manipulable. The user should not receive an output without first choosing their inputs. The interaction should be: "Given that you believe X about transmission rates and Y about compliance, here is what the model projects." This converts the simulation from an oracle (which will always disappoint) into a thinking tool (which clarifies the structure of uncertainty). The aha moment is not "the model says 2.2 million"; it is "oh, the difference between 200,000 and 2 million depends on whether we act in the next 14 days."

IV
Climate Science
Climate Models: Simulation at Civilizational Scale

How GCMs work

General Circulation Models (GCMs) are the most computationally ambitious simulations ever built. They discretize the Earth's atmosphere, ocean, and land surface into three-dimensional grid cells, then solve the Navier-Stokes equations for fluid dynamics, radiative transfer equations for energy balance, and coupled biogeochemical equations for carbon and water cycles. A modern GCM like those in CMIP6 (Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6) runs on grid cells as small as 25-50 km, with 30-80 vertical levels in the atmosphere and 40-60 in the ocean. A single century-long simulation can take weeks on thousands of processors.

But the product is not the model. The product is the scenario.

RCPs, SSPs, and the counterfactual as policy tool

The IPCC's innovation was to package climate simulation into explorable scenarios. The Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) from AR5 described four possible futures based on different greenhouse gas trajectories: RCP2.6 (aggressive mitigation), RCP4.5 and RCP6.0 (moderate), and RCP8.5 (business as usual). For CMIP6, these were paired with Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) that add socioeconomic assumptions: population growth, economic development, energy systems, land use.

The result is a matrix of possible futures. SSP1-1.9 represents a world of sustainable development with very low emissions. SSP5-8.5 represents fossil-fuel-driven development with high emissions. Each cell in the matrix produces a different temperature trajectory, sea level rise, precipitation pattern, and extreme weather frequency. The product question is: which future do you want to inhabit?

Climate simulation is the paradigm case of simulation as decision support at scale. The question "what happens if we reduce emissions by 40% by 2035?" is not an academic exercise. It is a multi-trillion-dollar investment question, a geopolitical question, and an existential question, all explored through the same simulation framework.

The UX of civilizational choice

The IPCC scenario framework works as a product because it does three things well. First, it bounds uncertainty rather than pretending to eliminate it: every scenario shows a range, not a point. Second, it connects actions to outcomes: the user can trace a specific policy (carbon tax, renewable mandate, deforestation halt) to a specific temperature trajectory. Third, it makes the counterfactual vivid: the difference between SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 is not an abstract number but a world with or without the Great Barrier Reef, with or without coastal cities, with or without predictable growing seasons.

Product pattern: Bounded scenario matrix with traceable causality

Climate models teach that simulation products at scale must present a structured menu of possible futures, not an open-ended sandbox. Users cannot explore infinite parameter space; they need curated scenarios that represent meaningfully different worlds. Each scenario must have a clear narrative (not just numbers) and traceable causal links from input assumptions to output consequences. The aha moment is comparative: it comes from seeing two futures side by side and understanding what choices separate them.

V
Urban Planning
City Simulation: From SimCity to Digital Twins

SimCity's accidental influence

When Will Wright released SimCity in 1989, he did not intend to build a planning tool. He intended to build a toy. But the game's underlying model, a simplified cellular automaton of land use, traffic flow, property values, and tax revenue, turned out to be a surprisingly effective intuition pump for urban dynamics. City planners noticed. SimCity was adopted as a teaching tool in urban planning programs. Its greatest contribution was not accuracy (the model was crude) but accessibility: for the first time, non-specialists could develop intuitions about feedback loops in urban systems. Zone residential near industrial and property values drop. Build highways and sprawl follows. Raise taxes and businesses leave.

The product lesson from SimCity is that a simulation does not need to be accurate to be transformative. It needs to be interactive enough to build intuition about system dynamics.

Digital twins: Simulation meets reality

Modern city simulation has left SimCity behind and entered the era of digital twins: high-fidelity, data-connected virtual replicas of real cities. Singapore's Virtual Singapore platform is the most ambitious deployment. Built using laser-scanning aircraft and ground vehicles, it models every building, road, tree, and utility line in three dimensions, with real-time data overlays from IoT sensors across the city-state. Planners use it to optimize solar panel placement (simulating shadow patterns throughout the year), model pedestrian flow through new developments, and simulate emergency evacuation routes.

Helsinki's 3D digital twin serves a different purpose: public engagement. Residents can visualize proposed developments in the context of their actual neighborhoods before construction begins. The simulation becomes a democratic tool: citizens can see and respond to planned changes, not just read about them.

What-if infrastructure

What if we add a metro line here? What if we allow 20-story buildings in this district? The twin shows downstream effects on traffic, sunlight, noise, and property values.

Disaster rehearsal

Simulate floods, earthquakes, fires. Route evacuations. Test where infrastructure fails under stress. Cities like Singapore and Seoul run these scenarios continuously.

Temporal navigation

The twin can show the city in the past, present, and proposed future. Citizens navigate time, not just space. This makes change legible.

Product pattern: Spatial-temporal sandbox with stakeholder views

City simulation teaches that the same underlying model must serve multiple users with different needs. The planner needs analytical views: traffic heat maps, infrastructure stress tests, cost models. The politician needs narrative views: "here is what the neighborhood looks like in 2035." The citizen needs experiential views: "here is the shadow my new neighbor's building casts on my garden." The product value is in providing coherent but differently framed views of the same simulated reality.

VI
Corporate Strategy
Business War Games: Shell and the Art of Prepared Minds

Pierre Wack and the invention of scenario planning

In 1965, Royal Dutch Shell established a planning activity based on the scenario method developed by Herman Kahn at RAND. By the early 1970s, a French planner named Pierre Wack had transformed it into something entirely new. Instead of producing single-point forecasts (the standard practice), Wack's team developed multiple, internally consistent narratives about how the future might unfold. These were not predictions. They were rehearsals for perception.

In 1972, the Group Planners delivered a message to Shell's managing directors: the price of oil, then at $2 per barrel, could soar to $10. The scenarios described the geopolitical conditions that would make this possible. When the Yom Kippur War triggered the 1973 oil embargo and prices quadrupled to $16 per barrel, Shell was the only major oil company that had already repositioned. They had shifted toward light fuels (harder to substitute), invested in cracking capacity to convert heavy into light fuels, and restructured their refinery operations.

In the early 1970s, Royal Dutch Shell was the seventh-largest oil company in the world. By the end of the decade, it had risen to second. The simulation did not predict the future. It prepared the organization to recognize the future when it arrived.
Shell Scenarios, 40 Years

The UX of corporate scenario planning

Wack's insight was that the purpose of scenarios was not to tell management what would happen but to change management's mental models so they could perceive what was happening. This is a profoundly different product concept from forecasting. A forecast says: "oil will be $10 in 1975." A scenario says: "here is a world in which oil is $10. Can you see how this world works? Can you recognize the early signals? Can you feel what it would be like to operate your business in this world?"

Shell's scenario practice used several UX patterns that persist in modern corporate war-gaming:

  • Named worlds: Each scenario got a memorable name and narrative identity, not a number. This made them mentally available and discussable.
  • Predetermined elements: Wack distinguished between things that were uncertain (oil prices) and things that were already decided but not yet manifest (demographic shifts, infrastructure investments with long lead times). The scenarios held predetermined elements fixed and varied the uncertainties.
  • Signposts: Each scenario came with observable indicators that would tell you which world was materializing. This converted the scenario from a thought experiment into a monitoring system.
  • Wind-tunneling: Once scenarios were built, Shell would "wind-tunnel" strategic decisions by asking: "Does this strategy work in World A? World B? Both? Neither?" Strategies that survived multiple scenarios were robust; those that only worked in one were bets.

McKinsey, BCG, and modern war-gaming

The consulting industry adopted and simplified Shell's approach. McKinsey and BCG now run corporate war games where executive teams role-play competitors, regulators, and market forces. The format is typically a one- to three-day exercise where teams make decisions in rounds, with a simulation engine computing market outcomes between rounds. The power of these exercises lies not in the accuracy of the simulation but in forcing executives to think from the adversary's perspective, the same red-teaming principle the military discovered.

Product pattern: Mental model transformation through narrative immersion

Shell's scenario planning teaches that the most valuable simulation product may be one that changes how users think, not what they know. The output is not a number or a chart but a reorganized perception. The UX must be narrative and immersive: users must feel what it is like to operate in each scenario. And the product must connect to action through signposts (what to watch for) and wind-tunneling (which strategies are robust across scenarios).

•
Synthesis
What "Simulation as Product" Looks Like for a Hedge Fund PM

The six patterns, distilled

1. Embodied entry

From aviation. The user does not look at the simulation. They enter it. The world surrounds them. This means: the PM should not see a spreadsheet of scenario outputs. They should see their portfolio, their positions, their P&L, responding in real time to a simulated world.

2. Adversarial honesty

From military. The simulation must contain intelligent opposition. "What does the market do if my thesis is wrong?" is not a sensitivity analysis. It is a red team. The simulation must be able to embarrass the user.

3. Assumption transparency

From epidemiology. Every output must trace back to explicit assumptions. The PM should never see a number without understanding which beliefs generated it. The interaction forces assumption choice before output display.

4. Bounded scenario matrix

From climate. Do not give the PM infinite parameter space. Give them a curated set of coherent worlds: "hawkish Fed + strong dollar," "stagflation," "China hard landing." Each world should have a name, a narrative, and traceable causality.

5. Multi-stakeholder views

From city planning. The same simulation must render differently for different users: the PM sees portfolio impact, the risk manager sees tail exposure, the CIO sees fund-level concentration. One model, many lenses.

6. Narrative transformation

From Shell. The deepest value is not the output but the changed mental model. After using the simulation, the PM should perceive the market differently, notice signals they previously ignored, hold multiple futures in mind simultaneously.

The product vision: World Model as instrument panel

Imagine a PM sits down and enters a simulation of the global financial system. Not a dashboard. Not a spreadsheet. A world. The PM says: "Show me what happens to my portfolio if the Fed raises rates 50bps while China devalues the yuan 8% and Brent spikes to $120."

The system does not return a single number. It constructs a coherent simulated future:

  • The rate hike strengthens the dollar. The PM's EM equity positions take a hit from currency translation.
  • But the yuan devaluation triggers capital flight from China, and some of that capital flows into US treasuries, partially offsetting the rate hike's impact on bond prices.
  • The oil spike feeds through to CPI with a lag. The PM's inflation-linked positions benefit, but their consumer discretionary shorts are already moving in the wrong direction because the market is pricing in demand destruction before the inflation print.
  • The cross-asset correlations shift. The PM's correlation assumptions from the last 12 months no longer hold. The simulation shows which hedges break.

The PM can then pause the simulation, rewind to any decision point, and ask: "What if I had put on a yuan hedge at this moment? What if I had doubled my oil position here?" Each counterfactual branches into a coherent alternative future.

The UX architecture

Layer 1: The cockpit. Borrowing from flight simulation, the PM's portfolio is the instrument panel. Every position is a live gauge. When the simulation runs, the gauges move. The PM watches their P&L respond to the simulated world in real time. This creates the embodied, visceral experience that makes simulation addictive: you feel the scenario in your portfolio, not just read about it.

Layer 2: The scenario selector. Borrowing from climate models, the system offers a curated matrix of named scenarios built from combinations of macro drivers. Each scenario has a narrative, a set of key assumptions, and signposts (from Shell) that would tell you the scenario is materializing in the real world. The PM can select a pre-built scenario or construct a custom one by adjusting drivers.

Layer 3: The red team. Borrowing from military wargaming, the simulation includes an adversarial engine that asks: "What is the market's response to your thesis? What does the smart money do when they see the same signals you see? Where is the crowded trade?" This is not a sensitivity analysis. It is an intelligent counterparty that responds to the PM's positioning.

Layer 4: The replay. Borrowing from flight simulation's after-action review, every simulation run is recorded and replayable. The PM can scrub through the timeline, examine decision points, and compare branching counterfactuals. The system highlights the moments where small changes in assumptions produced large divergences in outcomes, revealing the fragile joints in the PM's thesis.

Layer 5: The signpost monitor. Borrowing from Shell, each scenario produces a set of observable indicators. After the simulation session, these signposts are installed in a monitoring system. The PM is alerted when real-world data begins to match the early signatures of a specific scenario. The simulation is not a one-time exercise but an ongoing perceptual aid.

What makes it addictive

Every successful simulation product shares a common addictive loop:

HYPOTHESIS
The user forms a belief about how the world works. "If the Fed hikes, EM currencies will sell off."
SIMULATION
The user enters the simulated world and watches their hypothesis play out, or fail to play out, or play out with unexpected second-order effects.
SURPRISE
The simulation reveals something the user did not anticipate. This is the dopamine hit. The cross-asset correlation they assumed breaks. The hedge they trusted fails. The opportunity they missed appears.
REVISION
The user updates their mental model. They now perceive the financial system differently. They see connections and fragilities they previously missed.
RE-ENTRY
The user re-enters the simulation with their revised model and explores further. The loop continues. Each cycle sharpens their understanding.

This is the same loop that makes flight simulators, military war games, and SimCity compelling. The user is not passively consuming information. They are actively constructing understanding by exploring a responsive world. The simulation is not an answer. It is a thinking instrument.

The aha moment

The aha moment for a hedge fund PM using this product is the same aha moment that every simulation user across every industry eventually experiences: "I was thinking about this wrong."

The pilot who discovers their instinctive response to windshear would have killed everyone. The general who discovers his doctrine fails against asymmetric tactics. The epidemiologist who discovers that the timing of intervention matters more than its severity. The planner who discovers that the new highway induces the traffic it was supposed to relieve. The Shell executive who discovers that their strategy only works in one of three plausible futures.

The product is not the simulation. The product is the revised mental model that the user carries back into the real world. Everything else, the physics engine, the visual fidelity, the scenario library, the replay system, exists in service of that cognitive transformation.

A PM who has spent an hour in a world model exploring the second- and third-order consequences of a Fed hike does not trade differently because they have better numbers. They trade differently because they have better intuitions. They can feel the fragility in a position. They can sense when correlations are about to break. They have rehearsed the future, and when it arrives, they recognize it.

The Psychology of "Next Question" Loops

Seven mechanisms that make Perplexity, TikTok, ChatGPT, and slot machines irresistible -- and how a financial world model triggers all of them at once, with real money on the line.
