Develops constructive integration theory in the framework of formal topology, connecting Bishop's integral to point-free topology and enabling constructive probability theory in type-theoretic proof assistants.

Connection to Financial World Models

Bishop's constructive analysis provides the numerical backbone for a computational world model:

  • Built-in error bounds: Bishop reals carry convergence rates. Every computed price, risk measure, or expected value comes with a certified error bound—not an empirical estimate of error, but a proof that the approximation is within ε.
  • Constructive probability: probability distributions and expectations can be computed with certified accuracy. Monte Carlo is not the only option—constructive proofs of integrability yield deterministic algorithms with known convergence rates.
  • The approximate IVT for root-finding: calibrating models (finding parameters where model output matches market prices) is root-finding. The constructive IVT guarantees the bisection method converges at a known rate, with a certificate.
  • Moduli of continuity for stability: every constructive continuous function carries an explicit modulus of continuity. This directly quantifies model sensitivity: how much can inputs change before outputs change by more than ε?
Section 5

Homotopy Type Theory and Univalent Foundations

Origins and the Univalent Foundations Program

Homotopy Type Theory (HoTT) is the most significant recent development in the foundations of mathematics. It reinterprets Martin-Lof type theory through the lens of homotopy theory: types are spaces, terms are points, and identity proofs are paths. This gives a constructive foundation with a radically new conception of equality.

The Univalent Foundations Program. (2013)
Homotopy Type Theory: Univalent Foundations of Mathematics.
Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton. Available at homotopytypetheory.org/book.

The "HoTT book," written collaboratively during the 2012-2013 special year at IAS organized by Steve Awodey, Thierry Coquand, and Vladimir Voevodsky. It presents the synthetic theory of types-as-spaces, including the univalence axiom, higher inductive types, and applications to set-level mathematics.

Voevodsky, V. (2006)
A Very Short Note on Homotopy Lambda Calculus.
Unpublished note, September 2006. Available at math.ias.edu/vladimir/.
Voevodsky, V. (2010)
Univalent Foundations Project.
Modified version of an NSF grant application, October 2010. Available at math.ias.edu/vladimir/.
Awodey, S. and Warren, M.A. (2009)
Homotopy Theoretic Models of Identity Types.
Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society, 146(1), pp. 45-55.

The first published result establishing that the groupoid model of type theory generalizes to a full homotopy-theoretic model: identity types correspond to path spaces, and the elimination rule (J-rule) corresponds to path lifting.

Kapulkin, C. and Lumsdaine, P.L. (2021)
The Simplicial Model of Univalent Foundations (after Voevodsky).
Journal of the European Mathematical Society, 23(6), pp. 2071-2126.

The Univalence Axiom

Definition — Univalence axiom

For types A, B : Type in a universe U, there is a canonical map:

idtoeqv : (A =U B) → (A ≃ B)

mapping identity (paths in the universe) to equivalences. The univalence axiom states that this map is itself an equivalence:

(A =U B) ≃ (A ≃ B)

In words: identity is equivalent to equivalence. Two types that are equivalent (there exists a function between them with a two-sided inverse) are identical in the universe. This makes the universe's identity type non-trivial: there are multiple paths between equivalent types, corresponding to different equivalences.

Path Types and State Transitions

In HoTT, a path p : a =A b is an element of the identity type. Paths have rich structure:

  • Paths compose: given p : a = b and q : b = c, there is p · q : a = c
  • Paths invert: given p : a = b, there is p-1 : b = a
  • Higher paths exist: given p, q : a = b, one can form p = q (paths between paths)

This structure forms an infinity-groupoid: an algebraic structure with composition, inverses, and coherence at all levels.

Definition — Transport

Given a type family P : A -> Type and a path p : a =A b, there is a transport function:

transportP(p) : P(a) → P(b)

Transport moves data along a path. If P is a property of states and p is a transition between states, then transport carries the property from the old state to the new state. The computational content of the path determines how the property transforms.

Higher Inductive Types

Definition — Higher Inductive Type (HIT)

A higher inductive type is defined not only by its point constructors (as in an ordinary inductive type) but also by path constructors and possibly higher path constructors. For example, the circle S1:

data S1 : Type where
  base : S1
  loop : base = base

This has one point (base) and one non-trivial path from base to itself (loop). The resulting type has π1(S1) = Z (the fundamental group is the integers).

More complex HITs include:

  • Pushouts and quotients: for identifying states that should be considered equivalent
  • Truncations: ||A||n forgets information above level n
  • The Cauchy reals as a HIT: real numbers can be defined as a higher inductive type of Cauchy sequences quotiented by a path constructor identifying sequences with the same limit

Cubical Type Theory

Cohen, C., Coquand, T., Huber, S., and Mortberg, A. (2018)
Cubical Type Theory: A Constructive Interpretation of the Univalence Axiom.
Journal of Automated Reasoning, 60(2), pp. 127-171. (Conference version: TYPES 2015.)

This is the paper that made HoTT computationally viable. Cubical type theory gives the univalence axiom a computational interpretation—it computes, rather than being merely postulated. Paths are functions from an abstract interval [0,1], and the key operations (transport, composition) are defined by recursion on the type structure.

Vezzosi, A., Mortberg, A., and Abel, A. (2019)
Cubical Agda: A Dependently Typed Programming Language with Univalence and Higher Inductive Types.
Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages, 3(ICFP), Article 87.

Cubical Agda implements cubical type theory in a practical proof assistant, making HoTT directly executable. Code written in Cubical Agda can use univalence and HITs and still extract to executable Haskell.

Angiuli, C., Brunerie, G., Coquand, T., Hou (Favonia), K.-B., Harper, R., and Licata, D.R. (2021)
Syntax and Models of Cartesian Cubical Type Theory.
Mathematical Structures in Computer Science, 31(4), pp. 424-468.

The n-Type Hierarchy

Definition — Truncation levels

Types are classified by the complexity of their identity structure:

  • (-2)-types (contractible): there is exactly one element, up to paths. Trivial state spaces.
  • (-1)-types (mere propositions): either empty or contractible. Represents "truth values." Any two proofs of the same proposition are equal. Constraints and invariants live here.
  • 0-types (sets): identity between elements is a proposition. Ordinary data types (natural numbers, lists, records). Most state spaces are sets.
  • 1-types (groupoids): identity proofs between elements can themselves differ. State spaces with non-trivial symmetries (e.g., portfolios that are equivalent up to relabeling).
  • n-types: higher levels capture higher-order symmetries.

Connections to Topology and Sheaves

Shulman, M. (2018)
Brouwer's Fixed-Point Theorem in Real-Cohesive Homotopy Type Theory.
Mathematical Structures in Computer Science, 28(6), pp. 856-941.

Shulman shows that Brouwer's fixed-point theorem can be proven in a cohesive extension of HoTT, where types have genuine topological content. This "real-cohesive" HoTT can distinguish continuous from discontinuous maps internally.

Schreiber, U. (2013)
Differential Cohomology in a Cohesive Infinity-Topos.
arXiv preprint arXiv:1310.7930.
Rijke, E. (2022)
Introduction to Homotopy Type Theory.
arXiv preprint arXiv:2212.11082.
Connection to Financial World Models

HoTT provides a remarkably natural language for financial market modeling:

  • Path types as regime transitions: a path p : regime_A = regime_B in a universe of market models is not just a claim that regimes are equivalent—it is a specific, computable transformation between them. Different paths are different transition mechanisms.
  • Higher paths as meta-transitions: a path between paths alpha : p = q describes how one transition mechanism deforms into another. This models policy evolution: not just that the central bank changed rates, but how the rate-changing rule itself evolved.
  • Univalence for model equivalence: two market models that are structurally equivalent (there exists an equivalence between their state spaces preserving all observables) are identical as types. You can substitute one for the other in any context. This gives a rigorous notion of "model reduction" with guaranteed correctness.
  • HITs for quotient markets: markets with symmetries (e.g., indistinguishable assets, fungible instruments) are naturally modeled as higher inductive types where the path constructors encode the symmetries.
  • Transport for invariant propagation: if you prove a property (no-arbitrage, completeness) of model A, and you have a path p : A = B, then transport(p) automatically gives you the corresponding property of model B. Theorems propagate along equivalences for free.
  • Cubical type theory for computability: unlike axiomatic HoTT, cubical type theory makes all of the above compute. Transport along a path produces an actual algorithm transforming data from one model to another.
Synthesis

Unified Architecture: How These Foundations Compose

These five foundations are not independent pillars—they form an integrated stack for building a verified computational world model:

LAYER 5: HoTT / Univalent Foundations
       Model equivalence, regime transitions, continuous deformation
       Path types = transitions  |  HITs = quotient spaces  |  Univalence = model substitution
          |
LAYER 4: Martin-Lof Type Theory
       Dependent types for state-indexed computation
       Pi-types = parameterized models  |  Sigma-types = state bundles  |  Id-types = equality proofs
          |
LAYER 3: Typed Decomposition & Composition
       Session types (protocols) + Linear types (resources) + Open games (equilibria)
       Algebraic effects (modular side-effects) + Category theory (compositional semantics)
          |
LAYER 2: Bishop's Constructive Analysis
       Certified numerics with built-in error bounds
       Constructive reals + moduli of continuity + constructive probability
          |
LAYER 1: Constructive Logic (vs. Classical)
       Every proof is a program; every existence claim produces a witness
       BHK interpretation  |  No LEM  |  Decidability is a property  |  Realizability

The key insight is that constructive mathematics does not sacrifice power—it adds information. Every classical theorem that can be proved constructively automatically carries more content: algorithms, convergence rates, error bounds, and decision procedures. For building computational world models of financial markets, this additional content is exactly what distinguishes a formal specification from an executable system.

1. Foundational Papers by Per Martin-Lof

ML-1

"An Intuitionistic Theory of Types"

Per Martin-Lof. Written 1972 (unpublished; circulated as preprint). First widely available in: G. Sambin and J.M. Smith (eds.), Twenty-Five Years of Constructive Type Theory, Oxford University Press, 1998, pp. 127–172.

Key contributions Introduced the first version of intuitionistic type theory with a universe of all types (Type : Type). This version was shown inconsistent by Girard's paradox (analogous to Russell's paradox). Established the core idea of types as propositions and terms as proofs in a constructive setting. Introduced dependent function types and dependent sum types.

ML-2

"An Intuitionistic Theory of Types: Predicative Part"

Per Martin-Lof. In: H.E. Rose and J.C. Shepherdson (eds.), Logic Colloquium '73, Studies in Logic and the Foundations of Mathematics, vol. 80, North-Holland, 1975, pp. 73–118.

Key contributions The predicative correction of the 1972 theory. Introduced a hierarchy of universes (U0 : U1 : U2 : …) to avoid Girard's paradox. Defined the core type formers: Pi-types, Sigma-types, disjoint union, natural numbers, identity types, and W-types (well-founded trees). This is the paper that established the stable foundation for all subsequent MLTT work.

ML-3

"Constructive Mathematics and Computer Programming"

Per Martin-Lof. In: L.J. Cohen, J. Los, H. Pfeiffer, and K.-P. Podewski (eds.), Logic, Methodology and Philosophy of Science VI (Proceedings of the Sixth International Congress, Hannover 1979), Studies in Logic and the Foundations of Mathematics, vol. 104, North-Holland, 1982, pp. 153–175.

Key contributions Argued that MLTT simultaneously serves as (a) a logic for constructive mathematics, (b) a typed programming language, and (c) a specification language. Established the propositions-as-types principle in full generality for dependent types. Clarified the Brouwer-Heyting-Kolmogorov (BHK) interpretation: a proof of a proposition is a program that computes a witness. Showed that mathematical concepts (elements, sets, functions) correspond directly to programming concepts (data structures, data types, programs). This paper is the single most important bridge between constructive mathematics and computer science.

ML-4

"Intuitionistic Type Theory" (Bibliopolis lecture notes)

Per Martin-Lof. Notes by Giovanni Sambin of lectures given in Padua, June 1980. Studies in Proof Theory, vol. 1, Bibliopolis, Naples, 1984, ix + 91 pp. A retypeset PDF is available via archive-pml.github.io.

Key contributions The definitive pedagogical exposition of MLTT. Systematically presents: judgement forms (a : A, A type, a = b : A, A = B type), the four type formers (Pi, Sigma, +, Id) with their formation, introduction, elimination, and computation rules, natural numbers, finite types, universes, and W-types. Introduces the "meaning explanation" — a semantic justification where each judgement form is explained in terms of computation (canonical forms). This is the standard reference for the complete formal system.

ML-5

"On the Meanings of the Logical Constants and the Justifications of the Logical Laws"

Per Martin-Lof. Nordic Journal of Philosophical Logic, vol. 1, no. 1, 1996, pp. 11–60. Based on lectures given in Siena, April 1983.

Key contributions Philosophical foundation for MLTT. Distinguished between judgements and propositions, and between the act of judging and the content of a judgement. Provided the meaning-theoretic justification for the logical constants via introduction rules (which define meaning) and elimination rules (which are justified by meaning). Essential for understanding why constructive type theory has computational content.

ML-6

"Analytic and Synthetic Judgements in Type Theory"

Per Martin-Lof. In: P. Parrini (ed.), Kant and Contemporary Epistemology, Kluwer Academic Publishers, 1994, pp. 87–99.

Key contributions Connected MLTT to Kantian epistemology. Argued that the distinction between analytic and synthetic judgements can be made precise within type theory, where analytic judgements are definitional equalities (computed by reduction) and synthetic judgements require proof (construction).

2. The Curry-Howard Correspondence

CH-1

"The Formulae-as-Types Notion of Construction"

William A. Howard. Manuscript 1969; published in: J.P. Seldin and J.R. Hindley (eds.), To H.B. Curry: Essays on Combinatory Logic, Lambda Calculus and Formalism, Academic Press, 1980, pp. 479–490.

Key contributions Made explicit the syntactic correspondence between simply typed lambda calculus and natural deduction for intuitionistic propositional logic. Showed that (1) types correspond to propositions, (2) terms correspond to proofs, (3) beta-reduction corresponds to proof normalization, and (4) the type-inhabitation problem corresponds to provability. Extended Curry's earlier observation about combinators and Hilbert-style axioms to the full natural deduction setting. The "Rosetta Stone" between logic and computation.

CH-2

"Functionality in Combinatory Logic"

Haskell B. Curry. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, vol. 20, 1934, pp. 584–590.

Key contributions The earliest observation of the types-as-propositions connection: noticed that the type of the combinator K (λx y. x) corresponds to the axiom schema A → (B → A), and S corresponds to (A → (B → C)) → ((A → B) → (A → C)). This observation, initially just a curiosity, became the seed of the entire Curry-Howard paradigm.

The Correspondence in Full (with Dependent Types)

Logic (Propositions)Type Theory (Types)Programming (Data)
Implication A → BFunction type A → BFunctions
Conjunction A ∧ BProduct type A × BPairs / records
Disjunction A ∨ BSum type A + BTagged unions
Truth (⊤)Unit type 1Singleton value
Falsity (⊥)Empty type 0No inhabitants
∀x:A, B(x)Π(x:A). B(x)Dependent functions
∃x:A, B(x)Σ(x:A). B(x)Dependent pairs
a =A bIdA(a, b)Equality witnesses
Proof of PTerm t : PProgram of type P
Proof normalizationβ-reductionComputation / evaluation

Why Constructive Proofs Extract to Executable Algorithms

In classical logic, a proof of "there exists x such that P(x)" may use the law of excluded middle or double negation elimination, neither of which provides a concrete witness. In constructive (intuitionistic) logic, the BHK interpretation demands:

  • A proof of "A and B" is a pair (proof of A, proof of B)
  • A proof of "A or B" is either a proof of A or a proof of B, together with a tag saying which
  • A proof of "A implies B" is a function transforming any proof of A into a proof of B
  • A proof of "∃x:A, B(x)" is a pair (a, p) where a : A is a witness and p is a proof that B(a) holds

Since every proof is a construction (a computable function or data structure), the Curry-Howard correspondence guarantees that any constructive proof of an existential statement can be mechanically extracted into an executable algorithm that computes the witness. This is the basis of program extraction in Coq (via Extraction), Agda (programs are proofs directly), and Minlog (optimized extraction from classical-looking proofs with constructive content).

CH-3

"Adapting Proofs-as-Programs: The Curry-Howard Protocol"

Iman Poernomo, John Crossley, and Martin Wirsing. Monographs in Computer Science, Springer, 2005.

Key contributions Systematic treatment of how to adapt the Curry-Howard correspondence for practical software development. Covers program extraction, refinement, and specification languages based on type theory.

CH-4

"Lectures on the Curry-Howard Isomorphism"

Morten Heine Sorensen and Pawel Urzyczyn. Studies in Logic and the Foundations of Mathematics, vol. 149, Elsevier, 2006.

Key contributions Comprehensive textbook covering the correspondence from simply typed lambda calculus through System F, System Fω, and dependent types. Includes proof normalization, strong normalization theorems, and second-order logic connections.

3. Formal Definitions: Π-types, Σ-types, Identity Types

Π-type (Dependent Function Type)

Formation: If A : Type and B : A → Type (B is a family of types indexed by A), then Π(x:A). B(x) : Type

Introduction: If for any x : A we can construct t(x) : B(x), then λ(x). t(x) : Π(x:A). B(x)

Elimination: If f : Π(x:A). B(x) and a : A, then f(a) : B(a)

Computation (β): (λ(x). t(x))(a) ≡ t(a)

Uniqueness (η): f ≡ λ(x). f(x) : Π(x:A). B(x)

Intuition for state modeling: A Π-type Π(s:State). Transition(s) encodes: for every state s, there is a (possibly different) type of valid transitions from s. This captures state-dependent dynamics — the available moves depend on where you are.

Σ-type (Dependent Pair Type)

Formation: If A : Type and B : A → Type, then Σ(x:A). B(x) : Type

Introduction: If a : A and b : B(a), then (a, b) : Σ(x:A). B(x)

Elimination: Given p : Σ(x:A). B(x), we have fst(p) : A and snd(p) : B(fst(p))

Computation: fst(a, b) ≡ a,   snd(a, b) ≡ b

Intuition for state modeling: Σ(s:State). Property(s) represents "a state together with a proof that it satisfies some property." For example, Σ(s:State). IsReachable(s) is the type of reachable states — you cannot even construct one without proving reachability. This bakes invariants into the data.

Identity Type (Propositional Equality)

Formation: If A : Type and a, b : A, then IdA(a, b) : Type   (also written a =A b)

Introduction: For any a : A, refl(a) : IdA(a, a)   (reflexivity)

Elimination (J-rule): To prove a property C for all p : IdA(a, b), it suffices to prove C(a, a, refl(a)) for the reflexivity case.

Computation: J applied to refl reduces to the base case.

Intuition for state equivalence: IdState(s1, s2) captures when two system states are provably equal. In homotopy type theory, identity types generalize to paths, enabling a richer notion of state equivalence — states can be "equivalent up to isomorphism" via the univalence axiom, not just definitionally equal.

4. Dependent Types Encoding State Spaces

4.1 State Spaces as Indexed Type Families

The key insight is that a dynamical system's state space can be represented as a type family indexed by time, parameters, or discrete states:

-- A system with states indexed by a phase type
State : Phase → Type

-- A transition function that respects the phase structure
step : Π(p : Phase). State(p) → Event → Σ(q : Phase). State(q)

-- The return type (Σ) pairs the new phase with a state in that phase
-- This PREVENTS constructing a state in the wrong phase by construction

4.2 Π-types for State-Dependent Transitions

-- Policy: for each state, choose an action from the valid actions for THAT state
Policy : Π(s : State). ValidActions(s) → NextState(s)

-- The type ValidActions(s) varies with s -- a state where you are bankrupt
-- has different valid actions than a state where you are solvent
-- This is impossible to express in simply-typed systems without runtime checks

4.3 Σ-types for Constrained State Spaces

-- A feasible state is a state together with proof of feasibility
FeasibleState : Type
FeasibleState = Σ(s : State). IsFeasible(s)

-- A trajectory is a sequence of states where each transition is valid
Trajectory : Nat → Type
Trajectory 0     = FeasibleState
Trajectory (n+1) = Σ(prev : Trajectory n).
                    Σ(s : FeasibleState).
                    ValidTransition(last(prev), fst(s))

4.4 Identity Types for State Equivalence

-- Two market states are equivalent if they yield identical observables
MarketEquiv : Market → Market → Type
MarketEquiv m1 m2 = Id Observable (observe m1) (observe m2)

-- Bisimulation: two systems are behaviorally equivalent
Bisim : System → System → Type
Bisim s1 s2 = Π(a : Action).
    Id Observation (step(s1,a).obs) (step(s2,a).obs)
  × Bisim (step(s1,a).next) (step(s2,a).next)

DS-1

"Coalgebras and Codata in Dependent Type Theory"

Anton Setzer, Andreas Abel, Brigitte Pientka, David Thibodeau. Various papers 2012–2016 at TYPES, TLCA, and LICS.

Key contributions Coalgebraic methods formalize state-based dynamical systems in dependent type theory. A coalgebra for a functor F is a pair (S, step : S → F(S)), capturing exactly the structure of a state machine. M-types (the coinductive dual of W-types) in MLTT represent infinite behaviors (streams, processes, non-terminating systems).

DS-2

"Interactive Programs in Dependent Type Theory"

Peter Hancock and Anton Setzer. In: P. Clote and H. Schwichtenberg (eds.), Computer Science Logic (CSL 2000), LNCS 1862, Springer, 2000, pp. 317–331.

Key contributions Modeled interactive programs (which run forever, accept input, produce output) as coinductive objects in MLTT. Defined IO trees as greatest fixed points, where each node represents a state waiting for input. Directly relevant to modeling open dynamical systems that interact with an environment.

5. Formalizations in Agda, Coq, and Lean

FA-1

"Dependently Typed Programming in Agda"

Ulf Norell. In: P. Koopman, R. Plasmeijer, and D. Swierstra (eds.), Advanced Functional Programming (AFP 2008), LNCS 5832, Springer, 2009, pp. 230–266.

Key contributions Foundational paper on Agda as an implementation of MLTT. Demonstrates indexed types (Vec n, Fin n), with-abstraction for dependent pattern matching, and how the type checker serves as a proof checker. Agda's definitional equality includes pattern matching, making it powerful for encoding state machines where the type of valid operations depends on the current state index.

FA-2

"The Calculus of Constructions" / "Inductive Definitions in the System Coq"

Thierry Coquand and Gerard Huet, Information and Computation, vol. 76, 1988, pp. 95–120. Christine Paulin-Mohring, TLCA 1993, LNCS 664, pp. 328–345.

Key contributions Coq is based on the Calculus of Inductive Constructions (CIC), which extends MLTT with impredicative Prop, inductive types, and universe polymorphism. Coq's extraction mechanism (Letouzey, 2002) can produce OCaml, Haskell, or Scheme code from constructive proofs — directly implementing the Curry-Howard program extraction paradigm.

FA-3

"Modelling Bitcoin in Agda"

Fahad F.A. Alhabardi and Arnold Shereni. Preprint, arXiv:1804.06398, 2018.

Key contributions Formalized core Bitcoin protocol properties in Agda using dependent types. Demonstrated how MLTT can model a financial/cryptographic system with formally verified invariants — transactions must satisfy validity predicates baked into their types.

FA-4

"Adventures in Formalisation: Financial Contracts, Modules, and Two-Level Type Theory"

arXiv:1811.11317, 2018.

Key contributions Explored formalizing financial contracts using dependent type theory. Addresses how contract terms, obligations, and state transitions can be encoded as types, with contract execution modeled as type-level computation.

FA-5

"The Lean Theorem Prover (System Description)"

Leonardo de Moura, Soonho Kong, Jeremy Avigad, Floris van Doorn, and Jakob von Raumer. CADE-25, LNAI 9195, Springer, 2015, pp. 378–388.

Key contributions Lean implements a variant of the Calculus of Inductive Constructions with quotient types and a powerful tactic framework. Lean 4 (de Moura and Ullrich, 2021) is both a theorem prover and a general-purpose programming language, making the "proofs are programs" paradigm directly practical. Mathlib, Lean's mathematics library, contains extensive formalized mathematics relevant to dynamical systems (topology, analysis, measure theory).

FA-6

"Formalization of the Undecidability of the Halting Problem and Related Results in Coq"

Yannick Forster, Dominik Kirst, and Gert Smolka. ITP 2019, LIPIcs, vol. 141, 2019.

Key contributions Demonstrates state-machine formalization in Coq, including Turing machines and their state transitions as dependent types. Shows how computability theory itself can be formalized in CIC.

6. Recent Applications (2010–2025)

6.1 Economic and Financial Modeling

EC-1

"Quantifying Bounded Rationality: Formal Verification of Simon's Satisficing Through Flexible Stochastic Dominance"

arXiv:2507.07052, 2025.

Key contributions Applied formal verification techniques (rooted in type-theoretic reasoning) to Herbert Simon's satisficing model of bounded rationality. Demonstrated that dependent types can represent decision-theoretic concepts where the available choices and their properties are state-dependent, with proofs of stochastic dominance relations verified mechanically.

EC-2

System and Method for Modeling and Verifying Financial Trading Platforms

USPTO patents: US 10,109,010; US 10,424,019; US 10,769,726 (2018–2020).

Key contributions These patents describe using type-system-based logical programming to model and verify financial trading systems. Mathematical axioms are generated from axiomatic operational semantics, with the type system enforcing correctness of trading operations. Demonstrates industrial interest in type-theoretic verification of financial systems.

EC-3

"Certified Symbolic Management of Financial Multi-Party Contracts"

Patrick Bahr, Jost Berthold, and Martin Elsman. ICFP 2015, ACM, 2015, pp. 315–327.

Key contributions Formalized financial contract languages with certified evaluation. Contracts are represented as typed terms; contract execution is a type-preserving reduction. Extended in subsequent work to multi-party settings with dependent types ensuring that obligations match across counterparties.

6.2 Verified Numerical Computation

VN-1

"A Computer-Verified, Monadic, Functional Implementation of the Integral"

Russell O'Connor. arXiv:0809.1552, 2008; published in Theoretical Computer Science, vol. 411, no. 37, 2010, pp. 3386–3402.

Key contributions Implemented verified exact real arithmetic in Coq, including integration. Demonstrated that constructive proofs of convergence can be extracted to executable algorithms computing numerical results with guaranteed error bounds. The monadic structure handles effects (partial computation, precision management) in a dependently typed setting.

VN-2

"Exact Real Search: Formalised Optimisation and Regression in Constructive Univalent Mathematics"

arXiv:2401.09270, 2024.

Key contributions Formalized optimization and regression algorithms in constructive univalent mathematics (HoTT-based). Shows that numerical optimization can be carried out within a constructive type-theoretic framework, with the univalence axiom enabling transport of results across equivalent representations.

VN-3

"Computable Analysis in Coq" (C-CoRN project)

Luitzen de Vries, Bas Spitters, et al. Various papers 2001–2015, Radboud University Nijmegen.

Key contributions The C-CoRN (Constructive Coq Repository at Nijmegen) library formalized constructive real analysis, including the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, with extracted algorithms computing provably correct numerical results. Demonstrated that the entire chain from constructive proof to executable numerical computation can be mechanized.

6.3 Homotopy Type Theory and Univalent Foundations

HoTT-1

"Homotopy Type Theory: Univalent Foundations of Mathematics"

The Univalent Foundations Program. Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton, 2013. Available at homotopytypetheory.org.

Key contributions Extended MLTT with Voevodsky's univalence axiom: equivalent types are identical (ua : (A ≃ B) → (A =U B)). This makes identity types much richer — equality between types corresponds to isomorphism, not just syntactic identity. For dynamical systems, this means state spaces that are isomorphic can be freely substituted, enabling modular system composition. Higher inductive types allow quotienting state spaces by equivalence relations.

HoTT-2

"Cubical Agda: A Dependently Typed Programming Language with Univalence and Higher Inductive Types"

Andrea Vezzosi, Anders Mortberg, and Andreas Abel. ICFP 2019, ACM, 2019.

Key contributions Made univalence computational in Agda via cubical type theory. Unlike the original HoTT book's axiom (which blocks computation), cubical Agda gives univalence computational content — transport along equivalences actually computes. Programs that use state-space equivalences can be executed, not just type-checked.

6.4 Program Synthesis and Verification

PS-1

"Dependent Type Theory for Programming and Proving"

Robert Harper. Course notes, Carnegie Mellon University, Spring 2026. Available at cs.cmu.edu/~rwh/courses/atpl/.

Key contributions Harper's most recent treatment of dependent type theory as a unified framework for programming and proving. Covers bidirectional type checking, normalization by evaluation, and the relationship between computational and logical aspects of dependent types.

PS-2

"Practical Program Extraction from Classical Proofs"

Various authors. Electronic Notes in Theoretical Computer Science, Elsevier, 2006.

Key contributions Extended program extraction beyond purely constructive proofs, showing that even classically-proved theorems can sometimes yield computational content through refined extraction techniques (A-translation, modified realizability).

7. Connections to Active Inference and Bayesian Frameworks

AI-1

"Mathematical Foundations for a Compositional Account of the Bayesian Brain"

Toby St Clere Smithe. arXiv:2212.12538, 2022 (PhD thesis, University of Oxford).

Key contributions Used category theory (closely related to the categorical semantics of dependent type theory) to give compositional foundations for active inference and the Bayesian brain hypothesis. Defined statistical games, lenses, and optics as the mathematical structures underlying perception-action loops. While not directly using MLTT, the categorical structures (dependent products, dependent sums as fibrations) are the semantic counterparts of Π-types and Σ-types.

AI-2

"Generalised Free Energy and Active Inference"

Thomas Parr and Karl J. Friston. Biological Cybernetics, vol. 113, 2019, pp. 495–513.

Key contributions Defined generalized free energy for active inference agents. The state-dependent nature of action selection (different beliefs lead to different valid actions) has a natural dependent-type encoding: Policy : Π(b : Belief). ActionSpace(b), where the action space depends on the agent's current belief state.

AI-3

"Active Inference for Self-Organizing Multi-LLM Systems: A Bayesian Thermodynamic Approach to Adaptation"

arXiv:2412.10425, 2024.

Key contributions Recent work connecting active inference to multi-agent systems (LLM-based). The typed state space approach — where each agent's state type depends on its role and beliefs — is implicitly dependent-typed, though not formalized in MLTT.

Gap in the literature

There is no published work (as of August 2026) that directly formalizes active inference or the free energy principle within Martin-Lof type theory or a proof assistant. The categorical semantics of MLTT (fibrations, dependent products/sums) are the same structures used in compositional accounts of Bayesian inference (lenses, optics), but the explicit bridge — "here is active inference formalized in Agda/Coq" — has not been built. This represents an open research opportunity.

Section I

Soros's Reflexivity Theory

George Soros spent decades trying to get academia to take one idea seriously: that the act of observing and theorizing about financial markets changes those markets in ways the theories fail to account for. He finally formalized it as the interaction of two functions.

The Two Functions

The cognitive function runs from reality to perception: participants observe the state of the world — prices, fundamentals, sentiment — and form beliefs. But those beliefs are always incomplete and distorted. Soros calls this the principle of fallibility: human understanding of the world is inherently imperfect because we are part of the world we are trying to understand.

The participating function (Soros also calls it the manipulative function) runs in the opposite direction: participants act on their beliefs through buying, selling, lending, and capital allocation, and those actions change the very fundamentals they were trying to assess.

x = f(x) — perceptions are a function of the situation
y = φ(y) — the situation is a function of perceptions

Reflexivity: the independent variable of one function is the dependent variable of the other. Neither function has a genuinely independent variable. The relationship is circular.

This is not a metaphor. A rising stock price genuinely improves a company's access to capital, strengthens its balance sheet, attracts talent, improves credit ratings, and increases consumer confidence. The perception of strength creates actual strength, which validates the perception — until it doesn't.

The Boom-Bust Sequence

Soros's most actionable contribution is his model of how reflexive feedback produces boom-bust cycles in a structured, identifiable sequence:

  1. An underlying trend emerges. Some genuine change in fundamentals — a new technology, a deregulation, a shift in capital flows — creates a legitimate basis for asset price appreciation.
  2. A prevailing bias reinforces the trend. Participants develop a narrative that explains and extrapolates the trend. Rising prices validate the narrative; the narrative attracts more buyers; prices rise further.
  3. Successful reinforcement breeds complacency. The trend accelerates. Skeptics are punished. Leverage increases. The bias and the trend become self-reinforcing — a positive feedback loop.
  4. A moment of truth. Market expectations become so far removed from reality that participants are forced to recognize a misconception is involved.
  5. Twilight period. The bias erodes but inertia carries the trend forward briefly.
  6. The crash. The reversal triggers the same reflexive mechanism in the opposite direction. Because the bias must fully unwind, busts are typically faster and steeper than the preceding booms.

“I view such periods of stability as exceptional. Markets may just as easily tend away from a putative equilibrium as toward it.”

George Soros, “Fallibility, Reflexivity, and the Human Uncertainty Principle,” 2014

Reflexivity in Practice: The Trades

Black Wednesday, 1992

The UK had joined the European Exchange Rate Mechanism at an unsustainably high rate for the pound. British inflation was triple the German rate. Interest rates high enough to defend the peg were crushing domestic asset prices. Soros identified a textbook reflexive trap: the Bank of England was spending foreign reserves to maintain a price (the exchange rate) that was undermining the fundamentals (the economy) that would be needed to sustain it. The defense mechanism was destroying the thing it was defending.

Soros built a $1.5 billion short position, then escalated to $10 billion on the morning of September 16, 1992. The Bank of England burned an estimated 40% of its foreign reserves in a single day trying to prop up the pound. By evening, the UK withdrew from the ERM. The pound fell 15% against the Deutschmark, 25% against the dollar. Soros cleared over $1 billion.

The key insight was not contrarian — many people thought the pound was overvalued. The insight was reflexive: the act of defending the peg was making the peg less defensible, creating a one-way bet. The system was in a self-undermining loop that could only resolve by breaking.

The Asian Financial Crisis, 1997–98

Soros identified the same reflexive structure across Southeast Asian economies: fixed or pegged exchange rates maintained by governments whose economies depended on foreign capital inflows attracted by those same pegs. The peg attracted capital, which supported growth, which validated the peg — until current account deficits became unsustainable. When Thailand's baht broke, the reflexive loop reversed across the region: capital flight weakened currencies, weakened currencies increased the real burden of dollar-denominated debt, which triggered more capital flight.

Why Mainstream Economics Rejected Reflexivity

For decades, academic economics had no place for Soros's insight, for three interlocking reasons:

  • Equilibrium theory requires it. General equilibrium and efficient market models assume that prices converge to fundamental values via arbitrage. Reflexivity says prices can systematically diverge from fundamentals and alter those fundamentals in the process. Admitting this means abandoning the mathematical tractability that makes equilibrium models publishable.
  • Rational expectations forbid it. The Lucas school assumes agents have correct models of the economy on average. Reflexivity says agents' models are constitutively biased and that this bias is not noise — it is a structural force that shapes outcomes.
  • Soros was an outsider. He was a hedge fund manager writing philosophy books, not a professor publishing in the American Economic Review. The academy could afford to ignore him because his ideas did not arrive in the form of theorem-proof papers.

What changed: the 2008 financial crisis made it impossible to pretend that markets self-correct efficiently. Behavioral economics (Kahneman, Thaler) opened the door to biased agents. Complexity economics (Arthur, Beinhocker, the Santa Fe Institute) embraced feedback loops and emergent dynamics. The Adaptive Markets Hypothesis (Andrew Lo) explicitly incorporated evolutionary dynamics and regime changes. Soros is no longer on the fringe — he is a precursor.

Section II

Performativity in Economics

Soros argued from a trader's perspective. The sociologists of finance arrived at the same conclusion from the other direction: financial models don't describe markets. They construct them.

MacKenzie: An Engine, Not a Camera

Donald MacKenzie's 2006 book traces the history of the Black-Scholes-Merton option pricing model and demonstrates something extraordinary. Before Black-Scholes was published in 1973, option prices on the Chicago Board Options Exchange did not conform to the model's predictions. After the model was widely adopted — after traders started using it to price options — actual market prices converged toward the model's theoretical values.

The model was not a camera passively capturing reality. It was an engine that reshaped reality to match its assumptions.

MacKenzie coined the term Barnesian performativity (after sociologist Barry Barnes) to describe this phenomenon: a theory that makes itself true by being believed and acted upon. He distinguished three levels:

  • Generic performativity: The theory is used in practice (Black-Scholes is used to price options).
  • Effective performativity: Using the theory changes economic outcomes (prices actually shift toward model predictions).
  • Barnesian performativity: Using the theory makes the world more like the theory's assumptions (implied volatility surfaces flatten toward the model's constant-volatility assumption).

And then there is counterperformativity: when widespread adoption of a model eventually undermines the conditions that made it accurate. The Black-Scholes model assumed constant volatility and log-normal returns. By 1987, every major options desk was using the same model, creating a homogeneity of positions and hedging strategies. On Black Monday, the coordinated delta-hedging prescribed by Black-Scholes transformed a decline into a crash — the model's hedging prescription amplified the very volatility it assumed was constant. After October 19, 1987, the volatility smile appeared permanently in options markets — a structural scar recording the moment the model broke itself.

Key Insight The performativity cycle runs: Model adopted → market conforms to model → model appears validated → model adopted more widely → homogeneity of positions grows → model breaks itself in a crisis. This is reflexivity at the level of theory, not just price.

Callon: The Laws of the Markets

Michel Callon pushed the argument further in his 1998 collection. His central claim: economics does not describe an existing external economy — it brings that economy into being. Economic theories, models, and devices (spreadsheets, trading platforms, risk metrics) are not passive instruments of observation. They are active participants that format, frame, and construct the economic interactions they purport to measure.

Callon argued that the standard sociological critique of economics — that homo economicus is unrealistic — misses the point. The real question is not whether people are naturally rational maximizers, but how economic institutions, tools, and theories produce agents who behave as if they are. The calculative rationality economists assume is not a natural trait but an engineered outcome of the sociotechnical apparatus of markets.

For a world model, the implication is direct: the model is not outside the system it models. It is part of the sociotechnical apparatus that constitutes the system.

Section III

The Observer Effect in Complex Systems

The problem of observation changing the observed is not unique to finance. It is a structural feature of any system where the observer is part of the system. Finance is the most extreme case because the observer's actions (trades) are the system's primary substrate (price formation).

Goodhart's Law

Charles Goodhart, advising the Bank of England in 1975: “Any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes.” Later simplified to: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.

In finance, this is ubiquitous. An alpha signal that works precisely because no one is trading it stops working the moment it becomes a systematic strategy that many funds deploy. The VIX was a useful measure of implied volatility until it became a tradeable instrument with its own ecosystem of ETFs, options, and structured products — now VIX dynamics are partially driven by the mechanics of those instruments rather than the fear it was designed to measure.

The Lucas Critique

Robert Lucas (1976) formalized a version of this for macroeconomics: econometric relationships estimated under one policy regime will break down when the policy changes, because agents adjust their behavior in response to policy. A Phillips curve estimated during a period of low inflation cannot be used to predict what happens when the central bank deliberately targets higher inflation — because agents will change their wage-setting behavior in response to the new regime.

The Lucas Critique is reflexivity in regulatory drag. But it only goes one direction: it says the observed react to the observer's policy. It does not say the observer must model itself. Soros's insight is deeper — the observer's model is part of the observed system.

Campbell's Law

Donald Campbell (1979): “The more any quantitative social indicator is used for social decision-making, the more subject it will be to corruption pressures and the more apt it will be to distort and corrupt the social processes it is intended to monitor.” This captures not just the passive observer effect but the active gaming that measurement incentivizes. In finance: the moment a credit rating methodology becomes known, issuers restructure their obligations to optimize for the methodology rather than for actual creditworthiness. The measure creates the behavior it was supposed to passively detect.

The Common Thread Goodhart, Lucas, and Campbell all describe the same structural phenomenon from different angles: measurement in social systems is not passive extraction of information. It is an intervention that reshapes the system. A world model that treats its own outputs as passive observations is committing a category error about its own ontological status.
Section IV

Self-Referential Systems

Reflexivity in markets is an instance of a deeper phenomenon: self-reference. To understand why modeling reflexivity is fundamentally difficult — and why getting it right would be genuinely unprecedented — we need the theoretical machinery of self-referential systems.

Hofstadter's Strange Loops

Douglas Hofstadter's concept of a strange loop (1979, 2007) describes a system in which, by moving through levels of a hierarchy, you unexpectedly arrive back at the starting level. The classic examples: Gödel's incompleteness theorem (arithmetic contains statements about arithmetic that arithmetic cannot prove), Escher's drawing hands (each hand draws the hand that draws it), Bach's fugues (themes that modulate upward through keys and arrive back at the starting key).

A financial world model that includes itself as part of the world it models is a strange loop. The model produces outputs (predictions, signals). Those outputs drive actions (trades). Those actions change the world. The changed world is the input to the next iteration of the model. The model is simultaneously the map and part of the territory.

Autopoiesis

Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela (1972) coined autopoiesis to describe systems that produce and maintain themselves. A cell produces the membrane that contains the processes that produce the membrane. The system's boundary is produced by the system's own operations. Financial markets are autopoietic in this sense: market structure (prices, liquidity, volatility regimes) is produced by trading activity, which is shaped by market structure, which is produced by trading activity.

The important distinction from simple feedback: in a thermostat (negative feedback), the set point is external. In an autopoietic system, the system produces its own set points. Markets do not have externally given equilibrium prices. The “equilibrium” is an emergent property of the interactions that constitute the market, and it shifts as those interactions shift.

Luhmann's Social Systems

Niklas Luhmann (1984) extended autopoiesis to social systems, arguing that social systems consist of communications, not people. The economy is a system of payments, not a system of humans who happen to pay each other. Key insight: social systems are operationally closed but structurally coupled to their environment. The financial system processes everything as price signals — a pandemic, a war, a tweet — and can only respond to its environment through its own internal operations (trades, valuations, risk calculations).

For a world model, Luhmann's framework provides a crucial distinction: the model does not need to simulate the entire world. It needs to simulate the financial system's internal processing of the world — which includes the financial system's internal processing of the model's own outputs.

Self-Reference vs. Recursion

Technical Distinction Recursion is a function calling itself with different arguments: f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2). The structure is fixed; only the inputs change. Each level of the recursion operates by the same rules.

Self-reference is a system whose behavior depends on its own description of its behavior. The rules themselves are endogenous. A recursive system computes; a self-referential system computes about its own computation. This is why self-reference produces undecidability (Gödel), uncomputability (Turing), and the paradoxes of set theory (Russell). In finance: you cannot compute the “true” price of an asset if the true price depends on what everyone believes the true price is, and what everyone believes depends on the model they use to compute it, and the model is yours.
Section V

Technical Implementation

Everything above is theory. The question for RecWM is: how do you actually build it?

The Reflexivity Coefficient ε

Filimonov and Sornette (2012) provided the first rigorous quantification of reflexivity in financial markets using self-excited conditional Poisson processes (Hawkes processes). The core idea:

λ(t) = μ + Σi: ti<t φ(t − ti)

where λ(t) is the event intensity at time t,
μ is the background rate (exogenous events — genuine news),
φ(t − ti) is the triggering kernel (endogenous events — trades triggering trades).

The branching ratio n = ∫0∞ φ(s) ds   measures the average number of endogenous events triggered by each event.

The branching ratio n is the reflexivity coefficient. It ranges from 0 to 1:

  • n ≈ 0: Market is driven entirely by exogenous news. No reflexivity. Classical efficient market.
  • n ≈ 0.5: Half of price changes are triggered by other price changes. Moderate reflexivity.
  • n → 1: Market approaches criticality — the point where trading activity can diverge in the absence of any external news. Self-sustaining cascade. Flash crash territory.

Applied to E-mini S&P 500 futures from 1998 to 2010, Filimonov and Sornette found that exogenous information explained 70% of price changes in 1998 but less than 30% since 2007. The market became increasingly reflexive over time — more and more of the price action was generated endogenously by the market's own dynamics rather than by external news.

Critical Implication By 2007, more than 70% of price movements in the S&P 500 futures were endogenous — triggered by other price movements, not by news. Any model that treats price changes as responses to exogenous information is modeling less than a third of what is actually happening.

The Feedback Loop Architecture

In RecWM, the reflexive feedback loop operates as follows:

  1. Model predicts. The world model generates predictions about future states: price movements, volatility regimes, correlation shifts, liquidity conditions.
  2. PM acts. The portfolio manager (or execution system) acts on those predictions — entering positions, adjusting hedges, reallocating capital.
  3. Market changes. Those actions, however small, change the market microstructure: they consume liquidity, shift order flow, reveal information through price impact.
  4. Model updates. The world model ingests the new market state — which now includes the effects of its own previous predictions — and generates new predictions.

The challenge is step 4: the model must distinguish between market changes caused by its own actions and market changes caused by everything else. Without this distinction, the model will treat the consequences of its own predictions as new information, creating a spurious feedback loop that either amplifies its own biases (if it reinforces its previous view) or oscillates chaotically (if it reacts against its own signal).

Estimating Your Own Impact

This is the hardest technical problem. You need to model three things simultaneously:

1. Direct Market Impact

The price impact of your own trades. This is relatively well-understood: Almgren-Chriss models, the square-root law of market impact, Kyle's lambda. For a given trade size and liquidity conditions, you can estimate how much your execution moves the price.

2. Information Leakage Impact

The extent to which other market participants can infer your intentions from your order flow and position ahead of you. This is harder — it requires modeling other agents' inference processes about your behavior.

3. Structural Impact

The extent to which your strategy, if successful and scaled, changes the market dynamics it exploits. This is Goodhart's Law applied to alpha: a signal that works at $10M AUM may not work at $1B AUM because at $1B you are a significant fraction of the liquidity in the signal's universe. The signal's edge is not a fixed property of the market — it is a function of how many dollars are chasing it.

Active Inference Framing

The active inference framework (Friston, 2010) provides the natural theoretical architecture for reflexive world models. Under active inference:

  • The agent maintains a generative model of the world — a probabilistic model that generates predictions about sensory inputs.
  • The agent acts to minimize expected free energy — a quantity that combines prediction error (how surprised the agent is) with expected information gain (how much the agent expects to learn).
  • Crucially, the generative model includes the agent's own actions and their expected consequences. The agent does not just predict what will happen; it predicts what will happen given what it does.

This is exactly the structure needed for reflexive world modeling. The RecWM's generative model must include:

  • A model of the market (other agents, liquidity, information flow)
  • A model of itself (its own positions, its own signals, its own execution)
  • A model of how its own actions affect the market
  • A model of how other agents model it (second-order beliefs)
Comparison: Multi-Agent RL In multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), each agent's policy is part of every other agent's environment. The Nash equilibrium concept applies: your optimal policy depends on others' policies, which depend on yours. This is reflexivity in game-theoretic form. But MARL typically assumes a fixed game structure and seeks convergence to equilibrium. RecWM's reflexivity is deeper: the game structure itself changes as players adopt new strategies. The rules of the game are endogenous. This is closer to a metagame — a game about how the game is played — which is what Soros has been describing all along.

The ε Estimation Pipeline

Concretely, the reflexivity coefficient ε in RecWM would be estimated through a multi-scale pipeline:

  1. Microsecond scale: Hawkes process estimation on order flow data to measure the branching ratio of endogenous vs. exogenous trade arrivals.
  2. Daily scale: Causal impact analysis separating market movements attributable to the fund's own execution from movements attributable to other flows.
  3. Weekly/monthly scale: Signal decay analysis tracking the half-life of alpha signals as a function of the fund's own position size and the number of other participants running similar strategies.
  4. Regime scale: Structural break detection identifying when the relationship between the fund's signals and market outcomes has shifted — potentially because the fund's own success has attracted imitators who have crowded the signal.
Section VI

Why This Is the Single Most Innovative Feature

No existing financial product accounts for its own impact on the system it monitors. Not one.

Bloomberg terminals show data. They do not model how millions of people looking at the same data creates crowded trades, correlated positions, and synchronized deleveraging. The terminal is a camera pointed at a market it is actively shaping — and it has no awareness of the shaping.

Risk models compute Value at Risk, Expected Shortfall, stress scenarios. They do not model how everyone using the same risk model creates identical risk limits, identical hedging flows, and identical forced-selling triggers. The risk model is a fire alarm that, when it goes off, causes everyone to run for the same exit simultaneously — and it does not model the stampede.

Alpha models generate signals. They do not model their own decay — the process by which a profitable signal, once adopted by enough capital, moves prices to eliminate the very mispricing it detected. The alpha model is a fishing guide that does not account for overfishing.

The Analogies

A reflexive world model is like:

  • A flight simulator that accounts for how the pilot's training on the simulator changes their real-world behavior. Every hour in the sim changes the pilot. The sim must model a different pilot than the one who sat down.
  • A pandemic model that accounts for how people's reaction to the model's predictions changes the pandemic's trajectory. If the model predicts 2 million deaths, and the government locks down in response, the lockdown changes the trajectory — but the lockdown happened because of the prediction. The model must predict the world-including-the-model's-impact-on-policy.
  • A navigation app that accounts for how its own routing recommendations create the traffic it is trying to avoid. Waze sends everyone down the same side street, creating a new traffic jam. A reflexive Waze would predict the jam it creates and route around its own routing.

The Disasters of Ignoring Reflexivity

Case Study — 2007–08 Crisis

VaR Models and Correlated Deleveraging

By 2007, virtually every major bank and hedge fund used some variant of Value at Risk to set position limits and trigger deleveraging. VaR models estimated risk from historical correlations and volatilities, treating these as exogenous properties of the market. They did not model the reflexive reality: when losses hit VaR limits simultaneously across thousands of institutions using the same model, the forced selling those limits triggered changed the correlations and volatilities the models used as inputs. Selling drove prices down, which increased measured VaR, which triggered more selling, which drove prices down further. The risk model created the risk. By 2008, the endogenous feedback loop had amplified what might have been a contained subprime correction into a global financial crisis.

Case Study — 1998

LTCM: The Model That Didn't Model Its Imitators

Long-Term Capital Management's models were, by the standards of the time, state of the art. Merton and Scholes, Nobel laureates, built convergence-arbitrage strategies based on the assumption that mispricings between related instruments would mean-revert. The models were correct about the mispricing. They were catastrophically wrong about the reflexive dynamics: LTCM's early success attracted a cottage industry of imitators running similar convergence trades. When Russia defaulted in August 1998 and spreads widened, LTCM had to mark down its positions — but so did every imitator. The imitators' forced liquidations pushed spreads wider, which pushed LTCM's marks lower, which triggered margin calls, which forced LTCM to liquidate, which pushed spreads wider still. The model didn't account for the fact that its own success had created a crowded trade, and a crowded trade is a bomb with a reflexive fuse.

Case Study — August 2007

The Quant Meltdown

In the week of August 6, 2007, quantitative long/short equity hedge funds suffered unprecedented synchronized losses. The trigger: broader market stress from the subprime crisis forced multi-strategy funds and prop desks to raise cash. The most liquid part of their portfolios was quantitative equity. As they liquidated, they unwound the same factor exposures — long value, short momentum, or variations thereof — because they were all running similar models on similar data. The Khandani and Lo (2007) analysis showed that portfolio correlations among quant funds were far higher than factor model correlations suggested, because the funds had independently converged on similar positions. The models measured factor exposure; they did not measure crowding in factor exposure. The August 2007 meltdown was a reflexivity crisis: the quants' collective model-driven behavior had created a hidden fragility that the models were structurally incapable of detecting.

Case Study — January 2021

GameStop: Reflexivity Unmasked

GameStop was reflexivity in its purest, most visible form. Retail investors on r/WallStreetBets identified that GameStop's short interest exceeded 100% of the float — more shares were sold short than existed. They recognized that buying pressure would force short sellers to cover by buying, which would push the price up, which would force more covering, which would push the price up further. The feedback loop was explicitly identified and intentionally exploited. The stock went from $17 to $483 in two weeks. Market makers who had sold call options were forced to delta-hedge by buying the underlying, adding another reflexive layer: option demand created stock demand created option demand. The loop only broke when Robinhood and other brokers restricted buying on January 28, 2021 — an exogenous intervention that severed the feedback mechanism. GameStop demonstrated that reflexive dynamics are not subtle background effects. They are the dominant force in market microstructure when the conditions align.

“Every existing financial model treats the market as something that happens to you. A reflexive world model treats the market as something you happen to — and models the happening.”

RecWM Design Principle

The Competitive Moat

Building reflexivity into a world model is not a feature that can be bolted on. It requires the entire architecture to be designed around the circularity — the generative model must include itself as a causal actor. This means:

  • Most existing systems cannot retrofit it. A model built on the assumption that market data is exogenous cannot be patched to treat its own outputs as endogenous inputs. The assumption is load-bearing — it runs through every layer of the architecture.
  • The data requirement is recursive. You need data about your own impact to calibrate the reflexivity coefficient, but you can only generate that data by trading — which means the model improves as it trades and degrades if it stops. The model's accuracy is a function of its own operational history. This creates a compounding advantage that is extremely difficult for competitors to replicate.
  • The intellectual barrier is genuine. Most quantitative finance teams are trained in stochastic calculus and statistical learning — tools designed for systems where the observer is outside the system. Building reflexive models requires thinking from systems theory, cybernetics, and active inference — disciplines that most finance PhDs have never encountered.

A world model that models itself is not an incremental improvement over a world model that does not. It is a different kind of thing. It is the difference between a map and a map that includes the mapmaker and accounts for how the mapmaker's movements change the terrain. No one has built this. That is the opportunity.

Technical Research Brief

Compositional World Models

Why compositionality is the architectural key to generalization in AI world models, and why financial markets are the canonical domain where it matters.
