01

Object-Centric World Models

The fundamental premise: the world is not a monolithic pixel array. It consists of discrete objects that persist through time, interact causally, and can be composed into novel configurations. Object-centric world models exploit this structure by decomposing scenes into object-level representations, enabling combinatorial generalization that monolithic models cannot achieve.

Slot Attention: The Core Mechanism

Slot Attention (Locatello et al., 2020) introduced a differentiable mechanism for decomposing perceptual input into a set of object-level representations called slots. The mechanism is an iterative competitive attention process where K slots compete to explain the input features.

Given input features H ∈ RN×D (e.g., CNN features from an image), and K slot vectors sk ∈ RDs, each iteration performs:

1. Attention coefficients:
  A = softmaxslots( (1/√D) · k(H) · q(s)T )  ∈ RN×K

2. Normalize over slots (competition):
  Ã = A / Σk A:,k   (weighted mean, not softmax)

3. Aggregate & update:
  updates = ÃT · v(H)  ∈ RK×Ds
  s ← GRU(s, updates) + MLP(s)

The critical design choice is the softmax over the slot dimension (not the input dimension). This creates competition: each input feature is explained by exactly one slot, forcing the model to segment the scene. This is the opposite of standard cross-attention (where softmax is over keys), and it is what produces the object decomposition. The GRU update and iterative refinement (typically 3 iterations) allow slots to progressively sharpen their binding to specific objects.

The architecture is permutation equivariant: slots are initialized from a learned Gaussian distribution and their final assignment to objects is determined purely by the competitive attention, not by index position. This is essential — object identity should not depend on arbitrary ordering.

Extensions to Video: SAVi, STEVE, and Beyond

SAVi (Slot Attention for Video) (Kipf et al., 2022) extends slot attention to the temporal domain. Rather than independently decomposing each frame, SAVi propagates slot representations across time — the slots from frame t are used to initialize slots at frame t+1. This creates temporal persistence: a slot that "captured" a particular object in frame t continues to track it in frame t+1, implementing a form of object permanence. SAVi also introduces optional conditioning signals (e.g., optical flow, bounding boxes in the first frame) that help bootstrap the initial decomposition.

STEVE (Slot Transformer for Videos from Entities) (Singh et al., 2022) replaces the pixel-mixture decoder of standard slot attention with a Transformer-based discrete decoder (building on SLATE's dVAE + Transformer architecture). Where vanilla slot attention decodes each slot independently via a spatial broadcast decoder and combines them with alpha compositing, STEVE uses a Transformer that attends to all slots jointly, enabling it to model complex inter-object occlusions and lighting effects that the independent-decode assumption cannot capture.

MONet (Burgess et al., 2019) takes a different approach: a recurrent attention network sequentially generates attention masks, and a VAE encodes each masked region into a component representation. The attention network learns to "peel off" objects one at a time. GENESIS (Engelcke et al., 2020) uses a spatial mixture model formulation with an autoregressive prior over component masks, avoiding the sequential bottleneck of MONet while maintaining probabilistic coherence.

Object-Centric Dynamics: From Perception to World Models

The real power of object-centric representations emerges when they are coupled with dynamics models:

  • C-SWM (Contrastive Structured World Models) (Kipf et al., ICLR 2020) learns abstract state variables — one per object — and models transitions using a graph neural network where objects are nodes and interactions are edges. An object-level contrastive loss (energy-based, pushing apart representations of different states) trains the model without pixel reconstruction.
  • SlotFormer (Wu et al., ICLR 2023) applies a Transformer autoregressively over slot representations to predict future object states. The Transformer jointly processes all slots, learning interaction effects between objects. It achieves unsupervised visual dynamics simulation — predicting multi-step futures in latent space and decoding back to pixels.
  • DynaSlot / SOLD (2024) extends slot-based world models to robotic manipulation, learning relational dynamics between objects from pixels for planning.
Why this matters

Object-centric world models achieve what monolithic models cannot: combinatorial generalization. A model that has seen red cubes and blue spheres can immediately reason about blue cubes and red spheres, because the object representations factor color from shape from identity. Monolithic models must re-learn each combination from scratch. This is exactly the property needed for financial markets, where the "objects" are market fragments (liquidity regimes, momentum signals, credit conditions) that compose in exponentially many ways.

02

Modular & Compositional Architectures

Compositionality in architecture means building systems from specialized, reusable modules that can be dynamically assembled to handle novel inputs. This is fundamentally different from the monolithic approach where a single network processes everything.

Neural Module Networks

Neural Module Networks (NMNs) (Andreas et al., CVPR 2016) are the foundational compositional architecture. Given a question like "What color is the large object left of the cube?", NMNs:

  1. Parse the question into a compositional program: classify_color(filter_large(relate_left(find_cube)))
  2. Instantiate specialized neural modules for each operation: find, relate, filter, classify
  3. Compose these modules into a computation graph matching the program structure
  4. Execute the composed network end-to-end on the visual input

Each module type (attention, combination, classification) has its own learned parameters but shares structure across instances. The key insight: a module trained on "find(dog)" and "relate(left)" can immediately compose into "relate_left(find(dog))" even if this exact composition was never seen during training.

End-to-End Module Networks (Hu et al., 2017) and Stack-NMN (Hu et al., 2018) extended this by learning the module layout from data rather than requiring a parser. Compositional Attention Networks (MAC) (Hudson & Manning, ICLR 2018) simplified the approach into a recurrent cell with explicit read-and-write attention operations, achieving strong compositional reasoning without discrete module selection.

Mixture of Experts as Compositional Computation

The Mixture of Experts (MoE) paradigm implements a softer form of compositionality. The Sparsely-Gated MoE layer (Shazeer et al., 2017) introduced a noisy top-k gating mechanism:

G(x) = softmax( TopK( x · Wg + ε · softplus(x · Wnoise), k ) )
y = Σi G(x)i · Ei(x)

Each input token is routed to its top-k experts (out of thousands), so different inputs are processed by different subsets of parameters. This is compositional in a crucial sense: the effective network changes per input. A token representing a momentum signal might route to experts specialized in trend dynamics, while a token representing a credit event routes to credit-specialist experts.

The Switch Transformer (Fedus et al., 2022) simplified routing to top-1 (one expert per token) with a differentiable load-balancing loss, showing that hard routing could scale to trillion-parameter models. Mixtral 8x7B (Jiang et al., 2024) demonstrated that top-2 MoE in open-weights models could match dense models of equivalent active parameter count.

Recent work on Chain-of-Experts (2025) extends this further: rather than processing each token through a single expert selection, tokens pass through a sequence of expert selections, enabling deeper compositional chains. HC-SMoE (2025) uses hierarchical clustering to merge redundant experts post-training, revealing the underlying specialization structure.

The modular deep learning landscape

Pfeiffer et al. (2023) provide a comprehensive survey of modular deep learning, taxonomizing approaches along three axes: module computation (what each module does), module selection (how modules are chosen for each input), and module composition (how selected modules are combined). The survey identifies a convergence: the most successful architectures combine sparse selection (only a few modules active per input) with learned composition rules (how to wire active modules together). This is precisely the architecture a compositional world model for finance requires.

03

Compositional Generalization

A human who knows "purple," "elephant," "riding," and "bicycle" can immediately understand "a purple elephant riding a bicycle" — despite never encountering this combination. This is systematic compositionality: the meaning of the whole is determined by the meanings of the parts and the rules used to combine them (Frege's principle of compositionality). It is the single most important property separating human cognition from current AI systems.

The Failure of Monolithic Networks

Lake & Baroni (2018, "Still not systematic after all these years") demonstrated this failure rigorously using the SCAN benchmark. SCAN maps natural language commands to action sequences (e.g., "jump twice" → JUMP JUMP). Despite achieving near-perfect accuracy on the training distribution, sequence-to-sequence models catastrophically failed on systematic splits:

Test condition Human LSTM Transformer MLC (Lake 2023)
Simple (i.i.d.) 100% 99.8% 99.6% 99.9%
Add "jump" to compositions 100% 1.2% 0.8% 99.7%
Novel template length 100% 13.8% 15.2% 99.2%
Novel modifier + primitive 100% 2.5% 4.1% 98.8%

The failure is not about capacity — larger models fail equally. The problem is architectural: monolithic networks learn holistic input-output mappings rather than compositional rules. They memorize that "walk twice" → WALK WALK, but do not extract the rule "X twice → X X" that would generalize to "jump twice" → JUMP JUMP.

Solutions: From Meta-Learning to Neuro-Symbolic

MLC (Meta-Learning for Compositionality) (Lake & Baroni, Nature 2023) demonstrated that neural networks can achieve human-like systematic generalization — but only when explicitly optimized for it. MLC uses a meta-learning procedure where the model is trained on a distribution of compositional tasks, each requiring generalization to novel combinations. The key insight: compositionality is not an emergent property of scale but a structural constraint that must be explicitly induced.

Representational homomorphism (2025) provides a theoretical framework: a model generalizes compositionally when its internal representations are homomorphic to the compositional structure of the input domain. That is, the model's representation of "A and B" should be a deterministic function of its representations of "A" and "B" individually. Standard Transformers violate this because attention creates context-dependent representations — the representation of "A" changes depending on what else is in the input.

Other approaches include differentiable tree operations (Soulos et al., 2023) that impose syntactic tree structure on neural computations, and compositional generalization through abstract representations (Russin et al., 2022) showing that brain-like cortical representations achieve compositionality through factored representations where content and structure are separated.

04

The Binding Problem

The binding problem is the core technical challenge of compositional representation: how do you combine representations while maintaining their identity? If you represent a red triangle and a blue circle, how do you ensure "red" stays bound to "triangle" and "blue" to "circle"? This is trivially solved by symbolic systems (use a data structure) but profoundly difficult for distributed neural representations.

Greff et al.'s Taxonomy

Greff, van Steenkiste & Schmidhuber (2020, "On the Binding Problem in Artificial Neural Networks") provide the definitive taxonomy. They identify two fundamental aspects:

  • Segregation: separating the representation of distinct entities in a scene or input (which features belong to which object)
  • Relation binding: representing how entities relate to each other (spatial, causal, temporal relations)

They argue that the binding problem is not a single problem but a hierarchy of challenges, and that solving it requires representations with explicit object-like structure — precisely the slot-based representations described in Section 1. Standard neural networks fail because they use superposition: all objects are encoded in the same distributed activation vector, making it impossible to determine which features belong to which object (the "superposition catastrophe").

Tensor Product Representations (TPRs)

Smolensky's Tensor Product Representations (1990) provide the mathematical foundation for neural binding. A structured representation is encoded as:

r = Σi fi ⊗ ri

Where fi are filler vectors (the content: "red," "triangle") and ri are role vectors (the structural position: "color-of-object-1," "shape-of-object-1"). The tensor product ⊗ creates a matrix (or higher-order tensor) that uniquely binds each filler to its role.

Unbinding is exact when role vectors are linearly independent: to retrieve the filler in role rj, compute r · r̂j where r̂j is the dual vector of rj. The problem: rank explosion. Nested structures require tensor products of tensor products, and the dimensionality grows exponentially with nesting depth.

The TP-Transformer (Schlag et al., 2019) integrates TPRs into the Transformer architecture, using the Hadamard product (element-wise multiplication) as an approximation of the full tensor product to control dimensionality. The AID module (2024) improves TPR decomposition with attention-based iterative decomposition, using a routing mechanism to enhance structural representations for unseen compositions.

Holographic Reduced Representations

Plate's Holographic Reduced Representations (HRR) (1995) solve the dimensionality problem by using circular convolution as the binding operator:

(a ∗ b)j = Σk ak · b(j-k) mod D

Unlike the tensor product, circular convolution maps RD × RD → RD — the bound representation has the same dimensionality as its components. Unbinding uses circular correlation (convolution with the approximate inverse). The tradeoff: binding is lossy rather than exact, introducing crosstalk between bound pairs, but the fixed dimensionality makes deep composition tractable.

Vector Symbolic Architectures

Kanerva's Hyperdimensional Computing (2009) generalizes these ideas into Vector Symbolic Architectures (VSAs): a family of algebraic systems over high-dimensional vectors with three operations:

  • Binding (⊗): associates two vectors (XOR in binary, element-wise multiply in bipolar, circular convolution in continuous)
  • Bundling (+): creates a superposition (element-wise addition with majority decoding)
  • Permutation (π): creates a distinct variant (circular bit shift)

These three operations are sufficient to represent arbitrary data structures — sequences, trees, graphs — in fixed-dimensional vectors. The representations are holographic: the whole is distributed across all dimensions, and any subset of dimensions contains partial information about the whole. This is the mathematical substrate a compositional world model needs for binding market fragments to their contextual roles.

05

Emergence from Composition

The deepest reason compositionality matters is emergence: when simple components interact, the composite system exhibits behavior that is qualitatively irreducible to the behavior of the parts. This is not mysticism — it is a precise computational claim with profound implications for what kind of models can capture reality.

Anderson's Principle: More Is Different

Anderson (1972, "More is Different," Science) established the foundational argument: at each level of complexity, entirely new properties appear that require fundamentally new laws and concepts. The behavior of superconductors cannot be derived from the equations governing individual electrons, even in principle with unlimited computation, because the collective state (Cooper pairs, macroscopic phase coherence) is a symmetry-breaking phenomenon that has no analogue at the individual particle level.

This is not a failure of reductionism in the philosophical sense — the lower-level laws are still obeyed. It is a failure of constructionism: knowing the parts does not enable you to construct the behavior of the whole. The composition rules — how parts interact — create a system whose behavior is qualitatively richer than any extrapolation from the parts.

Computational Irreducibility

Wolfram (2002, A New Kind of Science) formalized this as computational irreducibility: for many systems, there exists no shortcut to determine the system's future state other than running the simulation step by step. Even with complete knowledge of the rules and initial conditions, you cannot predict the outcome without executing the computation.

This has a precise formal meaning tied to computational universality. If a system is capable of universal computation (and many simple systems are — Rule 110 cellular automata, for instance), then predicting its behavior is at least as hard as running the system itself. No model that is computationally simpler than the system can predict it. This is why world models — which simulate the system — are necessary, and why statistical models that try to shortcut the simulation necessarily miss emergent phenomena.

Examples Across Domains

Physics

The Ising model: individual spins with nearest-neighbor coupling H = -JΣ<ij> sisj. Simple components, simple interaction rule. Yet the composite system exhibits phase transitions, critical phenomena with universal scaling exponents, long-range correlations at criticality, and spontaneous symmetry breaking. The critical temperature Tc is an emergent property — no individual spin "knows" about it.

Biology

Gene regulatory networks: individual genes with simple binding rules (activator/repressor) compose into circuits that exhibit bistability, oscillations (circadian rhythms), and developmental pattern formation. Kauffman's NK models (1993) show that the ruggedness of the fitness landscape — and hence the evolvability of the system — is an emergent property of the interaction structure (K), not the number of genes (N) alone.

Economics

This is the domain where emergence matters most for our purposes. Agent-based models with simple trading rules (chartists following trends, fundamentalists mean-reverting) produce emergent statistical properties that match real markets (LeBaron, 2006; Farmer & Foley, 2009):

  • Fat-tailed returns: no individual agent has a fat-tailed strategy, but their interaction produces power-law tails in the aggregate return distribution
  • Volatility clustering: periods of high and low volatility cluster in time, an emergent temporal correlation structure
  • Bubbles and crashes: self-reinforcing feedback loops between momentum traders and liquidity providers create explosive price dynamics and sudden reversals

The Schelling segregation model (1971) is the cleanest demonstration: agents with only mild preferences for similar neighbors (e.g., wanting at least 30% similar) produce complete spatial segregation. The emergent macro-state is qualitatively different from (and far more extreme than) any individual agent's preference.

The simulation imperative

Computational irreducibility means that for emergent systems, there is no closed-form shortcut. You cannot predict a flash crash from a regression model, because the flash crash is an emergent property of the interaction between momentum strategies, liquidity provision, and order book dynamics. You must simulate the composition. This is why financial markets demand a world model, not a statistical model — and why that world model must be compositional.

06

Financial Markets as Compositional Systems

Financial markets are composed of interacting fragments — distinct, identifiable forces that individually have well-understood behavior but collectively produce dynamics that no linear combination can capture. The fragments are not latent factors to be estimated from returns (as in Fama-French or Barra models). They are causal mechanisms with their own internal dynamics that compose through non-linear, context-dependent interactions.

The Fragment Ontology

Fragment Internal dynamics Observable proxies
Liquidity Order book depth, bid-ask spread, funding costs, dealer balance sheet capacity VIX term structure, TED spread, OIS-Libor, primary dealer positions
Momentum Trend-following flows, CTA positioning, passive rebalancing, cross-asset momentum Rolling returns, flow data, CFTC positioning, momentum factor returns
Credit Default intensity, recovery rates, credit migration, covenant quality CDS spreads, IG/HY spreads, lending standards surveys
Sentiment Fear/greed cycles, narrative formation, herding dynamics Put/call ratios, AAII surveys, news sentiment scores, social media signals
Policy Rate expectations, QE/QT flows, fiscal impulse, regulatory changes Fed funds futures, central bank balance sheet, fiscal deficit projections
Structure Market microstructure, ETF flows, options hedging, passive/active ratio Gamma exposure, ETF creation/redemption, market maker inventory

Why Linear Factor Models Fail

The standard factor model assumes additive decomposition:

rt = α + β1F1,t + β2F2,t + ... + βkFk,t + εt

This assumes that the contribution of each factor is independent and additive. But the financial phenomena that matter most — crises, regime shifts, dislocations — are precisely the cases where factors interact non-linearly. When liquidity dries up and momentum is crowded and sentiment turns negative, the result is not βLΔL + βMΔM + βSΔS. It is a qualitatively different regime — a flash crash, a liquidity spiral, a credit crunch — that cannot be expressed as any linear combination of individual factor effects.

VAR models add temporal dynamics but still assume linear relationships between variables. Even augmented with regime-switching (Markov-switching VAR), the regimes are pre-specified and the within-regime dynamics remain linear. The model cannot discover novel interaction patterns.

Monolithic deep learning (a single large neural network mapping market features to predictions) can theoretically capture non-linear interactions, but in practice it memorizes surface correlations rather than learning compositional structure. It works on the training distribution but fails on novel compositions — exactly the same failure mode as Lake & Baroni's sequence-to-sequence models on SCAN. A model trained on 2005-2015 data has seen the GFC (credit × sentiment × liquidity interaction) but not COVID (pandemic × policy × structure interaction). Without compositional structure, it cannot generalize to novel crisis compositions.

07

Emergent Phenomena from Fragment Interaction

The alpha in financial markets lives not in the fragments themselves but in their composition. Below are the four canonical interaction types, each producing emergent behavior that linear models cannot capture.

Liquidity ⊗ Momentum

When momentum strategies crowd into thin liquidity, positive feedback creates explosive price dynamics. Momentum traders buy what is going up; their buying pushes prices further up; more momentum traders enter. In deep liquidity, this dissipates harmlessly. In thin liquidity, it cascades.

Emergent phenomena: Flash crashes, momentum ignition, stop-cascades, short squeezes.

Canonical example: The May 6, 2010 Flash Crash. Waddell & Reed's $4.1B sell algorithm executing into a thin E-mini order book triggered HFT momentum strategies, creating a feedback loop that crashed the Dow 1,000 points in minutes. Neither the sell order nor the thin order book alone was pathological — their composition was.

Brunnermeier & Pedersen (2009): funding liquidity ↔ market liquidity spiral. Kyle & Obizhaeva (2016): market microstructure invariance.

Credit ⊗ Sentiment

Credit risk is a slow variable (default probabilities evolve over quarters). Sentiment is a fast variable (fear can spike overnight). When sentiment interacts with credit, it creates self-fulfilling dynamics: if enough people believe a bank is insolvent, the resulting bank run makes it insolvent.

Emergent phenomena: Bank runs, credit crunches, wholesale funding freezes, contagion across counterparties.

Canonical example: The 2008 GFC. Subprime credit risk (slow, building over years) interacted with fear sentiment (fast, spiking after Lehman) to produce the wholesale funding freeze. The composition created a regime that neither variable alone could produce: fundamentally solvent institutions became illiquid because counterparties lost confidence.

Diamond & Dybvig (1983): bank runs as self-fulfilling equilibria. Gorton & Metrick (2012): securitized banking and the run on repo.

Policy ⊗ Risk

Central bank policy changes interact with existing risk positioning to create regime switches. The policy change itself may be small, but if risk is positioned for the old regime, the rebalancing flows can be enormous and self-reinforcing.

Emergent phenomena: Vol regime shifts, Volmageddon, taper tantrums, carry unwinds.

Canonical example: Volmageddon, February 5, 2018. Rising rate expectations (policy) interacted with massive short-volatility positioning (risk). The VIX spike forced short-vol ETPs (XIV, SVXY) into delta-hedging spirals, buying VIX futures which pushed VIX higher, creating a positive feedback loop that destroyed XIV (down 96% in a day). The policy signal was modest; the positioning made it catastrophic.

Adrian & Shin (2010): procyclical leverage. Brunnermeier et al. (2014): macroprudential regulation.

Structure ⊗ Liquidity

Market structure (ETFs, options, passive indexing) creates mechanical flows that interact with underlying liquidity. These are "plumbing" effects — the pipes through which capital flows shape the flow itself.

Emergent phenomena: Gamma squeezes, ETF liquidity mismatch, index rebalancing impact, passive ownership concentration effects.

Canonical example: GameStop, January 2021. Options market maker gamma hedging (structure) interacted with extremely thin short-interest liquidity. Retail call buying forced dealers to delta-hedge by buying shares; in a heavily shorted, thinly traded stock, this created a mechanical squeeze that amplified the underlying flow by 10-50x. The "memification" was the catalyst, but the gamma-liquidity composition was the mechanism.

Barbon & Buraschi (2021): gamma exposure and stock returns. Koijen & Yogo (2019): demand system approach to asset pricing.

The pattern

In every case, the emergent phenomenon arises because a slow variable (credit quality, risk positioning, market structure) creates conditions under which a fast variable (sentiment, momentum, policy signal) triggers self-reinforcing dynamics. The composition is not commutative (liquidity affecting momentum produces different dynamics than momentum affecting liquidity) and is highly state-dependent (the same policy signal in different positioning regimes produces qualitatively different outcomes). This is why a compositional world model must capture asymmetric, context-dependent interactions.

08

The Composition Operator ⊗

What must the composition operator do, mathematically, to capture financial fragment interactions? It is emphatically not simple multiplication. The operator must satisfy several properties that rule out most standard algebraic operations.

Required Properties

Context-dependence

The same two fragments compose differently depending on the current market regime. Liquidity ⊗ Momentum in a low-volatility, deep-liquidity regime produces gentle mean-reversion. The same composition in a high-volatility, thin-liquidity regime produces flash crashes. The operator must be parameterized by (or attend to) the ambient state:

(A ⊗c B) ≠ (A ⊗c' B)   for different contexts c, c'

Non-commutativity

Liquidity affecting momentum (thin liquidity amplifies momentum signals) is mechanistically different from momentum affecting liquidity (momentum crowding depletes liquidity). The operator must distinguish direction of causation:

A ⊗ B ≠ B ⊗ A   in general

State-dependence with memory

The composition depends not only on the current values of A and B but on their trajectories. A VIX at 25 that was at 15 yesterday composes differently with momentum than a VIX at 25 that was at 35 yesterday (even though the current values are identical). The operator needs access to path-dependent state.

Non-associativity (potential)

Whether (A ⊗ B) ⊗ C = A ⊗ (B ⊗ C) is an empirical question. In some cases, the order of composition matters: does credit risk first interact with sentiment and then the result interacts with liquidity? Or does credit interact with the liquidity-sentiment composition? These may produce different outcomes, especially near regime boundaries.

Mathematical Candidates

Given these requirements, the composition operator must be a learned, parametric function, not a fixed algebraic operation. Several architectures are candidates:

  • Attention-based composition: Each fragment "attends" to other fragments, with attention weights determining how strongly each pair interacts. This naturally implements context-dependence (attention weights depend on all fragments' current states) and non-commutativity (query-key asymmetry). This is the approach used by SlotFormer for object dynamics and is the most natural candidate for financial fragments.
  • Graph Neural Network message passing: Fragments as nodes, interactions as edges, with learned message functions. GNNs with directed edges naturally implement non-commutativity. The message function can be conditioned on global state for context-dependence. (Kipf et al., 2020; Battaglia et al., 2018)
  • Tensor Product Representations with learned roles: Fragments bound to context-dependent role vectors, composed via tensor products. The role vectors encode the "function" of each fragment in the current composition (e.g., "amplifier" vs. "dampener"). (Smolensky, 1990; Schlag et al., 2019)
  • Categorical composition: Morphisms in a category of market states, where composition is morphism composition. This is the most mathematically principled approach: each fragment interaction defines a morphism (state transformation), and compositions of interactions are compositions of morphisms, which are associative by construction but can be non-commutative. (Fong & Spivak, 2019, "An Invitation to Applied Category Theory")

The most practical implementation combines several of these: slot-based fragment representations (from object-centric world models) composed via Transformer-based attention (for context-dependent, non-commutative interaction), with GNN message passing for explicit pairwise interaction modeling within each attention layer.

09

Why Compositional World Models Win

The argument for compositional world models in finance rests on a single claim: financial crises are novel compositions of known fragments. Every crisis is different, but the ingredients are finite and recurring. A compositional world model that has learned the fragments and their interaction rules can simulate crisis types it has never seen — just as a human who knows "purple" and "elephant" can imagine a purple elephant.

Architecture What it captures What it misses Novel composition?
Factor models (Fama-French, Barra) Linear factor exposures, risk decomposition All interaction effects, regime switches, non-linear dynamics No
VAR / VECM Linear temporal dynamics, Granger causality Non-linear interactions, regime switches, tail events No
Regime-switching models Pre-specified regime dynamics Novel regimes, interaction-driven regime formation No
Monolithic deep learning Non-linear patterns in training distribution Novel compositions, out-of-distribution generalization No
Compositional world model Fragment dynamics + learned composition rules Truly novel fragment types (not novel compositions) Yes

The Architecture

A compositional world model for financial markets requires four components:

  1. Fragment encoder: Slot-based representations where each slot corresponds to one market fragment (liquidity, momentum, credit, sentiment, policy, structure). Unlike vision models where the number of objects varies, the fragment ontology is relatively stable, allowing fixed slot assignments with learned representations. Each slot encodes the current state and recent trajectory of its fragment from observable proxies.
  2. Composition engine: A Transformer-based interaction model that composes fragment slots. Self-attention between slots implements the ⊗ operator, with context-dependence emerging from the attention mechanism and non-commutativity from the query-key asymmetry. Multiple layers enable higher-order interactions (three-way, four-way fragment compositions). This is the financial analogue of SlotFormer's dynamics model.
  3. Hierarchical dynamics: Financial composition happens at multiple time scales. Microstructure effects (milliseconds to seconds), flow dynamics (hours to days), regime formation (weeks to months), structural shifts (quarters to years). The world model must compose across scales, using the output of faster-scale composition as input to slower-scale composition. This mirrors the hierarchical world models of Ha & Schmidhuber (2018) and Hafner et al.'s Dreamer (2020, 2023).
  4. Interventional interface: The world model must support counterfactual queries: "what happens if we inject liquidity here?" or "what if the Fed signals a rate cut?" This requires the fragment decomposition to be causally meaningful — intervening on one fragment's slot should propagate through the composition engine to affect other fragments, without the confounding that monolithic models exhibit. Object-centric world models naturally support this because interventions target specific slots. (Ke et al., 2021, "Systematic Evaluation of Causal Discovery in Visual Model Based Reinforcement Learning")
The core insight

A compositional world model does not need to have seen the 2020 COVID crash to simulate it. If it has learned how liquidity withdrawal works (from 2008, 2015, 2018), how policy intervention works (from QE episodes), and how structural fragility works (from flash crashes and ETF dislocations) — then it can compose these fragments in the novel configuration that was COVID: simultaneous liquidity withdrawal across all asset classes + unprecedented policy response + structural fragility from passive concentration. The compositional structure enables generalization to novel crises from known components — exactly as understanding "purple" and "elephant" enables imagining a purple elephant.

What This Means for Alpha

The alpha in a compositional world model comes from three sources:

  • Interaction alpha: Capturing non-linear fragment interactions that linear factor models miss. This is the primary source — the effects described in Section 7 (flash crashes from liquidity-momentum interaction, regime shifts from policy-risk interaction) are mispriced by factor models because they are invisible to additive decomposition.
  • Composition alpha: Predicting novel crisis types before they occur, because the world model can simulate fragment compositions it has never observed in data. This is the unique capability that compositional architecture enables.
  • Intervention alpha: Answering "what if" questions that statistical models cannot: what is the market impact of a specific trade? What happens if the Fed cuts rates in this specific positioning environment? The interventional interface enables strategy evaluation in the world model before deployment in the market.

Technical Research Brief — Compositional World Models — August 2026
Research Brief / August 2026

World Model Architectures:
The State of the Field

A survey of JEPA, Genie, World Labs, and the emerging application of world models to finance, economics, and social systems. Covering key papers, architectures, capabilities, and gaps from 2024 through mid-2026.

JEPA Genie 2 & 3 World Labs Finance & Economics Beyond Robotics Comparison
Architecture 1

JEPA -- Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture

Yann LeCun's JEPA is arguably the most theoretically ambitious world-model program. Its core thesis: predict in latent space, not pixel space. Instead of reconstructing raw inputs (as autoencoders and diffusion models do), JEPA learns to predict abstract representations of future states, discarding irrelevant detail and focusing on causal structure.

How it works: An encoder maps observation x to representation s_x. A predictor (conditioned on context and an optional variable z) predicts the target representation s_y. A target encoder (EMA-updated, no gradient) produces the ground-truth target. Collapse is prevented via energy-based contrastive or variance-covariance objectives. The key insight is that by predicting in latent space, the model can ignore stochastic, unpredictable details and learn the causal dynamics of the environment.

Timeline of instantiations:

I-JEPA (June 2023)

First instantiation on images. ViT backbone with random block masking; predictor fills in latent patches. Outperformed MAE on ImageNet linear probing with less compute.

V-JEPA (February 2024)

Extended masking to spatiotemporal tubes across video frames, forcing temporal reasoning about scenes. 1.5-6x more sample-efficient than pixel-generative video baselines. Open-sourced under CC-BY-NC.

V-JEPA 2 (June 2025)

The major scaling step: 1.2B-parameter ViT pretrained self-supervised on over 1M hours of video plus ~1M images. Runs ~30x faster than NVIDIA Cosmos on physical-reasoning benchmarks. The action-conditioned variant V-JEPA 2-AC adds a ~300M-param transformer predictor fine-tuned on <62 hours of robot data, achieving 65-80% zero-shot success on grasp/reach/pick-and-place in unseen labs.

arXiv 2506.09985 1.2B params Self-supervised

V-JEPA 2.1 & Extensions (2025-2026)

V-JEPA 2.1 (March 2026) adds dense predictive loss and deep self-supervision. VL-JEPA (late 2025) extends to vision-language with zero-shot classification and VQA. Audio-JEPA (ICME 2025) matches wav2vec 2.0 with <1/5 training data. Other variants include GeoJEPA (geospatial), MTS-JEPA (time-series anomaly detection), and LeWorldModel (JEPA for RL world models from pixels).

LeCun's Departure and Startup (November 2025)

After 12 years at Meta, LeCun departed to found an AI startup pursuing his Autonomous Machine Intelligence (AMI) vision. His thesis: next-token prediction is a dead end for world understanding. JEPA-based world models that predict at multiple abstraction levels, combined with hierarchical planning and intrinsic cost modules, form the path to AMI. Stated horizon: roughly a decade.

Relevance to Economics

JEPA's core design -- predicting in latent space, ignoring stochastic noise, learning causal dynamics -- is deeply relevant. MTS-JEPA already targets time-series anomaly detection. The architecture's ability to learn at multiple abstraction levels maps naturally to the multi-scale nature of economic systems (tick-level microstructure through macro cycles). The key limitation: JEPA currently requires dense spatiotemporal data (video, audio), and economic data is sparse, irregular, and multi-modal in different ways. An "Econ-JEPA" would need a fundamentally different encoder and masking strategy.

Architecture 2

Genie 2 & 3 -- Google DeepMind

DeepMind's Genie line represents the interactive generative approach to world models: generate photorealistic, action-controllable environments from a single image or text prompt, then let agents navigate them.

Architecture (Genie 2): An autoregressive latent diffusion model with three components: (1) a video autoencoder compressing frames into compact latent representations; (2) a transformer dynamics model trained with causal masking that takes past latent frames plus current action and predicts the next latent frame; (3) classifier-free guidance at inference to sharpen action controllability. Trained on a large-scale video dataset (undisclosed).

Genie 2 (December 2024)

Generates action-controllable, interactive 3D environments from a single image. Supports keyboard/mouse navigation with consistent worlds for up to ~60 seconds at 360p. Exhibits emergent behaviors: object interactions, physically plausible gravity/water/smoke, NPC behavior, and long-horizon memory (correctly rendering areas the agent revisits). No formal paper published -- blog post only with BibTeX citation.

Blog post only 360p / ~60s Internal system

Genie 3 (August 2025)

Major upgrade: 720p at 24 fps with one-minute memory (5x Genie 2). Integrates Google Street View data for realistic street environments. In January 2026, "Project Genie" launched as a web interface for Google AI Ultra subscribers via Google Labs.

Relevance to Economics

Genie demonstrates that autoregressive latent dynamics models can generate consistent, action-responsive environments. The architectural pattern -- encode state into latent space, predict next-state conditioned on actions, decode for interpretation -- is exactly the skeleton needed for an economic world model. Replace "keyboard input" with "policy intervention" and "video frame" with "economic state vector." The limitation: Genie is deeply tied to visual rendering; the conceptual leap is replacing the video autoencoder with an economic-state encoder.

Architecture 3

World Labs -- Spatial Intelligence

Founded by Fei-Fei Li in 2023, World Labs has raised ~$1.23B (valued at $5B as of January 2026) to build "Large World Models" that generate persistent, navigable, editable 3D environments -- distinct from video generation in that the output is a stable world, not a morphing sequence.

Marble (Large World Model)

Accepts text, photographs, video, panoramas, or rough 3D layouts and generates navigable, persistent, editable 3D environments. Limited beta November 2025; commercial launch February 2026. The World API (January 2026) exposes Marble programmatically.

RTFM -- Real-Time Frame Model (October 2025)

Generates video frames interactively as users navigate, using posed frames as spatial memory for unbounded persistence and consistency -- no explicit 3D reconstruction required.

Fei-Fei Li's Three-Type Taxonomy (June 2026)

A crucial theoretical contribution splitting "world models" into three functional roles:

Renderer -- generates sensory output
Simulator -- maintains persistent state evolving under actions
Planner -- maps observations to actions

Marble targets the Simulator role. Li argues that without a grounded simulator, planners produce actions disconnected from reality.

Relevance to Economics

Li's Renderer/Simulator/Planner taxonomy is directly applicable. An economic world model is fundamentally a Simulator: it maintains persistent economic state that evolves under policy/agent actions. The Renderer is the interpretive layer (dashboards, scenario reports), and the Planner is the policy-optimization component. The key difference: World Labs builds spatial simulators; an economic world model needs a relational/causal simulator operating over heterogeneous agent states and institutional constraints.

Architecture 4

Finance-Specific World Models

No one has built a true "world model for economics" in the JEPA/Genie sense, but several important efforts are converging on the idea from different directions.

MarS: Financial Market Simulation Engine (ICLR 2025)

By Microsoft Research (Li, Liu, et al.). A Large Market Model (LMM) operating at the order level, analogous to language modeling but for financial order flow. Generates realistic market dynamics for forecasting, anomaly detection, microstructure analysis, and agent training. Demonstrates strong scalability across data size and model complexity. This is the closest thing to a foundation world model for finance: a generative model learning market dynamics from order-level data.

arXiv 2409.07486 ICLR 2025 Microsoft Research Open-source

EconAgent: LLM-Empowered Macroeconomic Simulation

Constructs heterogeneous economic agents with perception (profiles), memory (multi-period experiences), and action (LLM-generated work/consumption propensities) modules. Agents operate in a shared market with endowments, skills, and wealth; their collective decisions produce macro dynamics through a rule-based environment acting as both central government (taxes) and central bank (interest rates).

LLM-as-agent Macro simulation

Bank of Japan: Generative AI in Economic Simulations (2025)

Created 1,000 consumer agents using GPT-4o mini to study wage/price effects on consumption. Separate experiment simulated monopoly vs. duopoly competition. Results were consistent with microeconomic theory. Critical caveat from BoJ researchers: LLMs "merely output responses that are statistically consistent with patterns in training data" -- they may fail in genuinely novel economic scenarios.

Three-in-One World Model for Marketing Intervention (May 2026)

Niimi (Meijo University). Uses a frozen Deep Boltzmann Machine as a belief representation that simultaneously supports energy-based consistency evaluation, outcome prediction, and counterfactual inference. Interventions enter only the adapter, never the DBM -- allowing counterfactual queries by fixing beliefs and toggling actions.

arXiv 2605.07199 DBM-based Counterfactual

Awesome-Econ-World-Models (Community Resource)

A curated GitHub repository with 737 validated papers organized across six capability levels (L1-L6): from fixed rule-based agents (L1) through LLM-based agents with beliefs and reasoning (L3) to self-evolving agents with online real-world correction (L6). L6 is currently empty -- no system yet achieves adaptive, self-correcting economic world modeling with real-world feedback loops.

github.com/FreedomIntelligence 737 papers L6 empty

MALLES & Agentic Economic Modeling (2025-2026)

MALLES extends the EconAgent paradigm to microeconomic retail/wholesale scenarios with alignment via transaction-data post-training. Agentic Economic Modeling (AEM) is a framework that aligns synthetic LLM choices with small-sample human evidence for reliable econometric inference. Eco3S targets complex socio-economic system simulation via agent-based models.

Gap Analysis

The finance world-model space has order-level generative models (MarS) and LLM-as-agent simulations (EconAgent, BoJ), but nothing that combines (a) learned latent dynamics, (b) action-conditioned prediction, (c) counterfactual reasoning, and (d) real-world feedback correction into a single system. The L6 gap in the Awesome-Econ-World-Models taxonomy -- adaptive, self-correcting economic world models -- remains unfilled.

Architecture 5

World Models Beyond Robotics

The world-model concept is rapidly escaping its robotics/gaming origins. Several 2025-2026 developments show the pattern generalizing to clinical, epidemiological, social, and policy domains.

Agentic World Modeling (April 2026)

Chu et al. (49 co-authors). Comprehensive survey of 400+ works proposing a "levels x laws" framework: L1 Predictor (one-step local transitions), L2 Simulator (multi-step, action-conditioned rollouts respecting domain laws), L3 Evolver (autonomously revises its own model when predictions fail). Applied across four law regimes: physical, digital, social, and scientific.

arXiv 2604.22748 400+ papers surveyed

Clinical World Models (November 2025)

Qazi, Nadeem, Yaqub. Capability rubric for healthcare: L1 temporal prediction, L2 action-conditioned prediction, L3 counterfactual rollouts, L4 planning/control. Most existing systems achieve only L1-L2. Identifies gaps in interventional validation and uncertainty calibration.

arXiv 2511.16333

Epidemiological World Models (April 2026)

"Toward World Models for Epidemiology" -- intervention-aware simulation allowing policy evaluation in terms of latent epidemic control rather than passive trend extrapolation.

arXiv 2604.09519

Policy4OOD: World Model for Opioid Crisis Intervention (February 2026)

A knowledge-guided world model for policy intervention simulation. Supports counterfactual reasoning by modifying policy inputs within historical sequences, re-running the model to produce counterfactual trajectories.

arXiv 2602.12373 Interventional

Social Dynamics Integration

A position paper at OpenReview argues that "world models should prioritize the unification of physical and social dynamics" -- modeling agent behavior, social norms, and institutional constraints is as important as modeling physics for real-world world models.

Counterfactual World Models via Digital Twins (November 2025)

Formalizes counterfactual world models that take interventions as explicit inputs, predicting temporal sequences under hypothetical modifications to observed properties. Uses video diffusion conditioned on digital twin state.

arXiv 2511.17481

Ethics of Counterfactual World Simulation (2025)

Springer Nature article examining the ethical implications of counterfactual world simulation models (CWSMs) that use multimodal evidence to answer causal questions by simulating what would have happened under alternative conditions.

Synthesis

Comparative Architecture Map

System Prediction Space Action-Conditioned Counterfactual Self-Correcting Domain
JEPA / V-JEPA 2 Latent embeddings Yes (V-JEPA 2-AC) Implicit No Vision, robotics
Genie 2 / 3 Latent diffusion Yes (actions) Yes (divergent rollouts) No 3D environments
World Labs Marble 3D spatial Yes (navigation) Editable worlds No Spatial intelligence
MarS (Microsoft) Order-level tokens Yes (orders) Scenario generation No Financial markets
EconAgent LLM text Yes (decisions) Scenario replay No Macroeconomics
Three-in-One (DBM) Energy-based latent Adapter only Yes (explicit) No Marketing
Policy4OOD Knowledge-guided Yes (policies) Yes (explicit) No Policy intervention
[L6 gap] ? Yes Yes Yes Economics

The table reveals a consistent pattern: no existing system is self-correcting. Every world model in the landscape is trained offline and deployed without real-world feedback loops. The "L3 Evolver" level from the Agentic World Modeling survey -- which autonomously revises its model when predictions fail -- remains aspirational across all domains.

Architectural Patterns Worth Importing

From JEPA: Latent-space prediction

Predict economic states in a learned abstract space rather than raw observables. This naturally handles the noise, missing data, and irrelevant variation in economic signals. The EMA target encoder provides a stable learning target without collapse.

From Genie: Action-conditioned autoregressive dynamics

The pattern of encoding state, conditioning on actions, and autoregressively generating next-states is the correct skeleton for an economic simulator. Replace "keyboard input" with "policy intervention" and "video frame" with "economic state vector."

From World Labs: The Simulator decomposition

Li's Renderer/Simulator/Planner taxonomy clarifies that the core intellectual challenge is the Simulator -- maintaining persistent, causally coherent state under interventions. The Renderer and Planner are separable engineering problems.

From Three-in-One: Frozen belief + intervention adapter

The DBM architecture's separation of learned beliefs (frozen world model) from intervention inputs (adapter only) is an elegant counterfactual mechanism. It ensures that counterfactual queries modify the intervention, not the agent's learned state.

From Policy4OOD: Explicit interventional conditioning

Taking interventions as first-class inputs (not just context) and re-running the model with modified policy sequences to produce counterfactual trajectories. This is exactly the pattern needed for economic policy evaluation.

Tail Risk Estimation, Extreme Value Theory & AI/ML in Finance

Literature Survey -- August 2026

Contents
  1. Classical EVT in Finance
  2. ML Approaches to Tail Risk Estimation
  3. AI for Stress Testing & Scenario Generation
  4. Deep Learning + EVT Integration
  5. Gaps in the Literature
  6. Master Citation Table

1. Classical EVT in Finance

Theoretical Foundations

Extreme Value Theory provides the mathematical framework for modeling the tails of probability distributions. Two core theorems underpin the field.

Fisher-Tippett-Gnedenko Theorem (Block Maxima)
The maximum of n i.i.d. random variables, properly normalized, converges to a Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) distribution with CDF: H(x) = exp(-(1 + ξx)^(-1/ξ)). The shape parameter ξ determines the tail type: ξ > 0 (Fréchet / heavy tail), ξ = 0 (Gumbel / light tail), ξ < 0 (Weibull / bounded tail). Financial returns typically exhibit ξ > 0, confirming heavy tails.
Pickands-Balkema-de Haan Theorem (Peaks Over Threshold)
Balkema, A.A. & de Haan, L. (1974). "Residual Life Time at Great Age." Annals of Probability, 2, 792-804.
Pickands, J. (1975). "Statistical Inference Using Extreme Order Statistics." Annals of Statistics, 3(1), 119-131.
For a distribution F in the maximum domain of attraction of a GEV, exceedances over a sufficiently high threshold u follow a Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD): G(y) = 1 - (1 + ξy/σ)^(-1/ξ). This is the theoretical basis of the Peaks Over Threshold (POT) method, generally preferred over Block Maxima in finance because it uses extreme data more efficiently.

Foundational Texts and Papers

Modelling Extremal Events for Insurance and Finance
Embrechts, P., Klüppelberg, C. & Mikosch, T. (1997). Springer-Verlag. 645 pp. ISBN 3-540-60931-8.
The seminal textbook that established EVT as a core tool for financial risk management. Covers heavy-tailed distributions, point processes, extremal processes, and applications to insurance and financial time series. Remains the standard graduate reference.
Estimation of Tail-Related Risk Measures for Heteroscedastic Financial Time Series: An Extreme Value Approach
McNeil, A.J. & Frey, R. (2000). Journal of Empirical Finance, 7(3-4), 271-300.
Introduced the GARCH-EVT two-stage methodology: (1) fit a GARCH model via pseudo-maximum-likelihood to filter out conditional heteroscedasticity, producing approximately i.i.d. standardized residuals; (2) apply POT/GPD to the upper tail of negated residuals. This yields conditional VaR and conditional Expected Shortfall estimates that account for time-varying volatility. This paper became the canonical approach for combining volatility models with extreme value tail estimation.
Quantitative Risk Management: Concepts, Techniques and Tools
McNeil, A.J., Frey, R. & Embrechts, P. (2005; 2nd ed. 2015). Princeton University Press.
The standard practitioner/academic textbook covering risk factors, loss distributions, aggregate risk, copulas, credit risk, and operational risk. Integrates EVT throughout as the primary tail modeling framework.
Value at Risk and Extreme Returns
Danielsson, J. & de Vries, C. (2000). Annales d'Économie et de Statistique, 60, 239-270.
Directly addresses the intersection of VaR computation and extreme value theory for financial returns. Also related: Danielsson, de Vries, de Haan & Peng (2001), "Using a Bootstrap Method to Choose the Sample Fraction in Tail Index Estimation," Journal of Multivariate Analysis, 76(2), 226-248.
Extreme Value Theory in Finance: A Survey
Rocco, M. (2014). Journal of Economic Surveys, 28(1), 82-108.
Comprehensive survey covering EVT applications in finance: VaR estimation, ES computation, asset allocation under safety-first constraints, portfolio tail risk, contagion under stress, and the choice between Block Maxima and POT approaches.
An Application of Extreme Value Theory for Measuring Financial Risk
Gilli, M. & Kellezi, E. (2006). Computational Economics, 27(2-3), 207-228.
Practical application of EVT methods (both Block Maxima/GEV and POT/GPD) to measure financial risk across equity indices, with detailed comparison of VaR estimates from parametric, historical simulation, and EVT approaches.
Estimating and Forecasting Conditional Risk Measures with Extreme Value Theory: A Review
Bee, M. et al. (2018). Risks, 6(2), 45.
Reviews the full pipeline of conditional EVT-based risk measures: GARCH filtering, threshold selection, GPD estimation (MLE, probability-weighted moments, L-moments), and backtesting of VaR/ES forecasts.

The EVT Pipeline for VaR and Expected Shortfall

The standard EVT pipeline for risk measurement:

  1. Volatility filtering. Fit an AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) or similar to returns. Extract standardized residuals z_t = (r_t - μ_t) / σ_t.
  2. Threshold selection. Use mean residual life plots or automated methods (e.g., Danielsson et al.'s bootstrap) to choose the threshold u for POT.
  3. GPD fitting. Fit GPD to exceedances above u via MLE: estimate shape (ξ) and scale (β) parameters.
  4. Risk measure computation. VaR_α = u + (β/ξ)[(n/N_u(1-α))^(-ξ) - 1];   ES_α = VaR_α/(1-ξ) + (β - ξu)/(1-ξ).
  5. Re-scaling. Convert back to conditional scale: VaR_t = μ_t + σ_t · VaR(z).

Key advantage over historical simulation or normal VaR: EVT provides theoretically justified extrapolation beyond observed data into the far tail (e.g., 99.9% quantiles), rather than being limited to the empirical distribution.

2. ML Approaches to Tail Risk Estimation

Deep Quantile Regression for VaR

Forecasting Value-at-Risk Using Deep Neural Network Quantile Regression
Chronopoulos, I., Raftapostolos, A. & Kapetanios, G. (2024). Journal of Financial Econometrics, 22(3), 636-669.
DNN Quantile Regression Uses a deep quantile estimator leveraging neural networks' universal approximation property to model non-linear associations between conditional quantiles and predictors. Supports different penalty functions and high-dimensional covariates. Outperforms linear, MIDAS, and other non-parametric quantile models in VaR forecasting. The key innovation is applying deep learning directly to the quantile loss function rather than to distributional assumptions.
VaR and ES Forecasting via Recurrent Neural Network-Based Stateful Models
Candelieri, A. et al. (2024). International Review of Financial Analysis, 92, 103054.
RNN LSTM Stateful Proposes stateful recurrent neural network architectures (LSTM, GRU) for jointly forecasting VaR and ES. The "stateful" design preserves hidden state across batches, capturing long-range dependencies in financial time series that standard RNN training misses.
Forecasting VaR and ES by Using Deep Quantile Regression, GANs-Based Scenario Generation, and Heterogeneous Market Hypothesis
Xu, Q. et al. (2024). Financial Innovation, 10, 19. (Springer)
Mogrifier RNN GAN Quantile Regression Combines quantile regression with "Mogrifier" recurrent neural networks to capture long memory and volatility clustering. Uses GAN-generated synthetic scenarios to augment training data for rare tail events. Integrates heterogeneous market hypothesis to weight different time horizons.

Deep Expected Shortfall Estimation

Deep Neural Expected Shortfall Regression with Tail-Robustness
Yu, M., Tan, K.M., Wang, H.J. & Zhou, W.-X. (2025). arXiv:2511.08772.
DNN Huber Loss Robust Nonparametric two-step ES regression: (1) estimate conditional quantile as nuisance parameter; (2) build ES estimator using feedforward ReLU networks. Key innovation: integrates a properly tuned Huber loss, yielding an estimator provably resistant to heavy-tailedness (non-asymptotic guarantees) and first-order insensitive to quantile estimation errors from stage one. Alleviates curse of dimensionality when underlying functions have hierarchical composition structure.
Enhancing Financial Tail Risk Forecasting: A Blending Ensemble Framework for Nonlinear Expectile Regression
Ma, F. et al. (2025). Journal of Forecasting. (Early view, Wiley)
Expectile Ensemble Uses expectile regression (a least-squares analogue of quantile regression) with ensemble blending to forecast tail risk. Expectiles are sensitive to tail behavior and can be converted to VaR/ES via the Efron-Tibshirani relationship.

Large-Scale ML for Tail Risk

ReSGA: A Large Tail Risk Model for Learning Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall
Zhang, Y., Zhu, K. & Zhu, Z. (2026). arXiv:2606.04576.
Autoencoder Retrieval Cross-sectional A retrieval-enhanced self-grouping autoencoder with millions of parameters for joint VaR-ES forecasting. (1) Learns latent group structures across assets so tail-risk information is shared among assets with similar financial behavior; (2) incorporates a retrieval mechanism enabling each asset to draw on long-term historical "experiences" from its own past and other grouped assets. Applied to US equities 1926-2023 with 153 firm characteristics. Outperforms 12 econometric and ML competitors. Key finding: improvements driven by data complexity rather than model complexity.
Learning About Tail Risk: Machine Learning and Combination with Regularization in Market Risk Management
Various authors (2024). Omega (Elsevier), 129, 103135.
Regularization Combination Investigates ML methods (random forests, gradient boosting, neural networks) combined with regularization for VaR/ES estimation. Model combination with regularization outperforms individual models for tail risk forecasting.

Hybrid Causal-Predictive Approaches

Causal and Predictive Modeling of Short-Horizon Market Risk and Systematic Alpha Generation Using Hybrid Machine Learning Ensembles
Various authors (2025). arXiv:2510.22348.
Causal ML Ensemble Demonstrates that short-term conditional drivers -- equity returns, interest rate sensitivities, commodity tail-risk measures -- dominate crash predictions. Combines causal identification with predictive ML ensembles for market risk forecasting.
CoFiE-NN: Cornish-Fisher Expansion with LSTM Neural Networks for Tail Risk Prediction
IMF Working Paper (2024).
LSTM Cornish-Fisher Combines Cornish-Fisher expansions (using higher moments -- skewness, kurtosis -- to adjust normal quantiles) with LSTM neural networks. Tested across four market regimes (GFC, European debt crisis, COVID-19, taper tantrum). Consistently outperforms traditional EVT, showing adaptability to regime changes.
Quantile-Based Modeling of Scale Dynamics in Financial Returns for VaR and ES Forecasting
Various authors (2025). arXiv:2603.02357.
Semiparametric Quantile A semiparametric approach modeling the conditional scale of financial returns via restricted quantile regression. Accepted in International Journal of Forecasting.

3. AI for Stress Testing & Scenario Generation

GANs for Financial Time Series and Stress Scenarios

Quant GANs: Deep Generation of Financial Time Series
Wiese, M. et al. (2020). Quantitative Finance, 20(9), 1419-1440.
GAN TCN Proposed QuantGAN using stacked temporal convolutional networks to capture long-range temporal dependencies in financial time series generation. Demonstrated that GANs can reproduce heavy-tailed distributions, volatility clustering, and leverage effects observed in real markets.
GANs for Scenario Analysis and Stress Testing in Financial Institutions
Review paper (2024). IJFMR, 6(3).
WGAN-GP Stress Testing Reviews conditional Wasserstein GANs with gradient penalty for stress scenario generation. The generator receives a noise vector plus a condition vector (severity level, geographic influence, duration) to produce synthetic stress scenarios. Addresses CCAR/DFAST regulatory requirements where historical data is insufficient.
Sig-Wasserstein GANs for Conditional Time Series Generation
Liao, S. et al. (2024). Mathematical Finance, 34(4). (Wiley)
Sig-WGAN Path Signatures Integrates Wasserstein GANs with path signatures -- a graded sequence of statistics providing a universal description of data streams. Enables conditional generation of financial time series preserving temporal dependence structure, useful for stress scenario generation conditioned on macroeconomic variables.
Generative Adversarial Networks Applied to Synthetic Financial Scenarios Generation
Various authors (2023). Physica A (Elsevier).
GAN Synthetic Data Evaluates GAN architectures for generating synthetic multivariate financial scenarios that preserve cross-asset correlations, marginal distributions, and tail dependencies for risk management and stress testing.
Can GANs Learn the Stylized Facts of Financial Time Series?
Various authors (2024). arXiv:2410.09850.
GAN Stylized Facts Empirically tests whether GAN-generated financial time series reproduce canonical stylized facts: heavy tails, volatility clustering, leverage effect, absence of autocorrelation in returns, long memory in absolute returns. Critical evaluation of where GANs succeed and fail in capturing tail behavior.
Time-Causal VAE: Robust Financial Time Series Generator
Various authors (2024). arXiv:2411.02947.
VAE Causal A variational autoencoder respecting temporal causal structure for generating financial time series. Designed to produce realistic scenarios for stress testing while maintaining the causal ordering of market dynamics.
Generative Adversarial Regression (GAR): Learning Conditional Risk Scenarios
Various authors (2025). arXiv:2603.08553.
GAR Conditional Extends GANs to conditional regression settings, learning to generate risk scenarios conditioned on specific covariate values. Directly applicable to "what-if" stress testing conditioned on specific macro-economic states.

Diffusion Models for Financial Data

Generation of Synthetic Financial Time Series by Diffusion Models
Various authors (2024). arXiv:2410.18897.
Diffusion Applies denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) to synthetic financial time series generation. Diffusion models offer advantages over GANs (training stability, mode coverage) and may better capture multimodal tail distributions.

Regulatory Context: CCAR and DFAST

The Federal Reserve's CCAR and Dodd-Frank Act Stress Tests require banks to project losses under severely adverse scenarios. Traditional approaches rely on historical or expert-designed hypothetical scenarios. AI/ML contributions include:

  • Scenario enrichment: GANs/VAEs generate plausible scenarios beyond historical experience, addressing the "we haven't seen it before" problem.
  • Conditional generation: Models generate scenarios conditioned on specific macro variables (unemployment spikes, rate shocks) that regulators specify.
  • Tail calibration: Generative models combined with EVT ensure synthetic scenarios respect extreme event statistics rather than producing unrealistic tail draws.
  • Multi-asset coherence: Modern generative architectures preserve cross-asset dependence structure under stress, avoiding independently shocked risk factors.

4. Deep Learning + EVT Integration

The emerging intersection where deep learning architectures are designed to respect or incorporate extreme value theory constraints -- arguably the most technically interesting frontier in the field.

Neural Networks with EVT Constraints

Modeling Extremes with d-max-decreasing Neural Networks
Hasan, A., Elkhalil, K., Ng, Y., Pereira, J.M., Farsiu, S., Blanchet, J.H. & Tarokh, V. (2021/2022). arXiv:2102.09042.
Constrained NN EVT Introduces a neural network architecture enforcing the d-max-decreasing property -- a stringent convexity constraint required by multivariate extreme value distributions. First class of non-parametric estimators maintaining the structural properties mandated by EVT. Achieves parametric-rate approximation of the dependence structure. Includes a generative sampling technique for high-dimensional extreme value distributions. Applications in environmental sciences and financial mathematics.
Deep Learning of Multivariate Extremes via a Geometric Representation
Murphy-Barltrop, C.J.R., Majumder, R. & Richards, J. (2024). arXiv:2406.19936.
Geometric Extremes DNN Uses geometric extremes -- inferring extreme dependence from deterministic limiting shapes of scaled sample clouds -- combined with deep learning. First approach to modeling limit sets using neural networks. Enables asymptotically-justified yet flexible semi-parametric models for extremal dependence of high-dimensional data. Extends geometric extremes beyond low-dimensional settings (previously limited to d < 5). Demonstrated on North Sea meteorological/oceanographic data.
Semi-parametric Bulk and Tail Regression Using Spline-Based Neural Networks (SPQRx)
Majumder, R. & Richards, J. (2025/2026). arXiv:2504.19994.
Spline NN Blended GPD SPQRx: semi-parametric quantile regression for extremes. Combines spline-based neural network density regression with a "blended generalized Pareto distribution" providing smooth transition between bulk and tail modeling without threshold selection. Complies with EVT standards while maintaining full distributional flexibility. Offers variable importance scores measuring covariate influence on bulk vs. tail behavior.

Deep Generative Models + EVT

Combining Deep Generative Models with Extreme Value Theory for Synthetic Hazard Simulation
Peard, A. & Hall, J. (2023). NeurIPS 2023 Workshop on Climate Change and ML. arXiv:2311.18521.
GAN EVT Hybrid Two-part architecture: (1) GAN models the dependence structure for multivariate hazards (wind speed, wave height, precipitation); (2) EVT handles tail extrapolation in a controlled manner. The GAN learns the copula/dependence, while EVT ensures realistic tail behavior. Generates thousands of realistic compound hazard events. Directly transferable to financial multivariate tail modeling.
Pasche & Engelke (2022); Richards & Huser (2022); Cisneros et al. (2024)
Multiple papers cited in Murphy-Barltrop et al. (2024).
Deep Generative EVT A cluster of recent papers constructing flexible, computationally-scalable models for univariate extremes using deep learning. Pasche and Engelke focus on conditional EVT models using neural networks; Richards and Huser on neural Bayes estimators for extreme value parameters.

EVT-Aware Loss Functions and Training

Standard neural network loss functions (MSE, cross-entropy) weight all observations equally or even downweight extremes. EVT-aware approaches:

  • Quantile/expectile loss: Asymmetric losses focusing on specific tail quantiles (Chronopoulos et al. 2024).
  • Huber-modified tail loss: Robust to heavy-tailed training data while focusing on ES estimation (Yu et al. 2025).
  • EVT-adapted loss functions: Koh et al. (2024, arXiv:2401.12195) proposed loss functions adapted to extreme values that prioritize the tail rather than the bulk of the data distribution.
  • Shape-constrained architectures: Enforcing d-max-decreasing or other EVT constraints directly in the network architecture (Hasan et al. 2022) rather than through loss functions.

5. Gaps in the Literature

Gap 1 -- Real-Time Tail Risk Monitoring with Causal Understanding

Existing work either models tails statistically (EVT) or predicts risk factors causally (causal ML), but almost no work integrates both into a real-time monitoring system. Current EVT-based VaR/ES is computed ex ante with fixed parameters; current causal ML identifies drivers but does not provide theoretically justified tail extrapolation. The missing piece: a system that simultaneously (a) identifies why tail risk is changing (causal mechanism), (b) quantifies how much it has changed (EVT-calibrated measures), and (c) updates in real time as new data arrives.

Gap 2 -- Adaptive EVT Under Regime Changes

Classical EVT assumes stationarity (or stationarity of GARCH residuals). When the data-generating process undergoes structural breaks -- regime changes, policy shifts, market microstructure changes -- EVT tail parameters (ξ, β) become non-stationary. The CoFiE-NN (2024 IMF) begins to address this but relies on pre-identified regimes. A fully adaptive system that detects regime changes endogenously and re-estimates tail parameters in real time remains absent. The key challenge: estimating GPD parameters with a sliding window when exceedances are very few per window.

Gap 3 -- Moving Beyond Historical Simulation

Despite decades of EVT research, the dominant industry practice remains historical simulation (HS) or filtered historical simulation (FHS). The gap is practical, not theoretical: EVT methods require threshold selection (fragile), GPD fitting (unstable with few exceedances), and distributional assumptions difficult to validate. ML approaches that automate or bypass these choices (like SPQRx's threshold-free approach) are promising but not yet industry-adopted.

Gap 4 -- Endogenous vs. Exogenous Tail Risk

Nearly all tail risk models treat risk as exogenous -- a shock arrives from outside the system. But financial crises often involve endogenous amplification (fire sales, margin spirals, liquidity feedback). The Cont & Schaanning (2017) fire-sale model addresses endogenous amplification, but this work is not integrated with EVT or ML tail estimation. A model capturing how endogenous feedback loops amplify exogenous shocks into extreme tail events is missing.

Gap 5 -- Multivariate Tail Dependence at Scale

Most EVT applications in finance are univariate. Multivariate EVT exists (copulas, spectral measures, geometric extremes) but is computationally challenging beyond 5-10 dimensions. Murphy-Barltrop et al. (2024) push this boundary with geometric extremes + deep learning but have not applied it to financial portfolios with hundreds of assets. Scaling multivariate tail dependence estimation to realistic portfolio dimensions remains open.

Gap 6 -- Generative Tail Calibration

GAN/VAE/diffusion models for financial scenario generation typically evaluate generated samples on aggregate statistical properties (autocorrelation, kurtosis, Wasserstein distance). Very few papers specifically evaluate whether the generative model's tail behavior is statistically consistent with EVT predictions. Peard & Hall (2023) is an exception, applied to climate not finance. A rigorous framework for calibrating generative financial models against EVT tail properties is needed.

Gap 7 -- Interventional Tail Risk

All current approaches are observational -- they estimate P(loss > x | data). None address the interventional question: P(loss > x | do(intervention)). What happens to tail risk if we change a policy, adjust a position, or modify a market structure? This requires integrating causal inference (do-calculus) with tail risk estimation, a combination absent from the literature.
