Innovation Deep Dive

The Financial State Estimation Engine

Continuous State Reconstruction of the Global Financial System — the core innovation of RecWM, modeled after power-grid state estimation and submarine fire-control systems.

0. The Central Claim

The financial system has a state at every instant — a compact mathematical object that, if known, would make every observable price, spread, flow, and signal a deterministic (or narrowly stochastic) consequence of that state. No one observes the state directly. We observe measurements: noisy, incomplete, heterogeneous projections of the state onto instrument prices, order books, news wires, and regulatory filings. The Financial State Estimation Engine (FSEE) solves the inverse problem: given the measurements, reconstruct the state.

This is not a prediction engine. A power grid state estimator does not predict tomorrow’s load — it tells the operator, with mathematical precision, what the grid looks like right now. A submarine’s fire control system does not predict where the enemy will be tomorrow — it constructs a firing solution for where the enemy is. The FSEE tells the portfolio manager: here is the state of the financial world at this instant. Here is what you can see. Here is what you cannot see. Here is your confidence in each component.

Everything else — scenario analysis, contingency simulation, regime detection, trade generation — is downstream of the state estimate. Get the state right and everything else follows. Get it wrong and nothing else matters.

1. The State Vector

1.1 What Constitutes “State” in Finance

In a power grid, the state vector x contains 2N−1 variables for an N-bus system: voltage magnitudes |Vi| and voltage angles θi at each bus (with one reference angle). These are the minimal set of quantities from which every measurable quantity (power flows, injections, currents) can be computed via the power flow equations.

The financial analogue requires identifying the minimal set of latent quantities from which every observable market quantity can (in principle) be derived. We define the state vector as a composite object living in a product space:

x(t) = (xL(t), xM(t), xR(t), xC(t), xS(t), xN(t), xP(t), ξ(t))

where each component corresponds to one of the seven fragments, and ξ(t) encodes the interaction structure between fragments. Concretely:

Fragment 1: Liquidity State xL ∈ RdL

xL = (δ1, ..., δK,   -- dealer inventory imbalances (K major dealers)
      ψ1, ..., ψJ,       -- funding stress indices (J funding markets)
      λ1, ..., λI, -- market depth parameters (I key venues)
      φ)                     -- aggregate liquidity regime indicator ∈ [0,1]

The dealer inventory imbalances δk are latent — no one publishes dealer books in real time. They are the analogue of bus voltage angles: not directly measurable, but inferable from observable quantities (bid-ask spreads, price impact coefficients, repo rates). Typical dimension: dL ~ 50–80.

Fragment 2: Momentum State xM ∈ RdM

xM = (μ1, ..., μA,          -- trend strengths across A asset classes
      σCTA,                -- CTA positioning intensity (scalar summary)
      fpassive1, ..., fP,    -- passive flow rates (P major ETF/index complexes)
      r1, ..., rG)            -- regime indicators for G trend groups

Trend strengths μa are defined as the signed magnitude of the log-signature truncation at depth 2 of the recent price path in asset class a (see Section 5 on the composition operator). Typical dimension: dM ~ 40–60.

Fragment 3: Risk State xR ∈ RdR

xR = (σ1, ..., σV,    -- implied vol levels (V key surfaces)
      κ1, ..., κV,    -- vol-of-vol parameters
      ρ,                      -- correlation state (vectorized upper triangle of
                                    the Nasset × Nasset correlation matrix)
      τ1, ..., τT)        -- tail risk measures (T instruments)

The correlation state ρ is the single most important subcomponent. In a power grid, when all generator rotors swing together, you have a coherent oscillation mode that threatens stability. In finance, when all asset correlations compress toward 1, you have a systemic stress event. The eigenvalue spectrum of the correlation matrix — particularly the ratio λ1 / Σ(λi) — is the financial analogue of the power system’s dominant oscillation mode damping ratio. Typical dimension: dR ~ 200–500 (dominated by the correlation vector).

Fragment 4: Credit State xC ∈ RdC

xC = (s1, ..., sE,            -- credit spread curves (E entity groups)
      π1, ..., πE,          -- implied default probabilities
      ω1, ..., ωF,    -- funding market stress indicators
      χ)                      -- credit cycle position ∈ [0, 2π] (cyclical)

Typical dimension: dC ~ 60–100.

Fragment 5: Structure State xS ∈ RdS

xS = (γ1, ..., γQ,    -- options dealer gamma exposure (Q underliers)
      θrebal,              -- rebalancing flow pressure (systematic strategies)
      βmicro1, ..., βW) -- microstructure regime params (W venues)

Dealer gamma exposure γq is the critical structural variable. When dealers are short gamma (γq < 0), their hedging amplifies price moves. When long gamma (γq > 0), their hedging dampens price moves. This is the exact analogue of the power system’s positive vs. negative damping on oscillation modes: negative damping means the system will amplify disturbances, and the state estimator must flag it. Typical dimension: dS ~ 30–50.

Fragment 6: Sentiment State xN ∈ RdN

xN = (η1, ..., ηH,        -- positioning survey indicators (H surveys)
      ζnews,                -- aggregate news tone (scalar, from NLP pipeline)
      ζsocial,              -- social media sentiment (scalar)
      α1, ..., αB)    -- analyst revision breadth (B sector groups)

Typical dimension: dN ~ 20–40.

Fragment 7: Policy State xP ∈ RdP

xP = (r*1, ..., r*C,  -- estimated neutral rates (C central banks)
      hawkish1, ..., hawkishC, -- hawkishness scores (from text analysis)
      fiscal1, ..., fiscalD,   -- fiscal impulse measures (D economies)
      reg1, ..., regU)         -- regulatory tightness indices (U domains)

Typical dimension: dP ~ 30–50.

1.2 The Interaction Structure

The interaction tensor ξ(t) captures how fragments influence each other. This is NOT a correlation matrix between fragments — it is a directed influence structure. Define:

ξij(t) ∈ R for i, j ∈ {L, M, R, C, S, N, P}

where ξij(t) measures the current strength of the causal channel from fragment j to fragment i. For example, ξL,P(t) measures how strongly current policy state is driving liquidity state.

The full interaction structure is a 7×7 matrix (49 parameters, minus the 7 diagonal elements which are absorbed into each fragment’s own dynamics, yielding 42 cross-fragment interaction parameters).

1.3 Total State Dimension

The total state vector lives in Rd where: 

d = dL + dM + dR + dS + dC + dN + dP + 42

  ~ 80 + 50 + 350 + 40 + 80 + 30 + 40 + 42

  = ~712

This is comparable in scale to a moderately large power system state estimation problem (a 350-bus system has ~700 state variables). It is tractable with modern computational methods.

State Estimation Architecture

2. The Measurement Model

2.1 The Observation Equation

In power systems, the measurement model is:

z = h(x) + e, e ~ N(0, R)

where z is the measurement vector, h is the (nonlinear) mapping from states to expected measurements, and R is the measurement noise covariance.

For the FSEE, we define a heterogeneous measurement model that handles the wildly different data types entering the system:

zk(t) = hk(x(t), θk) + ek(t)

where k indexes measurement channels, each with its own observation function hk, parameter vector θk, and noise process ek. The channels are:

Channel 1: Tick-level price data (continuous, high-frequency)

For instrument i with price pi(t):

log pi(t) = gi(xL, xM, xR, xS) + εi(t)

where gi is the pricing function that maps the relevant state components to the expected log-price, and εi(t) is microstructure noise. The function gi encodes the structural model: how liquidity, momentum, risk, and structure states combine to produce a fair price. For a liquid equity, gi might depend primarily on xR (risk state determines the discount rate) and xM (momentum determines the trend component). For a credit instrument, gi depends heavily on xC.

Channel 2: Spread data (continuous, medium-frequency)

Credit spreads, basis swaps, term premia:

sj(t) = fj(xC, xL, xP) + νj(t)

Spreads are measurements that are particularly informative about the credit and liquidity fragments.

Channel 3: Volatility surface data (continuous, medium-frequency)

Implied volatilities at strike K and maturity T:

σimpl(K, T, t) = Φ(xR, xS, xN) + w(K, T, t)

The entire volatility surface is a rich measurement of the risk and structure fragments. The skew (difference in implied vol between out-of-the-money puts and calls) is especially informative about tail risk expectations.

Channel 4: Flow and positioning data (discrete, low-frequency)

CFTC Commitments of Traders (weekly), fund flow reports (daily/weekly), 13F filings (quarterly):

Fm(tm) = Ψm(xM(tm), xL(tm)) + um

where tm is the reporting timestamp (which may lag the actual measurement time by hours to weeks). The lag is handled explicitly in the estimation framework — see Section 6.

Channel 5: Text-derived signals (discrete, event-driven)

NLP-processed central bank communications, earnings calls, news:

text_scoren(tn) = Ξn(xP(tn), xN(tn)) + vn

where the observation function Ξn maps the policy and sentiment states to an expected text score, and vn captures NLP model uncertainty. The noise variance for text channels is substantially larger than for price channels, reflecting the lossy nature of text-to-signal conversion.

2.2 The Unified Measurement Vector

At any estimation epoch t, the available measurements are assembled into a stacked vector: 

z(t) = [z1(t), z2(t), ..., zM(t)]T

with the corresponding stacked observation function:

h(x) = [h1(x), h2(x), ..., hM(x)]T

and block-diagonal noise covariance (assuming independence across measurement channels):

R = diag(R1, R2, ..., RM)

The dimension of z(t) is large — on the order of 10,000 to 50,000 measurements at any given instant (thousands of prices, hundreds of spreads, dozens of vol surface points, etc.). This is analogous to a large RTO’s 90,000 SCADA measurements.

2.3 Measurement Reliability Weighting

Not all measurements are equally reliable. The FSEE assigns each measurement a reliability weight that enters through the noise covariance R:

Rk = σk2 / wk

where σk2 is the intrinsic noise variance and wk ∈ [0, 1] is the reliability weight. The reliability weight is determined by:

  • Staleness: A measurement’s weight decays exponentially with age. A CFTC report from 3 days ago (reflecting positions from 5 days ago) has lower weight than today’s closing prices. The decay rate is calibrated per channel.
  • Source quality: Primary exchange data has wk near 1. Derived signals (sentiment scores, estimated flows) have lower wk. Pseudo-measurements (model-imputed values for missing data) have the lowest wk.
  • Market regime: During high-volatility regimes, the noise variance σk2 for price measurements increases (prices become noisier), while the information content of volatility surface measurements increases (the surface becomes more informative about tail risk). The R matrix is regime-dependent.

This is directly analogous to power system practice, where measurement weights reflect instrument accuracy classes, and pseudo-measurements (load forecasts used when telemetry is lost) are assigned very high noise variance.

3. The Transition Model

3.1 Why Financial State Dynamics Are Harder Than Physical Systems

In a power grid, the state transition model is derived from physics: the swing equation for generators, the power flow equations for the network, the thermal dynamics of transmission lines. These models are known. They may have uncertain parameters, but the functional form is dictated by Maxwell’s equations.

In finance, there is no Maxwell’s equations. The state dynamics are:

  • Endogenous: market participants’ beliefs about the state change the state (reflexivity)
  • Regime-dependent: the dynamics in a risk-off crash are qualitatively different from a low-vol grind
  • Non-stationary: the parameters of the dynamics themselves evolve as market structure changes

We address this with a regime-switching state-space model.

3.2 Regime-Switching Transition Model

Define a discrete regime variable r(t) ∈ {1, 2, ..., K} representing the current market regime. We use K = 4 base regimes: 

r = 1:  Low-vol expansion (risk-on, positive carry)
r = 2:  High-vol expansion (trending with volatility)
r = 3:  Orderly contraction (risk-off, negative carry, moderate vol)
r = 4:  Crisis/dislocation (high vol, correlation compression, liquidity withdrawal)

The state transition model is:

x(t + dt) = Ar(t)(x(t)) · x(t) + Br(t) · u(t) + w(t)

where:

  • Ar is the regime-dependent state transition matrix (possibly nonlinear, hence the functional notation Ar(x))
  • u(t) is a known input vector (scheduled events: central bank meetings, options expirations, index rebalances)
  • w(t) ~ N(0, Qr) is process noise with regime-dependent covariance

The regime transition is governed by a time-varying transition probability matrix:

P(r(t+dt) = j | r(t) = i, x(t)) = πij(x(t))

Critically, the regime transition probabilities depend on the current state. This means the state itself can trigger regime changes — a liquidity state crossing a threshold can trigger the transition from regime 1 (low-vol expansion) to regime 4 (crisis). This is the correct mathematical structure for modeling feedback loops like margin call cascades.

3.3 The Transition Matrix Structure

The transition matrix Ar has a block structure reflecting the fragment architecture:

Ar = | ArLL    ArLM    ...    ArLP |
     | ArML    ArMM    ...    ArMP |
     |   ...         ...       ...      ...     |
     | ArPL    ArPM    ...    ArPP |

The diagonal blocks Arii capture each fragment’s own dynamics (mean reversion of spreads, momentum persistence of trends, vol clustering). The off-diagonal blocks Arij capture cross-fragment transmission: how a credit state change propagates into liquidity, how a policy shock transmits into risk.

In regime 1 (low-vol expansion), most off-diagonal blocks are small — fragments evolve semi-independently. In regime 4 (crisis), the off-diagonal blocks are large — everything affects everything, correlations spike, the system becomes tightly coupled. This regime-dependent coupling is one of the most important features of the model: it captures the empirical fact that cross-asset correlations increase during stress.

3.4 Nonlinear Dynamics Within Fragments

Certain fragments have inherently nonlinear dynamics. Dealer gamma exposure (Fragment 5) is the clearest example:

d(γq)/dt = −Γq · (dpq/dt)2 + hedging_flowq

The gamma exposure is consumed by price moves (the −(dp)2 term) and replenished by new options trades. When γq crosses zero from positive to negative, the dynamics of the underlying price qualitatively change — from damped to amplified. This is a bifurcation in the dynamical system, analogous to a power system crossing its stability boundary.

For these nonlinear fragments, the transition model uses an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) or Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) formulation rather than a linear Kalman filter. Specifically:

EKF Linearization

At each step, compute the Jacobian:

Fr(t) = ∂Ar(x) / ∂x |x = x̂(t)

and use Fr in place of Ar for the covariance propagation:

P(t + dt) = Fr · P(t) · FrT + Qr

UKF Sigma Points

For the most nonlinear fragments (gamma exposure, tail risk measures), generate 2d+1 sigma points:

X0 = x̂
Xi = x̂ + √((d + κ) · P)i,         i = 1, ..., d
Xd+i = x̂ − √((d + κ) · P)i,     i = 1, ..., d

Propagate each through the nonlinear transition model, and reconstruct the predicted mean and covariance from the propagated sigma points. This avoids the linearization errors of EKF for highly nonlinear dynamics.

4. Observability Theory for Finance

4.1 The Observability Matrix

In linear systems theory, the system (A, H) is observable if and only if the observability matrix: 

O = | H        |
    | H·A      |
    | H·A2    |
    | ...       |
    | H·Ad-1  |

has rank d (the state dimension). This means: given the measurement function H and the dynamics A, can we reconstruct the full state from a sequence of measurements?

For the FSEE, observability is computed per-regime:

Or = | H            |
     | H · Ar      |
     | H · Ar2    |
     | ...           |
     | H · Ard-1  |

4.2 Fragment-Level Observability

A critical insight: we do not need full-system observability at every instant. We need fragment-level observability, which is a weaker condition. Define the fragment-level observability matrix for fragment i:

Or(i) = Πi · Or

where Πi is the projection onto fragment i’s state subspace. Fragment i is observable if rank(Or(i)) = di.

This decomposition matters because different fragments have different observability characteristics:

  • Risk (Fragment 3): Almost always observable. Volatility surfaces, correlation matrices, and tail measures are directly quoted in liquid markets. The Risk fragment is the analogue of bus voltage magnitudes in a power grid — the most directly measured state component.
  • Liquidity (Fragment 1): Partially observable. Bid-ask spreads and price impact are directly observable; dealer inventory positions are latent. Observability depends on the number and quality of proxy measurements (repo rates, dealer CDS, primary dealer survey data).
  • Structure (Fragment 5): Intermittently observable. Dealer gamma exposure can be estimated from options open interest and flow data, but the estimate degrades between options expiration cycles. This is analogous to power system observability loss when a key RTU goes offline.
  • Policy (Fragment 7): Observable only at discrete points. Between central bank meetings, the policy state must be propagated by the transition model with high uncertainty. On meeting days, the measurement update dramatically reduces uncertainty. This is analogous to a power system where certain buses are only telemetered intermittently.

4.3 The Minimum Sensor Set

What is the minimum set of market data required to make the financial state observable? We answer this by analogy with the power system measurement placement problem.

Define the essential measurement set E as the smallest set of data feeds such that, for each fragment i, rank(Or(i)(E)) = di for all regimes r.

Through structural analysis of the observation functions, we identify the following minimum sensor set:

Fragment Essential Measurements Power Grid Analogy
Liquidity SOFR-EFFR spread, cross-currency basis (3 major pairs), repo rates, bid-ask spreads (20 key instruments) Bus voltages at key substations
Momentum Price series (50 liquid futures across all asset classes), ETF flow data (10 major complexes) Generator MW output telemetry
Risk SPX vol surface (25 strikes × 8 tenors), VIX term structure, cross-asset realized correlation (10×10 matrix) PMU phasor measurements
Credit IG and HY CDX indices, 10 sovereign CDS, LIBOR-OIS spread Power flow measurements on key corridors
Structure SPX options open interest by strike, GEX estimates, end-of-month/quarter calendar Breaker status and transformer tap positions
Sentiment AAII survey, put/call ratio, news sentiment index Load forecast inputs
Policy Fed funds futures curve, ECB/BOJ/PBOC policy rate, fiscal deficit estimates Generator dispatch schedules

Total essential measurements: approximately 400–500 data points. This is the “measurement placement plan” for the financial state estimator — the minimum footprint for observability.

4.4 Observability Loss Detection

The FSEE continuously monitors its own observability. At each estimation epoch, it computes:

obs_scorei(t) = σmin(Or(i)(active_meas(t))) / σmax(Or(i)(active_meas(t)))

where σmin and σmax are the minimum and maximum singular values of the fragment-level observability matrix restricted to currently active measurements.

When obs_scorei(t) falls below a threshold (we use 0.01), the FSEE declares observability degradation for fragment i and:

  1. Increases the uncertainty (covariance) for fragment i’s state estimate
  2. Activates pseudo-measurements: model-imputed values based on historical patterns and cross-fragment inference
  3. Alerts the operator: “Liquidity state observability degraded — repo rate feed offline, using model-imputed values, confidence reduced to 60%”

This is the direct analogue of the power system state estimator’s response to telemetry loss: degrade gracefully, never silently. The 2003 Northeast Blackout’s root cause — silent failure of the state estimator — is the anti-pattern the FSEE is designed to prevent.

5. The Composition Operator

5.1 Why Concatenation Fails

The naive approach to combining seven fragment states is vector concatenation:

xnaive = [xL; xM; xR; xC; xS; xN; xP]

This treats the fragments as independent dimensions of a flat vector space. It fails because:

  1. Fragment interactions are not linear: the effect of a credit deterioration on liquidity depends on the current liquidity state (a credit shock when dealers are already stressed has a qualitatively different effect than when they are flush).
  2. Fragment states live in different geometric spaces: the correlation matrix (in Fragment 3) lives on a Riemannian manifold (the cone of positive-definite matrices), not in Euclidean space. The credit cycle position χ lives on a circle. Concatenation into a flat vector ignores this geometry.
  3. The composition must be coherent: the composed state must satisfy cross-fragment consistency constraints. A state where credit spreads are at crisis levels but volatility is at all-time lows is internally inconsistent — it should have low probability in the composed state, even if each fragment’s marginal distribution assigns it nonzero probability.

5.2 The Sheaf-Theoretic Composition

We define the composition operator using the mathematical structure of a cellular sheaf over the fragment interaction graph.

The fragment graph G = (V, E)

Vertices V = {L, M, R, C, S, N, P} are the seven fragments. Edges E represent causal channels between fragments. The graph is directed and weighted, with edge weights given by the interaction tensor ξij(t).

The sheaf F over G

To each vertex v ∈ V, assign the state space F(v) = Rdv (the fragment’s state space). To each edge e = (i, j), assign a restriction map:

ρe,i: F(i) → F(e)
ρe,j: F(j) → F(e)

where F(e) is the stalk space over the edge — the space of quantities that are jointly determined by both fragments. For example, the edge (Credit, Liquidity) has a stalk space containing “funding stress” — a quantity that is simultaneously a credit phenomenon and a liquidity phenomenon.

The restriction maps extract, from each fragment’s full state, the component relevant to the shared edge. For the (Credit, Liquidity) edge:

ρCL,C(xC) = ω(xC)     -- extract funding stress from credit state
ρCL,L(xL) = ψ(xL)       -- extract funding stress from liquidity state

Sheaf Consistency

The composed state is consistent if, for every edge e = (i, j):

|| ρe,i(xi) − ρe,j(xj) ||2 ≤ εe

That is, the two fragments agree on the shared quantities, up to tolerance εe.

The Sheaf Laplacian

Define the sheaf Laplacian matrix LF as:

(LF)vv = Σe incident to v ρe,vT · ρe,v
(LF)vw = −ρe,vT · ρe,w    for edge e = (v, w)

The quadratic form xT LF x measures the total inconsistency across all fragment pairs. The composed state is obtained by projecting the raw fragment estimates onto the consistency subspace:

xcomposed = argminx ||x − xraw||2W subject to xT LF x ≤ εtotal

where W is a weighting matrix reflecting confidence in each fragment’s raw estimate, and εtotal is the total inconsistency budget.

This is equivalent to the MinT forecast reconciliation approach used in hierarchical time series (Wickramasuriya et al., 2019), generalized from tree-structured hierarchies to arbitrary DAGs. The connection is exact: MinT’s reconciliation matrix is the pseudoinverse of the summing matrix, which is a special case of the sheaf Laplacian projection.

5.3 The Consistency Score

The sheaf consistency score is a scalar diagnostic:

C(t) = 1 − x(t)T LF x(t) / x(t)T x(t)

When C(t) is near 1, the fragments tell a coherent story — all measurement channels agree. When C(t) drops, the fragments are contradicting each other. A low consistency score is the financial analogue of a power system state estimator producing large normalized residuals: something is wrong, either in the measurements or in the model.

A PM glancing at the consistency score gets an instant read on whether the market’s signals are coherent. C(t) dropping from 0.92 to 0.71 in an hour means: the story is breaking apart. Credit is saying one thing, volatility another, flows a third. Either a regime change is underway or a data source has gone bad. In either case: pay attention.

6. Continuous vs. Discrete Updates

6.1 The Dual-Rate Architecture

Financial data arrives on two fundamentally different timescales:

  • Continuous: tick prices, order book updates, streaming news feeds (milliseconds to seconds)
  • Discrete: economic releases, earnings announcements, central bank decisions, regulatory filings (hours to quarters)

The FSEE handles this with a dual-rate estimation architecture inspired by multi-rate Kalman filtering.

Fast Loop (100ms cycle)

Processes continuous price and spread data. Updates the directly observable components of xR (volatility surface), xL (bid-ask spreads, market depth), and xS (microstructure metrics). Uses a linear Kalman update for computational speed:

x̂(t+) = x̂(t−) + K(t) · (zfast(t) − Hfast · x̂(t−))
K(t) = P(t−) · HfastT · (Hfast · P(t−) · HfastT + Rfast)−1
P(t+) = (I − K(t) · Hfast) · P(t−)

The fast loop only updates the subset of state variables that are directly observed by fast-rate measurements. All other state variables are propagated by the transition model without measurement update.

Slow Loop (5-minute cycle)

Performs the full nonlinear state estimation. Incorporates all measurement channels including text-derived signals, flow data, and cross-fragment consistency enforcement via the sheaf Laplacian projection. Uses the UKF formulation for the nonlinear fragments.

The slow loop also updates the regime probabilities:

P(r(t) = k | z1:t) = P(z(t) | r(t)=k, z1:t-1) · Σj [πjk(x(t-1)) · P(r(t-1)=j | z1:t-1)]
                      / P(z(t) | z1:t-1)

This is the standard Hamilton filter for Markov-switching models, with the critical extension that the transition probabilities πjk are state-dependent.

6.2 Event-Driven Updates

Discrete events (Fed announcements, earnings releases) trigger an event update outside the regular cycle:

x̂(tevent+) = x̂(tevent−) + Kevent · (zevent − hevent(x̂(tevent−)))

where zevent is the event measurement (e.g., the actual Fed funds rate decision vs. the expected rate embedded in the state estimate).

The event measurement function hevent maps the current state to the expected event outcome. The innovation zevent − hevent(x̂) measures the surprise. A fully expected rate hike produces zero innovation and no state update. A surprise 50bp emergency cut produces a large innovation that propagates through the entire state vector via the Kalman gain Kevent.

The event update also triggers a regime probability reassessment. A sufficiently large event innovation can cause an immediate regime transition:

if ||zevent − hevent(x̂)|| > thresholdregime:
    re-evaluate P(r | z1:t) with elevated transition probabilities

This captures the empirical reality that regime changes are often triggered by discrete events (Lehman bankruptcy, COVID lockdown announcement, unexpected rate decision).

6.3 Handling Delayed Measurements

Some measurements arrive with known delays. CFTC positioning data reports positions as of Tuesday but is released Friday. 13F filings report positions as of quarter-end but are filed 45 days later.

The FSEE handles delayed measurements using the fixed-lag smoother formulation. For a measurement zdelayed(t) that reports on the state at time t − τ:

x̂(t − τ | t) = x̂(t − τ | t-1) + Ksmooth · (zdelayed − h(x̂(t − τ | t-1)))

The smoother updates the historical state estimate at time t − τ, and then re-propagates forward through the transition model to update the current state estimate. This ensures that delayed measurements still contribute to the current state estimate, but with properly reduced influence reflecting the time lag.

7. Novelty Detection

7.1 The State Space Density Problem

A state estimate is only as good as the model that produces it. When the financial system enters a truly novel configuration — one that has never been observed in the training data — the model’s transition dynamics, noise parameters, and even fragment definitions may be inappropriate. The FSEE must detect when it is operating outside its competence.

Define the state space density at the current state estimate:

ρ(x̂(t)) = (1/N) · Σi=1N Kh(x̂(t) − xhistory(ti))

where Kh is a kernel function with bandwidth h, and {xhistory(ti)} is the set of historical state estimates. This is a kernel density estimate of the empirical distribution of states the system has previously visited.

7.2 The Novelty Score

The novelty score is:

ν(t) = −log ρ(x̂(t))

Low novelty (high density): the current state is similar to previously observed states. The model has been “here” before and its learned dynamics are likely appropriate.

High novelty (low density): the current state is in a sparsely visited region of state space. The model is extrapolating.

The novelty score is computed in a dimensionally reduced state space to avoid the curse of dimensionality. We use the top-k principal components of the historical state distribution (typically k = 20–30, capturing 90%+ of variance): 

xreduced(t) = UkT · (x̂(t) − x̄)

νreduced(t) = −log ρreduced(xreduced(t))

7.3 Component-Level Novelty

Beyond the scalar novelty score, the FSEE decomposes novelty by fragment and by interaction channel:

νi(t) = −log ρi(x̂i(t))       -- fragment-level novelty
νij(t) = −log ρij(x̂i(t), x̂j(t))  -- interaction novelty

This decomposition tells the PM where the novelty is. In March 2020:

  • νR (risk fragment novelty) was extremely high — vol levels exceeded anything in training data
  • νL (liquidity fragment novelty) was extremely high — Treasury market depth collapsed
  • νRL (risk-liquidity interaction novelty) was the highest signal — the combination of vol and illiquidity in Treasuries was genuinely unprecedented

The PM needs to know not just “this is novel” but “the novelty is concentrated in the interaction between risk and liquidity, specifically in sovereign bond markets.” That is an actionable signal.

7.4 The Mahalanobis Distance Approach

For a computationally efficient novelty measure, use the Mahalanobis distance of the current state from the historical mean:

DM(t) = √((x̂(t) − μhistory)T · Σhistory−1 · (x̂(t) − μhistory))

where μhistory and Σhistory are the mean and covariance of the historical state distribution.

Under Gaussian assumptions, DM follows a chi-distribution with d degrees of freedom. We flag states where:

P(DM > DM(t)) < α

for threshold α (typically 0.01, i.e., the current state is in the 1% tail of historical states).

The Mahalanobis approach is fast (single matrix multiplication per epoch) and naturally accounts for correlations between state components — a state that is extreme in two correlated dimensions is less novel than one that is extreme in two uncorrelated dimensions.

7.5 The Confidence Degradation Protocol

When novelty is detected (ν(t) exceeds threshold), the FSEE initiates a confidence degradation protocol:

  1. Inflate covariances: Multiply the state covariance P by a factor proportional to the novelty score:
    Pinflated = P · (1 + β · ν(t))
    This widens the uncertainty bounds, honestly communicating that the estimate is less reliable.
  2. Increase process noise: Multiply Qr by the same factor, reflecting that the transition model is less trustworthy in novel states.
  3. Activate ensemble estimation: Run multiple state estimators with perturbed model parameters (different regime transition matrices, different observation functions) and report the ensemble spread as an additional uncertainty measure.
  4. Flag to operator: “NOVELTY ALERT: Current state is in the 0.3rd percentile of historical states. Novelty concentrated in risk-liquidity interaction. State estimate confidence reduced. Transition model reliability: LOW.”

This is the “never fail silently” principle in action. The FSEE would rather tell the PM “I don’t know what’s happening” than produce a confident but unreliable state estimate in unprecedented conditions. In the 2003 blackout analogy: we would rather have a blinking “STATE ESTIMATOR UNRELIABLE” alarm than a frozen display of the last good state.

8. The Estimation Algorithm: Putting It Together

8.1 The Complete Estimation Cycle

At each slow-loop epoch (every 5 minutes), the FSEE executes:

Step 1: Predict

x̂(t|t-1) = Ar · x̂(t-1|t-1)  (propagate state via transition model)
P(t|t-1) = Fr · P(t-1|t-1) · FrT + Qr  (propagate covariance)

Step 2: Collect measurements

Assemble z(t) from all active channels, with reliability weights.

Step 3: Compute innovation

y(t) = z(t) − h(x̂(t|t-1))
S(t) = H · P(t|t-1) · HT + R  (innovation covariance)

Step 4: Bad data detection

For each measurement k, compute the normalized residual:

rkN = |yk| / √(Skk)

If rkN > 3.0 (χ-squared test at 99.7%), flag measurement k as suspect. Re-estimate with the suspect measurement removed. This is the direct analogue of largest normalized residual bad data detection in power system state estimation.

Step 5: Kalman update

K(t) = P(t|t-1) · HT · S(t)−1
x̂(t|t) = x̂(t|t-1) + K(t) · y(t)
P(t|t) = (I − K(t) · H) · P(t|t-1)

Step 6: Sheaf consistency projection

xcomposed(t) = argmin ||x − x̂(t|t)||2W s.t. xT LF x ≤ ε

Step 7: Regime update

Update P(r(t) = k | z1:t) via the Hamilton filter.

Step 8: Novelty assessment

Compute ν(t), νi(t), νij(t). If novelty exceeds threshold, activate confidence degradation protocol.

Step 9: Observability check

Compute obs_scorei(t) for each fragment. Flag any fragment where observability has degraded.

Step 10: Output

Publish to downstream systems:

  • State estimate x̂(t)
  • State uncertainty P(t)
  • Regime probabilities P(r(t) = k)
  • Consistency score C(t)
  • Novelty score ν(t) and its decomposition
  • Observability scores per fragment
  • Bad data flags

8.2 Computational Complexity

The dominant cost is the Kalman update step, which involves inverting the innovation covariance matrix S of dimension M × M (where M ~ 10,000–50,000 measurements). Direct inversion is O(M3), which is prohibitive.

We exploit the sparsity structure:

  1. Block-diagonal approximation: Since most measurements inform only one or two fragments, the Jacobian H is block-sparse. The innovation covariance S inherits this sparsity. Block-diagonal approximation reduces the inversion to 7 smaller inversions.
  2. Sequential processing: Process measurements one at a time (or in small batches), updating the state and covariance incrementally. This is the standard approach in real-time power system state estimation and reduces complexity from O(M3) to O(M · d2).
  3. Square-root filtering: Propagate the square-root of the covariance (Cholesky factor) rather than the covariance itself, improving numerical stability.

With these optimizations, the full estimation cycle completes in under 2 seconds on modern hardware, well within the 5-minute slow-loop budget.

9. The Vital Sign: Financial Frequency

9.1 Deriving a Single Aggregate Indicator

Power grid frequency encodes a fundamental truth: is generation equal to load? We need a single number that encodes a fundamental truth about the financial system.

Define the Financial Frequency (FF):

FF(t) = w1 · C(t) + w2 · (1 − νnorm(t)) + w3 · obsavg(t) + w4 · regime_stability(t)

where:

  • C(t) is the sheaf consistency score (Section 5.3)
  • νnorm(t) is the novelty score normalized to [0,1]
  • obsavg(t) is the average fragment observability score
  • regime_stability(t) = maxk P(r(t) = k) — the probability of the most likely regime (high when the regime is clear, low when multiple regimes are equally probable)
  • w1 through w4 are weights summing to 1 (calibrated empirically; default: 0.3, 0.2, 0.2, 0.3)

FF(t) ∈ [0, 1]. When FF is near 1, the financial system is “in tune”: fragments are consistent, the state is familiar, measurements are available, and the regime is clear. When FF drops, something is wrong — the analogue of grid frequency sagging when generation falls short of load.

The PM sees FF as a single number, a single color, a single sound. No interpretation required. Green means the world makes sense. Yellow means pay attention. Red means the picture is breaking down.

9.2 Frequency Response Bands

Like the power grid’s graduated response to frequency deviations:

FF Range Status Grid Analogue Action
0.85 – 1.00 Normal 59.95 – 60.05 Hz Routine monitoring
0.70 – 0.85 Alert 59.90 – 59.95 Hz Review positions, check hedges
0.50 – 0.70 Warning 59.50 – 59.90 Hz Reduce risk, activate contingency plans
< 0.50 Emergency < 59.50 Hz (UFLS territory) Capital preservation mode

10. From State Estimate to P&L

The state estimation engine is the foundation, not the product. The PM does not want to see a 712-dimensional state vector. They want to know: what trades should I put on? The state estimate enables this through three downstream systems:

Contingency Analysis

Take the current state estimate. Simulate perturbations (the N-1 and N-2 scenarios from the power grid analogue). For each perturbation, propagate through the portfolio to compute P&L impact. Rank contingencies by severity. Flag any that breach risk limits. Recommend hedges for the top-5 most damaging contingencies.

Regime-Conditional Positioning

Given P(r(t) = k) for each regime k, compute the optimal portfolio for each regime, then compute the probability-weighted blend. When regime 4 (crisis) probability rises from 5% to 20%, the blend shifts toward defensive positioning — automatically, continuously, like AGC adjusting generator output.

Anomaly-Driven Alpha

When bad data detection flags a measurement with a large normalized residual — a price that is inconsistent with the rest of the state estimate — one of two things is true: (a) the measurement is wrong (bad data), or (b) the measurement is right and the rest of the market has not yet adjusted. Case (b) is a trading opportunity. The state estimator’s residual analysis is, literally, an alpha signal: it identifies prices that are inconsistent with the global state, and therefore likely to revert to consistency.

This is the submarine’s firing solution. The state estimation gives you the target’s course, speed, and range. The downstream systems compute the torpedo’s course. The PM pulls the trigger.

11. What Makes This Different

The FSEE is not another risk model, factor model, or dashboard. Its innovations are:

1

State estimation, not prediction

It solves the inverse problem of reconstructing current reality from noisy measurements, rather than the forward problem of predicting the future. Prediction is downstream.

2

Observability-aware

It knows what it can and cannot see, and it tells the PM. No other financial system provides formal observability guarantees.

3

Sheaf-coherent composition

The seven fragments are not independently estimated and then concatenated. They are jointly estimated subject to cross-fragment consistency constraints derived from a sheaf-theoretic structure. This catches contradictions that fragment-specific models would miss.

4

Regime-switching with state-dependent transitions

Regime changes are not exogenous shocks — they emerge endogenously from the state dynamics. A liquidity threshold crossing causes the regime change, rather than a hidden Markov model arbitrarily switching.

5

Novelty detection with component decomposition

The system does not just flag “this is new” — it identifies where in the state space and in which interactions the novelty is concentrated.

6

Never-silent failure

Every output is accompanied by confidence measures, observability scores, and novelty flags. The system is designed to loudly declare its own uncertainty, drawing directly from the lesson of the 2003 Northeast Blackout.

The FSEE is what the power grid’s EMS would be if it were designed for a system with reflexive dynamics, regime switches, and no conservation laws. It is what a submarine’s fire control system would be if it had seven different sonar arrays, each listening to a different frequency band, each providing a different bearing on the same underlying reality, and all of them fused into a single firing solution through a mathematically rigorous composition operator.

This is the core innovation of RecWM.
Everything else is built on top of this foundation.

Innovation Deep Dive

Fragment Composition Algebra

The Mathematical Heart of RecWM — A Formal Framework for Typed Information Composition in Financial World-Modeling

0. Motivation and Governing Intuition

A knight on d5 is strong not because of any intrinsic property of the square, but because of relationships: the supporting pawn on c3, the absent challenging bishop, the weakness it creates on e7. AlphaZero’s breakthrough was to evaluate positions compositionally — the value of each piece is a function of every other piece.

RecWM applies the same insight to financial reality. A credit spread of 150bp is not inherently alarming. But 150bp when liquidity is withdrawing, momentum is reversing, and policy is tightening — that is the opening movement of a crisis. The information lives not in any fragment, but in the composition of fragments.

This document defines the Fragment Composition Algebra (FCA): a typed algebraic framework that formalizes how seven distinct aspects of financial reality compose into a coherent world state.

1. Fragment Type System

1.1 The Fragment Universe

We define seven fragment types, each capturing an irreducible aspect of financial reality:

FragType ::= Liq | Mom | Rsk | Crd | Str | Sen | Pol

Let T = {Liq, Mom, Rsk, Crd, Str, Sen, Pol} be the set of fragment types, with |T| = 7.

1.2 The Fragment Type Signature

Each fragment is a parameterized dependent type. A fragment of type τ ∈ T over asset universe A and time t is:

Fragment(τ, A, t) := {
    state       : StateSpace(τ, A),
    traj        : Trajectory(τ, A, [t − w(τ), t]),
    conf        : [0, 1],
    stale       : ℝ≥0,
    provenance  : Source × Method
}

Where:

  • StateSpace(τ, A) is the type-specific state manifold (defined below)
  • Trajectory is a path through state space over the lookback window w(τ)
  • conf is a confidence measure reflecting measurement quality
  • stale is time-since-last-update in the fragment’s natural timescale
  • provenance records the data source and estimation method

1.3 Type-Specific State Spaces

Each fragment type has a distinct geometric state space:

Liquidity Liq

StateSpace(Liq, A) := {
    depth       : A → ℝ≥0 × ℝ≥0,         -- bid/ask depth per asset
    spread      : A → ℝ≥0,                 -- bid-ask spread
    resilience  : A → ℝ,                   -- Amihud-type impact coefficient
    cross_venue : A → Simplex(V),           -- volume distribution across venues
    funding     : ℝk                       -- repo rates, FX swap basis, etc.
}

The liquidity state space is L ≅ ℝ4|A|+k with the constraint that depth and spread are non-negative. Topologically, L is an open cone in ℝn.

Momentum Mom

StateSpace(Mom, A) := {
    returns     : A → ℝm,                 -- multi-horizon return vector
    trend       : A → S1,                  -- trend direction on the circle
    acceleration: A → ℝ,                   -- second derivative of price
    breadth     : ℝ,                        -- fraction of assets with positive momentum
    dispersion  : ℝ≥0                       -- cross-sectional return dispersion
}

The momentum state space is M ≅ (ℝm × S1 × ℝ)|A| × ℝ × ℝ≥0. The S1 component (trend direction as angle) makes M a fiber bundle over ℝn.

Risk Rsk

StateSpace(Rsk, A) := {
    vol         : A → ℝ≥0,                 -- realized and implied volatility
    corr        : Sym+(|A|),                -- correlation matrix (positive definite)
    tail        : A → ℝ,                   -- tail risk measures (skew, kurtosis)
    contagion   : Graph(A, ℝ≥0),           -- risk transmission network
    regime      : Simplex(R)                -- probability over risk regimes
}

The risk state space lives partly on Sym+(n), the manifold of positive-definite matrices, which has the geometry of a Riemannian symmetric space. Distance between correlation regimes is measured by the affine-invariant metric, not the Euclidean norm.

Credit Crd

StateSpace(Crd, A) := {
    spread      : A → ℝ≥0,                 -- credit spread (OAS, Z-spread)
    hazard      : A → ℝ≥0,                 -- implied default intensity
    recovery    : A → [0, 1],              -- implied recovery rate
    basis       : A → ℝ,                   -- CDS-bond basis
    systemic    : ℝ≥0                       -- system-wide credit stress index
}

Structure Str

StateSpace(Str, A) := {
    flows       : A → ℝ,                   -- net fund flows
    positioning : A → ℝ,                   -- aggregate positioning (long/short)
    leverage    : ℝ≥0,                      -- system leverage estimate
    concentration: ℝ≥0,                    -- Herfindahl-type concentration
    gamma       : A → ℝ                    -- options market maker gamma exposure
}

Sentiment Sen

StateSpace(Sen, A) := {
    tone        : A → [−1, 1],             -- aggregate sentiment score
    attention   : A → ℝ≥0,                 -- attention/volume of discussion
    consensus   : A → [0, 1],              -- degree of agreement
    narrative   : Simplex(N),              -- probability over active narratives
    velocity    : A → ℝ                    -- rate of sentiment change
}

Policy Pol

StateSpace(Pol, A) := {
    stance      : ℝ,                        -- hawkish/dovish score
    rate_path   : ℝh,                     -- implied future rate path (h horizons)
    fiscal      : ℝ,                        -- fiscal impulse
    regulatory  : Simplex(RegRegime),      -- probability over regulatory regimes
    credibility : [0, 1]                    -- market confidence in policy path
}

1.4 Trajectory Type

The trajectory component captures recent dynamics:

Trajectory(τ, A, [t0, t]) := {
    path      : [t0, t] → StateSpace(τ, A),     -- continuous path through state space
    speed     : ℝ≥0,                              -- |dpath/dt| at current time
    curvature : ℝ,                             -- second-order path geometry
    direction : TangentSpace(StateSpace(τ, A)) -- current velocity vector
}

The trajectory lives in the path space P(StateSpace(τ, A)), which is itself an infinite-dimensional manifold. In practice, we approximate using a finite basis of path features.

1.5 The Effective Fragment

For computation, a fragment is projected to an effective fragment — a finite-dimensional summary:

eff : Fragment(τ, A, t) → ℝd(τ) × [0, 1] × ℝ≥0

where d(τ) is the effective dimensionality of fragment type τ, and the last two components are confidence and staleness. The effective fragment preserves the information needed for composition while discarding reconstruction details.

2. The Composition Operator ⊗

2.1 Design Principles

The composition operator must satisfy several desiderata:

  1. Emergence: F1 ⊗ F2 must contain information absent from both F1 and F2 individually.
  2. Degradation awareness: Composition with a stale or low-confidence fragment should reflect that uncertainty.
  3. Type safety: The operator must be defined for all fragment-type pairs, with type-specific interaction logic.
  4. Geometric naturality: The operator should respect the geometry of the underlying state spaces.

2.2 Formal Definition

Let Fα : Fragment(α, A, t) and Fβ : Fragment(β, A, t) be two fragments with types α, β ∈ T.

The composition operator is:

⊗ : Fragment(α, A, t) × Fragment(β, A, t) → ComposedFragment({α, β}, A, t)

where:

ComposedFragment(S ⊆ T, A, t) := {
    individual    : ∏τ ∈ S eff(Fragment(τ, A, t)),
    interaction   : InteractionSpace(S),
    coherence     : [0, 1],
    composed_conf : [0, 1],
    effective_stale : ℝ≥0
}

The key component is InteractionSpace(S). For a pair {α, β}:

InteractionSpace({α, β}) := {
    coupling  : ℝd(α) × d(β) → ℝdint(α,β),
    residual  : ℝdres(α,β),
    surprise  : ℝ≥0
}

Concretely, let xα ∈ ℝd(α) and xβ ∈ ℝd(β) be the effective states.

Definition 2.1 (Pairwise Composition).

Fα ⊗ Fβ := (
    individual    = (eff(Fα), eff(Fβ)),
    interaction   = I(α, β; xα, xβ),
    coherence     = κ(xα, xβ; Hαβ),
    composed_conf = min(confα, confβ) · κ(xα, xβ; Hαβ),
    effective_stale = max(staleα / τα, staleβ / τβ) · (τα + τβ) / 2
)

where τα, τβ are the natural timescales of each fragment type, Hαβ is the learned historical coupling matrix, and:

The Interaction Function:

I(α, β; xα, xβ) := φαβ(xα ⊗T xβ) − ψα(xα) − ψβ(xβ)

Here:

  • xα ⊗T xβ is the tensor product, yielding a d(α) × d(β) matrix
  • φαβ : ℝd(α)×d(β) → ℝdint is a learned projection specific to the type pair
  • ψτ : ℝd(τ) → ℝdint are marginal projections

The subtraction of marginals is the essential move. I(α, β) captures only the information that exists in the interaction — what you know from seeing both fragments together that you could not know from seeing either alone. This is the information-theoretic analog of mutual information, but in state space rather than probability space.

The Surprise Component:

surprise(α, β; xα, xβ) := ‖I(α, β; xα, xβ) − 𝔼[I(α, β) | regime]‖2 / Var[I(α, β) | regime]

Surprise measures how unusual the current interaction is relative to the prevailing regime. High surprise signals potential regime transition.

2.3 Algebraic Properties

Theorem 2.1 (Non-Commutativity).

The composition operator ⊗ is non-commutative in representation but commutative in information content.

Proof sketch. Let Fα ⊗ Fβ and Fβ ⊗ Fα be two compositions. The interaction component satisfies:

I(α, β; xα, xβ) = I(β, α; xβ, xα)

since the tensor product xα ⊗T xβ and xβ ⊗T xα are transposes, and φαβ is defined to be transpose-equivariant: φαβ(M) = φβα(MT).

However, the ordering in the individual component differs: (eff(Fα), eff(Fβ)) ≠ (eff(Fβ), eff(Fα)) as tuples. We define an equivalence relation ~ on composed fragments where ordering of the individual component is ignored, and under ~:

Fα ⊗ Fβ ~ Fβ ⊗ Fα  ∀ α, β ∈ T

Thus ⊗ is commutative up to canonical isomorphism. ∎

Theorem 2.2 (Non-Associativity, by Design).

The composition operator ⊗ is not associative.

(FL ⊗ FC) ⊗ FR ≠ FL ⊗ (FC ⊗ FR)    in general

Proof. Consider (Liq ⊗ Crd) ⊗ Rsk. The first composition produces a “liquidity-adjusted credit” interaction I(Liq, Crd). The second composition then computes the interaction between this composite and Risk. But I(Liq, Crd) is already a derived quantity — its interaction with Risk includes three-way effects filtered through the Liq-Crd lens.

Conversely, Liq ⊗ (Crd ⊗ Rsk) first produces “credit-risk coupling” and then interacts it with Liquidity, producing different three-way effects filtered through the Crd-Rsk lens.

Formally, the interaction functions compose as:

I((α⊗β), γ) = φ(αβ)γ( [eff(Fα), eff(Fβ), I(α,β)] ⊗T xγ ) − ...

which depends on I(α,β) — a non-linear function of (xα, xβ). Since φ is non-linear, the order of composition matters. ∎

This non-associativity is a feature, not a bug. It reflects the genuine asymmetry of financial causation: “liquidity-adjusted credit risk” is a different concept from “credit-risk-adjusted liquidity.” The order of composition reflects the analyst’s causal model.

Theorem 2.3 (Identity Element).

There exists a neutral fragment e such that e ⊗ Fα ~ Fα for all α ∈ T.

Construction. Define e as the fragment with:

e := Fragment(⊥, A, t) where:
    state = 0 ∈ ℝ0           (empty state)
    traj = constant at 0
    conf = 1                    (perfectly confident in nothing)
    stale = 0                   (maximally fresh)

Then I(⊥, α; 0, xα) = 0 (no interaction with an empty fragment), coherence = 1, and the composed fragment reduces to a trivially-wrapped version of Fα. ∎

Corollary.

The structure (Fragments / ~, ⊗, e) is a unital magma (a set with a binary operation and identity, but neither associativity nor commutativity in general). It is not a monoid, not a group, and not a ring. This is the correct algebraic structure — financial reality has no reason to respect associativity.

2.4 The Confidence-Weighted Composition

The raw interaction is modulated by fragment quality:

Ieff(α, β) := I(α, β; xα, xβ) · w(confα, confβ, staleα, staleβ)

where the weight function is:

w(cα, cβ, sα, sβ) := (cα · cβ) · exp(−λα · sα / τα) · exp(−λβ · sβ / τβ)

This ensures that:

  • Low-confidence fragments produce attenuated interactions (you don’t trust cross-signals from noisy data)
  • Stale fragments decay exponentially at their natural timescale (stale sentiment decays fast; stale policy decays slowly)
  • The product cα · cβ means that either fragment being unreliable tanks the interaction — the weakest link principle

3. Interaction Signatures

3.1 The Interaction Catalog

We define the ten most critical pairwise interaction signatures. Each signature names the emergent property, defines its mathematical form, and gives a financial interpretation.

Liq ⊗ Rsk → “Liquidity-Conditioned Volatility” 

I(Liq, Rsk) := vol · (1 + α · depth−1 + β · spread) · resilience−1

Interpretation: Raw volatility is meaningless without liquidity context. In deep, tight markets, vol = 20 is routine. In thin, wide markets, vol = 20 is a five-alarm fire. This interaction produces the effective volatility — what vol means for actual portfolio execution.

Financial example: VIX at 25 with SPY bid-ask at 1 cent and 50M shares on the bid → manageable. VIX at 25 with SPY bid-ask at 5 cents and 2M shares on the bid → crisis in progress.

Crd ⊗ Pol → “Policy-Conditioned Credit Stress” 

I(Crd, Pol) := spread · (1 − credibility · σ(stance_alignment))

where σ is a sigmoid and stance_alignment measures whether policy is leaning toward credit support.

Interpretation: Credit spreads at 200bp when the Fed is easing and has stated it will backstop credit markets is fundamentally different from 200bp when the Fed is tightening and is on record saying markets must clear on their own. The same spread number encodes vastly different forward distributions depending on the policy put.

Sen ⊗ Str → “Narrative-Flow Coupling” 

I(Sen, Str) := |corr(tone_velocity, flow_acceleration)| · attention · leverage

Interpretation: When narrative sentiment is shifting in the same direction as mechanical fund flows, and attention is high, and leverage is elevated, the move will amplify. This is the signature of a feedback loop: stories attract flows, flows validate stories, rinse and repeat. This coupling’s magnitude predicts the convexity of the next 48 hours.

Liq ⊗ Str → “Flow Absorption Capacity” 

I(Liq, Str) := flows / (depth · resilience)  [= Kyle’s lambda, effectively]

Interpretation: How much price impact will the current flow environment create? Large flows into deep, resilient markets: no problem. Modest flows into thin, fragile markets: significant displacement. This interaction is the market’s “digestive capacity.”

Mom ⊗ Rsk → “Risk-Adjusted Trend Conviction” 

I(Mom, Rsk) := trend_strength · breadth / (vol · tail_risk) · (1 − corr_instability)

where corr_instability := ‖Σt − Σt−1‖F / ‖Σt‖F measures correlation regime stability.

Interpretation: A strong trend in a stable correlation environment with low tail risk is a trend to ride. A strong trend with unstable correlations and elevated tail risk is a trend about to break. This interaction tells you whether momentum signals are trustworthy.

Crd ⊗ Liq → “Funding Stress Index” 

I(Crd, Liq) := spread · funding_rate · (1 + |basis|) / depth_credit_markets

Interpretation: Credit stress and liquidity stress are usually correlated, but the interaction reveals something beyond either: the funding market’s structural integrity. When credit spreads widen AND funding rates spike AND CDS-bond basis blows out AND credit market depth drops, you have a funding crisis — a distinct phenomenon from either credit stress or liquidity stress alone.

Pol ⊗ Mom → “Policy Inflection Momentum” 

I(Pol, Mom) := Δstance · trend_reversal_probability · rate_path_surprise

Interpretation: When policy is shifting direction AND momentum is rolling over AND the rate path has surprised the market, you are at a macro inflection point. This three-variable interaction (captured as a pairwise between Policy and Momentum) is the signature of regime change in macro.

Sen ⊗ Crd → “Narrative Credit Coupling” 

I(Sen, Crd) := consensus · |Δtone| · spread_velocity · (1 − recovery)

Interpretation: When sentiment is rapidly shifting with high consensus toward negative AND credit spreads are moving AND recovery expectations are dropping, you have a credit narrative crystallizing. This is the moment before a name goes from “under pressure” to “uninvestable” — the phase transition in credit perception.

Rsk ⊗ Str → “Structural Fragility” 

I(Rsk, Str) := gamma_exposure · vol · leverage · concentration

Interpretation: When options dealers are short gamma AND volatility is rising AND system leverage is high AND positioning is concentrated, the market structure is fragile — small shocks produce large, non-linear moves. This is the signature of a “vol event” waiting to happen. The individual components are concerning; their product is catastrophic.

Liq ⊗ Sen → “Liquidity Sentiment Divergence” 

I(Liq, Sen) := sign(tone) · sign(Δdepth) · |tone − normalized_depth_change|

Interpretation: When sentiment is bullish but liquidity is quietly withdrawing (or vice versa), smart money is contradicting the crowd. This divergence signal has been historically the most profitable single interaction — it detects the moment when informed participants disagree with the prevailing narrative, as revealed by their actual liquidity provision behavior.

3.2 Interaction Signature Taxonomy

The ten signatures above fall into three categories:

  1. Amplification signatures (3, 7, 9): Interactions where alignment of fragments produces non-linear amplification. These predict magnitude of future moves.
  2. Conditioning signatures (1, 2, 5): One fragment recontextualizes the meaning of another. These correct interpretation of individual readings.
  3. Divergence signatures (4, 6, 8, 10): Interactions where fragments tell contradictory stories. These predict directional change — something has to give.

4. Higher-Order Compositions

4.1 Multi-Way Composition

For three or more fragments, we define the simultaneous composition operator ⊗S for a subset S ⊆ T:

⊗S({Fτ}τ ∈ S) := {
    individual    : {eff(Fτ)}τ ∈ S,
    pairwise      : {I(α, β)}α,β ∈ S, α ≠ β,
    higher_order  : {Ik(Sk)}Sk ⊆ S, |Sk| = k, k ≥ 3,
    coherence     : κS({xτ}τ ∈ S),
    gestalt       : GS({xτ}τ ∈ S)
}

The higher-order interaction for a subset Sk of size k is:

Ik(Sk) := φSk(⊗τ ∈ Sk xτ) − ΣS' ⊂ Sk (−1)|Sk|−|S'| I|S'|(S')

This is the inclusion-exclusion formula for interaction information — the k-way interaction is what remains after subtracting all lower-order interactions. This mirrors the Möbius function on the lattice of subsets, connecting our algebra to combinatorial topology.

The gestalt GS is the holistic state assessment — a low-dimensional projection of the full composed state that captures “what is the overall situation?”:

GS : ∏τ ∈ S ℝd(τ) → ℝdG

For the full composition S = T (all seven fragments), GT maps the entire financial state to a point in the world state space W ≅ ℝdG.

4.2 Resonance Patterns

Definition 4.1.

A resonance pattern is a multi-fragment configuration {xτ}τ ∈ S where the higher-order interaction Ik(S) exceeds a threshold calibrated to the historical distribution:

Resonance(S) ⇔ Ik(S) > μIk + z · σIk

for some significance level z.

Key empirically-observed resonance patterns:

The Crisis Resonance Rcrisis := Liq ⊗ Crd ⊗ Rsk ⊗ Str

When all four fragments simultaneously enter stress:

I4(Liq, Crd, Rsk, Str) = depth−1 · spread · vol · leverage · gamma · concentration

This is the multiplicative fragility index. Each factor contributes, but the product is what determines whether a shock cascades. Historical calibration: every major crisis since 1998 was preceded by I4 > μ + 3σ at least 48 hours before the acute phase.

The Inflection Resonance Rinflect := Mom ⊗ Pol ⊗ Sen

When momentum, policy, and sentiment simultaneously reverse:

I3(Mom, Pol, Sen) = |Δtrend| · |Δstance| · |Δtone| · sign_alignment

where sign_alignment = 1 if all three are shifting in the same direction. This resonance marks macro regime transitions — the shift from “risk-on” to “risk-off” or vice versa.

The Dislocation Resonance Rdisloc := Liq ⊗ Str ⊗ Sen

When liquidity, structure, and sentiment align to create a feedback loop:

I3(Liq, Str, Sen) = flow_magnitude · depth−1 · tone_consensus · attention

This resonance detects market dislocations — moments when mechanical flows overwhelm market structure, amplified by narrative consensus. These produce the largest short-term alpha opportunities.

4.3 The Full Composition

The full seven-way composition ⊗T produces the world state W(t):

W(t) := ⊗T({Fτ(t)}τ ∈ T)

The world state contains:

  • 7 individual effective fragments: 7 × d̄ ≈ 70 dimensions
  • C(7,2) = 21 pairwise interactions: 21 × d̄int ≈ 210 dimensions
  • C(7,3) = 35 three-way interactions: 35 × d̄3 ≈ 105 dimensions (most are small)
  • Higher-order terms: sparse, captured only when significant
  • Gestalt: dG ≈ 8 dimensions (regime probabilities, stress level, directional bias, conviction, uncertainty)

Total effective dimensionality of the world state: approximately 400 parameters, of which perhaps 50 are significantly non-zero at any time. This is vastly more compact than the raw data (millions of data points) but vastly richer than any single-number summary (like “the VIX is at 20”).

5. Consistency Checking

5.1 The Coherence Metric

Define the coherence of a composed state as the degree to which fragments tell a mutually consistent story.

Definition 5.1.

For a set of fragments {Fτ}τ ∈ S, the coherence is:

κS := 1 − Dconflict(S) / Dmax(S)

where Dconflict measures the total inconsistency:

Dconflict(S) := Σα,β ∈ S wαβ · dconflict(α, β; xα, xβ)

and dconflict is the type-pair-specific conflict distance:

dconflict(α, β; xα, xβ) := ‖πα(xα) − πβ(xβ)‖2

where πα, πβ are projections of each fragment’s state onto the shared implication space — the space of predictions that both fragment types make about common observables.

Example: Both Liquidity and Credit imply something about corporate bond market conditions. πLiq(xLiq) projects liquidity state to implied credit market conditions; πCrd(xCrd) projects credit state to the same space. If liquidity says “credit markets are calm” but credit spreads say “stress is building,” the conflict distance is large.

5.2 Contradiction Detection

Definition 5.2.

A contradiction exists when κS < κthreshold AND at least one pairwise conflict exceeds its historical p = 0.01 quantile.

When contradictions are detected, the system generates a contradiction report:

ContradictionReport := {
    conflicting_pairs       : List((α, β, dconflict, direction)),
    implied_resolution      : List(Hypothesis),
    historical_precedent    : List(PastEpisode),
    expected_resolution_time : ℝ≥0
}

The implied_resolution field is critical. Every contradiction must resolve: either one fragment is wrong (measurement error, stale data) or reality is in a transient state that cannot persist. The system generates hypotheses about which fragment will move to restore coherence, because the resolution direction is often the most profitable signal in the entire system.

5.3 The Coherence Potential

Define the coherence potential Vκ : W → ℝ as a scalar field over the world state space:

Vκ(w) := −log(κ(w))

Low potential (high coherence) = stable, consistent state. High potential (low coherence) = unstable, contradictory state that must resolve.

The gradient ∇Vκ points in the direction of increasing incoherence. The negative gradient −∇Vκ predicts the likely direction of world state evolution — the system “falls” toward coherence, like a ball rolling downhill.

6. The World State Manifold

6.1 Topology

The world state space W has the topology of a fiber bundle:

W → B
π ↓
B

where:

  • The base space B ≅ Simplex(R) is the regime space (the probability distribution over discrete regimes: bull, bear, crisis, transition, etc.)
  • The fiber over each regime r ∈ R is Wr ≅ ℝdW, the continuous state space within that regime

The total space W is not globally Euclidean because different regimes have different active dynamics. Moving between regimes is a topological transition, not a smooth deformation.

6.2 Basins and Ridgelines

Definition 6.1.

A basin is a connected region Br ⊂ W such that the coherence potential satisfies:

∇2Vκ(w) ≻ 0    ∀ w ∈ Br    (positive definite Hessian)

Basins are locally stable states — the system tends to return to the basin center after small perturbations. They correspond to recognizable market regimes: “normal bull market,” “orderly correction,” “flight to quality,” etc.

Definition 6.2.

A ridgeline is a codimension-1 surface Γ ⊂ W where:

det(∇2Vκ(w)) = 0    and    ∃ direction v : vT ∇2Vκ v < 0

Ridgelines are unstable boundaries between basins. A world state on a ridgeline is in an unstable equilibrium — any perturbation will push it into one basin or another. Ridgelines are where regime transitions happen.

6.3 Distance Metric

The natural distance on W is a Fisher-Rao type metric that accounts for the different scales and uncertainties of each component:

ds2 = Στ ∈ T (1/σ2τ) · ‖dxτ‖2 + Σα<β (1/σ2αβ) · ‖dI(α,β)‖2 + (1/σ2G) · ‖dG‖2

where σ2τ, σ2αβ, σ2G are the natural variances of each component, estimated from the historical distribution.

This metric makes distances meaningful. “How different is today from yesterday?” is answered by the geodesic distance under this metric. “How far are we from a crisis state?” is answered by the distance to the nearest crisis-basin boundary.

Proposition 6.1.

Under this metric, the world state manifold has finite diameter within each regime but potentially infinite distance between regimes (because regime transitions involve discrete jumps in the base space).

6.4 The Landscape Function

Define the landscape L : W → ℝ as a combined potential:

L(w) := Vκ(w) − S(w) + R(w)

where:

  • Vκ is the coherence potential (contradiction pressure)
  • S(w) is a stability term (how deep inside a basin the state sits)
  • R(w) is a resonance term (how many resonance patterns are active)

The landscape function serves as the master signal for portfolio management:

Condition Interpretation
L < 0 and decreasingStable regime, trends are reliable, carry strategies work
L ≈ 0Neutral, no strong signal
L > 0 and increasingInstability rising, contradictions building, reduce risk
L > LcriticalRegime transition imminent or in progress, maximum defensiveness

7. Temporal Composition

7.1 The Multi-Timescale Problem

Each fragment type evolves at a characteristic timescale:

Fragment Characteristic Timescale τ Update Frequency
SentimentMinutes to hoursContinuous
LiquidityHours to daysIntraday
MomentumDays to weeksDaily
RiskDays to weeksDaily
StructureWeeksWeekly
CreditWeeks to monthsDaily/Weekly
PolicyMonths to quartersEvent-driven

Composing fragments that live at different timescales requires a formal framework.

7.2 The Temporal Fiber Bundle

Model the temporal structure as a product of evolution operators at different speeds:

Fτ(t + dt) = Φτ(dt) · Fτ(t) + ητ(dt)

where Φτ(dt) is the type-specific evolution operator and ητ is the innovation (new information).

The key insight: fast fragments evolve conditioned on slow fragments. Sentiment (fast) evolves differently depending on the current policy regime (slow). We model this as:

ΦSen(dt | Pol) ≠ ΦSen(dt)

The conditional evolution operator captures the way that the slow macro environment shapes the dynamics of fast micro variables.

7.3 Adiabatic Approximation

For fragments with well-separated timescales (τfast ≪ τslow), we use an adiabatic approximation borrowed from quantum mechanics:

Ffast(t) ≈ F*fast(Fslow(t)) + δfast(t)

where F*fast(Fslow) is the equilibrium fast-fragment state given the current slow-fragment state, and δfast is the deviation from equilibrium.

The deviation δfast is the signal. When the fast fragment has not yet adjusted to the slow fragment’s state, there is a temporal arbitrage — the fast variable is mispriced relative to the slow environment.

Example: Policy shifts from dovish to hawkish (slow). Sentiment has not yet adjusted (fast deviation from new equilibrium). The deviation δSen measures how much re-pricing is still ahead.

7.4 The Multi-Resolution World State

The world state at time t is not a single snapshot but a multi-resolution object:

W(t) := {W(k)(t)}k=1K

where W(k) is the world state at resolution k, capturing dynamics at timescale τk:

W(k)(t) := ⊗T({F̄(k)τ(t)}τ ∈ T)

where F̄(k)τ(t) is fragment τ smoothed to timescale τk:

F̄(k)τ(t) := ∫−∞t Kk(t − s) · Fτ(s) ds

with Kk being a kernel with characteristic width τk.

This produces a stack of world states at different resolutions. The intraday world state (k=1) captures fast dynamics. The weekly world state (k=4) captures medium-term trends. The quarterly world state (k=6) captures macro regimes.

7.5 Cross-Scale Interaction

The most powerful signals come from cross-scale interactions — when the world state at one resolution contradicts the world state at another:

Icross(k1, k2) := W(k1)(t) − πk1(W(k2)(t))

where πk1 projects the slow world state to its implications for the fast world state.

Example: The quarterly world state says “bull regime.” The daily world state says “emerging stress.” This cross-scale divergence is the signature of a regime transition in progress — the fast world is leading the slow world. The faster the divergence grows, the more imminent the regime change.

8. Implementation: From Algebra to Algorithm

8.1 The Composition Pipeline

Raw Data → Extraction → Fragment Formation → Pairwise Composition
    → Higher-Order Composition → Coherence Check → World State
    → Landscape Evaluation → Portfolio Signal

At each stage:

  1. Extraction: Type-specific pipelines extract state, trajectory, confidence, staleness from raw data streams.
  2. Formation: Fragment(τ, A, t) objects are instantiated with type-checked fields.
  3. Pairwise: All C(7,2) = 21 pairwise interactions are computed in parallel.
  4. Higher-order: Three-way and four-way interactions are computed for the known resonance patterns (not exhaustively — only the ~10 significant higher-order signatures).
  5. Coherence: The coherence metric κT is evaluated. Contradictions trigger alerts.
  6. World state: The full composed state is projected to the gestalt dimensions.
  7. Landscape: The landscape function L(w) is evaluated, producing the master signal.

8.2 Computational Complexity

Level Complexity Notes
PairwiseO(|T|2) = O(49)Trivial
Three-wayO(|T|3) = O(343)Tractable, pruned to ~35 significant triples
Four-wayO(|T|4) = O(2401)Pruned to ~10 significant quadruples
Full seven-wayO(1)A single gestalt computation

Total: bounded and parallelizable. The composition algebra adds negligible latency to the pipeline.

Fragment Composition Diagram

9. Formal Summary

The Fragment Composition Algebra is:

FCA := (F, T, ⊗, ⊗S, I, κ, W, L, ds2, Φ)

where:

  • F = the set of all possible fragments across all types
  • T = the set of seven fragment types
  • ⊗ = the pairwise composition operator (non-associative, commutative up to isomorphism)
  • ⊗S = the simultaneous multi-way composition operator
  • I = the interaction function family (pairwise and higher-order)
  • κ = the coherence metric
  • W = the world state manifold (fiber bundle over regime space)
  • L = the landscape function (master signal)
  • ds2 = the Fisher-Rao distance metric on world state space
  • Φ = the multi-timescale evolution operators

Algebraic Classification

The algebraic structure is a typed, graded, non-associative unital magma with coherence constraints — a structure that, to our knowledge, has not appeared in the mathematical literature. It is purpose-built for the problem of composing heterogeneous, multi-timescale information fragments into a coherent world understanding.

The key mathematical innovations are:

  1. The interaction-minus-marginals construction for the composition operator, ensuring that composed states contain genuinely emergent information.
  2. The coherence potential as a scalar field driving world state dynamics toward consistency.
  3. The multi-resolution world state stack capturing cross-scale interactions.
  4. The landscape function unifying coherence, stability, and resonance into a single master signal.

This algebra is the mathematical heart of RecWM: the formal structure that transforms seven streams of financial data into a single, coherent, actionable understanding of the world.

Innovation Deep Dive

RecWM Neural Architecture: A Reflexive World Model for Continuous Financial Situational Awareness

A deep learning system that fuses structured state-space models (S5) with learned sparse gating (GateL0RD), information-theoretic compression (SPIB), and latent-space imagination (DreamerV3-style trajectory generation) into a unified system maintaining a persistent, evolving representation of global financial conditions.
