Abstract

RecWM (Reflexive Constructive World Model) introduces a novel architecture that processes seven typed information fragments --- Liquidity Momentum Risk Credit Structure Sentiment Policy --- through specialized encoders, composes them via a novel bilinear tensor interaction network, evolves the resulting state through a multi-timescale structured state-space core, and generates branching forward simulations for scenario analysis.

Unlike existing financial models that treat prediction as a static regression problem, RecWM treats the market as a partially observable, non-stationary environment and maintains an explicit latent belief state that updates continuously and generates explanations in natural language.

Full Neural Pipeline Architecture

1. Fragment Encoder Stack

Each of the seven fragment types occupies a distinct point in the space of data modalities, sampling frequencies, and information density. A single encoder architecture cannot efficiently handle tick-level order book snapshots (microsecond-scale, highly structured) and central bank speeches (event-driven, unstructured natural language). All encoders share a common interface: they accept their native data format and output a fixed-dimensional fragment embedding fk ∈ ℝdf where df = 256.

1.1 Liquidity Encoder ℰLiq

Input: Streaming order book snapshots at configurable frequency (100ms--1s), consisting of L levels of bid/ask prices and quantities, plus derived features: bid-ask spread, book imbalance, cumulative depth, funding rates, repo rates.

Architecture: Hierarchical Temporal Convolution + Cross-Level Attention.

The liquidity encoder must capture both the instantaneous microstructure (the shape of the order book at a single moment) and its temporal evolution (how that shape changes, which reveals hidden liquidity dynamics).

Stage 1 --- Level Encoder. Each price level ℓ = 1, ..., L is represented as a feature vector. A shared 1D causal convolution network with dilated kernels processes the temporal sequence of each level independently:

xℓ(t) = [priceℓ, qtyℓ, sideℓ, depthℓ, Δpriceℓ, Δqtyℓ]

hℓ(t) = CausalConv1D(xℓ(t-T:t); θlevel)

Kernel sizes: [3, 5, 7]    Dilation factors: [1, 2, 4]
Horizons: 300ms, 1s, 4s    Output dim: dlevel = 64

Stage 2 --- Cross-Level Attention. The L level embeddings at time t are assembled into a matrix H(t) ∈ ℝL × dlevel and processed by a single-head attention layer where levels attend to each other:

H̃(t) = Attention(H(t) WQ, H(t) WK, H(t) WV) + H(t)

Stage 3 --- Aggregation. The cross-level output is aggregated via learned weighted pooling (not mean pooling --- near-touch levels are more informative) and concatenated with derived features:

fLiq(t) = MLP( [ Σℓ αℓ h̃ℓ(t) ; xderived(t) ] ) ∈ ℝ256

where αℓ = softmax(w⊤ h̃ℓ(t)) are learned attention weights
Design Decision

Causal convolutions were chosen over Mamba-style SSM for the level encoder because order book data has very short-range dependencies (relevant history is typically <10 seconds) and convolutions are more efficient at this scale. Cross-level attention is essential because order book dynamics are fundamentally about the interaction between levels.

1.2 Sentiment Encoder ℰSent

Input: Streams of text from news wires (Reuters, Bloomberg), social media (Twitter/X financial accounts), research reports, and earnings call transcripts. Each text item arrives as a (timestamp, source, text) triple.

Architecture: Frozen LLM Embeddings + Temporal Aggregation Network.

A frozen pre-trained language model (distilled 1.3B parameter model optimized for financial text) is used as a feature extractor; only the temporal aggregation network is trained.

Stage 1 --- Text Embedding:

ei = FrozenLLM(texti) ∈ ℝ768

êi = Wproj ei ∈ ℝ128
(CLS token, projected down through learned linear layer)

Stage 2 --- Source-Aware Weighting:

wi = σ(vsource(i)⊤ êi + bsource(i))

Learned vector per source category: wire, social, research, transcript

Stage 3 --- Exponential Decay Aggregation:

fSent(t) = LayerNorm( Σi: ti ≤ t wi · exp(−(t − ti) / τsource(i)) · êi )

τsource(i) = learned decay time constant per source. Projected to ℝ256 via final MLP.
Design Decision

End-to-end fine-tuning of the language model was rejected for three reasons: (a) catastrophic forgetting of general language understanding, (b) computational cost of backpropagating through 1.3B parameters at every training step, and (c) the ability to swap the frozen LLM for a better one without retraining the aggregation network.

1.3 Policy Encoder ℰPol

Input: Heterogeneous mixture of structured data (rate decisions, dot plots, economic projections) and unstructured data (FOMC minutes, speeches, press conferences).

Architecture: Dual-Stream Fusion Network.

Structured Stream:

hstruct = Conv2D_Net(Ddot) ⊕ MLP(xrates) ⊕ MLP(xprojections)

⊕ = concatenation + fusion MLP. Output: ℝ128

Unstructured Stream:

hunstruct = Wpol_proj · FrozenLLM(textpolicy) ∈ ℝ128

Fusion (Gated Combination):

g = σ(wg⊤ [hstruct; hunstruct] + bg)

fPol(t) = MLP(g · hstruct + (1 − g) · hunstruct) ∈ ℝ256

1.4 Remaining Encoders (Compact Specification)

Momentum Encoder

Processes price return series across multiple assets and timeframes. Architecture: Multi-scale S4 operating at [1min, 15min, 1hr, 1day] resolutions with cross-asset attention. The S4 backbone handles long-range dependencies in momentum signals (trend persistence can last weeks). Output: ℝ256

Risk Encoder

Processes realized volatility, implied volatility surfaces, correlation matrices, and tail risk indicators. Architecture: Volatility surface treated as image (strike x expiry) processed by lightweight CNN; correlations via GNN where assets are nodes and magnitudes are edge weights. Fused via MLP. Output: ℝ256

Credit Encoder

Processes CDS spreads, bond spreads, credit indices (CDX, iTraxx), and credit event indicators. Architecture: 1D temporal convolution on spread time series with entity-level attention (different issuers' spreads attend to each other to capture contagion dynamics). Output: ℝ256

Structure Encoder

Processes dealer gamma exposure, options open interest by strike, ETF flows, futures positioning (COT data). Architecture: Gamma profile processed as piecewise linear function via 1D convolution, combined with flow/positioning data via MLP. Output: ℝ256

2. The Composition Network: Tensor Interaction Operator ⊗

The seven fragment embeddings {fk}k=17 must be composed into a unified world state embedding s ∈ ℝds where ds = 512. Simple concatenation (7 × 256 = 1792 → MLP → 512) would ignore fragment interactions. A full pairwise attention mechanism would be black-box. We design a Bilinear Tensor Interaction Network that is both expressive and interpretable.

2.1 Pairwise Bilinear Interactions

For each pair of fragments (i, j), we compute a bilinear interaction score and interaction vector:

αij = fi⊤ Wij(α) fj ∈ ℝ     (interaction strength)

vij = ReLU(fi⊤ Wij fj) ∈ ℝdv     (interaction vector)

The 3-way interaction tensor Wij ∈ ℝ256 × 256 × dv is factorized using low-rank decomposition with rank R = 16:

Wij = Σr=1R ar(ij) ⊗ br(ij) ⊗ cr(ij)

ar, br ∈ ℝ256    cr ∈ ℝdv with dv = 64

Reduction: 2562 × 64 ≈ 4.2M per pair → 16 × (256+256+64) = 9,216 per pair
C(7,2) = 21 unique pairs. Total: 21 × 9,216 ≈ 194K params

2.2 Interpretability via Interaction Strengths

The scalar interaction strengths αij form a 7 × 7 symmetric matrix A. This matrix is directly interpretable: a large αLiq,Cred means "the Liquidity-Credit interaction is currently strong," which a portfolio manager can immediately translate to "funding stress is propagating to credit markets."

s = Wout( ⨁k=17 fk + Σi<j softmax(αij) · vij ) ∈ ℝ512

First term preserves individual fragment information; second injects pairwise interactions weighted by current strength.
Alternative Considered: GNN Composition

A complete-graph GNN was considered but rejected: (a) message-passing iterations make interaction order implicit and harder to interpret, and (b) with only 7 nodes, the graph is too small for GNN inductive biases to provide meaningful benefit. The bilinear tensor approach provides explicit, named interactions with a single forward pass.

3. S5 State Evolution Core

The world state embedding s(t) from the composition network is the observation at time t. The core of RecWM is a continuous-time latent state z(t) ∈ ℝdz with dz = 1024 that evolves according to a structured state-space model.

3.1 Multi-Timescale S5 Formulation

The standard S5 state equation:

dz/dt = Az(t) + Bu(t)
y(t) = Cz(t) + Du(t)

A ∈ ℝdz × dz state transition, B ∈ ℝdz × ds input matrix, u(t) = s(t)

Critical innovation: Multi-scale state partitioning. The latent state is partitioned into M = 4 blocks:

z(t) = [zfast(t) ; zmedium(t) ; zslow(t) ; zglacial(t)]
BlockDimensionTime Constant τFinancial Interpretation
zfast2561--60 secondsMicrostructure, order flow
zmedium2561--60 minutesIntraday momentum, sentiment shifts
zslow2561--24 hoursDaily regime, macro response
zglacial2561--30 daysStructural positioning, policy regime

Implemented by constraining eigenvalues of the block-diagonal A matrix with HiPPO initialization:

A = diag(λ1, ..., λdz)

For block m with time constant range [τmmin, τmmax]:
Re(λi) ∈ [−1/τmmin, −1/τmmax]    for i ∈ block m

Fast dims decay quickly (forgetting old microstructure); glacial dims persist (structural memory). Imaginary parts unconstrained for oscillatory dynamics.

3.2 Discretization for Irregular Timesteps

ZOH discretization with variable step size Δt = tn+1 − tn:

Ān = exp(A Δt),    B̄n = A−1(Ān − I)B

Since A is diagonal, both operations are elementwise: O(dz) --- no matrix exponential required.

3.3 GateL0RD Integration: Learned State Update Gating

Not every incoming observation warrants a state update. During quiet markets, the data stream is dominated by noise. GateL0RD provides principled sparse state updates.

Gate Mechanism:

ĝ(t) = σ(Wg [z(t); s(t); Δt] + bg)

Hard concrete relaxation for training:
gi(t) = min(1, max(0, (log u − log(1−u) + log ĝi(t)) / β))
where u ~ Uniform(0,1), β is temperature. At inference: threshold at 0.5.

Gated State Update:

z(tn+1) = g(tn) ⊙ (Ān z(tn) + B̄n s(tn)) + (1 − g(tn)) ⊙ z(tn)

gi = 0: state dimension carried forward unchanged. gi = 1: full S5 update.

L0 Regularization:

Lgate = λg Σt Σi E[gi(t)]

Analytically tractable under hard concrete distribution. Target: 15--25% update rate in normal conditions.

4. SPIB Compression Layer

The latent state z(t) has 1024 dimensions. The Symmetric Predictability Information Bottleneck compresses the state to a minimal sufficient statistic for predicting future states.

4.1 SPIB Objective Function

A stochastic encoder qφ(c | z(t)) maps the full state to compressed representation c ∈ ℝ128:

LSPIB = −I(c; z(t+δ)) + βIB · I(c; z(t))

Symmetric version adds reverse direction: compressed future → predicts current

LSPIBpractical = E[ −log pψ(z(t+δ) | c) + βIB · DKL(qφ(c | z(t)) || r(c)) ]

r(c) = N(0, I) is the marginal prior

4.2 Adaptive Compression Rate

βIB(t) = βbase · σ(wβ⊤ z(t) + bβ) + βmin

βbase = 1.0, βmin = 0.01. Model learns to reduce compression (lower βIB) during high uncertainty / transition dynamics.

4.3 Multi-Horizon Compression

LSPIBmulti = Σδ ∈ {1,5,20,60,240} wδ · LSPIB(δ)

δ values ≈ 1s, 5s, 20s, 1min, 4min. Weights inversely proportional to prediction variance.

5. Imagination Engine: Latent-Space Forward Simulation

The Imagination Engine generates branching trajectories in the compressed latent space c for scenario analysis --- RecWM's analogue of DreamerV3's imagination, adapted for multi-branching, conditional financial scenario analysis.

5.1 Latent Dynamics Model

ĉ(t+1) = fθ(c(t), a(t))

a(t) ∈ ℝda = optional action/intervention embedding. Dynamics: 2-layer GRU (not full S5 --- rollouts are short, 50--200 steps).

5.2 Conditional Branching --- Scenario Vocabulary

Policy Interventions

Fed cuts 25bp, Fed cuts 50bp, Fed holds, Fed hikes 25bp

Market Shocks

VIX spike to X, credit spread widening by Ybp, liquidity withdrawal

Macro Events

Payroll miss by Zk, CPI surprise by W%

Each scenario condition is encoded as a learned embedding ascenario ∈ ℝ64.

5.3 Branching Tree Structure

Branchk = {ĉk(t+1), ĉk(t+2), ..., ĉk(t+H)}    for k = 1, ..., K

v̂k = Vψ(Branchk) ∈ ℝ     (trajectory value head: expected portfolio impact)

5.4 Branch Pruning

Surprise criterion: if a branched trajectory at step h falls within 2σ of the baseline trajectory's state at the same horizon ("normal evolution" envelope), branching from that node is stopped. This focuses computation on genuinely divergent scenarios.

5.5 Trajectory Uncertainty

ĉ(t+1), σ̂2(t+1) = fθ(c(t), a(t))

Uncertainty grows with horizon. Trajectory terminated when predicted σ exceeds usefulness threshold.

6. Regime Detection Head

Monitors the compressed latent state c(t) for regime transition signatures. Operates on the learned representation (not raw data), providing cleaner and earlier signals.

6.1 Architecture: Latent-Space BOCPD

Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection adapted to operate in the learned latent space. SPIB compression strips away noise, making genuine regime shifts much more visible.

Run Length Distribution:
p(rt | c(1:t)) ∝ p(c(t) | rt, c(t−rt:t−1)) · p(rt | rt−1)

log p(c(t) | rt) ≈ −||c(t) − μrt(t)||2 / (2σrt2(t))

μ and σ from a small LSTM running for rt steps within current regime

6.2 Output Specification

RegimeAssessment {
  current_regime: Categorical // {calm, trending, volatile, crisis, transition}
  regime_probability: Float[5] // probability of each regime
  changepoint_probability: Float // prob of changepoint NOW
  estimated_transition_speed: Float // sudden vs. gradual
  regime_duration: Float // time since last changepoint
  next_regime_prediction: Categorical // most likely next regime
}

6.3 Training the Regime Head

  1. Supervised labels from historical regime annotations (a financial historian labels historical periods as calm/trending/volatile/crisis)
  2. Self-supervised signal from BOCPD changepoint probability (should spike when latent state undergoes rapid change)
  3. Auxiliary loss encouraging consistency with imagination engine's trajectory divergence (divergent trajectories should correlate with high transition probability)

7. Explanation Head: Latent-to-Language Translation

Translates the model's internal assessments into natural language. This is a first-class architectural component trained alongside the rest of the model, not a post-hoc explainability technique.

7.1 Conditional Language Model with Attribution

Input: Compressed state c(t), regime assessment, fragment interaction matrix A, optional query.
Architecture: Small decoder-only transformer (6 layers, 8 heads, dmodel = 512, ~50M params).

Latent state injected via cross-attention to "state tokens":

  1. Fragment contributions: Each fk projected to a "fragment token" --- 7 tokens for individual fragment information
  2. Interaction tokens: Top-k strongest interactions from matrix A, converted via interaction-specific projection
  3. Regime token: Regime assessment embedded as a single token
  4. Temporal context tokens: Rate-of-change Δc / Δt embedded for temporal context

7.2 Attribution Mechanism

Cross-attention weights provide natural attribution. Example output:

"Elevated risk assessment driven by:
 [Liquidity-Credit interaction: 34%] Funding stress propagating to credit
 [Structure fragment: 28%] Dealer gamma flipping negative at 5400
 [Policy fragment: 22%] Hawkish repricing after last FOMC
 [Momentum fragment: 16%] Bearish momentum divergence on 4H timeframe

7.3 Training the Explanation Head

Trained on (latent state, human-written assessment) pairs from:

  1. Historical market commentary from sell-side research, aligned to model's latent states at the same timestamps
  2. Synthetic explanations generated by large language model given raw fragment data + model outputs, filtered by human review
  3. Reinforcement from portfolio managers who rate explanations on 1-5 scale for accuracy, relevance, and actionability

Loss function:

Lexplain = LCE(generated, target) + λattr · Lattr_consistency

Lattr_consistency penalizes explanations whose attention-derived attributions contradict actual fragment contributions.

8. Training Architecture

8.1 Training Pipeline --- Four Phases

1

Fragment Encoder Pre-training

2 weeks | 8× A100 GPUs

Each fragment encoder trained independently via self-supervised next-step prediction:

Lencoder(k) = ||fk(t+1) − f̂k(t+1)||2
Forces representations where temporal dynamics are smooth and predictable.
2

Composition + S5 Core Training

4 weeks | 16× A100 GPUs

Composition network and S5 core trained jointly. Primary objective: multi-step state prediction.

Lcore = Σδ ∈ {1,5,20,60,240} wδ · ||z(t+δ) − ẑ(t+δ)||2 + LSPIBmulti + Lgate
3

Imagination Engine Training

2 weeks | 16× A100 GPUs

Dynamics model and trajectory value head trained on the learned latent space.

Limagine = Σh=1H γh · ||c(t+h) − ĉ(t+h)||2 + λunc · Lcalibration
γ = 0.99 discount. Lcalibration ensures predicted σ matches actual prediction error.
4

Head Training + End-to-End Fine-tuning

3 weeks | 32× A100 GPUs

Regime and explanation heads trained, then full system fine-tuned end-to-end.

Ltotal = Lcore + λ1Limagine + λ2Lregime + λ3Lexplain + λ4Lportfolio

8.2 Loss Function Details

Regime Detection Loss:

Lregime = −Σr yr log p̂r + λcp · BCE(ycp, p̂cp)

Portfolio Loss (Optional Reinforcement):

Lportfolio = −E[ Σt Rt · log πθ(at | c(t)) ]

Rt = realized Sharpe ratio. πθ = implied action distribution from trajectory value head rankings.

8.3 Data Requirements

Data SourceFrequencyHistoryApprox. Size
Order book snapshots (top 20 levels)100ms3 years~50 TB
Price/volume bars1-second10 years~500 GB
News wire textEvent-driven10 years~200 GB
Social media financial textStreaming5 years~1 TB
Options surfaces (strike x expiry)1-minute5 years~2 TB
CDS/bond spreads1-second10 years~100 GB

Total raw data: approximately 54 TB. After preprocessing and feature extraction: approximately 8 TB.

9. Compute and Inference Architecture

9.1 Latency Budget

ComponentLatency BudgetNotes
Fragment Encoding (all 7 parallel)15msParallelized across 7 encoder instances
Composition Network5msSingle forward pass, bilinear ops
Gate Computation3msSmall MLP on concatenated state+obs
S5 State Update2msDiagonal A: elementwise ops only
SPIB Compression5msEncoder forward pass
Regime Detection5msSmall LSTM + classifier
Total Core Pipeline35msWell within 100ms budget
Imagination (if triggered)40ms50-step rollout with 5 branches
Explanation (if requested)50msAutoregressive generation, ~100 tokens

9.2 Streaming Inference Architecture

Fragment Ingest Workers (7 processes)

One per fragment type. Each worker subscribes to its data stream, runs the fragment encoder, and publishes the fragment embedding to a shared buffer.

Composition + Core Worker (1 process, GPU)

Reads 7 fragment embeddings from shared buffer, runs composition, gate computation, S5 update, and SPIB compression. Maintains persistent latent state in GPU memory.

Regime Monitor (1 process, GPU)

Continuously monitors compressed state for regime transition signatures. Publishes alerts on a dedicated channel.

Imagination Worker (1 process, GPU)

Triggered by regime monitor or on a timer. Runs branching forward simulations and publishes scenario assessments.

Explanation Worker (1 process, GPU)

Triggered on-demand or by significant state changes. Generates natural language explanations.

State Manager

Handles checkpointing (every 60s), recovery (load + replay at 10x), and versioning (audit: "what did the model believe at 14:32:07 UTC?").

9.3 Hardware Specification

Inference Deployment (per market/asset class)

2× NVIDIA A10G GPUs (24GB each):
GPU 1: Fragment encoders + Composition + S5 Core + SPIB + Regime Detection
GPU 2: Imagination Engine + Explanation Head
64GB system RAM for state buffering and data queues. NVMe storage for checkpoints.

Total for global coverage (5 markets: US Equities, US Rates, FX G10, European Credit, Asia EM): 10× A10G GPUs. Estimated cloud cost: $15k--20k/month (AWS on-demand).

9.4 Fault Tolerance and Recovery

  1. State Checkpoint Protocol: Every 60s serialize full latent state, compressed state, regime history, gate stats to NVMe. Versioned, retained 7 days. On restart: load checkpoint, replay at 10x, then switch to real-time.
  2. Graceful Degradation: Failed fragment encoder receives zero vector and interaction matrix is reweighted. Failed imagination worker: real-time assessment continues without scenarios. Failed explanation worker: raw numeric assessments still available.

9.5 Model Versioning and Online Updates

  1. Shadow Mode: New model version runs in parallel on separate GPU, outputs compared against production for N hours.
  2. Gradual Cutover: If validated, traffic shifts 10% → 25% → 50% → 100% with automatic rollback if anomaly metrics degrade.
  3. Fragment Encoder Hot-Swap: Individual encoders can be updated independently (e.g., better Sentiment encoder) without retraining composition network, because the encoder interface (ℝ256) is fixed.

10.3 What Makes This Architecture Novel

1. Selective State Evolution

GateL0RD applied to multi-timescale S5 creates a model that simultaneously maintains fast-decaying microstructure memory and glacial structural memory, selectively updating only the relevant timescale for each observation. No existing architecture does this.

2. Adaptive Information Bottleneck

SPIB compression rate conditioned on the latent state itself creates a feedback loop: more aggressive compression in calm regimes (noise-dominated), opening up during transitions (previously irrelevant information becomes critical). Learned attention to relevance at the information-theoretic level.

3. Typed Fragment Composition with Interpretable Interactions

The bilinear tensor interaction network provides named, measurable interaction strengths between fragment types. A portfolio manager can inspect the 7×7 matrix and immediately understand which cross-domain dynamics drive the current assessment.

4. Imagination Grounded in Compressed State Space

Imagining trajectories in SPIB-compressed space (128d) rather than full latent space (1024d) means the imagination engine operates only on predictively relevant information --- both more efficient and more accurate.

5. End-to-End Trainability with Modular Deployment

Despite complex multi-component architecture, the entire system is end-to-end differentiable (straight-through estimators for GateL0RD gates). Yet individual components can be deployed, monitored, and updated independently.

Architectural Significance

This architecture is, to our knowledge, the first to combine structured state-space models, learned sparse gating, information-theoretic compression, and latent-space imagination into a single system designed for continuous, real-time operation on multi-modal financial data. It is not a forecasting model --- it is a world model: a persistent, evolving representation of the financial environment that can answer counterfactual questions, detect regime shifts before they manifest in raw data, and explain its assessments in the language of the portfolio managers who use it.

Innovation Deep Dive

24/7 Awareness Engine

Part of the RecWM Ten-Layer Innovation Stack

Overview

The Continuous Awareness Engine (CAE) is the always-on infrastructure layer of RecWM that maintains 24/7 situational awareness of global financial markets. It is modeled after the most battle-tested monitoring paradigms on Earth: power grid SCADA/EMS, NASA Mission Control, submarine watch standing, ICU patient monitoring, and F1 pit wall telemetry.

The core design principle: the world model is never allowed to go stale. Like a submarine's sonar picture that persists across watch changes, RecWM's state estimation of every fragment domain — liquidity, credit, momentum, volatility, macro — is continuously updated, versioned, and handed off across global market sessions without gap or discontinuity.

The fund using RecWM is too small to move markets. It is a pure reader — its edge comes from reading the world faster and more coherently than anyone else. The CAE exists to eliminate the PM's deepest anxiety: "What am I missing right now?"

1. The Console Architecture

Design Philosophy

NASA's Mission Control assigns each flight controller a specific subsystem domain. The EECOM watches power, thermal, and life support. GNC watches guidance, navigation, and control. CAPCOM is the sole voice to the crew. Each controller has full authority over their domain and escalates cross-domain issues to the Flight Director.

RecWM maps this model to financial fragment domains. Each "console" is an autonomous monitoring agent that owns a coherent slice of the financial world. Consoles run independently but share state through the central World Model Bus.

Console Definitions

LIQUIDITY Console (analog: EECOM — life support)

Liquidity is the oxygen of markets. When it fails, everything dies. EECOM's job was to keep the crew alive; the LIQUIDITY console's job is to detect when markets are suffocating.

Monitors:

  • Bid-ask spreads across all portfolio-relevant instruments (equities, options, futures, credit)
  • Market depth (Level 2/Level 3 order book data where available)
  • Repo market rates (SOFR, tri-party repo volumes, fails-to-deliver)
  • FX swap basis (USD funding stress indicator)
  • ETF premium/discount to NAV (canary for underlying illiquidity)
  • Volume profiles vs. historical norms (rolling 20-day, 60-day, 252-day percentiles)
  • Dark pool activity ratios
  • Dealer inventory proxies (primary dealer position data, published weekly, interpolated daily)

Escalation Thresholds:

Advisory: Bid-ask spreads widen beyond 75th percentile for asset class. Volume drops below 25th percentile.
Caution: Spreads beyond 90th percentile. Repo rate spikes > 2 standard deviations above trailing mean. ETF discounts appear in liquid names.
Warning: Multiple correlated spread-widening events across asset classes. Fails-to-deliver spike. FX swap basis blows out.
Critical: Liquidity conditions resemble a dated crisis episode (2008 Lehman week, March 2020 Treasury dislocation, March 2023 SVB weekend). This is detected by a learned crisis-similarity metric, not a static threshold.

Go/No-Go Criteria:

Go (Green): Portfolio can be fully liquidated within 3 days at < 50bps cost.
Conditional Go (Yellow): Liquidation feasible but cost estimate exceeds 50bps or time exceeds 5 days.
No-Go (Red): Liquidation cost estimate exceeds 200bps or time horizon exceeds 10 days. PM must review position sizing immediately.

RISK Console (analog: GNC — guidance, navigation, control)

GNC keeps the spacecraft on course. The RISK console keeps the portfolio within its risk envelope and detects when the risk landscape is shifting underneath positions.

Monitors:

  • Portfolio VaR (1-day, 10-day; 95th and 99th percentile; parametric, historical, Monte Carlo)
  • Factor exposures: market beta, sector, style (value/momentum/quality/size), rates duration, credit spread duration
  • Greeks for all options positions (delta, gamma, vega, theta, rho) — aggregated to portfolio level
  • Correlation matrix stability (eigenvalue tracking of the covariance matrix; a sudden shift in the top eigenvalues signals regime change)
  • Tail risk metrics: Expected Shortfall, maximum drawdown trajectory, Omega ratio
  • Concentration metrics: Herfindahl index by position, sector, geography, factor
  • Margin utilization and distance to margin call

Escalation Thresholds:

Advisory: Any single factor exposure drifts beyond target band. Correlation structure shifts (first eigenvalue explains > 5% more variance than trailing 60-day average).
Caution: Portfolio VaR exceeds soft limit (80% of hard limit). Multiple factor exposures outside target. Realized volatility diverges from implied by > 2 sigma.
Warning: VaR approaches hard limit. Margin utilization > 70%. Correlation breakdown detected (eigenvalue structure no longer resembles any historical regime in the library).
Critical: VaR breach. Margin call imminent. Unhedged tail exposure detected.

Go/No-Go Criteria:

Go: All risk metrics within target bands. Hedges performing as modeled.
Conditional Go: Minor drift in 1–2 metrics. Hedges slightly underperforming. Rebalance recommended within 24 hours.
No-Go: Hard limit breach or imminent breach. Immediate PM review and potential position reduction required.

CREDIT Console (analog: TELMU — telemetry)

TELMU monitored data integrity and spacecraft health signals. The CREDIT console monitors the health signals of counterparties, issuers, and the credit market ecosystem.

Monitors:

  • CDS spreads for all issuers in portfolio and their counterparties
  • Credit index levels (CDX IG, CDX HY, iTraxx)
  • Rating agency actions (watch, outlook, upgrade, downgrade) — real-time feed
  • Earnings surprise and guidance revision for portfolio names
  • Covenant compliance signals (debt/EBITDA ratios, interest coverage derived from quarterly filings)
  • Bank funding stress indicators (LIBOR-OIS successor spreads, commercial paper rates)
  • Sovereign credit signals for relevant geographies

Escalation Thresholds:

Advisory: CDS spread widens > 1σ for any portfolio name. Negative outlook change from one agency.
Caution: CDS spread widens > 2σ. Downgrade from one agency. Earnings miss > 2 standard deviations.
Warning: Multi-notch downgrade or downgrade from two agencies. CDS spread implies distress (> 500bps for IG-rated name). Covenant breach signal.
Critical: Default event. Cross-default trigger. Recovery rate estimate drops below assumption in position sizing model.

MOMENTUM Console (analog: FIDO — flight dynamics)

FIDO tracked trajectory. The MOMENTUM console tracks the trajectory of prices, flows, and positioning to detect when trends are forming, accelerating, or exhausting.

Monitors:

  • Price momentum signals across multiple timeframes (1-day, 5-day, 21-day, 63-day, 252-day)
  • Fund flow data (ETF flows, mutual fund flows — daily/weekly)
  • CFTC Commitment of Traders positioning (weekly, interpolated daily)
  • Short interest data
  • Options positioning (put/call ratios, skew, term structure of implied volatility)
  • Breadth indicators (advance/decline, new highs/lows, percent above moving averages)
  • Cross-asset momentum divergences (equity momentum vs. credit momentum for same issuer)

Escalation Thresholds:

Advisory: Momentum signal flips sign on any timeframe for a top-10 portfolio position.
Caution: Momentum divergence between price and flow (price rising on outflows, or vice versa). Positioning extreme (> 90th percentile long or short per CFTC data).
Warning: Multi-timeframe momentum reversal for portfolio-relevant names. Breadth divergence from index (index at highs but breadth deteriorating).
Critical: Momentum crash signal (multiple correlated momentum reversals resembling historical momentum crash episodes: August 2007, March 2009 reversal).

MACRO Console (analog: Flight Director — integrates all domains)

The Flight Director integrates information from all consoles to make Go/No-Go calls. The MACRO console integrates economic data, central bank signals, and geopolitical context to frame the environment in which all other consoles operate.

Monitors:

  • Economic data releases vs. consensus expectations (NFP, CPI, PMI, GDP, retail sales, housing)
  • Central bank communication (Fed, ECB, BOJ, PBOC, BOE) — statement analysis, dot plot tracking, forward guidance parsing
  • Yield curve shape and dynamics (2s10s, 3m10y, real rates, breakeven inflation)
  • Geopolitical event tracking (elections, trade policy, sanctions, military conflicts)
  • Fiscal policy changes (tax law, spending bills, regulatory shifts)
  • Cross-market regime indicators (risk-on/risk-off, reflation/deflation, growth/recession probability models)

Escalation Thresholds:

Advisory: Economic surprise index moves > 1σ. Central bank communication tone shifts detected by NLP.
Caution: Yield curve inversion deepens or un-inverts rapidly. Recession probability model crosses 30%.
Warning: Policy shock (unexpected rate decision, emergency meeting, capital controls). Geopolitical event with market-moving potential.
Critical: Regime change detected — the MACRO console believes the macroeconomic environment has fundamentally shifted and all other console thresholds need recalibration.

Cross-Console Communication

All consoles publish their state to the World Model Bus every update cycle. Any console can read any other console's state. Cross-domain escalation follows a defined protocol:

1
The originating console publishes an alert with a recommended severity level.
2
If the alert has implications for another console's domain, it tags the destination console.
3
The destination console independently evaluates whether the cross-domain signal changes its own assessment.
4
If two or more consoles simultaneously escalate to Warning or above, the system triggers an automatic "Flight Director Review" — a synthesized multi-domain assessment delivered to the PM.

2. The Watch Schedule

Global Market Session Map

The 24-hour watch cycle is depicted in the console architecture diagram above, showing Asia, Europe, US, and Overnight watches with their overlaps and update cadences. Below are the detailed watch definitions.

Watch Definitions

Asia Watch (00:00–08:00 UTC / 8:00 PM–4:00 AM ET)

  • Primary focus: JPY, CNY, AUD crosses. Nikkei, Hang Seng, Shanghai Composite. JGB yields. PBOC fixings.
  • Secondary focus: Commodity futures (metals open in Asia), overnight UST futures.
  • Update cadence: State estimation every 30 seconds during active trading. Every 5 minutes during pre/post market.
  • Staffing model: Fully automated. No human on console. Escalation alerts to the PM's phone via push notification if Warning or above.

Europe Watch (07:00–15:30 UTC / 3:00 AM–11:30 AM ET)

  • Primary focus: EUR, GBP, CHF crosses. Euro Stoxx, FTSE, DAX. Gilt and Bund yields. ECB/BOE communications.
  • Secondary focus: US equity futures, UST futures, crude oil.
  • Update cadence: State estimation every 15 seconds during active trading.
  • Staffing model: Automated with PM typically online from ~07:00 ET (12:00 UTC). Morning Briefing Protocol fires at PM's configured wake time.

US Watch (13:30–22:00 UTC / 9:30 AM–6:00 PM ET)

  • Primary focus: All US equities, options, futures. UST cash and futures. Investment-grade and high-yield credit. Fed communications.
  • Secondary focus: All global markets still open during overlap.
  • Update cadence: State estimation every 5 seconds during regular trading hours. Tick-level processing for portfolio positions.
  • Staffing model: PM is active. System operates in full interactive mode — PM can query, drill down, request scenarios.

Overnight/Weekend Watch (22:00–00:00 UTC + weekends)

  • Primary focus: Crypto markets (24/7), FX (Sunday 5 PM ET open), CME Globex futures.
  • Secondary focus: Breaking news, geopolitical events, natural disasters, elections in any timezone.
  • Update cadence: State estimation every 5 minutes. News scan every 60 seconds.
  • Staffing model: Fully automated. Reduced alarm thresholds (only Warning and Critical reach the PM). Advisory and Caution accumulate for Morning Briefing.

Watch Handoff Protocol

Every watch transition follows a structured handoff inspired by submarine watch relief and ICU bedside handoff. The outgoing watch produces a Watch Summary Package consumed by the incoming watch:

Watch Summary Package Contents
1
State Snapshot: Full world model state at handoff time, versioned and checksummed.
2
Active Alerts: All unresolved alerts with current severity, time since first trigger, trend direction (escalating/stable/de-escalating).
3
Contact Log: Every significant market event during the watch, with timestamp and assessed impact. (Analogous to submarine's contact tracking — every "contact" is a market event that was detected, classified, and tracked.)
4
Anomalies Without Explanation: Events detected that the system could not attribute to a known cause. These are flagged for human review. The outgoing watch is not permitted to dismiss unexplained anomalies.
5
Pending Events: Known upcoming events in the next watch's window (economic releases, earnings, central bank decisions, option expirations).
6
Degraded Systems: Any data feeds currently down or degraded, with estimated confidence impact.
7
Standing Orders: Any PM-specified instructions that persist across watches (e.g., "alert me immediately if AAPL drops below $180" or "suppress VIX alerts until after FOMC").
Acknowledgment Protocol

The incoming watch must acknowledge the handoff by:

1
Loading the state snapshot and verifying continuity with its own sensors.
2
Confirming all active alerts are reflected in its monitoring.
3
Flagging any discrepancy between the outgoing watch's state and its own initial assessment.

Handoff integrity is logged and auditable. A failed handoff (state discrepancy > tolerance threshold) triggers a system alert.

3. The Data Ingestion Pipeline

Multi-Frequency Data Fusion Architecture

The data ingestion pipeline fuses information across five frequency tiers, from microsecond tick data to weekly alternative data. Each source flows through its own normalizer/processor before entering the central State Estimator, which produces a unified World Model state consumed by all five consoles.

Tick Data
Microsecond
Normalizer → 1s OHLCV
Market Data
Second-level
Normalizer → SE
News & Text
Minute-level
NLP Pipeline → SE
Econ Releases
Event-driven
Surprise Calc → SE
Alt Data
Daily/Weekly
Batch Proc → SE
↓
State Estimator
5-second heartbeat → World Model → Consoles → Alarm Manager → PM
Persistence
Versioned State Snapshots + Immutable Event Log

Tier 1: Tick Data (Microsecond Cadence)

  • Sources: Exchange direct feeds (for portfolio positions), consolidated tape (SIP) for broad market.
  • Processing: Tick data is aggregated into 1-second OHLCV bars for state estimation. Raw ticks are retained for 90 days for replay. Beyond 90 days, only 1-second bars are kept.
  • Latency budget: Tick receipt to state estimator input: < 50ms. This is not HFT — we are reading, not racing. 50ms is generous and allows for robust normalization.
  • Volume estimate: ~500,000 ticks/second during peak US equity hours across monitored universe (~2,000 instruments).

Tier 2: Market Data (Second-Level Cadence)

  • Sources: Bloomberg B-PIPE or equivalent. Covers equities, fixed income (UST, IG, HY), FX, commodities, derivatives (options chains, futures curves).
  • Processing: Every incoming quote or trade updates the relevant instrument's state in the World Model. Derived quantities (implied volatility, yield curve points, credit spreads) are recalculated on every material update.
  • Latency budget: Source to World Model update: < 500ms.

Tier 3: News and Text (Minute-Level Cadence)

  • Sources: Newswire feeds (Reuters, Bloomberg, Dow Jones), SEC EDGAR filings (8-K, 10-Q, 10-K), social media financial feeds (filtered and scored), central bank publication feeds.
  • Processing: NLP pipeline classifies each item by: relevance to portfolio (binary + score), sentiment (positive/negative/neutral + confidence), entity extraction (which companies, sectors, countries), novelty (is this genuinely new information or a rehash).
  • Latency budget: Publication to classification: < 60 seconds. Publication to World Model impact assessment: < 120 seconds.
Critical Design Point

News is the most dangerous input for false alarms. The NLP pipeline must have a high precision threshold — it is better to miss a marginal story than to cry wolf. Novelty detection is essential: the same story reported by 50 outlets should generate one signal, not 50.

Tier 4: Economic Releases (Event-Driven)

  • Sources: Government statistical agencies (BLS, BEA, Census), central banks (Fed, ECB, BOJ, BOE, PBOC), pre-scheduled release calendar.
  • Processing: The system maintains a consensus expectation (from survey data) and a RecWM internal forecast for every release. On publication, it computes: surprise = (actual − consensus), model error = (actual − RecWM forecast). Both feed into the State Estimator.
  • Latency budget: Release publication to World Model update: < 5 seconds. This is time-critical because the market moves immediately on major releases (NFP, CPI, FOMC).
Special Handling

Embargo releases must not be processed early. The system clock is NTP-synchronized and release processing begins only at the scheduled time.

Tier 5: Alternative Data (Daily/Weekly/Irregular)

  • Sources: Satellite imagery (parking lots, shipping ports, oil storage), credit card transaction aggregates, web traffic data, job postings, patent filings, supply chain data.
  • Processing: Batch-processed on arrival. Each alternative data source has a source-specific model that translates raw data into a signal relevant to one or more fragment domains. Signals are expressed as deviations from expected values, with confidence intervals.
  • Latency budget: Arrival to signal integration: < 1 hour. This data is inherently slow-moving; the value is in the signal, not the speed.

Data Fusion: The State Estimator

The State Estimator is the heart of the CAE. It is directly analogous to the State Estimator in power grid EMS — the module that takes thousands of raw sensor readings and produces a single coherent estimate of the grid's state.

Design Principles
1
Frequency normalization: High-frequency data (ticks) is downsampled to the State Estimator's update cycle. Low-frequency data (alt data) is interpolated using a decay model — the signal's influence diminishes as it ages, but it never drops to zero until replaced by a newer observation.
2
Conflict resolution: When two data sources disagree (e.g., credit card data suggests strong retail spending but stock price of a retailer is declining), the system does not resolve the conflict. It flags it as a "divergence" and surfaces it to the relevant console. Human judgment resolves conflicts.
3
Missing data imputation: When a data source is absent (weekend, holiday, feed outage), the State Estimator uses the last known value with a confidence penalty that grows with time. The confidence penalty follows a source-specific decay curve (e.g., equity prices go stale faster than quarterly earnings data).
4
Update cycle: The State Estimator runs on a 5-second heartbeat during active market hours. Every 5 seconds, it ingests all data received since the last cycle, updates the World Model, and publishes the new state to all consoles.

4. The Alarm Philosophy

The Core Problem

The alarm fatigue literature is unambiguous: when false positive rates reach 85–99% (as documented in ICU monitoring), clinicians begin ignoring all alarms, including real ones. Three Mile Island's control room had over 100 alarms sounding simultaneously during the crisis — operators could not distinguish the critical from the trivial.

RecWM's alarm system is designed to be the opposite: fewer, smarter, context-aware alarms that the PM trusts enough to act on immediately.

Alarm Taxonomy

Level Name PM Experience Delivery Expected Frequency
0 Advisory Logged, visible in dashboard, no push Dashboard badge 50–100/day
1 Caution Visible in dashboard with highlight Dashboard + optional push 5–15/day
2 Warning Push notification + sound Phone + desktop 1–3/day
3 Critical Push + phone call escalation if unacknowledged in 5 min All channels < 1/week

Context-Dependent Thresholds

Static thresholds are the enemy of intelligent monitoring. A 2% move in the S&P 500 means different things in different contexts.

Regime-Aware Thresholding

The alarm system maintains a "context register" that adjusts thresholds based on:

  1. Scheduled events: Before FOMC, NFP, CPI, and earnings releases, the system widens thresholds for rate-sensitive and index-level movements. A 1% equity move during FOMC is normal; the same move on an uneventful Tuesday is notable.
  2. Current volatility regime: Thresholds are expressed in units of recent realized volatility, not absolute price moves. In a VIX-30 environment, larger moves are expected and the system does not alarm on them.
  3. Time of day: The first and last 30 minutes of US equity trading are inherently more volatile. Thresholds widen during these windows.
  4. Day of week/month: Options expiration days (monthly, quarterly) have known volatility patterns. Month-end rebalancing flows are expected.
  5. Historical analog: If the current market regime resembles a historical period (detected by the regime classification model), thresholds calibrate to that period's realized distribution.
Alarm Suppression Rules
  • During a scheduled event window (e.g., 2:00–2:30 PM ET on FOMC days), all Advisory and Caution alarms related to rates and equities are suppressed. Only Warning and Critical pass through.
  • When the PM has acknowledged an alert and marked it "monitoring," subsequent updates at the same severity level are batched, not individually pushed.
  • Correlated alarms are grouped. If 15 equity positions trigger Caution simultaneously because the index moved, the PM sees one alarm ("Broad equity decline — 15 positions affected") not 15 individual alarms.

The Double-Check Protocol

Before any alarm is escalated from Caution to Warning, the system runs a 30-second confirmation cycle:

1
Re-verify the data: Is the triggering data point confirmed by a second source? (Erroneous prints, data vendor glitches, and flash crashes should not cause Warning-level alerts.)
2
Check for reversion: Has the triggering condition already reverted in the 30 seconds since detection? Transient spikes in spreads or prices that immediately revert are logged but not escalated.
3
Cross-console check: Does any other console have information that explains this alarm? (Example: LIQUIDITY console sees spread widening, but MACRO console knows this is 30 seconds after a scheduled economic release — the widening is expected and transient.)

Only if the alarm survives all three checks is it delivered at Warning level. This protocol adds 30 seconds of latency to Warning alerts — an acceptable tradeoff for dramatically reduced false positives.

Alarm Performance Metrics

The system tracks its own alarm quality:

  • Precision: Percentage of Warning/Critical alarms that the PM, in retrospect, agrees were warranted. Target: > 80%.
  • Recall: Percentage of events the PM considers significant that were caught by the alarm system. Target: > 95%. Recall matters more than precision — missed real events are worse than occasional false alarms.
  • Alarm-to-action ratio: Percentage of Warning/Critical alarms that led to a portfolio action (trade, hedge adjustment, position reduction). Tracked but not targeted — some warranted alarms correctly result in "no action needed."

5. The State Persistence Layer

Design Principle

The submarine's sonar picture is never allowed to go stale. RecWM's world model state is never allowed to be lost. Every state transition is recorded in an immutable, append-only log. Any historical state can be reconstructed.

Architecture

The state persistence layer flows data through four stages:

State Estimator
Every update cycle
→
State Buffer
In-memory ring buffer
Last 1 hour
→
State Snapshots
TimescaleDB
Full state every minute
→
Cold Storage
S3 + Parquet
7-year retention

Additionally, every event flows to an Event Log (Kafka + S3, immutable append-only) in parallel with the state pipeline.

State Snapshot Design

Hot state (in-memory): The last 1 hour of state at full update-cycle resolution (every 5 seconds during market hours). This is a ring buffer in RAM. Purpose: immediate query response, real-time dashboard rendering.

Warm state (database): Every minute, the full world model state is serialized and written to TimescaleDB. Retained for 2 years at minute resolution. Purpose: intraday replay, historical analysis, backtesting.

Cold state (archive): Daily end-of-day snapshots are archived to S3 in Parquet format. Retained for 7 years (regulatory compliance). Purpose: long-term research, audit, regulatory inquiry.

State Recovery Protocol

On system restart (planned or unplanned):

1
Load the most recent warm state snapshot from TimescaleDB.
2
Replay all events from the Event Log that occurred after the snapshot timestamp.
3
Reconnect to all live data feeds.
4
Run a "catch-up" cycle: for each data source, request any data published during the outage window.
5
Run the State Estimator forward from the recovered state through all caught-up data.
6
Compare the recovered state with live market data. If discrepancy exceeds tolerance, flag the affected fragments as "recovery-degraded" and apply confidence penalties until the state converges with live data.

Recovery time objective: Full state recovery within 5 minutes for outages up to 4 hours. Within 30 minutes for outages up to 24 hours.

Historical State Replay

The PM can request: "Show me the world state at 2:00 PM ET on March 10, 2023."

The system:

1
Loads the nearest warm-state snapshot before the requested timestamp.
2
Replays events from the Event Log forward to the exact requested time.
3
Presents the reconstructed state in the same dashboard interface the PM uses for live monitoring.
4
Overlays what actually happened next — enabling hindsight analysis ("given what I knew at 2 PM, what should I have done?").

State Versioning and Audit Trail

Every state mutation is tagged with:

  • Timestamp (UTC, nanosecond precision)
  • Source (which data feed or computation triggered the change)
  • Previous value and new value (for each changed field)
  • Confidence score before and after
  • Causation chain (which upstream event caused this state change)

This audit trail is immutable. It enables both regulatory compliance ("show me every state change related to this security on this date") and system debugging ("why did the CREDIT console escalate to Warning at 3:15 PM?").

6. Degraded Mode Operations

Design Philosophy

Power grids run N−1 contingency analysis continuously: "If this one component fails, can the grid still operate?" RecWM applies the same principle to its data sources.

Every data source is registered with:

  • Its contribution to each fragment domain (which consoles depend on it)
  • Its redundancy status (are there alternative sources for the same information?)
  • Its staleness tolerance (how long before the absence of updates degrades confidence?)

Degradation Taxonomy

Level 1: Single Source Failure

One data feed is down or delayed beyond its staleness tolerance.

Response:

  • Switch to redundant source if available (e.g., if Bloomberg B-PIPE goes down, fall back to a secondary market data provider for price data).
  • If no redundant source, apply confidence penalty to affected fragment domains.
  • Log the outage. Display degradation indicator on affected consoles.
  • Example message to PM: "Repo market data feed offline since 10:32 AM. LIQUIDITY console confidence degraded from 94% to 78%. Using interpolated repo rates from last known values. ETA for recovery: checking with vendor."
Level 2: Multiple Source Failure

Two or more feeds serving the same domain are down simultaneously.

Response:

  • Affected console switches to "estimated mode" — using models and cross-domain inference rather than direct observation.
  • Console background color changes to amber in the PM interface.
  • Alarm thresholds for the affected domain widen (to avoid false alarms from model estimation error).
  • PM receives a Caution-level alert describing the degradation and its estimated impact.
Level 3: Domain Blackout

All data sources for a fragment domain are unavailable (example: all credit data feeds fail simultaneously).

Response:

  • Affected console switches to "stale mode" — displaying last known state with a prominent staleness warning.
  • Console background changes to red.
  • PM receives a Warning-level alert.
  • Cross-domain inference is maximized: the CREDIT console attempts to infer credit conditions from equity prices, option implied vols, and other available data.
  • System explicitly states its uncertainty: "CREDIT fragment is operating on inference only. Confidence: 35%. Recommend manual verification of credit conditions before any credit-sensitive trades."
Level 4: Complete Data Blackout

Market holidays, circuit breakers, or catastrophic infrastructure failure.

Response:

  • All consoles switch to "watch mode" — monitoring only news feeds and any data source that remains active (crypto markets, offshore FX).
  • State estimation freezes at last known market state.
  • The system focuses on detecting information that will affect markets when they reopen.
  • Weekend mode: on Friday close, the system generates a "Weekend Risk Report" — what could happen over the weekend that would affect Monday's open, ranked by probability and impact.

Confidence Score Computation

Each console maintains a real-time confidence score (0–100%) computed as:

confidence = base_confidence × Π(source_availability_weights) × staleness_decay_factor × cross_validation_factor

Where:

  • base_confidence — 100% when all sources are live and fresh.
  • source_availability_weights — reduce confidence proportionally when sources go down, weighted by each source's contribution to the domain.
  • staleness_decay_factor — a time-dependent function that reduces confidence as data ages beyond its staleness tolerance.
  • cross_validation_factor — captures whether available data sources agree with each other (high agreement = higher confidence even with some sources missing).

7. The Morning Briefing Protocol

Design Philosophy

This is the shift handoff. The overnight automated watch is handing off to the human PM. Like an ICU bedside handoff, it must be structured, complete, and prioritized.

Briefing Structure

The Morning Briefing fires at the PM's configured time (default: 6:30 AM local). It is delivered as a structured document with drill-down capability.

Section 1: Overnight Summary (30-second read)

One-paragraph narrative of what happened while the PM slept. Tone-calibrated: calm if nothing significant, urgent if action needed.

Example (calm)

"Quiet overnight. Asia session saw modest gains led by tech names in Tokyo. Europe opened flat. No unusual moves in rates or FX. Your portfolio is up 12bps on overnight futures."

Example (urgent)

"Significant overnight development. China announced unexpected reserve requirement ratio cut at 7 PM ET. Asia rallied sharply — Hang Seng +2.8%. Your EM exposure is up 45bps but your long USD/CNH hedge is down 30bps. Net portfolio impact: +15bps. The RRR cut was not in our model — MACRO console has flagged this as a potential regime signal for China easing cycle."

Section 2: What Changed (2-minute read)

Ranked list of the 5–10 most significant state changes across all fragment domains since the PM last reviewed.

Each item includes: what changed, magnitude, assessed cause, portfolio impact, and recommended attention level.

Organized by console: LIQUIDITY changes, RISK changes, CREDIT changes, MOMENTUM changes, MACRO changes.

Section 3: What Did NOT Change That Should Have (1-minute read)

This is the most intellectually distinctive section. The system maintains expectations for what should change given the overnight developments, and flags when expected changes did not materialize.

Example

"Given the China RRR cut, we expected AUD/USD to rally. It didn't — currently flat. This non-reaction may indicate the market had already priced in easing expectations, or that USD strength is overpowering the signal. Worth monitoring."

This section directly addresses the PM's fear of "what am I missing?" by surfacing absent signals, not just present ones.

Section 4: Portfolio Health Score (30-second read)

A single composite score (0–100) summarizing portfolio health across all dimensions.

Breakdown by component: Liquidity Health, Risk Budget Utilization, Credit Quality, Momentum Alignment, Macro Positioning.

Trend: is the health score improving, stable, or deteriorating? Over what timeframe?

Comparison to 30-day average.

Section 5: Top 3 Attention Items (2-minute read)

The three things the PM should focus on today, ranked by urgency and importance.

Each item includes: the situation, why it matters, what options the PM has, and a recommended action.

These are not generic observations — they are specific, actionable, and tied to the PM's actual portfolio.

Section 6: Scenario Updates (1-minute read)

RecWM maintains a set of active scenarios (user-defined and system-generated). This section reports how each scenario's probability has changed overnight.

Example

"Scenario 'Fed pauses in September' — probability increased from 62% to 71% based on overnight Fed commentary. Your portfolio is positioned to benefit from this scenario."

Section 7: Today's Calendar (30-second read)

Key events scheduled for today: economic releases with times and consensus expectations, earnings reports, central bank speeches, option expirations, index rebalances.

RecWM's pre-event positioning assessment: "You have significant rates exposure and CPI is at 8:30 AM. Consider whether current positioning reflects your CPI view."

Briefing Delivery

The Morning Briefing is delivered in three formats simultaneously:

1
Dashboard: Full interactive version with drill-down capability.
2
Summary push notification: Section 1 (overnight summary) + Section 5 (top 3 items) delivered as a push notification. The PM can read this in 90 seconds on their phone.
3
Structured data: All briefing data available via API for integration with the PM's other tools.

Monitoring the Monitor

The CAE monitors its own health using a separate, independent heartbeat system:

  • Every component publishes a heartbeat every 10 seconds.
  • An independent watchdog (running on separate infrastructure) monitors heartbeats.
  • If any component misses 3 consecutive heartbeats (30 seconds), the watchdog triggers an infrastructure alert — distinct from market alerts — delivered to both the PM and the technical operations team.
  • The watchdog itself is monitored by an external uptime service (e.g., Pingdom, UptimeRobot) as a final failsafe.
The 2003 Northeast Blackout Lesson

This addresses the 2003 Northeast Blackout lesson: the monitoring system's alarm processor had crashed, and nobody noticed for 90 minutes. RecWM's watchdog ensures that if the monitoring system itself fails, the failure is detected within 30 seconds.

Appendix: Console Status Dashboard Layout

+------------------------------------------------------------------+ | RecWM Continuous Awareness Engine | | Watch: US Active | 2026-08-09 14:32:17 ET | +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | | | LIQUIDITY [GREEN] RISK [GREEN] CREDIT [YELLOW] | | Confidence: 94% Confidence: 97% Confidence: 82% | | Spreads: Normal VaR: 62% of limit CDS: 1 name wide | | Depth: Normal Beta: 0.95 Rating: Stable | | Repo: Normal Margin: 45% IG Spread: +2bps | | | | MOMENTUM [GREEN] MACRO [GREEN] | | Confidence: 91% Confidence: 96% | | Trend: Intact Regime: Risk-On | | Breadth: Healthy Recession P: 18% | | Flows: Neutral Next Event: CPI | | (tomorrow 8:30 AM) | | | +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | ACTIVE ALERTS | | [CAUTION] CREDIT: XYZ Corp CDS +45bps (2.1 sigma) -- 14:28 ET | | [ADVISORY] MOMENTUM: Breadth divergence in small caps -- 13:55 | +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | PORTFOLIO HEALTH: 87/100 (stable, 30-day avg: 85) | +------------------------------------------------------------------+

Design Summary

The Continuous Awareness Engine is not a dashboard bolted onto a data feed. It is a cognitive architecture — a system that maintains a continuously updated mental model of the financial world, detects when that model diverges from reality, and communicates the divergence to a human decision-maker with appropriate urgency.

Its design draws on decades of operational learning from domains where monitoring failures have catastrophic consequences: blackouts that leave 50 million people without power, spacecraft that must keep crews alive 250,000 miles from home, submarines that must track contacts in three dimensions continuously, and intensive care units where a missed alarm means a missed intervention.

The financial application is less dramatic but no less demanding: the PM who uses RecWM should never again wonder "what am I missing?" The system is always watching, always updating, always ready to tell them.

Real-Time Detection, Classification, and Response to Structural Breaks in Financial Markets

Contents

1. What IS a Regime? 6. The Contagion Network 2. Pre-Transition Signatures 7. The Early Warning Timeline 3. The Cascade Model 8. The Regime Memory 4. Transition Speed Classifier 9. Implementation Architecture 5. The New Regime Classifier 10. What Makes This Different

1. What IS a Regime? A Mathematical Definition

1.1 Formal Definition

A regime is a maximal connected region in world-state space over which the generating dynamics of financial observables are approximately stationary.

Let the world state at time t be denoted W(t) — the full RecWM world model state comprising all fragment states (Liquidity, Credit, Risk, Structure, Flow, Narrative, Macro). Define the dynamics of each fragment f as:

dFf(t) = μf(W(t), θr) dt + σf(W(t), θr) dBf(t) + Jf dNf(t)

where:

  • θr — the regime-specific parameter vector
  • μf — the drift (expected change) of fragment f
  • σf — the diffusion (volatility structure) of fragment f
  • Jf — the jump size distribution
  • Nf — a Poisson counting process for discontinuous events
  • Bf — a (possibly correlated) Brownian motion

A regime R is then characterized by the tuple:

R = (θ, Σ, Λ, T)
  • θ = parameter vector governing fragment dynamics
  • Σ = cross-fragment correlation matrix (the co-movement structure)
  • Λ = jump intensity vector (how often discontinuities occur per fragment)
  • T = the transition kernel — probabilities of moving to other regimes

Two time periods t1 and t2 belong to the same regime if and only if there exists no changepoint between them — formally, if:

KL( P(·|θt1), P(·|θt2) ) < ε

where KL is the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the data-generating distributions and ε is a stationarity tolerance calibrated empirically.

1.2 Regime Taxonomy

Regimes are not purely discrete labels nor purely continuous — they exist on a hybrid lattice. We define regimes along three independent axes:

Axis 1: Volatility State
Low • Normal • Elevated • Crisis
Axis 2: Growth / Risk Appetite
Risk-On-Expansion • Neutral • Risk-Off-Contraction
Axis 3: Monetary / Liquidity
Accommodative • Neutral • Restrictive

This yields a 4 × 3 × 3 = 36 canonical regimes, though in practice many cells are rarely visited. The occupied cells cluster into approximately 8–12 empirically distinct regimes.

Within each canonical regime, the system tracks a continuous regime coordinate — a point on a manifold that captures sub-regime variation. The transition between regimes is not a binary event but a trajectory across this manifold, though it often passes through narrow “transition corridors” where the dynamics are highly unstable.

The 36-Cell Regime Lattice

Volatility ACCOMMODATIVE NEUTRAL RESTRICTIVE
Risk-On Neutral Risk-Off Risk-On Neutral Risk-Off Risk-On Neutral Risk-Off
Low Goldilocks
2012–17		 Steady Growth Rare Mid-Cycle Calm Drift Rare Rare Rare Rare

1.3 Regime Catalog — Historical Examples

Low-Vol-Growth-Accommodative (“Goldilocks”)

Period: 2012–2017, portions of 2019

Fragment signatures: VIX 10–14, credit spreads tight and compressing, equity-bond correlation negative (bonds diversify), carry strategies profitable, trend strategies suffer, realized vol << implied vol

Correlation structure: Cross-asset correlations low, sector dispersion moderate

Winning strategies: Short volatility, carry, credit long, equity momentum, risk parity

Fragment states: Liquidity = Abundant, Credit = Benign, Risk = Compressed, Structure = Stable, Flow = Passive-dominated, Narrative = Complacent, Macro = Steady-growth

Credit-Stress-Deleveraging (“2008 Mode”)

Period: Sep 2008 – Mar 2009, briefly Mar 2020

Fragment signatures: VIX 40+, credit spreads >500bp, TED spread elevated, correlations spike to ~1.0 across risk assets, basis trades blow out, funding stress acute

Correlation structure: Everything-correlated — diversification fails

Winning strategies: Long volatility, long treasuries, short credit, cash

Fragment states: Liquidity = Frozen, Credit = Distressed, Risk = Panic, Structure = Breaking, Flow = Forced-selling, Narrative = Catastrophic, Macro = Recession

Fed-Tightening-Repricing (“2022 Mode”)

Period: Jan 2022 – Oct 2022

Fragment signatures: Rising rates, equity-bond correlation flips positive (both down together), growth-to-value rotation, duration punished, credit resilient initially then weakening

Correlation structure: Equity-bond correlation positive (historically unusual), within-equity: value beats growth

Winning strategies: Short duration, value over growth, commodities, trend-following

Fragment states: Liquidity = Draining, Credit = Tightening, Risk = Repricing, Structure = Rotating, Flow = Duration-exit, Narrative = Inflation-fear, Macro = Overheating

Speculative-Euphoria (“AI Bubble / Late 1999”)

Period: Nov 2023 – present (as of design), late 1999, late 2020/early 2021

Fragment signatures: Narrow market leadership, extreme concentration, retail inflows, options skew inverted for leaders, VIX moderate but single-stock vol elevated, credit tight, IPO/SPAC activity elevated

Correlation structure: Intra-index correlation low (few names driving), thematic clustering high

Winning strategies: Momentum in leaders, long gamma on leaders, but tail risk enormous

Fragment states: Liquidity = Selective-abundance, Credit = Benign, Risk = Concentrated, Structure = Fragile-beneath-surface, Flow = Narrative-chasing, Narrative = Euphoric, Macro = Mixed-but-ignored

2. Pre-Transition Signatures: The Financial P-Waves

The central insight: structural deterioration precedes price deterioration. The world model's fragments are designed to detect exactly this — the gap between what price says and what structure says.

2.1 The Fragment Inconsistency Detector

Define the inter-fragment coherence score as:

C(t) = 1 − (1/N) Σi<j |si(t) − E[si | sj(t), Rcurrent]|

where si(t) is the normalized state of fragment i and E[si | sj(t), Rcurrent] is the expected state of fragment i given fragment j’s state under the current regime’s correlation structure.

When C(t) is high (~1.0), fragments are behaving consistently. When C(t) drops below ~0.7, fragments are sending contradictory signals — the hallmark of an impending transition.

Historical Example — Pre-GFC (June 2007)

  • Price fragment: S&P 500 at all-time highs. Risk = “calm.”
  • Credit fragment: ABX indices declining since February. BBB tranche spreads widened 400bp.
  • Liquidity fragment: Repo haircuts on structured credit increasing. Bear Stearns hedge funds reporting difficulties.
  • Structure fragment: Dealer balance sheets at record leverage. Counterparty exposure concentrated.

The coherence score C(t) would have collapsed: Price says calm, Credit says distress, Liquidity says tightening, Structure says fragile. This four-way disagreement is the P-wave.

Historical Example — Pre-COVID (February 2020)

  • Price fragment: S&P 500 at all-time highs through Feb 19.
  • Macro fragment: China PMI collapsed in January. South Korean exports declined.
  • Flow fragment: Smart money (corporate insiders, hedge fund positioning) showed net selling.
  • Narrative fragment: COVID news accelerating, markets ignoring — narrative-price gap widening.

2.2 Volatility-of-Volatility: The Meta-Instability Signal

Define the vol-of-vol metric:

VoV(t) = στ[RV(s)]  for s ∈ [t−τ, t]

where RV is realized volatility and τ is a rolling window (typically 20 trading days). Before major transitions, VoV rises while headline vol may remain low. The system is “trembling.”

Critical Slowing Down

Near a phase transition, the system’s return to equilibrium slows down. If the system state x(t) evolves as:

dx/dt = −λ(p)(x − x*) + η(t)

where p is a control parameter approaching a bifurcation value pc, then the restoring force λ(p) → 0 as p → pc. Observable consequences:

1. AUTOCORRELATION

AR(1) coefficient of fragment residuals increases toward 1.0

2. VARIANCE

Var(x) ~ σ²/(2λ) → ∞ as λ → 0

3. FLICKERING

System samples the alternative regime state before fully transitioning

RecWM monitors all three of these critical slowing down indicators across every fragment.

2.3 Correlation Structure Destabilization

Define the correlation stability index:

CSI(t) = ||Σ(t) − Σregime||F / ||Σregime||F

where Σ(t) is the rolling cross-fragment correlation matrix and Σregime is the expected matrix for the current regime. ||·||F is the Frobenius norm. When CSI exceeds 0.3–0.5, the correlation structure is no longer consistent with the current regime.

A more sensitive variant: the absorption ratio — the fraction of total variance explained by the top k eigenvectors:

ARk(t) = Σi=1k λi(t) / Σi=1n λi(t)

Kritzman et al. (2011) showed this ratio spiked before every major crisis since 1998.

2.4 The Transition Probability Score

Combine the above into a single real-time Transition Probability Ptrans(t):

Ptrans(t) = σ(w1·(1 − C(t)) + w2·VoVnorm(t) + w3·CSI(t) + w4·ARk(t) + w5·Liqstress(t) + b)

where σ is the sigmoid function, weights w are learned from historical transitions via logistic regression, and Liqstress is a composite liquidity deterioration metric.

Ptrans Range Classification Action
0.0 – 0.2Stable regimeNo action needed
0.2 – 0.4Elevated awarenessMonitor more frequently
0.4 – 0.6Pre-transitionAlert PM. Begin scenario analysis.
0.6 – 0.8Transition likely imminentRecommend hedging. Activate circuit-breakers.
0.8 – 1.0Transition underwayFull cascade monitoring active

3. The Cascade Model: How Regime Transitions Propagate

3.1 The Domino Sequence

Regime transitions do not occur simultaneously across all fragments. They cascade. Typical cascade for a risk-off transition:

1. Liquidity → 2. Credit → 3. Volatility → 4. Correlation → 5. Price → 6. Narrative → 7. Flow → 8. Structure
Stage 1 — Liquidity Leads

Funding conditions tighten before anything else. Repo rates tick up. Dealer balance sheet capacity shrinks. Bid-ask spreads widen in less-liquid instruments. Invisible to anyone watching equities.

Stage 2 — Credit Amplifies

Credit spreads widen, initially in the weakest credits (CCC, distressed), then propagating up the quality spectrum. Equity may still be near highs.

Stage 3 — Volatility Responds

Implied vol rises in rates and credit first, then equity vol follows. Vol surface reshapes — skew steepens, term structure inverts.

Stage 4 — Correlations Spike

Previously independent risk factors become correlated. Diversification benefits disappear. This is when many risk models break.

Stage 5 — Price Adjusts

Risk assets finally reprice. The newspaper reports “markets crashed” — but structural deterioration has been underway for days or weeks.

Stage 6 — Narrative Catches Up

Financial media shifts from “buy the dip” to “crisis.” Narrative fragment lags price, creating overshoot risk.

Stage 7 — Flow Follows

Retail and systematic flows respond. Redemptions, margin calls, CTA trend-following all kick in, amplifying the move.

Stage 8 — Structure Breaks

Market microstructure deteriorates. Circuit breakers trigger. Liquidity providers withdraw. The market’s ability to process information degrades.

Key insight for RecWM: By the time a PM sees Stage 5 (price moving), Stages 1–4 have already occurred. The engine’s job is to detect Stages 1–2 and alert at Stage 3.

3.2 Cascade Dynamics — The Mathematical Model

Model the cascade as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) with probabilistic propagation. Let each fragment f have a stress level sf(t) ∈ [0, 1] and a transition threshold τf. Stress propagation follows:

dsf/dt = αf·I(sf > τf) + Σg→f βgf·I(sg > τg)·h(sg) + γf·ξf(t) − δf·sf
  • αf — self-excitation rate once the fragment transitions
  • βgf — contagion coefficient from fragment g to fragment f
  • h(sg) — contagion intensity function (typically concave)
  • γf — exogenous shock sensitivity
  • ξf(t) — white noise (random perturbations)
  • δf — mean-reversion rate
  • I(·) — indicator function

The critical insight is the βgf matrix — the contagion structure. This matrix is itself regime-dependent. In calm times, β values are small. In stress, β values increase — contagion becomes more efficient precisely when you need it to be less so. This positive feedback is what makes cascades nonlinear.

3.3 The Self-Sustaining Cascade Threshold

Define the cascade eigenvalue as the largest eigenvalue of the effective contagion matrix B(t) = {βgf(t)}. When this eigenvalue exceeds 1.0, the cascade is self-sustaining:

λmax(B(t)) > 1  ⇒  self-sustaining cascade

This is directly analogous to the basic reproduction number R0 in epidemiology. When R0 > 1, the epidemic grows exponentially. When λmax > 1, the financial stress cascade grows exponentially.

Cascade Eigenvalue (R0) Visualization

λmax < 0.5 — Normal
0.5 < λmax < 0.8 — Elevated
0.8 < λmax < 1.0 — Critical
λmax > 1.0 — Self-Sustaining
CRITICAL THRESHOLD: λmax = 1.0

Analogous to R0 in epidemiology — above 1.0, stress propagation creates more stress than mean-reversion can absorb

λmax Status Interpretation
< 0.5NormalPerturbations die out quickly
0.5 – 0.8ElevatedSystem becoming more “contagious”
0.8 – 1.0CriticalNear self-sustaining threshold; any moderate shock could trigger a cascade
> 1.0Cascade ActiveSelf-reinforcing stress loop; only external intervention or exhaustion of selling can stop it

3.4 Feedback Loops That Accelerate Cascades

Loop 1: The Dealer Hedging Vortex

Dealers sell options → must delta-hedge → selling into falling markets → pushes price lower → triggers more hedging → more selling. The “gamma trap” where dealer hedging amplifies moves. The engine tracks aggregate dealer gamma exposure and flags when gamma is sufficiently negative that hedging flows amplify any move by more than 2x.

Loop 2: The Margin-Liquidation Spiral

Price falls → margin calls → forced selling → more price falls → more margin calls. When estimated margin utilization exceeds 85%, any 3% further decline triggers forced selling that itself causes a further Y% decline. When Y > 3%, the spiral is self-sustaining.

Loop 3: The Liquidity Black Hole

Vol rises → risk models cut position limits → market makers withdraw → liquidity drops → same order flow moves price more → vol rises further. When the ratio of market depth to realized volatility falls below a critical level, the market enters a “liquidity black hole.”

4. The Transition Speed Classifier

4.1 Speed Classes

Not all transitions are equal. The detection algorithm, response, and PM notification must be calibrated to the transition speed.

Class Speed Examples Detection Method Lead Time PM Notification
S1 Weeks to months Fed policy pivot (2021–22), China slowdown, demographic shifts BOCPD with long run-length priors; EWMA with λ=0.97 30–90 days “Advisory: Macro regime shifting. Recommend gradual adjustment.”
S2 Days to weeks SVB collapse (Mar 2023), EM currency crises, sector rotation BOCPD moderate priors; rolling correlation breakdowns (τ=10d) 3–14 days “Alert: Credit-Stress transition detected. Recommended actions: [list].”
S3 Hours to days Flash crashes (Oct 2014 Treasury), sudden geopolitical events, margin cascades High-freq fragment monitoring; VPIN; real-time options flow 1–24 hours “URGENT: Rapid regime transition underway. Immediate review recommended.”
S4 Minutes May 2010 Flash Crash, Aug 2007 quant meltdown, algo cascades Microstructure metrics; order book imbalance; ETF arb spread breakdown Seconds to min Real-time dashboard alert. Auto-activate pre-authorized hedging protocols.

4.2 Speed-Adaptive Detection Algorithm

The unified detection algorithm runs BOCPD (Adams & MacKay, 2007) at multiple timescales simultaneously:

P(rt = r | x1:t) ∝ P(xt | rt=r, xt−r:t−1) · P(rt=r | rt−1) · P(rt−1 | x1:t−1)

where rt is the “run length” (time since last changepoint) and xt is the observation vector. The key innovation: rather than running BOCPD on price data (noisy and late), we run it on the fragment state vector.

Four parallel BOCPD instances:

BOCPD-S1

Weekly fragment summaries
H(τ) = 1/250 (~250 weeks)

BOCPD-S2

Daily fragment states
H(τ) = 1/60 (~60 days)

BOCPD-S3

Hourly fragment updates
H(τ) = 1/120 (~120 hours)

BOCPD-S4

Minute-level microstructure
H(τ) = 1/480 (~480 min)

5. The New Regime Classifier

5.1 Template Matching

Once a transition is detected, the system must answer: what is the new regime?

Approach 1 — Nearest Historical Analog: Compute the distance between the current fragment state vector and historical regime onsets:

d(Wnow, Whist) = Σf wf · ||Ff(now) − Ff(hist)||² + λ · ||Σ(now) − Σ(hist)||F²

The nearest historical analog provides both a label and a playbook — “This looks like October 2018 (vol shock + growth scare). In Oct 2018, the drawdown was 20%, recovery took 4 months, value outperformed growth by 8% during the transition.”

5.2 Novel Regime Detection

Critical capability: detecting when the current state does not match any historical template. Define the novelty score:

N(t) = minR ∈ catalog d(W(t), WR)

If N(t) exceeds the 95th percentile of historical within-regime distances, the engine classifies the current state as Novel Regime:

WARNING: Novel Regime Detected

“Current market state does not match any historical regime template. You are operating without historical precedent. Default to maximum risk reduction until the new regime stabilizes.”

Examples of novel regimes:

  • March 2020: Pandemic-driven crash with simultaneous Treasury market dysfunction — no analog combined these features
  • 2022: Simultaneous inflation shock with negative equity-bond correlation breakdown — not seen since the 1970s, but with completely different market microstructure

5.3 Regime Stability Assessment

Once in a new regime, the PM needs to know: will it persist? The engine computes a stability score based on:

  1. Fragment consensus: Are all fragments consistent with the new regime, or are some still in the old?
  2. Policy response probability: Is the new regime likely to trigger a policy response that would cause another transition?
  3. Historical regime duration: For matched analogs, what was the typical duration?
  4. Transition momentum: Is the system still moving toward the new regime, or has it stabilized?
Stability(t) = (Cnew(t))α · (1 − Ppolicy(t))β · (telapsed / thist_median)γ · (1 − |dW/dt| / |dW/dt|transition)δ
