6. The Contagion Network

6.1 Network Architecture

The contagion network is a directed weighted graph G = (V, E, w) where:

Nodes (V) — Contagion Units
  • Asset class: Equities, Credit (IG, HY, EM), Rates, FX, Commodities, Crypto, Real Estate
  • Geographic: US, Europe, Japan, China, EM-Asia, EM-LatAm, EM-EMEA
  • Sector: Tech, Financials, Energy, Healthcare, etc.
  • Participant: Dealers, Hedge Funds, Pension/Insurance, Retail, Sovereign Wealth, Central Banks
Edges (E) — Contagion Channels
  • Funding links: Prime brokerage, repo counterparties, dollar funding chains
  • Collateral chains: Rehypothecation, margin call triggers
  • Common ownership: Mark-to-market cascades
  • Basis trades: Treasury cash-futures, ETF-underlying, CDS-bond
  • Hedging links: Cross-asset hedging flows

Edge weights (w) are the contagion probabilities:

w(A→B, t) = P(stressB(t+Δt) > τB | stressA(t) > τA, regime(t))

Estimated from:

  1. Historical co-stress frequencies (empirical Bayes)
  2. Known structural links (funding, collateral, ownership from regulatory filings)
  3. Granger causality tests on fragment stress indicators
  4. Real-time market-implied contagion (options-implied correlation, CDS-equity co-movement)

6.2 Contagion Probability Computation

For a given stress event at node A, compute contagion probability to node B using a multi-step propagation model:

P(A→B, k steps) = 1 − Πpaths p: A→B, |p|≤k (1 − Πedges e ∈ p w(e))

For computational efficiency, approximate using the network Laplacian:

L = D − W

where D is the degree matrix and W is the weighted adjacency matrix. The eigenvalues of L characterize contagion properties: small algebraic connectivity (Fiedler value) means the network has bottlenecks that can contain contagion; large algebraic connectivity means contagion propagates easily.

6.3 Super-Spreader Identification

A super-spreader is a node whose stress causes maximum contagion. Define contagion centrality:

CC(v) = Σu ∈ V, u≠v P(v→u, kmax) · Impact(u)

Historical super-spreaders:

2008

AIG (collateral chains), Lehman (funding links), money market funds (common ownership, funding)

2020

Treasury market dealers (funding, hedging), corporate bond ETFs (basis trades, flow)

2023

Silicon Valley Bank (funding links, common depositor base, narrative contagion)

6.4 Dynamic Network — Regime-Dependent Topology

The contagion network is not static. Its topology changes with the regime:

In Calm Regimes

Network is sparse. Edge weights are low. Fiedler value is small — fragmented network, contagion containable.

In Stress Regimes

Network densifies. Edge weights increase. New edges appear. Fiedler value increases — contagion propagates easily.

RecWM maintains a library of regime-specific network topologies, estimated from each historical regime period. When the regime classifier identifies the current regime, the corresponding network topology is loaded as the primary contagion model.

7. The Early Warning Timeline

7.1 A Composite Timeline — Anatomy of a Regime Transition

Using the 2023 SVB crisis as a worked example:

T-45 days Late January 2023: First tremors
  • Liquidity: Regional bank CDS spreads widening 15–20bp. Velocity 2σ above normal.
  • Credit: FHLB advances spiking — a sign of deposit stress not visible in public data.
  • RecWM display: Yellow indicator. Ptrans = 0.12. “Unusual funding stress detected in regional banking sector.”
T-30 days Early February: Fragment inconsistencies emerge
  • Macro: Fed still hiking. Yield curve deeply inverted.
  • Flow: Insider selling at several regional banks accelerating.
  • Risk: KRE equity vol rising while broad market vol remains low.
  • RecWM: Coherence C(t) drops to 0.65. Ptrans = 0.28.
T-14 days Late February: Multiple signals converge
  • Credit: Silvergate announces delayed 10-K. Similar banks’ CDS jumps.
  • Structure: Duration mismatch at historically extreme levels (HTM portfolios vs. short-duration deposits).
  • Correlation: Regional bank stocks & Treasury yields turning strongly positive (unusual).
  • RecWM: Ptrans = 0.48. “Pre-transition state detected. Contagion centrality 85th percentile.”
T-7 days Early March: Threshold exceeded
  • Liquidity: SVB deposit outflow accelerates. Silvergate announces voluntary liquidation (Mar 8).
  • Flow: Put buying on KRE, SIVB, FRC spikes.
  • VoV: Financial sector vol-of-vol jumps to 90th percentile.
  • RecWM: Ptrans = 0.71. λmax = 0.78. “WARNING: Regime transition likely imminent. Historical analog: Continental Illinois (1984).”
T-1 day March 9: Cascade initiated
  • Event: SVB announces $1.8B loss on bond portfolio sale and $2.25B capital raise attempt.
  • Credit: SVB CDS gaps to 500bp. All regional bank CDS widening.
  • Flow: $42B deposit withdrawal in a single day (unprecedented velocity).
  • Narrative: Social media “bank run” sentiment explodes. Narrative contagion faster than financial contagion.
  • RecWM: Ptrans = 0.94. λmax = 1.12 (self-sustaining). Contagion to broader financials: 73%.
T-0 March 10–13: Full transition
  • SVB seized by FDIC. Signature Bank closed. First Republic under extreme pressure.
  • KRE down 30% from pre-crisis levels. Broad market volatility spikes.
  • The transition structurally visible 45 days ago has now become a price event.

7.2 Generalized Timeline Template

T-N    Fragment anomaly (single fragment, single sub-sector)
        → Yellow indicator, daily briefing mention

T-N/2  Fragment inconsistency (2+ fragments disagree)
        → Orange indicator, coherence score alert

T-N/3  Multi-signal convergence (3+ independent warnings)
        → Ptrans crosses alert threshold, PM receives structured briefing

T-N/5  Cascade dynamics detectable (stress propagation between fragments)
        → Red indicator, cascade model activated, contagion mapping

T-1    Cascade eigenvalue approaching or exceeding 1.0
        → Critical alert, hedging recommendations, scenario analysis

T-0    Price-visible event (headline news, large moves)
        → Full transition report, new regime classification, strategy update

The value N depends on speed class: N ≈ 45 days for S1 transitions, N ≈ 7 days for S2, N ≈ 24 hours for S3.

8.2 Feature Importance Learning

After each transition, the engine performs a retrospective analysis:

1. Gradient-Based Feature Attribution

Which input features contributed most to Ptrans in the lead-up? Uses SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values on the logistic model.

2. Lead-Lag Analysis

Which fragment transitioned first? How much lead time did it provide? Update the canonical cascade sequence for this regime pair.

3. False Positive Analysis

In the 90 days prior, were there Ptrans spikes that did not result in a transition? What distinguished them from the true signal?

Output: a continuously updated feature importance ranking. Early transitions rely on hand-crafted weights; after ~20 observed transitions, learned weights dominate.

8.3 Near-Miss Analysis

Perhaps the most valuable category: transitions that almost happened but reversed. Cases where Ptrans exceeded 0.4 but subsequently declined.

September 2019 Repo Spike

Overnight repo rates spiked to 10%. All hallmarks of a liquidity crisis present. Fed intervened within 24 hours with emergency repo operations. Ptrans likely reached ~0.65 before intervention reversed it.

March 2023 — Broader Contagion

After SVB, crisis could have spread to money center banks. Ptrans for a full financial crisis likely reached 0.5–0.6. The Fed’s Bank Term Funding Program (BTFP) broke the contagion chain.

For each near-miss, the engine records:

  • What was the maximum Ptrans reached?
  • What intervention reversed it?
  • What distinguished this from a true transition?

This catalog is critical for two reasons: (1) it prevents over-fitting to completed transitions (rare events) while ignoring far more numerous near-misses, and (2) it enables policy response modeling — estimating whether a current pre-transition state is likely to elicit an effective policy response.

8.4 Continuous Model Update Protocol

Timing Actions
Immediate (T+0 to T+1d) Log all fragment states, cascade sequence, and contagion network snapshot. Classify speed and match analogs.
Short-term (T+1 week) Retrospective analysis. Compute feature importance. Update BOCPD hazard functions. Recalibrate Ptrans weights.
Medium-term (T+1 month) Post-mortem. Final outcome, regime duration, strategy performance, optimal hedging strategy, counterfactual analysis.
Long-term (T+3 months) Update regime catalog. Add novel regimes to template library. Update analog distance metrics. Retrain full model.

10. What Makes This Different

Existing regime detection approaches suffer from three fatal flaws:

Flaw 1: They detect transitions in price, not structure.

Hidden Markov Models on returns, GARCH regime-switching models, even sophisticated Bayesian approaches — they all wait for the statistical properties of price to change. By then, structural deterioration has been underway for days or weeks. RecWM detects transitions in the generating structure (fragments), not the generated output (price).

Flaw 2: They don’t model cascade dynamics.

Existing approaches treat regime transitions as instantaneous jumps. In reality, transitions cascade across interconnected systems over time. The cascade model — with its contagion network, feedback loops, and self-sustaining threshold — captures this dynamics. It tells the PM not just “a transition happened” but “a transition has started in Liquidity, will reach Credit in 2 days, and has a 70% chance of becoming self-sustaining.”

Flaw 3: They don’t learn.

Most regime models are static — defined once, never updated. RecWM’s regime memory creates a continuously improving system. Every transition and near-miss enriches the catalog, refines feature importance rankings, and sharpens detection algorithms. After 50 transitions, the engine has a rich library of templates, cascade patterns, and early warning signatures that no static model can match.

The Regime Transition Engine is not an incremental improvement. It is a fundamentally different approach — one that treats regime detection not as a statistical exercise on returns, but as a structural monitoring problem on the world model itself.

It detects the earthquake’s P-wave, not the shaking. It identifies the grid’s sagging transmission line, not the blackout. It measures R0 before the pandemic is declared.

This is how a world-model hedge fund survives the moments when the rules change.

INNOVATION DEEP DIVE

Scenario Branching Engine

Part of the RecWM Ten-Layer Innovation Stack

0 Design Philosophy

RecWM does not predict the future. It maps the topology of possible futures so that no category of event arrives without a pre-computed response. The operating metaphor is not a crystal ball but a chess engine: AlphaZero does not know what move its opponent will play, but it has evaluated every plausible line deeply enough to respond instantly to any of them.

The Scenario Branching Engine (SBE) runs continuously, 24/7, consuming every fragment state update from the RecWM World Model, re-branching the scenario tree, pruning dead lines, and maintaining a live Contingency Matrix that maps every high-impact scenario to a pre-computed portfolio response.

The PM never sees the tree. The PM sees: "Here are the 5 scenarios that matter most to your portfolio right now, ranked by expected impact multiplied by probability. Here is what you should do in each case. Here is what it costs to hedge. Here is the scenario you are NOT hedged for."

1 The Scenario Tree Structure

1.1 Defining "Moves" in the Financial Game Tree

In chess, moves are discrete and well-defined. In markets, the "move space" is continuous and high-dimensional. The SBE discretizes the move space into Fragment Regime Transitions (FRTs) -- the atomic unit of scenario branching.

A Fragment Regime Transition is a change in the regime state of any RecWM fragment. The canonical fragment set:

FragmentRegime StatesTransition Triggers
Liquidity Abundant / Normal / Tight / Crisis Fed balance sheet changes, repo rate spikes, dealer inventory shifts, money market stress
Credit Expansionary / Stable / Tightening / Distress Spread widening, default rate changes, rating agency actions, covenant violations
Volatility Suppressed / Normal / Elevated / Dislocation VIX regime shifts, realized vs implied divergence, correlation breakdown, gamma exposure imbalance
Rates Easing / Stable / Hiking / Inversion-Stress Central bank actions, inflation data, term premium shifts, yield curve shape changes
Sentiment Risk-On / Neutral / Risk-Off / Panic Flow data, positioning extremes, narrative shifts, contagion signals
Macro-Growth Acceleration / Trend / Deceleration / Contraction GDP nowcasts, PMI shifts, employment data, earnings revision breadth
Geopolitical Stable / Elevated / Acute / Systemic Conflict escalation, sanctions, trade policy shifts, election outcomes, commodity supply disruption

Each fragment maintains a transition probability matrix updated in real time by the World Model. A "move" in the game tree is one or more fragments transitioning simultaneously.

1.2 Scenario Parameterization

Scenarios are NOT parameterized as simple directional moves ("stocks go down 10%"). They are parameterized as fragment regime vectors with associated dynamics.

A scenario is a tuple:

S = (Fregime_vector, Thorizon, Ppath, Δcorrelation) Where: Fregime_vector = [Liquidity: Tight, Credit: Tightening, Vol: Elevated, Rates: Hiking, Sentiment: Risk-Off, Growth: Deceleration, Geo: Stable] Thorizon = time horizon over which transition completes (1d, 1w, 1m, 1q) Ppath = transition path type (gradual, sudden, oscillating) Δcorrelation = correlation regime shift matrix (how cross-asset correlations change in this scenario)
Path matters. A gradual credit tightening over 3 months is a fundamentally different scenario from a sudden credit dislocation over 3 days, even if the endpoint regime is the same.

1.3 Tree Depth (Time Horizons)

The tree has four depth layers, each with different branching factors and evaluation precision:

Layer 0 (NOW) : Current fragment state. Single node. Full precision evaluation. Layer 1 (1 day) : 12-20 branches. High precision. Updated every 5 minutes. Layer 2 (1 week) : 8-15 branches per Layer 1 node. Medium precision. Updated hourly. Layer 3 (1 month) : 5-10 branches per Layer 2 node. Lower precision. Updated every 4 hours. Layer 4 (1 quarter): 3-5 branches per Layer 3 node. Directional precision. Updated daily.

Total theoretical tree size at full expansion: ~20 × 15 × 10 × 5 = 15,000 leaf scenarios at quarterly horizon. After pruning, the live tree maintains 200-500 active leaf scenarios at any time.

1.4 Tree Width (Branching Factor)

The branching factor is adaptive, not fixed. It depends on the current state of each fragment:

  • Near transition boundary: Higher branching factor. When the Liquidity fragment is near the Normal/Tight boundary, the engine explores more Liquidity branches.
  • Deep in regime: Lower branching factor. When Liquidity is firmly Abundant, fewer Liquidity branches are needed.
  • High uncertainty: Higher branching factor. When the World Model's confidence in fragment state is low, explore more.
  • Event-driven: Spike branching around known catalysts. FOMC day: Rates fragment gets 3× normal branching factor.

The branching factor allocation algorithm:

for each fragment F: base_branches(F) = 2 # minimum: stay or transition boundary_proximity = distance_to_nearest_transition(F) if boundary_proximity < threshold: branch_bonus += 3 × (1 - boundary_proximity / threshold) uncertainty_bonus = world_model_entropy(F) × 2 catalyst_bonus = upcoming_catalyst_weight(F, horizon) × 4 total_branches(F) = min(base_branches + branch_bonus + uncertainty_bonus + catalyst_bonus, MAX_BRANCHES_PER_FRAGMENT)

2 Pruning Heuristics

The raw tree is computationally intractable. Pruning is the core intellectual contribution of the SBE -- it determines what the system thinks about and what it ignores. Four pruning strategies operate simultaneously.

2.1 Portfolio-Relevance Pruning

Principle: Only explore scenarios that materially affect THIS portfolio. A scenario where emerging market currencies collapse is irrelevant to a portfolio with zero EM exposure -- unless the second-order effects (risk-off contagion, dollar strength) propagate.
def portfolio_relevance_score(scenario, portfolio): # First-order: direct exposure direct_impact = sum( position.notional × fragment_beta(position, scenario.fragment_changes) for position in portfolio.positions ) # Second-order: contagion and correlation contagion_impact = estimate_contagion( scenario.fragment_changes, portfolio.correlation_matrix, scenario.delta_correlation ) # Third-order: liquidity-adjusted impact # In a crisis, you can't just mark positions -- you have to exit them liquidity_penalty = sum( position.notional × liquidity_haircut(position, scenario) for position in portfolio.positions if position.days_to_exit(scenario) > position.days_to_exit(current_state) × 2 ) relevance = abs(direct_impact) + abs(contagion_impact) + liquidity_penalty return relevance # Prune if relevance < 0.5% of portfolio NAV PRUNE if portfolio_relevance_score(scenario) < 0.005 × portfolio.nav
Critical subtlety: The pruning threshold is asymmetric. Negative-impact scenarios are pruned at a HIGHER threshold (0.5% NAV) than positive-impact scenarios (2% NAV). The PM cares more about downside surprises than upside surprises.

2.2 Probability Pruning

Principle: Don't waste computation on scenarios with negligible probability -- but never prune a scenario just because it hasn't happened before.
PRUNE if: scenario.probability < base_threshold AND scenario.max_impact < catastrophic_threshold Where: base_threshold = 0.1% for Layer 1 (1-day scenarios) base_threshold = 0.5% for Layer 2 (1-week) base_threshold = 1.0% for Layer 3 (1-month) base_threshold = 2.0% for Layer 4 (1-quarter) catastrophic_threshold = 10% of NAV (never prune a scenario that could lose 10%+ of NAV regardless of probability)
The catastrophic override is essential. A 0.01% probability scenario that wipes out 50% of NAV must always remain in the tree. This is the lesson of every financial crisis: the "impossible" scenario is the one that matters most.

2.3 Novelty Pruning (Inverse)

Principle: Spend MORE computation on unprecedented scenarios. This is the opposite of chess engines, which prune unusual positions because they are likely bad. In finance, unprecedented scenarios are likely the most dangerous because the portfolio is least prepared for them.
def novelty_score(scenario): # How similar is this scenario to any historical episode? min_distance = min( scenario_distance(scenario, historical_episode) for historical_episode in scenario_memory.episodes ) # How similar is this to scenarios we've explored recently? exploration_recency = max( exploration_decay(scenario, explored) for explored in recently_evaluated_scenarios ) # High novelty = high distance from history + low recent exploration return min_distance × (1 - exploration_recency) # BOOST computation (anti-prune) for high-novelty scenarios computation_allocation(scenario) ×= (1 + novelty_score(scenario) × NOVELTY_WEIGHT)

This creates a natural exploration-exploitation balance: familiar scenarios are evaluated efficiently using cached historical analogs, while novel scenarios receive disproportionate computational attention.

2.4 Sensitivity Pruning

Principle: Focus on scenarios where small changes in assumptions produce large changes in outcomes. These are the "phase transition" scenarios -- the ones where being slightly wrong about the world leads to dramatically wrong portfolio positioning.
def sensitivity_score(scenario): base_evaluation = evaluate_portfolio(scenario) perturbations = generate_perturbations(scenario, ε=0.05) perturbed_evaluations = [evaluate_portfolio(p) for p in perturbations] # Gradient magnitude: how much does the outcome change # per unit change in assumptions? gradient = max( abs(perturbed - base_evaluation) / ε for perturbed in perturbed_evaluations ) return gradient # NEVER prune high-sensitivity scenarios PRESERVE if sensitivity_score(scenario) > SENSITIVITY_THRESHOLD

High-sensitivity scenarios are where the portfolio is most exposed to model error. They represent the "knife edge" where the difference between a good outcome and a bad outcome depends on getting the scenario exactly right -- which is precisely what you cannot do.

3 The Scenario Evaluation Function

Each scenario leaf in the tree is evaluated by a multi-objective evaluation function that produces a Scenario Impact Profile (SIP).

3.1 The Six Evaluation Dimensions

SIP = { pnl_impact: float, # Expected P&L change (dollars) max_drawdown_path: float, # Worst peak-to-trough on the path to this scenario liquidity_score: float, # 0-1, can you actually exit positions? risk_limit_status: dict, # Which risk limits are breached? margin_call_prob: float, # Probability of margin call from prime broker opportunity_cost: float # What alpha opportunities open up in this scenario? }

P&L Impact

Not a simple linear calculation. Uses the full RecWM fragment model to propagate scenario regime changes through to asset prices, accounting for non-linear payoffs (options), cross-asset correlations under the scenario's correlation regime, and funding costs.

def compute_pnl_impact(scenario, portfolio): # Step 1: Map fragment regime changes to asset price distributions asset_distributions = fragment_to_asset_model.propagate( scenario.fragment_vector, scenario.delta_correlation ) # Step 2: Evaluate each position under the distribution position_pnls = [] for position in portfolio.positions: if position.is_linear: pnl = position.δ × asset_distributions[position.asset].expected_move elif position.is_option: pnl = reprice_option( position, asset_distributions[position.underlying], scenario.implied_vol_surface ) - position.current_value elif position.is_structured: pnl = monte_carlo_reprice(position, asset_distributions, n_paths=1000) position_pnls.append(pnl) # Step 3: Aggregate with funding cost adjustment gross_pnl = sum(position_pnls) funding_adjustment = compute_funding_cost(scenario.rates_regime, portfolio) return gross_pnl - funding_adjustment

Maximum Drawdown Path

The terminal P&L might be acceptable, but the path might be catastrophic. A scenario where the portfolio drops 30% before recovering to -5% will trigger margin calls and forced selling that prevents the recovery. The MDP evaluator simulates the intra-scenario path:

def compute_max_drawdown_path(scenario, portfolio): # Simulate 100 intra-scenario paths paths = generate_intra_scenario_paths(scenario, n=100) max_drawdowns = [] for path in paths: cumulative_pnl = [evaluate_portfolio_at_time(portfolio, path, t) for t in path.timestamps] running_max = accumulate_max(cumulative_pnl) drawdowns = [running_max[i] - cumulative_pnl[i] for i in range(len(path))] max_drawdowns.append(max(drawdowns)) return percentile(max_drawdowns, 95) # 95th percentile worst drawdown

Liquidity Score

Measures whether you can actually trade in this scenario. Uses the Liquidity fragment's regime-dependent market depth model.

def compute_liquidity_score(scenario, portfolio): total_exit_cost = 0 total_notional = 0 for position in portfolio.positions: market_depth = liquidity_model.depth( position.asset, scenario.liquidity_regime, scenario.volatility_regime ) # How many days to exit at <2% market impact? days_to_exit = position.notional / (market_depth.daily_capacity × 0.02) # Slippage cost over exit period exit_cost = estimate_slippage(position, days_to_exit, market_depth) total_exit_cost += exit_cost total_notional += abs(position.notional) # Score: 1.0 = fully liquid, 0.0 = completely trapped return max(0, 1 - total_exit_cost / (total_notional × 0.05))

Risk Limit Status

Maps each scenario to the portfolio's risk limits and identifies breaches.

def check_risk_limits(scenario, portfolio, risk_limits): breaches = {} scenario_risk = compute_risk_metrics(scenario, portfolio) for limit in risk_limits: if limit.type == 'VAR': if scenario_risk.var_99 > limit.threshold: breaches[limit.name] = { 'current': scenario_risk.var_99, 'limit': limit.threshold, 'overage_pct': (scenario_risk.var_99 - limit.threshold) / limit.threshold } elif limit.type == 'GROSS_EXPOSURE': if scenario_risk.gross > limit.threshold: breaches[limit.name] = {...} elif limit.type == 'CONCENTRATION': for sector, exposure in scenario_risk.sector_exposures.items(): if exposure > limit.threshold: breaches[f'{limit.name}_{sector}'] = {...} return breaches

3.2 Composite Scoring

The six dimensions combine into a single Scenario Urgency Score (SUS) that determines how prominently the scenario is surfaced to the PM:

SUS = w1 × normalize(pnl_impact) + w2 × normalize(max_drawdown_path) + w3 × (1 - liquidity_score) + w4 × count(risk_limit_breaches) + w5 × margin_call_prob - w6 × normalize(opportunity_cost) # Opportunities reduce urgency Default weights: w1=0.25, w2=0.25, w3=0.20, w4=0.15, w5=0.10, w6=0.05

SUS weight distribution:

P&L 25% MDD 25% Liq 20% Risk 15% Marg 10% Opp

The weights are PM-configurable. A PM running a market-neutral book might weight liquidity higher; a PM running a directional book might weight P&L impact higher.

Every scenario with SUS above the alert threshold has an associated Response Playbook computed and maintained in real time.

4.2 Response Optimization Algorithm

For each high-SUS scenario, the engine solves a constrained optimization:

minimize: portfolio_loss(scenario, current_portfolio + hedge_adjustments) subject to: hedge_cost < max_acceptable_cost execution_time < scenario_onset_window liquidity_consumed < available_market_depth × 0.25 # Don't move the market risk_limit_compliance(adjusted_portfolio) = True # Feasibility constraints for each adjustment in hedge_adjustments: adjustment.instrument must be tradeable in scenario conditions adjustment.size must be executable given market depth

The optimizer runs a two-stage process:

Stage 1 -- Candidate Generation: Enumerate candidate hedge instruments from a pre-defined universe (index options, single-name CDS, rate swaps, FX forwards, futures). Score each by hedge effectiveness per unit cost.

Stage 2 -- Portfolio Optimization: Solve the constrained optimization using sequential quadratic programming. The non-linear constraints (liquidity, feasibility) are handled via penalty functions.

4.3 Response Ordering

When a scenario involves multiple actions, ordering matters. The engine ranks actions by a priority function:

priority(action) = impact_per_dollar(action) × urgency_decay(action) × liquidity_window(action) Where: impact_per_dollar = reduction in scenario loss per dollar of hedge cost urgency_decay = exponential decay based on how quickly the hedge becomes unavailable liquidity_window = estimated time window in which the action is executable

Actions with the shortest liquidity windows execute first. This prevents the common crisis failure mode where you execute the easy hedges first and find the critical ones are no longer available.

6 Red Team / Adversarial Analysis

6.1 The Adversarial Module

The Red Team module asks: "If a sophisticated, well-capitalized adversary knew our exact portfolio, what would they do to maximize our losses?"

This is modeled as a minimax game:

maxadversary minportfolio Loss(portfolio, adversary_action) Where: adversary_action is drawn from the set of feasible market actions: - Large directional trades that move prices against our positions - Withdrawal of liquidity in our key markets - Information release that triggers regime transitions - Coordinated action with other large participants

The adversary is constrained to be realistic: they cannot violate market mechanics or regulations, but they CAN exploit knowledge of our positions (the "crowded trade" scenario).

6.2 Adversarial Scenario Generation

Attack Vector 1: Position Crowding

Find positions where we (and likely others) are concentrated. Large holder exits trigger stop-losses and margin calls.

def generate_adversarial_scenarios(portfolio): scenarios = [] # Attack vector 1: Position crowding for position in portfolio.positions: if position.size > market_depth(position.asset).daily_volume × 0.1: scenarios.append(AdversarialScenario( type="CROWDED_EXIT", target=position, mechanism="Large holder exits, triggering stop-losses and margin calls", our_vulnerability=position.size / market_depth(position.asset).daily_volume, estimated_impact=compute_crowded_exit_impact(position, portfolio) ))

Attack Vector 2: Correlation Exploitation

Find hidden correlations that would hurt us. Stress correlations diverge significantly from normal-regime correlations.

# Attack vector 2: Correlation exploitation stress_correlations = compute_stress_correlation_matrix(portfolio) normal_correlations = compute_normal_correlation_matrix(portfolio) correlation_surprises = find_largest_divergences( stress_correlations, normal_correlations ) for surprise in correlation_surprises: scenarios.append(AdversarialScenario( type="CORRELATION_BREAKDOWN", assets=surprise.asset_pair, mechanism=f"Correlation shifts from {surprise.normal_corr:.2f} " f"to {surprise.stress_corr:.2f}", estimated_impact=compute_correlation_impact(surprise, portfolio) ))

Attack Vector 3: Liquidity Trap

Find positions that become illiquid under stress. Market depth evaporates; position becomes untradeable.

# Attack vector 3: Liquidity trap for position in portfolio.positions: stress_liquidity = liquidity_model.stress_depth(position.asset) if position.days_to_exit(stress_liquidity) > 10: scenarios.append(AdversarialScenario( type="LIQUIDITY_TRAP", target=position, mechanism="Market depth evaporates; position becomes untradeable", days_trapped=position.days_to_exit(stress_liquidity), estimated_impact=compute_trapped_position_impact(position, portfolio) ))

Attack Vector 4: Basis Risk

Find hedges that fail under stress. Hedge effectiveness can drop catastrophically in correlated stress events.

# Attack vector 4: Basis risk for hedge_pair in portfolio.identified_hedges: basis_risk = compute_basis_risk_under_stress(hedge_pair) if basis_risk.hedge_effectiveness < 0.5: scenarios.append(AdversarialScenario( type="HEDGE_FAILURE", hedge=hedge_pair, mechanism=f"Hedge effectiveness drops from " f"{hedge_pair.normal_effectiveness:.0%} to " f"{basis_risk.hedge_effectiveness:.0%}", estimated_impact=basis_risk.unhedged_exposure )) return sorted(scenarios, key=lambda s: s.estimated_impact, reverse=True)

7 Monte Carlo Simulation Layer

7.1 Path Generation Architecture

The Monte Carlo layer generates 10,000 forward paths per simulation cycle. Paths are NOT simple geometric Brownian motion. They incorporate:

Regime-switching dynamics

Each path draws from the fragment transition probability matrix. At each time step, the path may undergo a regime transition with probability given by the World Model.

Fat tails

Return distributions use a mixture model -- normal returns 85% of the time, drawn from a Student-t distribution with 4 degrees of freedom 12% of the time, and drawn from a jump-diffusion process 3% of the time.

Correlation regime-switching

Cross-asset correlations are drawn from the correlation regime associated with the current fragment state. In stress regimes, correlations increase (the well-documented "correlations go to 1 in a crisis" phenomenon).

Reflexivity

Paths incorporate feedback loops. A large drawdown triggers margin calls, which trigger forced selling, which triggers further drawdown. The simulation models these cascading effects.

def generate_path(portfolio, horizon, dt=1/252): path = [current_state()] t = 0 while t < horizon: current = path[-1] # Step 1: Check for regime transitions for fragment in fragments: transition_prob = world_model.transition_probability( fragment, current.regime[fragment], dt ) if random.random() < transition_prob: current.regime[fragment] = sample_new_regime( fragment, current.regime[fragment] ) # Regime transition triggers correlation update current.correlation_matrix = get_regime_correlation( current.regime ) # Step 2: Generate returns dist_type = sample_distribution_type() # normal / fat-tail / jump if dist_type == 'normal': returns = multivariate_normal( current.expected_returns, current.correlation_matrix × current.vol_vector ) elif dist_type == 'fat_tail': returns = multivariate_t( current.expected_returns, current.correlation_matrix × current.vol_vector, df=4 ) elif dist_type == 'jump': returns = multivariate_normal(...) + jump_component(current.regime) # Step 3: Apply reflexivity portfolio_pnl = compute_portfolio_pnl(portfolio, returns) if portfolio_pnl < -margin_buffer × 0.5: # Margin pressure → forced selling → additional market impact forced_selling_impact = compute_forced_selling( portfolio, portfolio_pnl, current.market_depth ) returns += forced_selling_impact # Feedback loop # Step 4: Update state new_state = apply_returns(current, returns) path.append(new_state) t += dt return path

7.2 Simulation Frequency and Triggers

The Monte Carlo runs on two schedules:

Scheduled runs: Full 10,000-path simulation every 15 minutes during market hours, every hour outside market hours.

Triggered runs: Immediate re-simulation when:

  • Any fragment transitions to a new regime
  • Portfolio composition changes (new trade, position closed)
  • A scheduled macro data release occurs (NFP, CPI, FOMC)
  • VIX moves more than 2 points in any 30-minute window
  • Any position approaches a risk limit

8 Scenario Memory

8.1 The Scenario Ledger

Every scenario that reaches evaluation (survives pruning) is logged in a persistent Scenario Ledger with full metadata:

ScenarioLedgerEntry = { scenario_id: uuid, created_at: timestamp, fragment_vector: dict, probability_at_creation: float, sus_score: float, pre_computed_response: PlaybookRef, # Tracking fields (updated as reality unfolds) did_occur: bool, occurrence_date: timestamp | null, actual_impact: float | null, predicted_impact: float | null, prediction_error: float | null, # actual - predicted response_executed: bool, response_effectiveness: float | null, # Meta-learning fields was_novel: bool, # No historical analog existed was_pruned_initially: bool, # Was this pruned and later restored? surprise_factor: float, # How surprised was the system? }

8.2 Accuracy Tracking and Calibration

The Scenario Memory system tracks prediction accuracy across three dimensions:

Impact Accuracy

When scenario X occurred, did the predicted P&L impact match reality?

impact_accuracy = 1 - median( abs(actual_impact - predicted_impact) / abs(actual_impact) for scenario in occurred_scenarios ) Target: impact_accuracy > 0.70 (within 30% of actual impact)

Probability Calibration

Of the scenarios assigned 10% probability, did roughly 10% occur?

For each probability bucket [0-5%, 5-15%, 15-25%, ...]: assigned_count = count(scenarios in bucket) occurred_count = count(scenarios in bucket that occurred) calibration_error = abs(occurred_count/assigned_count - bucket_midpoint) Target: calibration_error < 5% for each bucket

Coverage Tracking

What fraction of actual significant events were pre-explored in the scenario tree?

coverage = count(significant_events that matched a pre-explored scenario) / count(all significant_events) Target: coverage > 0.85 (at most 15% of significant events should be surprises)

8.3 Scenario Evolution Rules

Based on the Scenario Memory, the engine evolves its scenario generation over time:

Rule 1 -- Miss Incorporation: When a significant event occurs that was NOT in the scenario tree, the engine permanently adds that event class to its generation rules.

Example: March 2023 -- SVB failure was not in the scenario tree.
Action: Added "Regional bank failure cascade" as a permanent scenario class. Sub-scenarios: Single bank failure, Regional contagion, Systemic bank stress. These are now evaluated in every N-1 and N-2 contingency cycle.
Rule 2 -- Probability Recalibration: When the calibration tracking shows systematic over- or under-estimation of probabilities for certain scenario types, the transition probability matrices are adjusted.

Example: The system consistently assigned 2% probability to credit spread blowouts, but they occurred 5% of the time.
Action: Multiplicative recalibration of credit stress transition probabilities by factor 2.5.
Rule 3 -- Impact Model Correction: When impact predictions are systematically biased (typically underestimating), the evaluation function is recalibrated.

Example: Liquidity stress impacts were underestimated by 40% on average.
Diagnosis: The liquidity model used normal-regime market depth estimates even in stress scenarios.
Fix: Added regime-conditional market depth to the liquidity scoring model.
Result: Impact accuracy improved from 0.55 to 0.78.
Rule 4 -- Pruning Audit: Quarterly review of pruned scenarios that subsequently occurred. Any pattern of dangerous pruning triggers a modification to the pruning heuristics.

Example: Three scenarios were pruned as "low probability" that subsequently occurred within the same quarter.
Analysis: All three involved the Geopolitical fragment, which had been assigned overly stable transition probabilities.
Fix: Reduced the probability pruning threshold for Geopolitical scenarios from 0.5% to 0.1%.

10 Design Principles (Axiomatic)

1

Asymmetric attention

The system spends 80% of its compute on downside scenarios and 20% on upside. Survival comes first; opportunity comes second.

2

Never prune the catastrophic

Any scenario that can lose more than 10% of NAV stays in the tree regardless of probability. The PM may choose to ignore it; the system may not.

3

Pre-compute, don't predict

The system does not claim to know which scenario will occur. It claims to have a good response ready for whichever one does.

4

Path over destination

A scenario that ends at -5% but passes through -30% is more dangerous than one that ends at -10% smoothly. Drawdown paths matter because they trigger margin calls, forced selling, and behavioral errors.

5

Reflexivity is real

The system models the fact that its own actions (and those of similar portfolios) affect market outcomes. A hedge that "everyone" is putting on is not actually a hedge -- it is a crowded trade that will unwind violently.

6

Novelty is danger

The most dangerous scenario is the one that has never happened before, because no one is positioned for it, no hedges exist for it, and no playbook covers it. The system deliberately over-invests in exploring novel scenarios.

7

Memory makes it smarter

Every scenario that actually occurs -- whether predicted or missed -- improves the system. The feedback loop from Scenario Memory to Scenario Generation is the primary learning mechanism.

8

The PM decides, the system prepares

The SBE never executes trades. It presents options, costs, and tradeoffs. The PM retains full agency. The system's job is to ensure the PM is never in a position where they have to make a critical decision without having thought about it before.

Innovation Deep Dive

Opponent & Flow Modeling

Abstract

Financial markets are heterogeneous ecosystems populated by participants with fundamentally different objective functions, constraint sets, time horizons, and information processing capabilities. The Opponent & Flow Modeling framework provides a systematic methodology for decomposing observed market flows into their constituent participant-level components, modeling the constraints that force specific behaviors, and identifying the interaction dynamics that create predictable cascade patterns. By treating each market participant class as an agent with observable signatures, quantifiable constraints, and modelable behavioral responses, we transform the opaque aggregate of "the market" into a transparent network of identifiable, anticipatable flows.

The Multi-Participant Market Ecosystem (MPME) framework developed here integrates nine distinct participant taxonomies, a flow decomposition engine, behavioral constraint models, crowding metrics, interaction graphs, Schelling point detection, and predictive flow calendars into a unified system for understanding and anticipating market microstructure dynamics. This framework is designed not merely as an analytical tool but as a source of persistent, structural alpha derived from understanding who must do what and when.

1. Participant Taxonomy

1.1 Design Principles

Submarine Sonar Analogy: Just as a submarine identifies surface vessels through their acoustic signatures — propeller cavitation patterns, hull resonance frequencies, engine harmonics — a sophisticated market participant can identify counterparties through their trading signatures. Each participant class leaves a distinctive "acoustic" footprint in the data: order timing, size clustering, instrument selection, and reaction patterns to exogenous events.

Every participant class in our taxonomy is defined by four core components:

1. Objective Function

What the participant is trying to optimize: return maximization, risk minimization, mandate tracking, hedging exposure, or policy implementation.

2. Constraint Set

The binding restrictions that limit degrees of freedom: regulatory requirements, mandate rules, risk limits, capital constraints, behavioral biases.

3. Observable Signatures

The data trails each participant class leaves: regulatory filings, order flow patterns, positioning data, timing regularities.

4. Behavioral Model

The mathematical or heuristic model that maps states to actions: reaction functions, replication portfolios, decision rules.

1.2 The Nine Participant Classes

CLASS 1

Central Banks

Objective Function

Price stability (inflation targeting, typically 2%), financial stability, and in some jurisdictions a dual mandate including maximum employment. Central banks operate as the ultimate macro-level participant whose actions cascade through every asset class.

Constraint Set
  • Political constraints: Central bank independence varies by jurisdiction; communication must balance transparency with forward guidance optionality
  • Institutional constraints: Balance sheet composition limits, collateral eligibility frameworks, legal mandates
  • Communication constraints: FOMC dot plots, press conferences, minutes release schedules create pre-committed information revelation points
Observable Signatures
  • COFER data: IMF Currency Composition of Official Foreign Exchange Reserves (quarterly, 6-month lag)
  • H.4.1 release: Federal Reserve balance sheet (weekly)
  • SOMA holdings: System Open Market Account (monthly)
  • NLP of speeches: Sentiment analysis of FOMC member communications (real-time)
  • OIS curves: Overnight index swap pricing of rate path expectations (real-time)
  • Swap line usage: USD liquidity provision to foreign central banks (weekly)
  • TIC data: Treasury International Capital flows (monthly, 2-month lag)
Behavioral Model

Regime-switching Taylor rule reaction function incorporating real-time inflation expectations, output gap estimates, and financial conditions. The model captures the shift between hawkish and dovish regimes via Markov-switching dynamics. Forward guidance is modeled as a state-contingent commitment device that constrains near-term policy path variance.

Detection Protocol

Monitor OIS-implied policy rates vs. stated forward guidance for divergence signals. Track FOMC member speech frequency and hawkish/dovish score shifts relative to blackout periods. Detect balance sheet operation changes via H.4.1 weekly deltas exceeding 2-sigma from trend.

CLASS 2

CTAs / Trend Followers

Objective Function

Capture persistent price trends across asset classes through systematic momentum strategies. CTAs seek to extract returns from the tendency of prices to continue in their established direction, profiting from both uptrends and downtrends across commodities, fixed income, equities, and FX.

Constraint Set
  • Moving average lookback windows: Typically 3-month and 12-month crossover signals; shorter signals (10/50-day) for faster funds
  • Inverse-volatility position sizing: Position size = target risk / (asset vol x notional), creating mechanical scaling
  • Portfolio volatility target: 10–15% annualized portfolio volatility, hard-coded in risk management systems
  • Daily rebalancing requirement: Position adjustments computed end-of-day, executed at close or next open, creating predictable timing
Observable Signatures
  • CFTC Commitments of Traders (COT): Weekly positioning data for managed money across futures markets
  • CTA index returns: SG CTA Index, Barclay CTA Index correlation with trend signals
  • Moving average levels: Key MA crossover points where mechanical buying/selling triggers
  • Volume patterns: Elevated volume near MA crossover points, clustered at session close
Behavioral Model

Replication portfolio: Construct a replica CTA portfolio using known signal parameters (3m/12m MA crossover, inverse-vol sizing to 12% vol target). Track replica vs. SG CTA Index returns. When replica correlates >0.85, the model is well-calibrated.

Trigger level computation: For each major futures market, compute the price levels where MA crossovers flip signals. These are the levels where CTAs must buy or sell, regardless of fundamental conditions.

Detection Protocol

Monitor the distance between current price and key MA crossover levels. When price approaches within 1% of a crossover level, flag potential CTA flow. Volume clustering at session close on crossover days confirms CTA participation.

Calibration

Correlation of 0.85+ between replica portfolio returns and SG CTA 3m/12m crossover strategy. Estimated AUM: $350 billion. Back-test validation: correctly predicted direction of CTA flow in 78% of MA crossover events since 2010.

CLASS 3

Risk Parity / Vol-Targeting Funds

Objective Function

Maintain a constant portfolio volatility target, typically 10–12% annualized. Risk parity funds allocate capital inversely proportional to each asset's realized volatility, while vol-targeting funds mechanically lever or delever the entire portfolio to hit a fixed risk budget.

Constraint Set
  • Mechanical deleveraging: When realized vol exceeds target, positions must be cut — no discretion, no timing optimization, pure mechanical response
  • 1–3 month lookback: Realized vol calculated over 1 to 3 months of daily returns; shorter windows create faster, more violent responses
  • Procyclical dynamics: Selling into falling markets (rising vol) and buying into rising markets (falling vol) creates a systematic feedback loop
Observable Signatures
  • VIX correlation: Strong negative correlation between VIX changes and estimated risk parity equity exposure (ρ ≈ −0.70)
  • AUM estimates: $200 billion+ in dedicated risk parity strategies; additional $500B+ in vol-targeting overlays
  • Deleveraging events: Sharp equity selling coincident with vol spikes, particularly when 1-month realized vol breaches 20%
Behavioral Model

Replica portfolio: Construct a 4-asset risk parity replica (equities, bonds, commodities, gold) with inverse-vol weighting targeting 10% portfolio vol. The deleveraging curve maps realized vol levels to equity exposure reductions:

Vol < 12%: Full allocation (leverage 1.5-2.0x) Vol 12-16%: Begin reduction (-5% exposure per 1% vol increase) Vol 16-20%: Accelerated reduction (-8% exposure per 1% vol increase) Vol > 20%: Emergency deleveraging (-12% exposure per 1% vol increase) Vol > 30%: Near-zero equity exposure, all-bonds allocation
Detection Protocol

When 1-month realized vol crosses above 15%, activate risk parity deleveraging monitor. Estimate selling flow = AUM x leverage x delta(exposure)/delta(time). Confirm with equity futures volume spikes during European/early US session (typical execution window).

CLASS 4

Passive / Index Funds

Objective Function

Minimize tracking error relative to a benchmark index. Passive funds have a single, unambiguous objective: replicate the performance of their target index as closely as possible, making their behavior the most deterministic of all participant classes.

Constraint Set
  • Exact weight matching: Must hold securities in precisely the weights specified by the index methodology
  • Rebalancing triggers: Index reconstitution dates (Russell in June, S&P quarterly), corporate actions, IPOs, delistings
  • Target-date glidepath: For target-date funds, a pre-determined equity-to-bond glide schedule based on years to retirement
  • Cash management: Must invest inflows and raise cash for outflows within 1-2 days to minimize tracking error
Observable Signatures
  • ETF creation/redemption baskets: Daily authorized participant activity showing exact fund flows (T+1)
  • 13F filings: Quarterly holdings showing exact replication portfolios
  • Fund flow reports: ICI weekly, EPFR daily, showing aggregate passive flow direction
  • Russell reconstitution: Annual June event with $100B+ in notional rebalancing, announced weeks in advance
Behavioral Model

Deterministic rebalancing: Given index methodology, every rebalancing trade can be computed exactly in advance. For the Russell reconstitution, the adds/deletes list is published weeks before implementation, allowing precise flow prediction.

Target-date glidepath: For a fund with 20 years to target date, the equity allocation follows a pre-published schedule (e.g., 90% equity at T-20, declining ~2% per year). Monthly rebalancing to glidepath creates a steady, predictable flow from equities to bonds as the cohort ages.

Detection Protocol

Track ETF creation/redemption vs. NAV premium/discount. Large creation activity (premium) indicates passive inflows; large redemption activity (discount) indicates outflows. Confirm with ICI weekly flow data and EPFR daily estimates.

CLASS 5

Dealer Hedging Desks

Objective Function

Maintain delta-neutral positioning on the firm's options book. Dealer desks do not express directional views — they exist to warehouse client option positions and hedge away directional risk, creating mechanical flows that are entirely determined by the structure of outstanding options positions.

Constraint Set
  • Gamma-dependent hedging frequency: Hedging frequency scales with gamma exposure; near-expiry, high-gamma positions require continuous rehedging
  • Basel III capital requirements: Risk-weighted asset calculations constrain total book size and leverage
  • VaR limits: Daily Value-at-Risk caps force position reduction when market volatility spikes
  • Intraday risk limits: P&L stop-losses and delta limits create forced hedging within the trading day
Observable Signatures
  • Options open interest (OI): Exchange-reported OI by strike and expiry reveals the structure of dealer inventory
  • Gamma Exposure (GEX) estimates: Computed from OI data — net dealer gamma at each strike level
  • CFTC large trader data: Dealer/intermediary positions in futures (weekly)
  • Strike pinning: Price clustering near high-OI strikes approaching expiration reveals dealer hedging flow
  • Vanna and charm flows: Predictable hedging flows driven by changes in implied volatility and time decay
Behavioral Model
GEX Computation: GEX = Σ (OI_call_i × Γ_call_i - OI_put_i × Γ_put_i) × 100 × S² × 0.01 Gamma Flip Level: Level where aggregate dealer gamma transitions from positive to negative. Above flip: dealer hedging dampens moves (buy dips, sell rallies) Below flip: dealer hedging amplifies moves (sell into declines, buy into rallies) Hedging Flow per 1% Move: ΔF = GEX × 0.01 × S At GEX = +$5B: 1% down move triggers ~$50M in dealer buying (stabilizing) At GEX = -$5B: 1% down move triggers ~$50M in dealer selling (amplifying) Vanna/Charm Estimates: Vanna flow = Σ OI_i × Vanna_i × ΔIV Charm flow = Σ OI_i × Charm_i × Δt
Detection Protocol

Compute GEX daily from options OI data. Track the gamma flip level and current distance from it. When price crosses the gamma flip level from above, expect transition from stabilizing to destabilizing dealer flows. Monitor intraday hedging via futures volume correlation with delta changes.

Calibration

Back-test GEX model against intraday S&P 500 reversals: in positive gamma regimes, intraday reversals from 0.5% moves occur 72% of the time vs. 38% in negative gamma regimes. Gamma flip level correctly predicted regime shifts in 85% of cases since 2018.

CLASS 6

Discretionary Hedge Funds

Objective Function

Generate absolute returns uncorrelated with market beta, typically targeting 8–15% net annualized returns with a Sharpe ratio above 1.0. Discretionary funds employ fundamental analysis, event-driven strategies, macro themes, and conviction-based positioning.

Constraint Set
  • VaR and risk limits: Internal risk budgets (typically 1–3% daily VaR) constrain position sizes
  • Redemption cycles: Quarterly or monthly redemption windows create forced selling pressure when performance deteriorates
  • Factor exposure limits: Risk models cap exposure to known factors (momentum, value, size, quality, volatility)
  • Behavioral constraints: Anchoring, loss aversion, herding into consensus positions, career risk driving closet indexing
Observable Signatures
  • 13F filings: Quarterly equity holdings with 45-day lag — reveals crowded positions, sector tilts, and concentration
  • Prime broker (PB) data: Aggregated long/short ratios, gross/net exposure, sector tilts (Goldman, Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan reports)
  • Crowding metrics: HF ownership concentration, 13F overlap scores, factor crowding indices
  • Short interest: Exchange-reported short positions (bi-monthly), securities lending data (daily)
Behavioral Model

Positioning surveys: Aggregate PB data into HF net equity exposure index (0–100 percentile). Extremes (>90th or <10th percentile) indicate crowded positioning vulnerable to unwind.

Factor crowding analysis: Compute overlap between HF portfolio factor exposures and known factor indices. High overlap (>0.70 correlation) indicates crowded factor bets prone to simultaneous unwind.

13F analysis: Track quarter-over-quarter changes in top holdings across the 100 largest equity hedge funds. Identify stocks where hedge fund ownership exceeds 25% of float (crowding risk).

Residual flow estimation: Total observed flow minus estimated mechanical flows (CTA + risk parity + passive + dealer) = residual attributed to discretionary + retail.

Detection Protocol

Monitor PB aggregate exposure data daily. When gross leverage exceeds 250% and net exposure exceeds 70%, flag elevated crowding risk. Track 13F filing changes for concentration shifts. Redemption pressure indicators: fund return drawdown > 5% approaching quarter-end.

CLASS 7

Corporate Hedgers

Objective Function

Reduce or eliminate exposure to specific financial risks (FX, interest rate, commodity price) that could impact operating earnings. Corporate hedging programs are designed to reduce cash flow volatility, not to profit from market moves.

Constraint Set
  • Treasury policy mandates: Board-approved hedging policies specifying instruments, tenors, and minimum/maximum hedge ratios
  • Hedge ratios: Typically 50–100% of next 12 months' projected exposure, with declining ratios for further-out quarters
  • Instrument restrictions: Many corporates limited to vanilla forwards and options; exotic instruments require special approval
  • FASB hedge accounting rules: ASC 815 requirements for hedge effectiveness testing constrain strategy flexibility; losing hedge accounting treatment has material P&L consequences
Observable Signatures
  • 10-K/10-Q disclosures: Notional hedging amounts, maturity schedules, hedge instruments used (annual/quarterly)
  • Seasonal hedging patterns: Airlines hedge jet fuel Q1 for full-year coverage; food companies hedge grain post-harvest
  • FX forward activity: Quarter-end hedging roll activity concentrated in last 2 weeks of quarter
Behavioral Model

Hedging calendars: Map corporate fiscal year-ends, budget cycles, and hedging policy roll dates to predict hedging flow timing. US multinationals with December fiscal year-end concentrate EUR/JPY hedging in Q4. Mining companies roll commodity hedges on a quarterly cycle aligned with production schedules.

Detection Protocol

Monitor FX forward points at quarter-end for unusual demand. Track seasonal patterns in commodity options buying by sector. Cross-reference 10-K hedging disclosures with observed options/forward activity timing.

CLASS 8

Retail Traders

Objective Function

Heterogeneous and often poorly defined. Retail objectives range from long-term wealth accumulation to short-term speculation, social media-driven momentum plays, and lottery-ticket option buying. Unlike institutional participants, retail traders frequently lack a coherent optimization framework.

Constraint Set
  • Regulation T margin: 50% initial margin, 25% maintenance — creates forced liquidation at deterministic price levels
  • Behavioral biases: Disposition effect (sell winners early, hold losers), overconfidence, recency bias, herding
  • Social media influence: Reddit (WallStreetBets), Twitter/X, TikTok financial influencers create coordinated positioning surges
  • Call buying preference: Persistent retail preference for buying short-dated, out-of-the-money call options, creating asymmetric gamma exposure for dealers
Observable Signatures
  • Retail order flow: SEC Rule 606 reports, PFOF (payment for order flow) data from wholesalers (Citadel, Virtu)
  • Options skew anomalies: Retail call buying compressed call-side skew; unusual small-lot options activity (1–10 contracts)
  • Social media metrics: Reddit mention frequency, Twitter ticker volume, Google Trends, Stocktwits sentiment
  • Meme stock ETF flows: BUZZ ETF, MEME ETF, Robinhood top-held lists as real-time retail attention proxies
Behavioral Model

Sentiment-driven flow model: Retail flow = f(social media volume, recent returns, option implied volatility attractiveness). Positive feedback loop: price up → social media volume up → retail buying → price up.

Gamma squeeze dynamics: When retail buys large volumes of short-dated calls, dealers must delta-hedge by buying the underlying. If the stock rises, dealer delta increases, requiring more buying, creating a reflexive squeeze.

Disposition effect model: Retail sells at a higher rate when positions are profitable (anchored to purchase price). This creates predictable selling pressure as stocks approach round-number prior highs.

Detection Protocol

Monitor options OI for small-lot call buying surges (>3x normal volume in <$10 premium strikes). Track social media mention acceleration (Reddit, Twitter). Cross-reference with retail broker platform data (when available) and small-lot order flow from wholesaler reports.

CLASS 9

Sovereign Wealth Funds (SWFs)

Objective Function

Long-term real wealth preservation and intergenerational transfer. SWFs invest sovereign savings (typically commodity revenues or trade surpluses) with multi-decade horizons, targeting real returns of 3–5% above inflation while maintaining capital preservation.

Constraint Set
  • Strategic Asset Allocation (SAA) bands: Board-approved allocation ranges per asset class (e.g., equities 40–60%, fixed income 20–30%, alternatives 10–20%)
  • Geographic allocation targets: Home bias, diversification mandates, sanctions-compliant investment universes
  • Currency hedging policy: Typically partial hedge (30–70%) of foreign currency exposure, creating predictable FX flows
  • ESG mandates: Increasingly binding exclusion lists (coal, tobacco, weapons) and engagement requirements
Observable Signatures
  • Annual reports: NBIM, GIC, ADIA, CIC publish allocation data with 6–12 month lag
  • 13F filings: US equity holdings reported quarterly (NBIM, GIC are top filers)
  • COFER data: IMF reserve composition data captures SWF currency allocation shifts
  • Block trade activity: SWFs trade in large blocks — unusual block activity in low-vol names during Asian/European hours suggests SWF flow
Behavioral Model

Allocation shift model: When oil prices rise, oil-exporting SWFs (Norway, Abu Dhabi, Kuwait) receive larger inflows, which must be allocated per SAA targets. Estimate inflow = f(oil price, production volume, fiscal breakeven) and allocate across asset classes per published SAA weights.

Rebalancing flow estimation: When equities outperform bonds by >5% in a quarter, SWFs at the top of their SAA equity band must sell equities and buy bonds. Estimate rebalancing flow = AUM × (current weight − target weight) for NBIM ($1.7T), GIC ($700B+), ADIA ($900B+).

Detection Protocol

Monitor block trade activity in European morning session (SWF execution window). Track NBIM real-time equity benchmark vs. actual performance for rebalancing timing. Cross-reference COFER data with FX forward market flows for currency hedging activity.

Participant Interaction Network

2. Flow Decomposition Engine

2.1 Architecture: Three Time Scales

Tick-Level (Microseconds to Minutes)

Market microstructure: order flow imbalance, trade classification (Lee-Ready), toxicity metrics (VPIN), queue position dynamics. Dominated by HFT and dealer hedging flows.

Session-Level (Hours to Days)

Participant-attributed flow decomposition: CTA signals, risk parity deleveraging, passive rebalancing, retail sentiment surges. The primary time scale for our MPME framework.

Multi-Day (Weeks to Months)

Structural positioning shifts: SWF allocation changes, central bank policy regimes, corporate hedging cycles, passive fund flow trends. Drives medium-term return forecasts.

2.2 Decomposition Methodology

The core decomposition equation attributes total price change to the weighted sum of individual participant flows:

dP(t) = Σi=1..N λi(t) · Fi(t) + ε(t) Where: dP(t) = observed price change at time t λi(t) = price impact coefficient for participant i at time t Fi(t) = estimated flow from participant i at time t ε(t) = residual (unattributed flow + noise) N = number of participant classes (9 in our taxonomy) Price impact coefficients are time-varying and depend on: - Market liquidity (bid-ask spread, depth) - Participant urgency (VWAP vs. market orders) - Correlation with other flows (cascade amplification) Estimation: Kalman filter with regime-switching λi dynamics Validation: Out-of-sample R² > 0.60 at session level, > 0.45 at daily level

2.3 Worked Example: S&P 500 −2% Session

Consider a session where the S&P 500 declines 2%. Our flow decomposition engine attributes the move as follows:

Participant Class Estimated Contribution Confidence Mechanism
CTA / Trend Followers 40% HIGH 50-day MA breached; mechanical selling triggered across $350B AUM
Dealer Gamma Hedging 25% HIGH GEX flipped negative at 4,480; dealer selling amplified decline
Risk Parity / Vol-Target 15% MEDIUM 1-month realized vol crossed 18%; deleveraging curve activated
Discretionary HF 12% LOW Estimated from residual flow minus mechanical components
Retail 8% MEDIUM Put buying surge + margin call liquidation (Reg T triggers)
Forward Implications:
  • CTA (next 1–3 days): 200-day MA at 4,350 is next trigger level. If breached, additional $15–20B in CTA selling estimated. Distance to trigger: 1.2%.
  • Dealer (next 24h): GEX will become more negative as puts gain delta approaching expiry. Expect continued amplification until post-OpEx gamma unwind.
  • Risk Parity (next 1–5 days): If realized vol remains above 18%, additional 3–5% exposure reduction expected over next week. Total selling estimate: $8–12B.
  • Discretionary (next 1–4 weeks): Gross leverage at 235%; below forced deleveraging threshold (250%). Watch quarter-end redemption window in 3 weeks.
  • Retail (next 1–2 days): Social media sentiment at 6-month low. Historically, retail capitulation at sentiment extremes precedes 3–5 day bottoms.

Net Assessment: This session's decline was 65% mechanically driven (CTA + dealer + risk parity), meaning the "fundamental" catalyst accounts for only 35% of the observed price change. The mechanical nature of the dominant flows creates a specific forward path: if the 200-day MA holds, CTA selling pressure abates; if it breaks, expect a further 3–5% cascade as all three mechanical participants accelerate. The key variable is realized vol over the next 3 trading days — if it mean-reverts below 15%, risk parity reverses from seller to buyer, creating a powerful V-shaped recovery setup.

3.2 Forced Flow Detection

These are the specific triggers that force participants to trade regardless of market conditions or fundamental views:

Trigger Participant Signal Estimated Magnitude
MA Crossover CTAs Price crosses 50/200-day MA or 3m/12m crossover flips $15–30B per major asset class
VIX Spike >25 Risk Parity 1-month realized vol exceeds target by >50% $10–20B equity selling over 1–5 days

3.3 Constraint Interaction Matrix

The most dangerous market episodes occur when constraints across multiple participant classes trigger simultaneously, creating cascade effects. Here is the canonical cascade sequence:

Cascade Example: The Volatility Doom Loop
1 &rdarr; CTA Mechanical Selling: Price crosses below 50-day MA → CTAs sell $15–20B across equity futures
2 &rdarr; Volatility Spike: CTA selling drives prices lower → realized volatility increases from 12% to 18%
3 &rdarr; Risk Parity Deleveraging: Vol exceeds target → risk parity sells $8–12B in equities over 3 days
4 &rdarr; Negative Gamma Activation: Price falls below gamma flip level → dealers must sell into decline
5 &rdarr; Dealer Hedging Cascade: Dealer selling drives price further down → more gamma exposure → more selling. Self-reinforcing until gamma exhausted at next major strike cluster.

Total amplification: The initial CTA trigger of $15–20B generates a total cascade flow of $40–60B over 3–5 days. The price impact is 2–4x what the initial trigger alone would produce. Stopping condition: price reaches a major put strike cluster (pin zone) or a value buyer threshold absorbs selling pressure.

4. Crowding and Positioning Model

4.1 Four Crowding Metrics

FCI — Factor Crowding Index

Measures the degree to which hedge fund portfolios are concentrated in the same factor exposures (momentum, value, quality, size, volatility). Computed from 13F overlap analysis and PB aggregate exposure data.

Calibration:
FCI > 0.70 preceded the August 2007 Quant Quake (factor crowding unwind), the February 2018 VIX spike (vol-short crowding), and the March 2020 COVID crash (momentum crowding in growth/tech). In all three episodes, the crowded factor experienced a >3 standard deviation reversal within 5 trading days.
PCS — Position Concentration Score

Measures the concentration of hedge fund positioning in individual names. Computed as the percentage of float held by hedge funds (from 13F data) weighted by the number of funds holding the position.

Calibration:
PCS > 0.30 (i.e., hedge funds collectively hold >30% of float) has preceded an average 12% drawdown within 60 days in 68% of historical instances. The top-20 most crowded names underperform the market by 3–5% per quarter.
SIC — Short Interest Concentration

Measures the severity of short-side crowding. Days-to-cover (short interest / average daily volume) indicates how long it would take to close all short positions at normal trading volume.

Calibration:
SIC > 10 days-to-cover has been associated with 85% of historical short squeeze events (defined as >20% price appreciation in <10 trading days). GameStop (Jan 2021): days-to-cover reached 17, preceding a 1,600% price spike.
OPS — Options Positioning Skew

Measures the imbalance between call and put open interest, weighted by gamma. Extreme call skew indicates speculative long positioning (gamma squeeze potential); extreme put skew indicates hedging demand (crash protection).

Calibration:
Extreme call skew (>2 standard deviations) preceded the unwinding of meme stock gamma squeezes with >50% declines in 78% of cases. Extreme put skew (>2 SD) preceded VIX mean-reversion rallies within 10 days in 72% of cases.

4.2 Exit Congestion Model

When crowded positions unwind, the critical question is whether exit liquidity is sufficient. The Exit Congestion Ratio (ECR) measures this:

ECR = Estimated Position Size / (Average Daily Volume × Participation Rate) Where: Estimated Position Size = total HF holdings (from 13F) or short interest Average Daily Volume = 20-day ADV in shares Participation Rate = maximum fraction of volume a liquidating seller can capture (typically 10-20%) Thresholds: ECR < 3: Orderly exit likely; position can unwind in <3 days ECR 3-5: Some price impact; expect 2-5% adverse move during exit ECR 5-10: Significant exit congestion; expect 5-15% adverse move ECR > 10: Severe congestion; orderly exit unlikely, probable gap/cascade
Reflexive Spiral: When ECR > 5, exits become self-defeating. Selling pressure drives the price lower, triggering stop-losses at other holders, which increases selling volume, which further depresses the price. This reflexive dynamic means that the actual exit cost can be 2–5x the static ECR estimate. The model incorporates a reflexivity multiplier: Effective ECR = Static ECR × (1 + ρ × ln(Static ECR)) where ρ captures the reflexivity coefficient (calibrated at 0.3–0.6 for equity markets).

5. Interaction Graph

5.1 Feedback Loop Taxonomy

Amplifying Loops (Positive Feedback)

1. Gamma Cascade

Amplification factor: 1.5–3.0x

→ Price decline below gamma flip → dealer short gamma → dealer sells futures to hedge → price declines further → more delta to hedge → more selling

Historical examples: February 5, 2018 (XIV blow-up, 4.1% SPX decline amplified by negative gamma); March 2020 (sustained negative gamma regime amplified COVID selling by estimated 1.8x); September 2020 ("SoftBank whale" — massive call buying created positive gamma squeeze of 2.5x).

2. Volatility Spiral

Amplification factor: 1.3–2.5x

→ Price decline → realized vol increases → risk parity deleverages → selling drives price lower → vol increases further → more deleveraging

Historical examples: August 2015 (China devaluation triggered risk parity cascade, 11% S&P drawdown over 6 days); Q4 2018 (Fed hawkishness + trade war triggered 20% drawdown with significant risk parity amplification).

3. Liquidity Vacuum

Amplification factor: 2.0–5.0x

→ Forced selling → market makers widen spreads / reduce depth → price impact per unit flow increases → more stop-losses triggered → more forced selling into thinner book

Historical examples: Flash Crash May 2010 (liquidity evaporated, amplification reached 5x for brief period); Treasury Flash Rally October 2014 (12-sigma move in 12 minutes as depth collapsed).

4. Retail Gamma Squeeze

Amplification factor: 3.0–10.0x

→ Retail buys OTM calls → dealers delta-hedge by buying stock → price rises → call delta increases → dealers buy more stock → short sellers forced to cover → price spikes → more social media attention → more retail call buying

Historical examples: GameStop January 2021 (1,600% move, estimated 8x amplification from gamma + short squeeze); AMC June 2021 (500% move, 5x amplification); Multiple "meme stock" episodes 2021–2024.

Dampening Loops (Negative Feedback)

1. Value Buyer Absorption

Dampening factor: 0.3–0.7x

→ Price declines to value threshold → fundamental buyers step in (pension funds, endowments, corporate buybacks) → buying absorbs forced selling flow → price stabilizes

Activation condition: price reaches value-based support levels (e.g., forward P/E at cycle lows, dividend yield at 2+ standard deviations). Typically absorbs 30–70% of mechanical selling over 2–5 days.

2. Dealer Positive Gamma

Dampening factor: 0.5–0.8x

→ Price rises above gamma flip level → dealer long gamma → dealers sell rallies and buy dips → price oscillation dampened → realized vol compressed

This is the default regime for ~60% of trading days. Positive gamma environments exhibit lower realized vol, smaller intraday ranges, and more frequent mean-reversion. The "pinning" effect near high-OI strikes is the clearest manifestation.

3. Central Bank Backstop

Dampening factor: 0.5–1.0x (can fully arrest cascades)

→ Market stress exceeds threshold → central bank intervenes (rate cuts, QE, emergency facilities, forward guidance) → liquidity injection stabilizes funding markets → risk premium compression → selling pressure absorbed

The "Fed put" has been the ultimate dampening mechanism since 1987. However, it is the least predictable in timing and magnitude, and its effectiveness depends on the nature of the stress (monetary policy is less effective against real economic shocks).

5.2 Cascade Probability Estimator

The Fragility Score combines four factors into a single 0–100 score estimating the probability of a cascade event:

Fragility Score = w1 × GammaRegime + w2 × VolState + w3 × CrowdingLevel + w4 × LiquidityDepth Where: GammaRegime (0-25): 0 = strong positive gamma, 25 = deep negative gamma VolState (0-25): 0 = VIX <12, 25 = VIX >30 CrowdingLevel (0-25): 0 = no crowding, 25 = FCI >0.70 and PCS >0.30 LiquidityDepth(0-25): 0 = deep book, 25 = book depth <20% of 90-day average Weights: w1 = w2 = w3 = w4 = 1.0 (equal weighting; tuned via backtest)

Calibration: Since 2010, the fragility score has exceeded 80 on 12 occasions. Of these 12, 10 were followed by a >3% drawdown within 10 trading days (83% hit rate). The two misses occurred when the central bank backstop activated before the cascade could develop (September 2019 repo crisis, March 2023 SVB — in both cases, Fed intervention within 48 hours arrested the cascade). Average drawdown following score >80: 6.2%. Average time to drawdown trough: 8 trading days.

6. Schelling Point Detector

6.1 Concept

A Schelling point is a focal price level where multiple participant classes coordinate — not through communication, but through shared awareness of the same technical, structural, and calendar features. These levels act as gravitational attractors during normal markets and breakout triggers during stressed markets. Identifying Schelling points in advance reveals where the market is most likely to pause, reverse, or accelerate.

6.2 Technical Level Clustering

Multiple technical reference points cluster at specific price levels, creating focal points for participant attention:

  • Round numbers: Psychological levels (S&P 4,000; 4,500; 5,000) attract attention and order clustering from all participant classes
  • Moving averages: 50-day, 100-day, 200-day MAs serve as CTA trigger levels and widely-watched support/resistance
  • Prior highs/lows: All-time highs, 52-week highs/lows, prior swing points serve as reference for discretionary traders
  • Fibonacci retracement levels: 38.2%, 50%, 61.8% retracements of major moves concentrate technical trader attention
Technical Density Score (TDS): TDS(P) = Σi wi × exp(-|P - Li|² / 2σ²) Where: P = price level being evaluated Li = technical reference level i (MA, round number, prior high/low) wi = weight (round numbers: 1.0, 200-day MA: 2.0, ATH: 1.5) σ = proximity bandwidth (typically 0.5% of price) High TDS (>3.0) indicates a major Schelling point with multiple technical levels clustered.

6.3 Options Strike Concentration

Options open interest concentrations create "pinning" effects as dealers hedge around high-OI strikes:

  • Pinning mechanism: As expiration approaches, dealer hedging around high-OI strikes creates a gravitational pull. If price is above a high-OI call strike, dealer selling caps upside; if below, dealer buying provides support.
  • Pin Risk Score: Computed as the ratio of OI at a given strike to total OI across all strikes. Strikes with >5% of total OI have significant pinning potential. Combined call + put OI at a single strike creating a "magnet" effect.

6.4 Calendar Focal Points

Recurring calendar events create temporal Schelling points where participant attention concentrates:

FOMC Meetings

8 per year. Pre-meeting positioning, statement release vol spike, press conference gamma. Typical VIX compression 2 days before, expansion on release.

Options Expiration

Monthly (3rd Friday), quarterly (triple/quad witch). Gamma unwind post-expiry creates directional moves. Quad witch is the largest single-day volume event.

Index Rebalancing

Russell (June), S&P (quarterly), MSCI (quarterly). Pre-announced, deterministic flows creating predictable price impact on adds/deletes.

Month-End / Quarter-End

Pension fund rebalancing, window dressing, FX hedging rolls. Last 2–3 days of month see systematic flow from institutional rebalancing.

Earnings Season

4 weeks starting mid-January, April, July, October. Elevated single-stock vol, sector rotation, guidance-driven positioning shifts.

6.5 Confluence Score

The Confluence Score integrates all three Schelling point sources into a single measure of focal-point strength at any given price level and time:

Confluence(P, t) = α × TDS(P) + β × PinRisk(P) + γ × CalendarProximity(t) Where: TDS(P) = Technical Density Score at price P PinRisk(P) = Options pinning risk at price P (function of OI, DTE, gamma) CalendarProximity(t) = Weighted sum of approaching calendar events α, β, γ = Calibrated weights (0.35, 0.40, 0.25 respectively) Interpretation: Confluence < 1.0: Weak focal point; price likely to pass through Confluence 1.0-2.0: Moderate; expect some pause/reaction Confluence 2.0-3.0: Strong; likely support/resistance, reversal probable Confluence > 3.0: Extreme; major Schelling point, high-conviction level

7. Predictive Flow Calendar

7.1 Architecture: Three Flow Categories

Deterministic Flows

Timing and direction are known in advance with high confidence. Can be computed exactly.

  • Index reconstitution (Russell June, S&P quarterly)
  • Options expiration gamma unwind
  • Futures roll windows
  • Dividend reinvestment dates
  • Target-date fund glidepath rebalancing
Conditional Flows

Direction depends on market state; timing is known but magnitude is state-contingent.

  • Quarter-end rebalancing (direction depends on asset return dispersion)
  • CTA trigger levels (known levels, direction depends on which side crossed)
  • Vanna/charm flows (known timing, direction depends on IV level)
  • Month-end pension rebalancing
Probabilistic Flows

Timing and direction depend on market conditions; modeled as probability distributions.

  • Risk parity deleveraging (conditional on vol state)
  • HF redemption flows (conditional on performance)
  • Retail gamma squeeze (conditional on social media momentum)
  • Central bank intervention (conditional on stress level)
