7.3 Alert Framework

GREEN Alerts (Informational)

Upcoming deterministic flows. No immediate action required but awareness needed.

Example: "Russell reconstitution adds/deletes list published. Net buying in adds estimated at $3.2B. Implementation on June 28. Top 5 adds: [list]. Top 5 deletes: [list]."

AMBER Alerts (Conditional)

State-contingent flows approaching trigger levels. Action may be needed if conditions evolve.

Example: "CTA trigger level at SPX 4,480 (200-day MA). Current price: 4,510. Distance: 0.7%. If breached, estimated selling: $18B over 48h. Risk parity deleveraging conditional on resulting vol spike."

RED Alerts (Active)

Active forced flow event. Cascade risk elevated. Immediate positioning review recommended.

Example: "CTA 200-day MA breached at 10:42 ET. GEX turned negative at 4,475. Risk parity deleveraging estimated to begin within 24h. Fragility score: 78 (SEVERE). Cascade probability: 65%. Recommended: reduce gross exposure, add tail hedges, prepare to fade at 4,350 (next Schelling point)."

8. Information Edge: From Modeling to Alpha

8.1 Informed vs. Uninformed Flow

The critical distinction in flow analysis is between informed flow (driven by new information or superior analysis) and uninformed flow (driven by constraints, mandates, or behavioral patterns). Our framework primarily targets uninformed flow, which is:

  • Predictable: Constraint-driven flows follow deterministic rules that can be modeled in advance
  • Non-informational: These flows do not reflect new fundamental information — they represent mechanical portfolio adjustments
  • Temporary: Once the constraint is satisfied, the flow stops. Price impact from uninformed flow tends to partially reverse
  • Sizeable: Mechanical flows often dwarf fundamental-driven flows, especially during stress events
The Alpha Proposition: If 60–70% of short-term market flow is mechanically driven, and if these mechanical flows are partially predictable, then the information required to generate alpha is not "what will earnings be?" but "what will CTAs, dealers, and risk parity do next?" This reframes the alpha problem from fundamental forecasting to flow forecasting — a domain where structural analysis dominates.

8.2 Five Specific Trade Structures

Trade Structure 1

Front-Running Mechanical Flows

Expected edge: 50–150 bps per event  |  Frequency: 20–40 events per year

Position ahead of known deterministic flows: index additions (buy the add before passive funds must execute), Russell reconstitution (buy adds / sell deletes before rebalancing date), futures roll (position for roll premium/discount). The edge comes from executing before the constrained participants must act.

Risk management: Size positions to limit loss to 30 bps if the flow fails to materialize. Use limit orders to manage execution. Accept that crowding in this strategy compresses the edge over time — rotate across asset classes and events.

Trade Structure 2

Fading Mechanical Selling

Expected edge: 1–3% per event  |  Win rate: 65–75%

When the flow decomposition engine identifies that a price decline is dominated by mechanical selling (CTA + risk parity + dealer ≥60% of attributed flow), position for mean reversion once the mechanical flow exhausts. The key is timing: buy when the mechanical selling is 70–80% complete (estimated from position size models and volume analysis).

Entry criteria: Flow attribution ≥60% mechanical, price at or near a Schelling point (confluence score >2.0), fragility score declining from peak, volume profile showing exhaustion (decreasing volume on down ticks).

Trade Structure 3

Crowding Unwind

Expected edge: 3–10% per event  |  Frequency: 2–5 events per year

When crowding metrics (FCI >0.70, PCS >0.30, ECR >5) indicate extreme positioning, establish positions that profit from the unwind. Short the most crowded names (high HF ownership, high factor loading), buy the neglected mirror names. Use options to limit downside while maintaining convexity to large unwind events.

Historical edge: Long neglected / short crowded portfolio has generated 8–12% per year over the past 15 years, with the returns heavily concentrated in 2–3 unwind events per year. Sharpe approximately 0.7–1.0 with significant positive skew.

Trade Structure 4

Expiration Flow Capture

Expected edge: 0.5–2% per event  |  Frequency: 12 events per year (monthly OpEx)

Exploit the predictable gamma unwind that occurs at options expiration. In positive gamma regimes, sell volatility ahead of expiry (premium decay accelerates); in negative gamma regimes, buy volatility or position for the post-expiry directional move. Vanna and charm flows create predictable patterns in the 3–5 days before expiry.

Key insight: The transition from pre-expiry (high gamma, pinning, compressed vol) to post-expiry (gamma vacuum, directional freedom, vol expansion) creates a regime change that is both predictable in timing and tradeable in magnitude.

Trade Structure 5

Discretionary vs. Mechanical Conflict

Expected edge: 2–5% per event

The highest-conviction trades occur when discretionary (informed) and mechanical (uninformed) flows point in opposite directions. When the flow decomposition shows mechanical selling driving prices lower while discretionary HF positioning is increasing (informed buyers accumulating), the mechanical flow creates an entry point for informed buying. Position with the informed flow, expecting price to reverse when mechanical flow exhausts.

Detection: Monitor the residual flow component (discretionary estimate) for divergence from aggregate flow direction. When residual is positive during aggregate selling, informed accumulation is occurring.

8.3 Edge Decay and Adaptation

Why is this edge durable rather than arbitraged away? Four structural reasons:

  1. Mandate-driven constraints are permanent. CTAs must follow their signals. Risk parity must target vol. Passive funds must track indices. These mandates are fiduciary obligations that cannot be relaxed, ensuring the flows recur perpetually.
  2. Scale mismatch. The participants generating mechanical flows manage trillions. The capital available to exploit them is orders of magnitude smaller. Even if every flow trader front-runs a Russell reconstitution, the $100B+ in passive rebalancing flows dwarfs the front-running capital.
  3. Timing uncertainty. While we can identify trigger levels and calendar events, the exact timing of conditional flows depends on market state. This uncertainty limits crowding in the exploitation strategy itself.
  4. Multi-dimensionality. The full MPME framework integrates 9 participant classes, dozens of data sources, and complex interaction dynamics. Partial replication captures some edge but the full system’s value exceeds the sum of its parts due to interaction effects and cascade modeling.

9.2 Calibration and Validation

1. Historical Back-Test

Run flow decomposition on historical sessions with known outcomes. Validate attribution accuracy against post-hoc analysis. Target: ≥60% session-level R², ≥70% correct cascade prediction.

2. Out-of-Sample Validation

Rolling 12-month out-of-sample tests for all signal models. Walk-forward optimization to prevent overfitting. Report degradation metrics vs. in-sample performance.

3. Event Study Analysis

Study each forced flow trigger (MA crossover, OpEx, VIX spike, etc.) across 100+ historical instances. Compute average hit rate, edge, and decay profile. Reject strategies with <55% hit rate or <0.3 Sharpe.

4. Real-Time Paper Trading

6-month live paper trading before capital deployment. Track signal accuracy, execution slippage, and edge realized vs. modeled. Adjust position sizing and timing based on observed performance.

10. Conclusion

The Opponent & Flow Modeling framework transforms the portfolio manager's view of markets from a single aggregate entity into a transparent ecosystem of identifiable participants with modelable behaviors. By decomposing flows into their constituent components, mapping the constraints that force specific actions, and modeling the interaction dynamics that create cascades, we create an information advantage that is structural rather than ephemeral. The key insight is that the majority of short-term market flow is not driven by new fundamental information but by mechanical portfolio adjustments dictated by mandates, risk limits, and behavioral patterns that are observable and predictable.

The integration of these components — participant taxonomy, flow decomposition, constraint modeling, crowding analysis, interaction graphs, Schelling point detection, and predictive flow calendars — is itself the edge. Any single component can be replicated; the synthesis cannot. The system provides not just a model of what has happened but a framework for anticipating what must happen next, converting structural market knowledge into persistent, repeatable alpha across multiple time horizons and trade structures. This is the foundation upon which the full Reflexive Constructive World Model builds its market understanding: knowing who is doing what, why they must do it, and when they will be forced to act.

INNOVATION DEEP DIVE

Portfolio Health Score

Part of the RecWM Ten-Layer Innovation Stack

Design Philosophy

The NEWS2 score saves lives in hospitals because it reduces six continuous physiological variables to a single integer that any nurse can act on. A score of 5 means "increase monitoring frequency." A score of 7 means "call the rapid response team." No interpretation required. No ambiguity. The escalation protocol is hardwired to the number.

RecWM's Portfolio Health Score (PHS) applies the same architecture to financial portfolios. Seven fragment vital signs, each scored 0–3 based on deviation from regime-normal ranges, compose into a single 0–21 base score. An interaction penalty of up to +9 captures dangerous multi-fragment stress combinations. A portfolio-conditioning layer adjusts the score relative to the PM's actual positions. A trajectory classifier projects where the score is heading. The result is a single number, updated continuously, that tells the PM: "Your portfolio is this healthy, relative to the state of the world, right now."

The design draws from six systems that have solved the early warning problem in other domains:

NEWS2Hospital medicineAdditive scoring bands with escalation protocols
APACHE IIICU severityChronic condition modifiers (portfolio-specific conditioning)
MEWSWard deteriorationSimplicity enables adoption; catches decline 6–24h early
Power grid frequencyEnergySingle number encodes system-wide supply/demand balance
F1 tire degradationMotorsportCliff detection — sudden failure after gradual decline
TCASAviationEscalating alerts with specific evasive action instructions

1.1 Liquidity Fragment

Primary Metric: Composite Liquidity Stress Index (CLSI)

The CLSI blends three signals into a single z-score:

  • Dealer inventory capacity (40% weight): Primary dealer net positions as a fraction of trailing 12-month average, sourced from NY Fed weekly reports interpolated daily via proxy (corporate bond ETF bid-ask spreads and Treasury repo rates). When dealers are stuffed, new risk absorption is constrained.
  • Bid-ask resilience (35% weight): Median bid-ask spread across the portfolio's top-20 holdings, normalized by trailing 60-day median. Captures real-time liquidity available to THIS portfolio, not abstract market liquidity.
  • Funding spread (25% weight): 3-month SOFR-OIS spread plus cross-currency basis (EUR/USD, JPY/USD). Captures wholesale funding stress that propagates into asset price liquidity with a 2–5 day lag.
ScoreCLSI z-scoreLabelInterpretation
0−1.0 to +1.0NormalLiquidity conditions unremarkable
1+1.0 to +1.5Mildly stressedSpreads widening, execution costs rising
2+1.5 to +2.5Moderately stressedDealer capacity constrained, large orders will move markets
3> +2.5Severely stressedMarket-making withdrawal underway, liquidation would incur significant slippage
Historical calibration: CLSI hit 3 in Sept 2008 (Lehman), March 2020 (COVID), March 2023 (SVB week). It hit 2 in Aug 2007 (quant quake), Dec 2018 (Fed tightening selloff), Sept 2019 (repo spike). False positives at score 2: approximately 4 per year. False positives at score 3: approximately 0.5 per year.

1.2 Momentum Fragment

Primary Metric: Regime Coherence Index (RCI)

The RCI measures whether price momentum across asset classes is coherent (trending together in an interpretable pattern) or incoherent (contradictory signals suggesting regime transition).

  • Trend strength (35% weight): Average absolute value of 20/60/120-day momentum z-scores across the portfolio's factor exposures (equity beta, duration, credit, commodity). High absolute values = strong trend. Near-zero = no trend. The danger zone is moderate-and-declining.
  • CTA trigger proximity (35% weight): Distance of key asset prices from known CTA trend-following entry/exit levels (estimated via SocGen CTA index replication). When multiple assets are near CTA flip points simultaneously, mechanical flow can create cascades.
  • Passive flow pressure (30% weight): Month-end / quarter-end rebalancing pressure estimated from known index reconstitutions, pension rebalancing calendars, and option expiry gamma exposure.
ScoreRCI ConditionLabelInterpretation
0Coherent trend, no CTA triggers nearStable trendMomentum tailwind or headwind is clear and persistent
1Weakening coherence OR 1–2 CTA triggers nearTrend softeningMomentum regime may be shifting; conviction should decrease
2Incoherent signals AND multiple CTA triggers nearRegime transitionHigh probability of abrupt momentum reversal within 5 days
3Active CTA cascade detected AND passive flow opposingMomentum crisisMechanical flows dominating price discovery; fundamental signals unreliable

1.3 Risk Fragment (Volatility)

Primary Metric: Vol Surface Distortion Score (VSDS)

Rather than using VIX level alone (which captures only ATM implied vol for SPX), VSDS measures the shape of the volatility surface relative to its own history.

  • Skew steepness (30% weight): 25-delta put/call skew for SPX, normalized by 2-year rolling percentile. Steep skew = demand for downside protection is elevated.
  • Term structure inversion (35% weight): Ratio of 1-month to 3-month implied vol. When short-dated vol exceeds long-dated vol, markets are pricing imminent risk. This is the single most reliable vol-based crisis indicator.
  • Realized-implied gap (35% weight): Difference between trailing 10-day realized vol and 30-day implied vol. When realized exceeds implied, hedging is underpriced. When implied massively exceeds realized, fear is elevated but not yet confirmed by price action.
ScoreVSDS ConditionLabelInterpretation
0Skew normal, term structure normal contango, realized < impliedCalmVol surface consistent with normal risk appetite
1Skew elevated (>75th pctile) OR mild term structure flatteningNervousMarket is pricing incrementally more risk than fundamentals suggest
2Skew extreme (>90th pctile) AND term structure invertedFearfulDemand for crash protection is acute; vol selling is dangerous
3Term structure deeply inverted AND realized > implied AND cross-asset vol correlation >0.8PanickedVol regime shift underway; all correlations going to 1

1.4 Credit Fragment

Primary Metric: Credit Cascade Probability (CCP)

Credit stress is uniquely dangerous because it exhibits threshold effects — stable, stable, stable, then sudden repricing as a critical mass of credits breach distress thresholds.

  • Spread velocity (40% weight): 5-day rate of change in IG and HY OAS, normalized by trailing 60-day vol of spread changes. Velocity matters more than level because spread levels can persist at elevated ranges (e.g., 2001–2003) without crisis, but rapid widening signals information arrival.
  • Default probability clustering (35% weight): Fraction of CDS names in the CDX IG/HY indices with >200bps 5Y CDS spread. When this fraction crosses 10% for IG or 25% for HY, the distribution of defaults shifts from idiosyncratic to correlated.
  • Crossover migration rate (25% weight): Trailing 90-day rate of downgrades from BBB to BB (the "fallen angel" pipeline). This captures the slow buildup of credit stress that precedes acute crises by 3–6 months.
ScoreCCP ConditionLabelInterpretation
0Spread velocity < 1σ, clustering < 5% IG / 15% HYNormalCredit markets functioning normally
1Spread velocity 1–2σ OR clustering approaching thresholdsTighteningCredit conditions deteriorating; new issuance may slow
2Spread velocity > 2σ AND clustering above thresholdsStressCredit market access impaired for weaker borrowers; contagion risk rising
3Spread velocity > 3σ AND clustering >15% IG / >35% HY AND fallen angel pipeline acceleratingCrisisCredit market dysfunction; self-reinforcing downgrade/spread-widening loop probable

1.5 Structure Fragment (Market Microstructure)

Primary Metric: Structural Fragility Index (SFI)

Captures the mechanical and structural features of markets that amplify or dampen shocks.

  • Gamma exposure (GEX) (40% weight): Net market-maker gamma exposure estimated from options open interest. When GEX is deeply negative, dealer hedging amplifies moves. When GEX is deeply positive, dealer hedging dampens moves. The absolute magnitude and sign both matter.
  • Rebalancing pressure (30% weight): Estimated forced buying or selling from systematic strategies (risk parity, vol targeting, CTA) given recent price moves. Computed from AUM estimates, known strategy rules, and recent returns.
  • Market depth (30% weight): Top-of-book depth in SPX futures (E-mini and Micro) relative to trailing 60-day average. Thin books magnify the impact of any flow.
ScoreSFI ConditionLabelInterpretation
0GEX positive, no rebalancing pressure, depth normalStabilizingMarket structure is dampening volatility
1GEX near zero OR moderate rebalancing pressureNeutralStructure neither helping nor hurting
2GEX negative AND rebalancing pressure in same direction as recent moveAmplifyingMarket structure is amplifying moves; overshoots likely
3GEX deeply negative AND heavy rebalancing selling AND depth < 50% of normalCascadingStructural cascade risk is acute; flash-crash conditions possible

1.6 Sentiment Fragment

Primary Metric: Positioning Divergence Score (PDS)

Sentiment is dangerous not when everyone is bearish or bullish, but when positioning is extreme AND divergent from narrative (everyone says they're cautious but positioning data shows they're levered long).

  • Positioning consensus (40% weight): CFTC commitment of traders net speculative positioning in major futures, aggregated across equity, rates, and FX. Extreme readings indicate crowded trades vulnerable to unwinds.
  • Narrative divergence (30% weight): Gap between NLP-derived sentiment from sell-side research, financial media, and earnings calls vs. actual positioning data. When the narrative is bearish but positioning is bullish, the unwind when narrative is confirmed will be violent.
  • Put-call ratio / fear-greed composite (30% weight): CNN Fear & Greed analogue built from put/call ratio, VIX term structure, junk bond demand, stock price breadth, and safe haven demand. Extreme readings in either direction are scored as stressed.
ScorePDS ConditionLabelInterpretation
0Positioning moderate, narrative-position alignedBalancedNo crowding risk; sentiment consistent with positioning
1Positioning extended OR mild narrative divergenceLeaningCrowd is developing; reversal risk incrementally higher
2Positioning extreme AND narrative divergentCrowded-and-complacentClassic contrarian setup; unwind trigger unknown but impact will be large
3Positioning at historical extremes AND narrative violently divergent AND fear-greed at extremeFragile consensusAny catalyst will trigger aggressive repositioning; the crowd is on the wrong side

1.7 Policy Fragment

Primary Metric: Policy Surprise Potential (PSP)

Policy risk is fundamentally about surprises — known policy is priced; surprises are not.

  • Hawkish/dovish score (30% weight): NLP-derived central bank communication score tracking the hawk-dove spectrum for Fed, ECB, BOJ, and PBOC. Calibrated against historical rate decisions. The score measures not the level but the delta — how much more hawkish/dovish than the market expects.
  • Policy surprise probability (40% weight): Implied probability of a rate move different from market pricing, derived from options on SOFR futures. When the options market is pricing a bimodal outcome (hold vs. emergency cut), this spikes.
  • Fiscal impulse (30% weight): Trailing 6-month change in cyclically-adjusted primary deficit as a fraction of GDP, for US, EU, China, and Japan. Fiscal impulse is the most underappreciated macro variable because it moves slowly and is not priced until it is.
ScorePSP ConditionLabelInterpretation
0Communication consistent with market pricing, low options-implied surprise probabilityPricedNo material policy surprise risk
1Mild communication shift OR options pricing bimodalShiftingPolicy path may diverge from consensus within 1–2 meetings
2Significant communication shift AND high surprise probability AND fiscal impulse reversingDivergingPolicy surprise within next meeting is probable; positioning for consensus path is risky
3Emergency language detected OR inter-meeting action priced >30% OR major fiscal reversal underwayCrisis-modeCentral bank in reactive mode; policy is a source of volatility, not stability

2. The Composite Health Score

2.1 Base Score Computation

The base Portfolio Health Score is the sum of all seven fragment scores:

PHSbase = L + M + R + C + S + Se + P

Where L=Liquidity, M=Momentum, R=Risk, C=Credit, S=Structure, Se=Sentiment, P=Policy.

Range: 0 to 21.

Unlike APACHE II (which uses complex weighting), the base score is unweighted additive, following the NEWS2 design. The reasoning: in NEWS2, weighting was tested extensively and found to add complexity without improving predictive accuracy. The power of the score comes from aggregation across independent systems, not from fine-tuning weights. The interaction penalty (Section 3) captures the nonlinear effects that weighting would attempt to approximate.

2.2 Single-Fragment Trigger

Following NEWS2's "single parameter score of 3" rule: any individual fragment score of 3 automatically elevates the composite to at least CAUTION level (score 9), regardless of the base sum. This prevents a critical failure in one system from being masked by calm readings in others.

Implementation: PHSeffective = max(PHSbase + interaction_penalty, 9) if any fragment = 3.

2.3 Composite Score Interpretation

PHS RangeLevelColorMeaning
0–4NOMINALGreenWorld conditions are benign relative to portfolio. Normal operations.
5–8ELEVATEDYellowOne or more fragments showing stress. Increased vigilance warranted.
9–12CAUTIONAmberMultiple stress signals or one critical signal. Active risk review required.
13–16WARNINGOrangeSystemic stress developing. Hedging and de-risking should be actively considered.
17–21CRITICALRedRare, extreme stress. Crisis protocols. Historical frequency: <2% of trading days.
22–30CRITICAL+Dark RedInteraction penalties pushing score beyond base maximum. Multi-system cascade. 2008/2020 territory.

3. The Interaction Penalty

3.1 Rationale

In 2008, liquidity stress alone was manageable. Credit stress alone was manageable. But liquidity stress + credit stress created a self-reinforcing spiral: credit losses forced selling, selling overwhelmed liquidity, illiquidity forced mark-to-market losses, losses triggered more selling. The interaction was more dangerous than the sum of the parts.

The interaction penalty captures these nonlinear combinations. It is added to the base score.

3.2 Dangerous Pair Interactions

Each pair interaction is computed as: penalty = weight × min(scoreA, scoreB), where the penalty only applies when both fragment scores are ≥ 2. This ensures the penalty activates only when both fragments are meaningfully stressed.

Liquidity
+ Credit
Weight: 1.5x
The death spiral. Illiquidity makes credit losses real; credit losses destroy liquidity. 2008 GFC: Lehman bankruptcy created simultaneous liquidity freeze and credit repricing.
Risk
+ Structure
Weight: 1.5x
Gamma cascade. Negative gamma + vol spike = dealer hedging amplifies the move, which increases vol, which increases hedging. Feb 2018 Volmageddon.
Momentum
+ Structure
Weight: 1.0x
CTA cascade into thin markets. Systematic momentum reversal into poor market depth. Aug 2015: China deval triggered CTA selling into illiquid markets.
Credit
+ Sentiment
Weight: 1.0x
Crowded credit unwind. Everyone positioned for carry simultaneously; exit is a stampede. March 2020: IG credit ETFs gapped to massive discounts.
Policy
+ Risk
Weight: 1.0x
Policy shock into elevated vol. Surprise policy move when vol is already high creates non-linear repricing. Dec 2018 Fed hike; June 2022 75bp surprise.
Liquidity
+ Structure
Weight: 0.75x
Illiquidity amplified by structural fragility. Poor depth + negative gamma + wide spreads. March 2020 Treasury market: record vol in the "safest" asset.
Sentiment
+ Momentum
Weight: 0.75x
Crowded momentum unwind. Consensus positioning in a trending market reverses violently. Jan 2021: GameStop / short squeeze cascade.

3.3 Triple Interaction: The Crisis Triad

When three specific fragments are simultaneously at score ≥ 2, an additional +3 penalty applies:

Liquidity (≥ 2) + Credit (≥ 2) + Structure (≥ 2) = +3 additional penalty
This is the 2008 pattern: credit losses + liquidity freeze + structural amplification (forced selling from leveraged vehicles). When all three activate, the system is in a self-reinforcing crisis mode.

Maximum theoretical interaction penalty: +9 (all dangerous pairs at max + crisis triad). This means the theoretical maximum PHS = 21 (base) + 9 (interaction) = 30.

3.4 Penalty Computation Example

Scenario

Liquidity=2, Credit=3, Risk=2, Structure=2, Momentum=1, Sentiment=1, Policy=0.

Base score: 2 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 11

Interaction penalties (both fragments ≥ 2):

  • Liquidity(2) + Credit(3): 1.5 × min(2, 3) = 3.0
  • Risk(2) + Structure(2): 1.5 × min(2, 2) = 3.0
  • Liquidity(2) + Structure(2): 0.75 × min(2, 2) = 1.5
  • Crisis triad (L=2, C=3, S=2): +3.0

Total interaction penalty: 3.0 + 3.0 + 1.5 + 3.0 = 10.5, capped at 9.

PHSfinal = 11 + 9 = 20 CRITICAL+

This correctly identifies a scenario with the 2008 fingerprint as extreme, even though no individual fragment is at its theoretical maximum of 3.

4. Portfolio-Specific Conditioning

4.1 The Exposure Vector

The raw PHS describes the state of the world. The conditioned PHS describes the state of the world relative to this portfolio. A long-vol portfolio is healthy when the Risk fragment spikes. A short-vol portfolio is critical.

The conditioning layer computes a portfolio sensitivity vector:

S = [sL, sM, sR, sC, sS, sSe, sP]

Where each si is a signed multiplier in the range [−1.0, +2.0]:

  • si = 1.0: Portfolio has average sensitivity to this fragment (default)
  • si > 1.0: Portfolio is MORE exposed than average (e.g., concentrated credit portfolio has sC = 1.5–2.0)
  • si = 0.0: Portfolio is neutral to this fragment (e.g., market-neutral equity portfolio has near-zero sM)
  • si < 0.0: Portfolio BENEFITS from this fragment's stress (e.g., long-vol portfolio has sR = −0.5, meaning vol spikes reduce its health risk)

4.2 Sensitivity Derivation

FragmentSensitivity Derived FromExample
Liquidity (sL)Portfolio-weighted average daily volume / position size. Concentrated illiquid positions → higher sL$500M in small-cap: sL = 1.8
Momentum (sM)Net beta + trend-following factor loading. High beta, pro-trend → higher sM. Mean-reversion → lower.Momentum-loaded quant: sM = 1.5
Risk (sR)Net vega exposure. Long vol → negative sR. Short vol → high positive sR.Short straddle: sR = 1.8. Long puts: sR = −0.3
Credit (sC)Portfolio DTS (duration times spread). High-yield overweight → higher sC.IG-only, short dur: sC = 0.6. Levered HY: sC = 2.0
Structure (sS)Portfolio's estimated contribution to dealer gamma. Large option positions → higher sS.Delta-hedged options: sS = 1.6. Cash equity: sS = 0.4
Sentiment (sSe)Cosine similarity between portfolio factor loadings and CFTC crowded-positioning vector.Consensus tech longs: sSe = 1.5. Contrarian value: sSe = 0.3
Policy (sP)Portfolio duration + rate sensitivity. Long duration → higher sP.30Y bond OW: sP = 1.8. Bills-only: sP = 0.2

4.3 Conditioned Score Computation

PHSconditioned = Σi max(0, fragment_scorei × si) + interaction_penaltyadjusted

The max(0, ...) ensures that fragments where the portfolio benefits (negative sensitivity) contribute zero, not a negative score. We do not award health points for beneficial stress — the score is a measure of risk, not expected return.

The interaction penalty is adjusted proportionally: if both interacting fragments have sensitivities > 1.0, the penalty is amplified. If either has sensitivity < 0.5, the penalty is reduced.

4.4 Gross Exposure Modifier

A final modifier scales the conditioned score by gross exposure:

PHSfinal = PHSconditioned × exposure_multiplier
Gross Exposure (% NAV)MultiplierRationale
< 100%0.8Low leverage provides buffer
100–200%1.0Normal hedge fund leverage
200–400%1.2Elevated leverage amplifies all risks
400–800%1.5Extreme leverage (typical of macro/rates funds); small fragment moves create large P&L impact
> 800%2.0Systemic-level leverage; portfolio is a source of market risk, not just exposed to it

5. Trajectory Scoring

5.1 The Cliff Detection Problem

In F1, tire performance follows a characteristic pattern: gradual, linear degradation for 25 laps, then a sudden "cliff" where grip falls off non-linearly. The driver who pits one lap before the cliff gains 2 seconds. The driver who pits one lap after loses 15 seconds.

Portfolio health exhibits the same cliff dynamics. The 2008 crisis appeared to develop gradually through 2007 (Bear Stearns hedge funds, BNP Paribas, Northern Rock) then fell off a cliff in September 2008. The PHS trajectory system must distinguish between gradual deterioration (manageable) and approaching-cliff deterioration (requires immediate action).

5.2 Trajectory Metrics

Three metrics computed over the PHS time series:

Velocity (V): First derivative. Rolling 24-hour change in PHS.

V = PHS(t) − PHS(t − 24h)

Acceleration (A): Second derivative. Change in velocity.

A = V(t) − V(t − 24h)

Cliff Probability (CP): A trained classifier (logistic regression on historical episodes) that estimates the probability of a >5-point PHS increase within the next 48 hours, given current PHS level, velocity, acceleration, and the specific pattern of fragment scores.

The cliff probability model is trained on 20 historical crisis episodes (2000–2025) and validated on out-of-sample events. Features include:

  • Current PHS and its percentile rank over the trailing year
  • V and A values
  • Which specific fragments are contributing (some combinations are more cliff-prone)
  • Day of week and proximity to major events (FOMC, opex, quarter-end)
  • Cross-asset correlation regime (rising correlations are a cliff precursor)

5.3 Trajectory Classification

ClassSymbolCriteriaPM Implication
Stable---|V| < 1.0 AND |A| < 0.5No trajectory concern. Focus on level.
Improving↓V < −1.0 AND A ≤ 0Conditions improving. May reduce hedges.
Deteriorating↑V > 1.0 AND A ≤ 0Conditions worsening at constant rate. Monitor.
Accel. Deterioration↑↑V > 1.0 AND A > 0.5Worsening and getting worse faster. Proactive hedging recommended.
Cliff Warning⚠CP > 40% OR (V > 2.0 AND A > 1.0 AND PHS > 8)High probability of sudden, large score increase. Defensive positioning urgent.

5.4 Trajectory Override

  • A PHS of 6 (ELEVATED) with Cliff Warning trajectory is treated as CAUTION (escalated one level)
  • A PHS of 10 (CAUTION) with Accelerating Deterioration is treated as WARNING
  • A PHS of 5 (ELEVATED) with Stable trajectory and Improving trend may be de-escalated to NOMINAL after 48 hours of sustained improvement

6. The Escalation Protocol

6.1 NOMINAL (PHS 0–4)

Monitoring frequency: Fragment scores updated every 15 minutes during market hours. Composite score recomputed every 15 minutes. Full recalibration daily at 16:30 ET.

Notifications: None pushed. Daily morning briefing (07:00 ET) includes PHS summary: "Portfolio Health Score: 3 (NOMINAL). All fragments green. No trajectory concerns."

Actions available: PM can drill into any fragment for detail. Historical percentile rank shown. "Your PHS is at the 35th percentile over the trailing year — typical for low-vol summer conditions."

Staffing: Automated monitoring only. No human analyst review triggered.

6.2 ELEVATED (PHS 5–8)

Monitoring frequency: Fragment scores updated every 5 minutes. Composite score recomputed every 5 minutes. Intra-day recalibration at 09:30, 12:00, 15:00 ET.

Notifications: Score change pushed to PM dashboard with specific fragment(s) driving the elevation. Example: "PHS elevated to 6. Drivers: Liquidity(2) — bid-ask widening in EM credit holdings; Momentum(1) — CTA signals near reversal level for equity indices."

Actions recommended:

  1. Review fragment drill-down for the elevated fragments
  2. Verify hedges are current and sized appropriately
  3. Note any upcoming events that could push scores higher (FOMC in 3 days, opex Friday)

Escalation to PM: Passive — appears on dashboard. No push notification to mobile unless PHS has been ELEVATED for >4 continuous hours (suggesting persistent stress, not transient noise).

6.3 CAUTION (PHS 9–12)

Monitoring frequency: Fragment scores updated every 2 minutes. Composite updated continuously. Trajectory classification updated every 5 minutes.

Notifications: Push notification to PM mobile. Message includes: PHS value, trajectory class, top contributing fragments, and estimated P&L impact of a 1-standard-deviation adverse move in the dominant risk factor.

Example notification: "CAUTION — PHS 11 (↑↑ Accelerating). Credit(3) + Liquidity(2) + Structure(2). Interaction penalty +4.5. At current positioning, a further 50bps HY spread widening would generate −$12M P&L. Recommended: review credit hedges."

Actions triggered automatically:

  1. Scenario analysis engine generates 5 stress scenarios tailored to current fragment stress pattern
  2. Hedging recommendation engine computes optimal hedges for current risk profile
  3. Position-level risk decomposition refreshed and displayed
  4. Correlation regime monitor activated (tracking whether cross-asset correlations are rising)

Escalation chain: PM + risk manager notified. If PHS remains at CAUTION for >2 hours OR trajectory is Accelerating Deterioration, CIO is also notified.

6.4 WARNING (PHS 13–16)

Monitoring frequency: Continuous real-time. All fragments streaming. Trajectory recomputed every 60 seconds.

Notifications: Immediate push to PM, risk manager, and CIO. Audible alert on trading desk. Message includes specific recommended actions, not just information.

Example notification: "WARNING — PHS 15 (⚠ Cliff Warning). Pattern matches pre-crisis fingerprint (Liquidity+Credit+Structure interaction). Recommended immediate actions: (1) Reduce gross by 20%, prioritizing illiquid positions (2) Buy 1-week SPX put spread, $X notional (3) Close CDX HY short protection gap."

Actions triggered automatically:

  1. Pre-computed hedging trades generated with live executable prices
  2. Liquidation schedule generated: "If PHS reaches 17, sell the following positions in this order..."
  3. Counterparty exposure report generated
  4. Margin and collateral headroom calculated under stress
  5. Risk limits automatically tightened by one tier (e.g., max position size reduced 25%)

Escalation chain: PM + risk manager + CIO + COO. Conference bridge auto-opened if PHS remains at WARNING for >30 minutes.

6.5 CRITICAL (PHS 17+)

Monitoring frequency: Tick-level. Every price update recomputes relevant fragment scores.

Notifications: All hands. Flashing dashboard. SMS to all senior investment staff. The notification includes:

  • Current PHS and trajectory
  • Estimated max drawdown under current conditions (using tail-risk model)
  • Pre-computed hedge execution package (ready to send to broker with one click)
  • Comparison to historical episodes: "Current PHS pattern most closely matches March 16, 2020 (PHS peaked at 24). Portfolio drawdown in that episode from equivalent starting point: −18%."

Actions triggered automatically:

  1. Portfolio enters "defensive mode" — new position initiation blocked pending PM override
  2. All limit orders reviewed for potential adverse fills
  3. Margin excess computed hourly and projected under further stress
  4. Redemption/withdrawal pressure estimated (if fund structure relevant)
  5. Communication template generated for investors/clients

Crisis protocol:

  • PM must acknowledge alert within 15 minutes or CIO is auto-escalated
  • Every 30 minutes, PM must log a decision: "maintaining positions because X" or "reducing position Y by Z because W"
  • All decisions timestamped and stored for post-crisis review

7.2 False Positive Analysis

ThresholdDays Above (2000–2025)% of DaysFalse Positive RateActionable?
PHS > 4 ELEVATED~1,26020%N/A (monitoring)Yes — increased vigilance is appropriate 20% of the time
PHS > 8 CAUTION~63010%~60%Acceptable — cost of false CAUTION (reviewing positions) is low

The false positive rates are calibrated to match NEWS2's empirical performance: NEWS2 ≥ 7 has a positive predictive value of approximately 30% for cardiac arrest within 24 hours, but the cost of a false positive (calling the rapid response team) is much lower than the cost of a false negative (missing a cardiac arrest). The PHS applies the same asymmetric loss function.

7.3 Backtesting Framework

Monthly rolling backtest:

  1. Reconstruct PHS daily for trailing 20 years
  2. At each PHS level, compute: probability of >2%, >5%, >10% drawdown within next 5, 10, 20 trading days
  3. Compute ROC curve for each threshold
  4. Optimize threshold levels to maximize area under the curve, subject to constraints:
    • Maximum CAUTION frequency: 15% of days
    • Maximum WARNING frequency: 5% of days
    • Maximum CRITICAL frequency: 2% of days
    • Minimum lead time at CAUTION for actual crises: 48 hours (median)
  5. Recalibrate scoring bands quarterly to account for structural market changes

8. Anti-Alarm-Fatigue Design

8.1 The Core Problem

In hospitals, alarm fatigue causes 72–99% of clinical alarms to be ignored. In trading, alert fatigue is equally dangerous — the PM who gets 50 risk alerts per day reads none of them. The PHS must produce alerts that are rare enough to be noticed, specific enough to be useful, and credible enough to be trusted.

8.2 Maximum Alert Frequency

LevelMax Alerts / DayCooldownRationale
ELEVATED3 state-change notifications2 hoursPM needs to know when conditions shift, but not every fluctuation
CAUTION2 initial + hourly if sustained1 hourBalance urgency with avoiding noise
WARNING1 initial + 30-min updates + trajectory changes15 minutesHigh urgency; every update should contain new information
CRITICALContinuous until acknowledged0 (persistent)Life-or-death equivalent; cannot be silenced

8.3 Context-Aware Suppression

Known-event windows: During FOMC announcements, NFP releases, and CPI prints, the PHS suppresses ELEVATED and CAUTION notifications for a window of T−15min to T+60min, unless the score reaches WARNING. Rationale: the PM already knows volatility is coming. Alerting on expected volatility is noise. But if the score reaches WARNING, the reaction has exceeded expectations and the alert is genuine.

Event calendar integration: The system maintains a calendar of known events (FOMC, ECB, BOJ, opex, quad-witch, index rebalance, major earnings). Each event has a pre-assigned "expected vol" level. Alerts are suppressed only for score moves consistent with the expected vol. Moves exceeding the expected vol by >2 standard deviations are never suppressed.

Market hours: Score computation is continuous, but push notifications outside market hours (18:00–07:00 ET) are suppressed for ELEVATED. CAUTION notifications outside hours are batched to a single summary at 06:30 ET. WARNING and CRITICAL are never suppressed.

8.4 Information Density Requirements

Every alert must contain:

  1. The PHS value and its change since last alert
  2. The single most important driver (the fragment contributing most to the change)
  3. The portfolio-specific implication (estimated P&L impact or position at risk)
  4. One specific recommended action (not "review your portfolio" but "your CDX HY short is 40% of the score — consider adding to it or taking profit")

Alerts that cannot populate all four fields are suppressed. This prevents vague, uninformative alerts.

8.5 Credibility Tracking

The system maintains a rolling credibility score for each alert level:

Credibility = (true positives) / (true positives + false positives)

Where a "true positive" at CAUTION is defined as: a >3% portfolio drawdown occurred within 10 trading days of the alert.

If credibility drops below thresholds, the system auto-adjusts:

LevelMin CredibilityAction if Below
CAUTION25%Tighten threshold by 1 PHS point
WARNING45%Tighten threshold by 1 PHS point
CRITICAL70%Flag for manual recalibration; do not auto-adjust

This creates a self-correcting system: if the PHS is generating too many false positives at CAUTION (say, credibility drops to 20%), the threshold automatically tightens from PHS > 8 to PHS > 9. This restores credibility at the cost of slightly later detection — the correct tradeoff when the PM is beginning to ignore alerts.

8.6 The PM Trust Dashboard

A dedicated panel shows the PM:

  • Rolling 90-day alert history: how many alerts at each level, how many were "real"
  • Average lead time: when alerts did precede drawdowns, how much warning did the PM get?
  • Largest miss: the worst drawdown that occurred without a prior WARNING. This is the most important number — it tells the PM what the system's worst failure looked like.
  • Comparison to naive VIX-only system: "PHS gave you 3 additional days of warning compared to a VIX > 25 rule in 8 of 12 episodes"

This transparency is critical for trust. A PM who understands the system's track record — including its failures — will use it more effectively than one who receives alerts from a black box.

9.3 Display Design

The PHS is displayed as a single large number (font size: dominant element on screen) with:

  • Color background matching the level (green/yellow/amber/orange/red)
  • Trajectory arrow (---, ↑, ↑↑, ⚠)
  • Sparkline of the last 24 hours of PHS
  • Below: seven small fragment gauges showing individual scores (0–3 each)
  • On click/tap: drill into any fragment for the full decomposition

The design follows the power grid control room principle: the single most important number is the largest thing on the screen. Everything else is subordinate.

10. Governance and Override

10.1 PM Override

The PM can override the PHS level downward by one tier (e.g., acknowledge a WARNING as CAUTION) with a logged justification. This:

  • Reduces alert frequency to the lower tier
  • Does NOT change the displayed score (the number stays honest)
  • Requires re-acknowledgment every 4 hours
  • Is logged and included in post-incident review
The PM cannot override CRITICAL. This is the aviation principle: TCAS resolution advisories cannot be overridden by the pilot. When the system says "pull up," you pull up.

10.2 Manual Fragment Override

The PM can manually set a fragment score if they believe the automated scoring is wrong (e.g., "I know the liquidity score is 2, but I have a committed credit facility that makes me immune to this particular liquidity stress"). This:

  • Changes the composite score accordingly
  • Flags the override visually on all displays
  • Requires written justification
  • Auto-expires after 24 hours unless renewed
  • Is included in compliance reporting

10.3 Post-Incident Review

After every episode where PHS reached WARNING or higher, a structured review is conducted:

  1. Timeline reconstruction: when did each fragment first elevate?
  2. Lead time assessment: how much warning did the PM get?
  3. Action assessment: what did the PM do in response? Was it timely?
  4. False positive assessment: was the alert justified by subsequent events?
  5. Calibration adjustment: should any thresholds be changed?

This creates the feedback loop that makes the system smarter over time — the financial equivalent of the NTSB investigation process that makes aviation progressively safer.

Innovation Deep Dive

Decision Tempo Engine

Part of the RecWM Ten-Layer Innovation Stack

Executive Design Summary

The Decision Tempo Engine (DTE) is RecWM's action layer -- the system that translates the world model's continuous assessment of financial reality into decisions at the speed the portfolio manager needs. The design draws from Boyd's OODA loop, Endsley's Situational Awareness model, submarine fire control, ER triage, and F1 pit wall strategy to build a system whose central design thesis is:

The PM's edge is not being smarter. It is completing the Observe-Orient-Decide-Act cycle faster than competitors while maintaining higher decision quality. RecWM compresses cognitive latency from hours to seconds.

The fund is too small to move markets. Decision quality, not market impact, is the entire game. The DTE is engineered to maximize the ratio of decision quality to decision latency.

OODA Loop Architecture with Orientation Engine Subsystems

1. The OODA Architecture: Mapping the Loop to System Components

1.1 OBSERVE -- Financial Battlespace Awareness

The Observe phase is not a data terminal. Bloomberg is a data terminal. Bloomberg gives the PM Level 1 perception in Endsley's framework: raw numbers, prices, yields, spreads. The PM must then synthesize meaning from thousands of data points while simultaneously managing a portfolio, taking calls, and reading research. RecWM's observation layer is fundamentally different: it observes so the PM does not have to.

Data Feeds (Sensor Array)

Feed Category Sources Refresh Rate Signal Type
Price / Volume Exchange direct feeds, consolidated tape Real-time Quantitative
Order Flow Dealer inventories (TRACE, DTCC), dark pool prints T+15min to real-time Structural
Macro State FRED, BLS, Census, Treasury auctions Event-driven Regime
Positioning COT, 13F, options open interest, ETF flows Daily to quarterly Behavioral
Narrative Fed speeches, earnings calls, sell-side notes Event-driven Semantic
Cross-Asset FX, commodities, rates, equities, credit Real-time Correlation
Volatility Surface Options chains across tenors and strikes Real-time Expectation

How Observation Differs from Bloomberg

Bloomberg shows the PM 30,000 data points and says: "Here is reality." RecWM's observation layer performs three transformations that Bloomberg cannot:

1. Relevance Filtering. Of the 30,000 data points, RecWM identifies the 7-12 that are currently load-bearing for this portfolio at this moment. The rest are noise. The filter is dynamic -- what matters shifts as the regime shifts.
2. Change Detection. The observation layer does not report levels. It reports deviations from the world model's expectations. "5Y yield is 4.23%" is Bloomberg. "5Y yield is 14bp above where the model expected it given today's CPI print and current term premium" is RecWM. The deviation is the signal.
3. Cross-Domain Coherence Checking. The observation layer continuously checks whether signals across domains tell the same story. When equity vol is falling but credit spreads are widening and dealer inventories are shrinking, the observation layer flags the incoherence before the PM notices it -- often before any single-domain analyst notices it.

Observation Output Format

The observation layer does not produce a dashboard. It produces a continuously updated Observation Digest -- a prioritized list of deviations, anomalies, and coherence failures. Each entry has three fields:

[OBSERVATION] Signal: 5Y breakeven inflation dropped 8bp in 2 hours Deviation: -2.1 sigma from model expectation given current inputs Relevance: HIGH -- portfolio has long real rates position via TIPS

Only observations above a configurable deviation threshold surface to the PM. Everything else is logged but suppressed.

1.2 ORIENT -- The Schwerpunkt

Boyd identified orientation as the center of gravity of the entire OODA loop. Orientation is where information becomes understanding. It is the mental model through which the decision-maker interprets observations and generates decisions. A superior orientation enables faster and better decisions from the same observations.

RecWM's orientation engine is the single most innovative component of the Decision Tempo Engine. It is described in full in Section 2 below.

Orientation Output: Not data. Not charts. Synthesized understanding delivered in natural language with quantified confidence:

"The current macro-credit configuration most closely resembles Q4 2018 (73% similarity) -- specifically the period after the October selloff when the Fed was still guiding toward further hikes but positioning had already shifted defensive. The key difference from Q4 2018 is that dealer balance sheets are 40% smaller relative to outstanding issuance, meaning any forced selling will meet thinner bids. The implication for the current HY long position is that downside tail risk is larger than the vol surface implies. The model estimates a 23% probability of a spread-widening event exceeding 80bp in the next 30 days, versus the 11% implied by current option prices."

1.3 DECIDE -- The Decision Menu

The Decide phase presents the PM with a structured set of options, ranked by risk-adjusted expected value. The system does not decide. The PM decides. But the system compresses the cognitive work of generating and evaluating alternatives from hours to seconds.

The Decision Menu is described in full in Section 3 below.

1.4 ACT -- Action Readiness

The Act phase connects decision to execution. The gap between "I've decided" and "it's done" is where edge leaks. RecWM's action layer pre-stages execution so that once the PM decides, the action is one confirmation away.

Action Readiness System

  • Pre-Staged Orders. For each item on the Decision Menu, RecWM pre-computes the execution plan: which instruments, what size, what order type, what venue, what timing. These are stored as executable templates, not live orders.
  • Hedging Templates. For the current portfolio, RecWM maintains a library of pre-computed hedges: "To reduce duration by 0.5 years, sell $X of ZN futures" or "To hedge the credit leg, buy $Y of CDX.IG protection at current offer." These update continuously as the portfolio and market move.
  • Execution Timing. RecWM recommends optimal execution windows based on liquidity patterns: "Dealer activity peaks in the next 45 minutes based on historical patterns for this security. Delay beyond 2pm risks wider bid-ask."
  • Confirmation Protocol. The PM confirms with a single action. The system shows: what will be executed, estimated fill price, estimated slippage, estimated market impact (minimal for our size), and the portfolio state after execution.

The Kill Chain

Mapping to the military kill chain: Sensor (observation) to decision-maker (PM with orientation and decision menu) to shooter (execution). RecWM compresses this chain from a typical cycle of hours (observe in morning, orient during the day, decide in afternoon, act next morning) to minutes or seconds when needed.

Traditional Kill Chain

Bloomberg terminal → PM reads → PM thinks → PM calls desk → Desk executes

Latency: 2-8 hours typical, 30-60 minutes urgent

RecWM Kill Chain

Observation digest → Orientation synthesis → Decision menu → One-click execute

Latency: Seconds (pre-computed), Minutes (novel situation requiring PM judgment)

2. The Orientation Engine

2.1 Design Philosophy

The Orientation Engine is RecWM's replacement for the PM's internal mental model -- or more precisely, it is an augmentation of that mental model. The PM still has judgment, intuition, and experience. The Orientation Engine provides the structured analytical scaffolding that makes that judgment faster and more precise.

The engine has four subsystems, each producing a distinct type of understanding.

2.2 Historical Pattern Matching -- "This Resembles..."

The pattern matcher compares the current multi-dimensional state vector (macro regime, positioning, flows, vol surface, credit conditions, cross-asset correlations) against a library of historical episodes. It does not match on price patterns. It matches on structural configurations.

Output Format

HISTORICAL PATTERN MATCH ======================== Primary match: Q4 2018 post-October selloff (73% structural similarity) Secondary match: Q3 2015 China deval aftermath (58% similarity) Anti-match: March 2020 COVID shock (only 12% similarity despite surface-level resemblance in credit spreads) Key similarities to Q4 2018: - Fed rhetoric hawkish but positioning already shifting defensive [match: 0.89] - Credit spreads widening from tight levels without macro deterioration [match: 0.82] - Equity vol elevated but not crisis-level [match: 0.77] Key differences from Q4 2018: - Dealer balance sheets 40% smaller relative to issuance [CRITICAL] - Treasury supply schedule 3x heavier in next 60 days [SIGNIFICANT] - No equivalent to 2018 EM contagion catalyst [MODERATE] Historical outcome of Q4 2018 analog: - HY spreads widened 120bp over 8 weeks before Fed pivot - IG spreads widened 45bp - Duration rallied 35bp in 10Y once pivot signaled - Best trade: long duration + short credit (Sharpe 2.1 over 90 days)
Why this matters: The PM reads this in 30 seconds and immediately has a structural framework for interpreting today's market. Without it, building this mental model from raw data takes 2-3 hours of reading research, checking charts, and thinking.

2.3 Anomaly Detection -- "This Is Unprecedented Because..."

Not all situations match historical patterns. The anomaly detector identifies configurations that have no good historical analog and explains why.

Output Format

ANOMALY ALERT [severity: ELEVATED] =================================== The current combination of: (1) Negative term premium at -45bp (2) Credit spreads at 95th percentile tightness (3) Dealer inventory at 10th percentile lows (4) Realized vol 2x implied vol in rates ...has NO historical precedent in the post-2000 dataset. Nearest partial matches: - (1)+(2) occurred in Q1 2020 pre-COVID (spreads snapped 400bp in 3 weeks) - (2)+(3) occurred in Q2 2007 (spreads began widening 4 months later) - (1)+(4) has never co-occurred Interpretation: The market is pricing perfection in credit while rates markets are showing stress signals. This divergence is structurally unstable. The model assigns 67% probability that it resolves via credit repricing wider rather than rates calming down. Confidence: MODERATE (novel configuration reduces backtest reliability)

2.4 Narrative Coherence Engine -- "The Stories Don't Match"

Markets are driven by narratives. At any moment, multiple narratives compete. The Narrative Coherence Engine tracks the dominant narratives, identifies where they conflict, and assesses which narrative the positioning data supports.

Output Format

NARRATIVE COHERENCE REPORT ========================== Active narratives (ranked by market pricing weight): 1. SOFT LANDING (priced at ~55% by rates + equity markets) Implication: Gradual rate cuts, earnings hold up, credit fine Supporting: Employment data, consumer spending, corporate margins Contradicting: Regional bank stress, CRE defaults, manufacturing ISM 2. REACCELERATION (priced at ~25% by commodities + breakevens) Implication: No cuts, possibly more hikes, dollar strength Supporting: Services inflation sticky, wage growth, fiscal deficit Contradicting: Leading indicators declining, credit tightening 3. HARD LANDING (priced at ~15% by credit curves + vol) Implication: Rapid cuts, earnings collapse, spread blowout Supporting: Yield curve shape, loan officer survey, LEI trend Contradicting: Labor market still adding jobs 4. SYSTEMIC EVENT (priced at ~5% by tail hedging flow) Implication: Emergency response, circuit breakers, intervention Supporting: Dealer leverage, concentration risk in mag-7 Contradicting: Bank capital ratios at highs, Fed facilities in place COHERENCE SCORE: 0.42 (LOW -- narratives are unusually divergent) Critical divergence: Equity markets price soft landing while credit curves price rising default risk. Historically, when this divergence exceeds 1.5 sigma (current: 1.8 sigma), credit has been right 68% of the time. Portfolio implication: Current long-credit positioning is aligned with the equity narrative. If credit curves are right, the position faces estimated -340bp of excess spread widening.

2.5 Causal Reasoning -- "A Causes B Causes C"

The causal engine traces transmission mechanisms. It does not just correlate -- it models the structural pathways through which one event propagates to affect portfolio positions.

Output Format

CAUSAL CHAIN ANALYSIS ===================== Trigger: Bank of Japan signals faster balance sheet reduction Transmission chain: BOJ reduces JGB purchases → Japanese institutional investors repatriate from foreign bonds → Selling pressure on UST and European govies → Term premium rises 15-25bp (model estimate) → Mortgage rates rise, housing slows further → Consumer confidence drops → HY default expectations rise → Portfolio impact: -45 to -70bp on HY long position Chain confidence by link: BOJ → repatriation: HIGH (0.85) -- announced policy Repatriation → UST: HIGH (0.78) -- Japanese are largest foreign holder UST → term premium: MODERATE (0.65) -- magnitude uncertain Term premium → housing: MODERATE (0.60) -- lagged effect, 3-6 months Housing → consumer: LOW-MODERATE (0.50) -- depends on wealth effect Consumer → defaults: LOW (0.35) -- long causal chain, many offsets Overall chain probability: 18% (product of conditional probabilities) Expected portfolio impact if chain completes: -58bp (midpoint) Probability-weighted expected impact: -10bp Time horizon: 3-6 months for full chain completion Early warning indicators: Japanese MOF flow data, UST auction tail sizes

3. The Decision Menu

3.1 Design Principles

The Decision Menu is not a recommendation engine. It is a structured presentation of the PM's option space, ranked by the model's assessment of risk-adjusted expected value. The PM always decides. The system compresses the work of generating and evaluating alternatives.

The menu follows three design principles:

  1. Never more than 5 items. Miller's Law. The PM cannot evaluate more than 5 options effectively under time pressure.
  2. Every item includes its own counter-argument. No option is presented without the strongest case against it.
  3. Time sensitivity is explicit. Some decisions are time-sensitive. Others can wait. The menu distinguishes.

3.2 Decision Menu Format

3.3 Information Hierarchy

The Decision Menu uses a strict information hierarchy inspired by ER triage (ABCDE):

Layer Content When Shown
A (Airway) Is the portfolio in immediate danger? Always -- top of screen, red if yes
B (Breathing) What is the health trend? Always -- health score with direction arrow
C (Circulation) What are the top 1-3 actions? Always -- the Decision Menu
D (Disability) What assumptions are most fragile? On demand -- one click deeper
E (Exposure) Full position detail, raw data, model internals On demand -- two clicks deeper

This hierarchy ensures the PM never drowns in data. The most critical information is always visible. Detail is always available but never forced.

4. Time Pressure Mode -- Crisis Operations

4.1 Activation Criteria

Time Pressure Mode activates automatically when any of the following conditions are met:

  • Portfolio health score drops below 4.0
  • Regime transition probability exceeds 65%
  • Observation layer detects a coherence failure exceeding 2.5 sigma
  • A pre-defined scenario trigger fires (e.g., sovereign credit event, major central bank surprise, systemic counterparty stress)
  • The PM manually activates it

4.2 Crisis Display

When Time Pressure Mode activates, the interface transforms. Non-essential information is stripped. The display compresses to three panels:

Panel 1: SITUATION (left, 40% of screen)

CRISIS MODE ACTIVE -- Trigger: Regime transition probability 72% Time in crisis mode: 00:04:32 WHAT IS HAPPENING: Credit spreads widening sharply. HY +45bp in 90 minutes. Dealer bids pulling back across the board. ETF outflows accelerating (LQD -$800M, HYG -$1.2B today). WHAT IT MEANS: Pattern match: This resembles the opening phase of a credit deleveraging event. The analog is Feb 2018 vol shock crossed with Q4 2018 credit repricing. The model estimates a 58% probability that spreads widen another 50-100bp before stabilizing.

Panel 2: ACTIONS (center, 35% of screen)

IMMEDIATE ACTION REQUIRED: [1] REDUCE HY BY 50% -- Execute now at current bids Est. cost: 8bp slippage vs mid Est. savings if spreads widen 75bp more: $1.4M [2] HEDGE REMAINING VIA CDX -- 5Y protection Cost: 35bp running (elevated from 22bp this morning) Payoff if spreads +100bp: $620K [3] DO NOTHING -- Accept current exposure Est. loss if model is right: -$1.8M to -$3.2M over 1 week Est. gain if model is wrong: +$340K carry over 1 week → Asymmetry favors action

Panel 3: PLAYBOOK STATUS (right, 25% of screen)

ACTIVE PLAYBOOK: Credit Stress Alpha Triggered: 10:43 ET Pre-computed steps: [x] Alert PM (push notification sent) [x] Calculate optimal liquidation sequence [x] Stage hedge orders [ ] PM confirmation required for execution [ ] Post-execution rebalance COST OF DELAY: ████████████░░░░░░ ~$12K per minute at current widening rate (Based on $200M notional, 3.5bp/hour widening)

4.3 Pre-Computed Playbooks

RecWM maintains a library of pre-computed playbooks for known crisis archetypes. Each playbook contains:

  • Trigger conditions (what activates it)
  • Situational assessment template (what to check first)
  • Rank-ordered action list (what to do, in what sequence)
  • Pre-staged orders (ready for one-click execution)
  • Communication template (what to tell LPs/risk committee)

Playbook archetypes include: Credit Stress, Rates Shock, Liquidity Crisis, Counterparty Failure, Flash Crash, Sovereign Event, Correlation Breakdown, and Forced Selling (detected via flow analysis).

4.4 The Inaction Cost Calculator

At every moment, the system displays the estimated cost of inaction. This is critical because the dominant failure mode for PMs during crises is paralysis -- waiting for more information when the cost of waiting exceeds the value of additional information.

The F1 Pit Wall Analogy: "The cost of being wrong by one lap is 2-3 seconds. The cost of waiting one extra lap for certainty is also 2-3 seconds. The option value of additional information is approximately zero."
INACTION COST ESTIMATOR ═══════════════════════ Current trajectory: HY spreads widening 3.5bp/hour If you do nothing for: 15 minutes: -$3K (noise -- not actionable) 1 hour: -$12K (uncomfortable but recoverable) 4 hours: -$48K (material -- equivalent to 2 weeks of carry) 1 day: -$85K (significant -- 15% of quarterly target) Break-even: You should act now UNLESS you believe there is a >72% chance that spreads reverse within 4 hours. Model estimates reversal probability at 18%. VERDICT: ACT. The expected cost of delay exceeds the expected value of additional information.

5. The Cognitive Load Manager

5.1 Attention Budget

The PM has a finite attention budget. The Cognitive Load Manager allocates that budget to maximize decision quality. The system tracks three attention states:

State Description Max Items Depth Refresh
Scan Quick check, everything nominal 3 items Headline only Every 30 min
Monitor Something developing, need to track 5 items Summary + key metric Every 5 min
Engage Active decision required 3 items Full detail + options Real-time

5.2 Progressive Disclosure

Every piece of information in the system exists at three levels of detail:

Level 1 -- Headline (5 words or fewer)
Credit spreads widening sharply
Level 2 -- Summary (2-3 sentences)
HY spreads have widened 45bp since market open, driven by ETF outflows and dealer inventory reduction. The pattern matches Q4 2018 credit stress. Portfolio impact: -$180K mark-to-market.
Level 3 -- Full Analysis (paragraph + data)
[Full orientation engine output including pattern match details, causal chain analysis, positioning data, historical analogs, confidence intervals, and recommended actions]

The PM controls depth with a single interaction: tap for Level 2, long-press for Level 3, or voice command "tell me more about credit."

5.3 Quiet Mode

When all systems are nominal -- health score above 7, no anomalies, no coherence failures, no time-sensitive decisions -- the system enters Quiet Mode. In Quiet Mode:

  • The display shows only the health score and a single line: "All systems nominal. Next scheduled check: [time]."
  • No alerts, no menus, no decisions required.
  • The PM can focus on other work, take meetings, or think strategically.
  • Quiet Mode breaks automatically if any trigger fires.
The system actively resists the temptation to fill silence with noise. Showing the PM information when no action is needed degrades decision quality by creating alert fatigue.

6. The Argument Engine -- Adversarial Reasoning

6.1 Design

Every position, every view, every recommendation in RecWM has an adversarial counterpart. The Argument Engine exists to prevent confirmation bias -- the most dangerous cognitive failure in portfolio management.

The engine has three outputs:

6.2 The Counter-Brief

For every orientation output, the engine generates the strongest possible counter-argument:

COUNTER-BRIEF ═════════════ Your current view: Credit is overvalued and due for repricing. The strongest case against you: 1. Corporate balance sheets are the healthiest since 2005. Leverage ratios are falling. Interest coverage is rising. Default rates are below long-term averages. The fundamental case for tight spreads is sound. 2. The technical picture supports tight spreads. Insurance companies and pension funds are structurally short duration and need to buy credit. This demand floor has persisted through multiple cycles. 3. The Q4 2018 analog you're relying on ended with the Fed pivoting and spreads recovering everything within 3 months. If you sold Q4 2018 stress, you locked in a loss that was recovered by February 2019. 4. Your model's regime transition probability of 72% has historically had a 35% false positive rate. One in three times, the model signals stress and it doesn't materialize. Steelman probability: The counter-argument is correct with estimated 28-35% probability. This is not negligible.

6.3 The Key Assumptions Dashboard

The most important display in the adversarial reasoning system. It shows every load-bearing assumption in the current portfolio positioning, with confidence levels and invalidation criteria.

KEY ASSUMPTIONS DASHBOARD ═════════════════════════ ASSUMPTION CONFIDENCE FRAGILITY INVALIDATOR ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Fed holds rates through Q4 72% HIGH CPI >3.8% or payrolls >300K Credit cycle has more room 45% CRITICAL IG default rate >0.8% or 3 consecutive months of spread widening China stimulus is sufficient 55% MODERATE PMI <48 for 2 months Dealer liquidity is adequate 38% CRITICAL Primary dealer fails to bid at auction Correlation regime is stable 60% HIGH Cross-asset correlation exceeds 0.85 MOST DANGEROUS ASSUMPTION: Dealer liquidity (38% confidence, CRITICAL fragility). If wrong, estimated portfolio impact: -$2.1M to -$4.3M. Monitor: Daily primary dealer position reports, TRACE volume data.

6.4 Pre-Mortem Generator

Before any major position change, the engine runs a pre-mortem: "Assume this decision turned out badly. What went wrong?"

PRE-MORTEM: Reducing HY by 30% ══════════════════════════════ If this decision loses money, the most likely reasons are: 1. (42% probability) The Fed signals a dovish pivot sooner than expected, spreads tighten 60bp, and you sold the bottom. 2. (28% probability) The current widening is a brief technical dislocation from ETF rebalancing, not a regime change. Spreads recover within 2 weeks. 3. (15% probability) You re-enter the position at worse levels, paying the round-trip transaction cost for no benefit. Total probability of regret: ~55% But: The expected cost of being wrong (foregoing ~45bp of carry over 1 quarter = $225K) is much smaller than the expected cost of NOT acting and being right (~$1.8M drawdown). The asymmetry favors action even at 55% regret probability.

7. Decision Journaling -- The Learning Loop

7.1 Automatic Capture

Every time the PM takes an action through RecWM, the system captures a complete decision record:

DECISION RECORD #2026-0811-001 ══════════════════════════════ Timestamp: 2026-08-11 10:52:14 ET Action: Reduced HY exposure by 30% ($60M notional) Execution: Sold via CDX.HY at 385bp, 2bp inside bid-side mid World state at decision: Health score: 6.2 (declining) Regime: TRANSITIONAL Top pattern match: Q4 2018 (73% similarity) Anomaly level: ELEVATED Narrative coherence: 0.42 (LOW) Model recommendation: Reduce HY by 30% (ranked #1, confidence 68%) PM action: Matched recommendation exactly PM reasoning: [captured via voice note or text entry] "Dealer bids are thinning. Don't want to be the last one through the door." Key assumptions at time of decision: Fed holds: 72% confidence Credit cycle turn: 45% confidence Dealer liquidity: 38% confidence

7.2 Outcome Tracking

At T+1 day, T+1 week, T+1 month, and T+1 quarter, the system revisits each decision and scores the outcome:

DECISION REVIEW: #2026-0811-001 (T+1 week) ═══════════════════════════════════════════ Action taken: Sold $60M HY at 385bp Current spread: 420bp (+35bp since decision) P&L impact: +$490K avoided loss (vs. hold-to-current) Model accuracy: Direction correct, magnitude within confidence interval Decision grade: A- (acted on correct signal, slightly early on timing but execution quality was good given liquidity conditions) Lessons: - Model's Q4 2018 analog was directionally correct - Spread widening has been more gradual than 2018 analog predicted - Dealer liquidity assumption (38% confidence) was validated -- bids continued to thin as predicted Feedback to model: - Increase weight on dealer positioning signals (+0.05) - Q4 2018 analog spread velocity was 1.3x too fast -- adjust analog calibration for post-2020 market structure

7.3 The Learning Loop

Decision outcomes feed back into the orientation engine through three channels:

1. Analog Calibration. How well did historical pattern matches predict outcomes? Adjust similarity weights.
2. Confidence Calibration. When the model said 68% confidence, was it right 68% of the time? Adjust confidence scoring.
3. PM Alpha Tracking. When the PM overrides the model's recommendation, does the PM beat the model? Track the PM's comparative advantage and learn from it.

Over time, the system becomes a hybrid intelligence: the model's structural analysis augmented by the PM's calibrated intuition.

8. The Morning Briefing -- The Most Important Daily Interaction

8.1 Design Philosophy

The Morning Briefing is a 2-minute structured information delivery designed to bring the PM from zero to full situational awareness in 120 seconds. It is the single most important daily interaction with RecWM.

The design draws from military shift-change briefings: incoming watch officer must understand the tactical situation completely before the outgoing officer leaves. The PM "takes the watch" each morning from the system that monitored overnight.

8.2 Format Specification
