8.3 Delivery Mechanism

The Morning Briefing is delivered through three channels simultaneously:

  1. Visual. The RecWM interface shows the briefing as the default view when the PM first opens the system each day.
  2. Audio. A synthesized voice reads a compressed version (90 seconds) while the PM commutes or prepares for the day. The audio version omits numbers and focuses on narrative: "Your portfolio health dropped overnight. Credit is the main concern. The BOJ signal is adding pressure. The model thinks you should reduce HY further. You have a decision to make before the auction at 1pm."
  3. Push notification. A single notification summarizing the health score and the number of items requiring attention: "RecWM: Health 6.2 (down from 7.1). 3 items need attention. HY position decision needed today."

8.4 The Baffles Check

Named after the submarine's baffles -- the blind spot directly behind the boat where the sonar cannot see. Every morning briefing includes one item the PM is not currently tracking that the model believes deserves attention.

The Baffles Check is deliberately limited to one item. If the system flagged five blind spots every day, the PM would stop reading them. One item, carefully chosen, ensures it gets read and considered.

Selection criteria for the Baffles Check:

  • Must be something not currently on the PM's watchlist or in the Decision Menu
  • Must have a plausible transmission mechanism to the portfolio
  • Must have shown recent movement that is not yet widely discussed
  • Preference for slow-burn developments over sudden events (sudden events get caught by the main alerting system)

9. System Integration: The Complete Decision Tempo Loop

9.1 Submarine Fire Control Analogy

The full system operates like a submarine's fire control computer. The sonar (observation layer) detects contacts. The TMA (target motion analysis, analogous to the orientation engine) runs multiple solutions, converging on a firing solution. The captain (PM) evaluates the solution's confidence and decides whether to shoot.

Submarine Fire Control

Sonar contact
  ↓
TMA (multiple runs)
  ↓
Firing solution
(bearing, range, confidence)
  ↓
Captain: "Shoot/Hold"
  ↓
Torpedo away
  ↓
BDA (battle damage assessment)

RecWM Decision Tempo Engine

Observation digest
  ↓
Orientation engine (pattern match,
anomaly, narrative, causal)
  ↓
Decision menu
(action, outcome, confidence)
  ↓
PM: "Execute/Hold"
  ↓
Order executed
  ↓
Decision journal + outcome tracking

The key insight from fire control: The captain does not need a perfect solution. The captain needs a solution that is good enough to act on, with a clear understanding of the confidence interval. Waiting for a perfect solution means the target maneuvers and the solution degrades. The Decision Tempo Engine is designed around this principle: good enough, fast enough, with explicit uncertainty.

9.2 Tempo Advantage Quantification

The system's value is measured in tempo advantage -- how much faster RecWM completes the OODA loop compared to the PM's competitors.

OODA Phase Traditional PM RecWM-Augmented PM Tempo Advantage
Observe 45-90 min (read screens, chat, research) 0 min (continuous, pre-filtered) 45-90 min
Orient 60-180 min (synthesize, think, discuss) 2-5 min (read orientation output) 55-175 min
Decide 30-120 min (generate options, evaluate) 5-15 min (review decision menu) 25-105 min
Act 15-45 min (call desk, negotiate, execute) 1-3 min (confirm pre-staged order) 14-42 min
Total 2.5-7 hours 8-23 minutes ~10-20x faster

This tempo advantage means RecWM-augmented PMs can complete 3-5 OODA cycles per day while competitors complete one. Over a quarter, this compounds into a significant information and decision advantage.

9.3 Failure Modes and Safeguards

The system is designed with explicit safeguards against its own failure modes:

1. Model overconfidence. Every confidence estimate includes a "calibration score" based on historical accuracy. If the model says 70% confidence but has historically been right only 55% of the time at that stated confidence level, the calibration warning is displayed.
2. Automation bias. The PM may defer too much to the model. The system periodically forces the PM to articulate their own view before showing the model's recommendation: "Before I show you the Decision Menu, what is your current assessment of the HY position?"
3. Alert fatigue. The Cognitive Load Manager enforces strict limits on alert frequency. If the system generates more than 5 alerts per day in normal mode, it automatically raises its threshold.
4. Feedback loop corruption. Decision journaling could create a system that optimizes for past patterns rather than novel situations. The anomaly detector explicitly counterweights the pattern matcher -- when something is genuinely new, the system says so rather than forcing a historical fit.
5. Speed-accuracy tradeoff. The system tracks whether faster decisions correlate with worse outcomes. If they do, it recommends the PM slow down: "Your last 5 decisions made in under 10 minutes have underperformed your decisions made in 30+ minutes. Consider taking more time on this one."

10. Summary: The Decision Tempo Engine as Competitive Moat

The Decision Tempo Engine is not a dashboard, not an analytics platform, not a research tool. It is a cognitive augmentation system that compresses the PM's OODA loop from hours to minutes while maintaining or improving decision quality.

The competitive moat is not in any single component. It is in the integration:

  • Observation that filters signal from noise in real-time
  • Orientation that synthesizes understanding, not just information
  • Decision support that presents options with explicit uncertainty and adversarial counter-arguments
  • Action readiness that eliminates the gap between deciding and doing
  • Learning that improves every cycle based on outcomes

The PM who uses RecWM does not work harder. They do not read more research or watch more screens. They work at a higher level of abstraction -- at the level of understanding and decision rather than data collection and synthesis. The system handles the mechanical work of observation and analysis. The PM provides judgment, intuition, and accountability.

This is Boyd's vision applied to finance: the side that cycles OODA faster, with higher quality orientation, wins. RecWM is the orientation machine.

Innovation Deep Dive

Cognitive Extension UX

Part of the RecWM Ten-Layer Innovation Stack

Classification: Internal Product Architecture

Design Philosophy: Extended Cognition (Clark & Chalmers 1998) applied to financial markets

Objective: Build an interface so deeply integrated into the PM's cognitive workflow that it becomes a literal component of their financial perception — the blind person's cane, the surgeon's scalpel, the pilot's HUD — not a tool they use but an organ they think with.

Part I

The Screen Architecture

Design Principle: The Triad of Awareness

RecWM deploys across three screens arranged in a cognitive hierarchy that mirrors the brain's own attentional architecture. The primary screen occupies peripheral vision (ambient processing, preattentive features). The secondary screen sits at arm's length, receiving intermittent focal attention. The tertiary screen is the "desk" — pulled forward only when the PM needs to interrogate a specific question.

This mirrors the F1 pit wall: the race engineer's telemetry wall, the strategist's timing screen, and the team principal's aggregate dashboard are three different cognitive instruments serving three different decision timescales.

Primary Screen: The World Canvas

What the PM sees at a glance — the equivalent of the sonar waterfall.

The primary screen is a single, continuous, slowly-evolving visual field. No tables. No numbers in the default state. It is a topological map of the financial world as RecWM perceives it.

Layout

The screen is dominated by a large circular topology — think of a radar display crossed with a gravitational field map. At the center is the portfolio. Radiating outward are concentric rings representing proximity of influence: the innermost ring holds positions and their direct drivers; the middle ring holds macro fragments (rates, credit, volatility regimes); the outer ring holds exogenous forces (geopolitical, regulatory, structural).

Each fragment is represented as a node — a softly glowing circle whose properties encode information through preattentive visual features:

Color
Color encodes health state. A custom palette moves from deep blue (stable, favorable) through teal (neutral) to amber (watchful) to a pulsing coral (stress). This is not a traffic-light system — the transitions are continuous gradients, because markets do not jump from green to red. The PM's peripheral visual system learns to detect the slow drift from blue to teal without conscious attention, the same way a sonar operator detects a tonal shift in the waterfall display.
●
Size encodes magnitude of relevance to the portfolio. A fragment that has grown in influence over the past 48 hours physically expands on the display. The PM does not need to read a number to know that "something in the credit space is getting louder."
Motion
Motion encodes rate of change. Stable fragments are still. Fragments in transition wobble gently, like a gyroscope losing its axis. Fragments in rapid transition pulse — a slow, rhythmic expansion and contraction, like breathing. This motion is designed to trigger the peripheral motion detection circuits of the visual cortex (area MT/V5), which operate below conscious awareness. The PM will feel that something is moving before they know what it is.
Links
Connections between fragments are rendered as thin lines whose opacity encodes correlation strength and whose color encodes sign (blue for positive coupling, a muted copper for negative). During regime transitions, these lines thicken and brighten — the PM sees the system's coupling tighten in real time. During a liquidity crisis, the display will visually contract as correlations spike, fragments pulling toward each other like stars collapsing into a dense cluster. The PM does not need to read a correlation matrix. They see the universe shrinking.
Tex
Texture encodes uncertainty. High-confidence fragments have clean, sharp edges. Low-confidence fragments have a soft, slightly grainy boundary — like looking at something through frosted glass. The PM learns to distrust the fuzzy ones without being told to.

The Waterfall Strip

Along the bottom of the primary screen runs a horizontal time-series strip — the direct descendant of the submarine sonar waterfall. This strip shows the last 24 hours of the world canvas state, compressed into a scrolling band. Each vertical slice is a snapshot of the topology at that moment, rendered as a color column. The PM can see, at a glance, whether the world has been stable (uniform color bands) or turbulent (jagged, shifting patterns). This strip becomes the PM's time-sense for the market — they develop an intuitive feel for the rhythm of the day.

The Heartbeat Line

A single waveform runs across the top of the primary screen: the portfolio health score as a continuous trace, rendered like an ECG. The PM's eye catches the shape of this line — steady and rhythmic during normal conditions, erratic during stress — without reading a single number. This is the ICU monitor principle: the waveform IS the patient.

Secondary Screen: The Portfolio Console

The working surface — what the PM reads when they lean in.

The secondary screen is structured like a Bloomberg terminal reimagined for the world-model era. It is organized into four quadrants:

Top-left: Position Matrix

Every position in the portfolio, displayed as a compact grid. Each cell shows the position name, current P&L (color-coded), and a tiny sparkline of the last 5 days. But the critical addition is the RecWM health indicator: a small colored dot next to each position reflecting the health of the fragments that drive it. The PM sees not just "this position is up 2%" but "this position is up 2% and the fragments supporting it are deteriorating." This is Level 2 SA — comprehension, not just perception.

Top-right: Fragment Composition Panel

The active fragment compositions — the causal narratives RecWM has constructed. Each composition is displayed as a compact card showing: the composition name ("Fed Pivot Thesis," "China Credit Stress," "Energy Dislocation"), its current probability, its trajectory arrow (improving/stable/degrading), and its portfolio impact estimate. These cards are sorted by absolute portfolio impact. The PM scans this quadrant to answer: "What stories is the world telling me, and which ones matter for my book?"

Bottom-left: Scenario Tree

RecWM's forward-looking scenario projections, displayed as a branching tree diagram. The trunk is the current state. Branches represent divergent futures, with branch thickness encoding probability and branch color encoding portfolio impact (blue for favorable, copper for adverse). The PM can see, spatially, the shape of the future — whether it is narrow (high confidence, few scenarios) or wide (deep uncertainty, many branches). A narrow tree with blue branches means "stay the course." A wide tree with mixed colors means "hedge or reduce."

Bottom-right: Action Queue

Recommended actions, ranked by urgency and impact. Each action card shows what to do, why (linked to a fragment composition), expected impact, and a confidence level. Actions are color-coded by type: blue for opportunity, amber for risk management, coral for urgent defense. This quadrant is the bridge between perception and action — RecWM's translation of its world model into the PM's operational language.

Tertiary Screen: The Deep Dive Theater

The investigation surface — opened on demand, closed when done.

The tertiary screen is a flexible workspace that reconfigures based on what the PM is investigating. By default, it shows a blank dark surface with a subtle RecWM logo — an invitation, not a demand. When the PM clicks on any element from the primary or secondary screens, the tertiary screen populates with a deep-dive view.

Fragment Deep Dive

When a fragment is selected, the tertiary screen shows its full anatomy: the data sources feeding it, the historical trajectory (with annotated regime changes), the causal links to other fragments, the confidence decomposition (what is well-supported, what is inferred), and the counterfactual analysis ("if this fragment were in state X instead of state Y, the portfolio impact would be Z").

Scenario Deep Dive

When a scenario branch is selected, the tertiary screen shows the full scenario narrative — the chain of events that leads to this future, the key decision points, the historical analogues, and the specific portfolio impact under this scenario. The PM can toggle between scenarios and see, side by side, how different futures would reshape their book.

Participant Model View

When a market participant is selected (e.g., "Federal Reserve," "China PBOC," "Systematic Vol Sellers"), the tertiary screen shows RecWM's model of that participant: their inferred objectives, constraints, likely actions under different conditions, and historical behavior patterns. This is the "theory of mind" view — the PM seeing the market through the eyes of its other players.

Part II

The Ambient Awareness Layer

Design Principle: Below Consciousness, Above Ignorance

The ambient layer is designed to exploit the human visual system's preattentive processing capabilities. Research by Healey and Enns (2012) identified visual features that can be detected in under 200 milliseconds without focused attention: color, orientation, size, motion, shape, and spatial grouping. RecWM's ambient layer uses exclusively these features to convey market state.

Visual Metaphors for Abstract States

Liquidity Stress

The world canvas literally contracts. Fragment nodes pull closer together. Connection lines thicken and brighten. The visual metaphor is gravitational collapse — the same instinct that makes a school of fish tighten into a ball when a predator approaches. The PM's peripheral vision registers "the world is getting smaller" without conscious analysis. As stress deepens, the background color of the canvas shifts from its default dark charcoal toward a deep, bruised purple — subtle enough that the PM might not notice the exact moment it changes, but visceral enough that they feel it.

Regime Transition

The texture of the entire display changes. During stable regimes, the canvas has a calm, still quality — nodes glow steadily, connections are thin and translucent. When RecWM detects a regime transition, the display develops a subtle shimmer — a low-frequency oscillation across all elements, like heat haze over a highway. This is designed to trigger the "something is different" response before the PM can articulate what changed. The shimmer intensifies as transition probability increases.

Momentum Shift

When a fragment reverses its trajectory, its node develops a rotational quality — it begins to slowly spin, then reverses direction. The visual effect is of a wheel decelerating, stopping, and beginning to turn the other way. The PM's motion-detection circuits pick up the deceleration before the reversal, giving them a preconscious lead time.

Consensus Divergence

When participant models begin to disagree — when the "crowded trade" starts to fragment — the relevant nodes develop a flickering quality, alternating between two colors at a rate just below the fusion threshold. The effect is visual dissonance: the PM feels that something is unstable without knowing why.

Tail Risk Accumulation

The outer ring of the world canvas normally fades into darkness at its edges. When tail risks accumulate, the edges of the canvas begin to glow faintly — a dim, warm light at the periphery, like dawn on the horizon. This exploits the fact that humans are hardwired to notice changes at the edges of their visual field (an evolutionary adaptation for predator detection). The PM's peripheral awareness registers "something is building at the edges" long before any formal alert triggers.

The Ambient Audio Layer

Optionally (and this is a PM preference setting), RecWM can provide an ambient audio channel — not alarms, not speech, but a continuous, low-volume sonic texture that encodes market state. Think of it as the sonar operator's headphones.

During normal conditions, the audio is a low, steady hum — barely audible, like a distant machine. As volatility increases, the pitch rises slightly and the texture becomes more granular. During stress, a subtle rhythmic pulse emerges. During crisis, the frequency spectrum widens into a broader, more complex sound.

This is not background music. It is a data sonification layer that the PM's auditory cortex can process in parallel with their visual attention. Research by Hermann et al. (2011) on auditory display has shown that continuous sonification can provide monitoring capabilities that supplement visual attention, particularly for detecting slow trends and sudden changes.

Part III

The Progressive Disclosure Model

Level 0 — The Glance (0.5 seconds)

The PM looks up from their phone, their conversation, their lunch. In half a second, they absorb:

  • The heartbeat line shape: Steady, erratic, or trending. No numbers needed.
  • The world canvas color: Predominantly blue (calm), mixed (watchful), or amber-coral (stress).
  • The canvas geometry: Expanded (normal) or contracted (correlated stress).
  • Any pulsing elements: Motion attracts attention. A pulsing node means "look at me."

This level is designed for the preattentive visual system. Zero cognitive load. The PM returns to their conversation knowing "everything is fine" or "I should look more closely in a minute."

Level 1 — The Scan (5 seconds)

The PM shifts their gaze to the secondary screen and reads:

  • Top 3 fragment compositions by portfolio impact — just the names and trajectory arrows.
  • Any action items in coral (urgent) in the action queue.
  • The scenario tree shape — narrow (predictable) or branching (uncertain).
  • Position P&L heatmap — who is winning, who is losing.

This level requires focal attention but minimal reading. The PM answers the question: "What is the state of the world and my portfolio right now?"

Level 2 — The Read (30 seconds)

The PM engages with the secondary screen in detail:

  • Fragment composition cards: Read the probability estimates, the supporting evidence summaries, the impact estimates.
  • Scenario narratives: Read the one-sentence summary of each major scenario branch.
  • Action queue rationale: Read why each recommended action is suggested.
  • Position risk decomposition: Which fragments are driving each position's risk.

This level requires active reading and analytical thinking. The PM answers: "What should I be thinking about, and what might I need to do?"

Level 3 — The Deep Dive (5 minutes)

The PM pulls forward the tertiary screen and investigates:

  • Full fragment anatomy: Data sources, historical context, confidence bounds.
  • Scenario counterfactuals: "What if X doesn't happen? What if Y happens instead?"
  • Participant model interrogation: "What is the Fed likely to do, and how confident is the model?"
  • Historical analogue comparison: "When has the world looked like this before, and what happened next?"
  • Portfolio simulation: "If I execute this trade, how does my risk profile change across scenarios?"

This is the deep work. The PM is now using RecWM as a full analytical partner, not just a display.

Part IV

The Morning Ritual Integration

Design Principle: Sacred Augmentation

The morning ritual for a PM is already deeply embedded: wake, check phone (futures, overnight moves), Bloomberg terminal scan, morning meeting, position review. RecWM does not replace this ritual. It layers onto it, making each step richer. The goal is that within three months, the PM cannot remember what the ritual felt like before RecWM.

Phase 1: The Pre-Dawn Push (6:00 AM)

The PM's phone buzzes once — not an alarm, not a notification, a single haptic pulse. They see a lock-screen widget showing three things:

1 The Health Number: A single integer, 1–10, representing overnight portfolio health. Color-coded. If it is 7 or above, the PM relaxes. Below 5, they are already reaching for their phone.

2 The Headline Fragment: One sentence — the single most important thing that changed overnight. "Credit stress in Asia-Pacific intensified; HY spread fragment shifted from blue to amber." This is RecWM's editorial judgment: out of everything that happened, THIS is what matters for YOUR portfolio.

3 The Delta Count: How many fragments changed state overnight. "3 fragments shifted" tells the PM whether the world moved or held still while they slept.

This takes 3 seconds. The PM knows whether to hurry to the desk or take their time.

Phase 2: The Commute Brief (6:30–7:30 AM)

On the tablet (or phone in landscape mode), RecWM presents the Morning Brief — a structured, scrollable document designed for commute reading. This is the new Bloomberg FIRST function, but built for the world-model era.

Structure of the Morning Brief

1. Overnight Narrative (200 words): What happened, told as a coherent story, not a list of data points. "Asian credit markets showed continued stress overnight, driven by property developer liquidity concerns that have now propagated into the broader HY complex. The Liquidity Stress fragment moved from 4.2 to 5.8, crossing the amber threshold. European open reflected this with a 15bp widening in iTraxx crossover. The rate trajectory fragment remained stable, suggesting this is isolated credit stress rather than a broader risk-off event."
2. Fragment State Changes (tabular): Each fragment that changed, with before/after state, driver, and portfolio relevance.
3. Scenario Tree Update: Which branches grew or shrank overnight. Any new branches that emerged. Any branches that were pruned (events that ruled out certain futures).
4. Today's Watch List: Specific events, data releases, or thresholds that could trigger fragment transitions today. "If 10Y breaks 4.50%, the rate regime fragment transitions to 'restrictive,' triggering a cascade into equity risk premium and credit spread fragments."
5. Recommended Pre-Open Actions: Any trades or hedges that the model suggests executing before the market opens, with rationale and urgency level.

The PM reads this during their commute and arrives at the desk already briefed, already thinking, already forming hypotheses. The morning meeting becomes sharper because the PM has already absorbed the situational context.

Phase 3: The Console Activation (7:30 AM)

The PM sits down. The screens wake. The world canvas populates with a brief animation — fragments appearing and connecting, the topology assembling itself like a living organism awakening. This is a deliberate design choice: the animation takes 3 seconds and serves no informational purpose. It is a ritual element. The console is waking up. The day is beginning. The PM's cognitive extension is coming online.

The first thing the secondary screen shows, for exactly 30 seconds before reverting to the standard quadrant layout, is the "Delta View" — a focused summary of what changed since the PM last looked at the console. This is RecWM saying: "Here is what happened while you were away." After 30 seconds, or after the PM clicks anywhere, the console transitions to its standard operating mode.

Part V

The Language of RecWM

Design Principle: Language as Cognitive Scaffolding

When Bloomberg users say "I'll pull it up on the BBAL," they are not just describing an action — they are invoking a shared cognitive framework. RecWM must create its own language that becomes equally natural.

The Core Lexicon

Fragment States (Color Language)

StateColorMeaning
Deep blue Blue Stable, favorable, well-understood
Teal Teal Neutral, watchful, monitoring
Amber Amber Stressed, transitioning, requires attention
Coral Coral Critical, active deterioration, demands action
Usage in conversation: "The credit fragment went amber overnight" is a complete, meaningful sentence to anyone in the RecWM ecosystem. It conveys state, trajectory, urgency, and domain in four words.

Health Score (Numerical Language)

ScoreLabelMeaning
9–10StrongPortfolio is well-positioned across all scenarios
7–8SoundMinor concerns, no action required
5–6WatchfulMeaningful risks present, monitoring closely
3–4StressedActive risks require response
1–2CriticalImmediate action required
Usage: "We are running at a 6 with credit pulling us down" becomes the opening line of the morning meeting.

Fragment Composition Names

RecWM generates human-readable names for its causal compositions. These names are designed to be memorable, specific, and evocative:

NameDescription
Liquidity VortexWhen multiple liquidity indicators converge into a self-reinforcing stress pattern
Rate Regime PivotWhen the model detects a fundamental shift in rate expectations
Correlation StormWhen cross-asset correlations spike simultaneously
The UnwindWhen a crowded positioning fragment begins to reverse
Slow BurnWhen a risk accumulates gradually below threshold but with persistent trajectory

These names enter the PM's vocabulary. They become shorthand. "Are we in a Slow Burn?" is faster, more precise, and more actionable than "Is there a gradually building risk that hasn't triggered any alerts yet?"

Scenario Shorthand

RecWM labels scenario branches with historical analogues when appropriate: "We are on the March-2020 branch" immediately communicates: rapid, correlated, liquidity-driven drawdown. "We are on the 2013-Taper-Tantrum branch" communicates: rate-driven repricing, disorderly but contained.

Tribal Markers

RecWM users will develop linguistic tells:

  • "What color is your book?" (asking about fragment health, not P&L)
  • "The canvas is contracting" (correlation stress building)
  • "I've got shimmer on the rates fragment" (regime transition detected)
  • "We need to prune the tree" (reduce scenario count through decisive action)

These phrases mark the speaker as a RecWM user the way "Can you pull up a GP?" marks a Bloomberg user. Language creates tribe. Tribe creates loyalty.

Part VI

The Stradivarius Effect — Mastery Progression

Design Principle: The Tool That Grows With You

A Stradivarius does not sound better than a student violin to a beginner. It reveals its qualities as the player's skill increases. RecWM must work the same way — always useful, but increasingly powerful as the PM develops fluency.

Week 1: The Dashboard Phase (Level 1 SA — Perception)

What the PM does:

Treats RecWM as a sophisticated dashboard. Checks the health score. Reads the morning brief. Looks at position P&L.

What RecWM does:

Provides clean, clear, immediately useful information. Does not overwhelm. The world canvas is beautiful but mostly decorative to the new user. Fragment compositions are presented simply: name, status, impact.

Milestone trigger:

The PM checks RecWM before Bloomberg for the first time. This is not forced — it happens naturally because the morning brief is more narratively coherent than scanning Bloomberg screens.

Month 1: The Comprehension Phase (Level 2 SA — Comprehension)

What the PM does:

Begins reading fragment compositions in detail. Starts asking "why?" — clicking through to the tertiary screen. Begins using fragment names in conversation ("the credit fragment is amber").

What RecWM reveals:

Deeper causal analysis. The PM discovers that clicking on a fragment shows its upstream drivers. They see the causal chain: "Credit is amber BECAUSE liquidity stress is building BECAUSE dealer balance sheets are constrained BECAUSE of quarter-end dynamics." This is the first taste of Level 2 SA — comprehension of the current situation, not just perception of data points.

Milestone trigger:

The PM makes a trade decision influenced by a fragment composition rather than by a single data point. They say, in the morning meeting: "The model is showing a credit stress composition that concerns me."

Month 3: The Projection Phase (Level 3 SA — Projection)

What the PM does:

Actively uses the scenario tree for decision-making. Begins asking "what if?" — running counterfactual analyses. Starts to feel the rhythm of the world canvas — they notice, preconsciously, when something shifts.

What RecWM reveals:

Predictive compositions. The PM discovers that RecWM does not just describe the current state — it projects forward. The scenario tree becomes a decision-making tool, not just a display. The PM begins simulating trades against scenarios: "If I add this position, how does my health score change across the top three branches?"

Milestone trigger:

The PM catches a risk that they would not have seen without RecWM. The "it saw it before I did" moment. This is the first deep bonding event.

Month 6: The Extension Phase (Cognitive Extension Achieved)

What the PM does:

Stops thinking about RecWM as a separate tool. Their morning ritual is seamlessly integrated. Their vocabulary has changed. Their decision process has changed. When someone asks how they knew to hedge before the drawdown, they cannot separate their own judgment from RecWM's contribution — because there is no separation. The tool is part of the cognition.

What RecWM reveals:

The PM begins to notice that RecWM is adapting to them. The morning brief emphasizes the things they care about. The action queue prioritizes the types of trades they favor. The scenario tree highlights the branches they find most relevant. RecWM is learning the PM's investment personality and becoming a more precise cognitive extension as a result.

Milestone trigger:

RecWM goes down for scheduled maintenance on a Saturday night. On Monday morning, the PM arrives at their desk and feels blind. The muscle memory is there — they reach for the world canvas with their eyes — but the screens are dark. This is the "I cannot go back" moment. It lasts 4 hours. When RecWM comes back online, the PM feels a wave of relief that they would describe, if pressed, as "getting my vision back."

Year 1: The Mastery Phase (Permanent Cognitive Alteration)

What the PM does:

Their mental model of the market has been permanently restructured. They think in fragments, compositions, and scenarios even when RecWM is not in front of them. When they read a news article, they automatically translate it into fragment impacts. When they hear a macro argument, they evaluate it against RecWM's scenario tree. They are faster, more precise, and more calibrated than they were a year ago, and they attribute much of this to RecWM — not because RecWM told them what to think, but because it organized the way they think.

Milestone trigger:

The PM tries a competing product. Within 30 minutes, they close it. Not because it is worse in any measurable way — but because it does not think the way they think. RecWM has become their cognitive dialect. Everything else is a foreign language.

Part VII

The Crisis Interface

Design Principle: The System That Becomes What You Need

In normal conditions, RecWM is a perception engine — ambient, continuous, low-demand. In crisis conditions, RecWM transforms into an action engine — focused, urgent, high-bandwidth.

Automatic Mode Transition

RecWM operates in three modes, with transitions triggered by the aggregate state of the fragment network:

Normal Mode (Health 7–10)

Full ambient display, standard information density, exploratory tools available. The PM browses, explores, thinks.

Elevated Mode (Health 4–6)

The world canvas subtly intensifies. The background darkens slightly. The heartbeat line becomes more prominent. The action queue moves from the bottom-right quadrant to the top-right, displacing the fragment composition panel (which moves to the tertiary screen). The message: "Pay attention. You may need to act."

Crisis Mode (Health 1–3)

The interface transforms.

The world canvas contracts sharply — fragments pull together, connections blaze bright, the peripheral glow at the edges flares. On the secondary screen, the four-quadrant layout collapses into two panels:

Left panel: The Situation Board

A real-time, auto-updating narrative of what is happening. Not data feeds — a continuously generated human-readable account: "Credit stress has cascaded from Asia HY into European IG. Dealer liquidity indicators suggest market-making capacity has dropped 40% from yesterday. The Fed Pivot scenario has been pruned — the model now assigns 85% probability to a Liquidity Vortex composition. Portfolio health is 2 and declining."

Right panel: The Action Board

Pre-computed playbooks that have been activated, each available as a one-click execution package. "Playbook: Defensive De-risk. Actions: Reduce HY exposure by 30%, add 3M put spread on HYG, increase cash to 15%. Estimated cost: 45bp of carry. Estimated health improvement: from 2 to 5. Execute?"

At the top of the secondary screen, a communication bar appears: one-click buttons for "Alert CIO," "Alert Risk Team," "Alert Traders," each pre-loaded with a context-appropriate message generated from RecWM's situational assessment.

The tertiary screen becomes the "war room" — a full-screen scenario simulation environment where the PM can stress-test responses in real time: "If I execute the defensive playbook AND the Vortex deepens, where do I end up?"

The Debrief

After crisis mode ends (health returns above 6), RecWM automatically generates a "Crisis Debrief" — a structured post-mortem document:

  • Timeline of events and fragment state transitions
  • Actions taken (by both RecWM recommendations and PM decisions)
  • Portfolio impact analysis (what was lost, what was saved by defensive action)
  • Model performance assessment (what did RecWM predict correctly, what did it miss)
  • Lessons for future playbooks

This debrief becomes a learning artifact — both for the PM and for RecWM's own model improvement.

Part VIII

The Bonding Moments

Design Principle: Engineered Serendipity

Bonding moments cannot be forced, but they can be designed for. RecWM's architecture creates the conditions for specific types of bonding experiences.

Moment 1: "It Saw It Before I Did"

Design

RecWM's fragment network has a broader perceptual field than any human PM. It monitors hundreds of data streams simultaneously. The "early detection" moment is when RecWM highlights a pattern — say, a subtle shift in dealer positioning data combined with an unusual options flow pattern — that the PM has not noticed.

Product experience

The PM sees a fragment shift from blue to teal. They investigate. They discover a risk they had not considered. They take action. The next day, the risk materializes. The PM tells the story at the morning meeting: "RecWM flagged the dealer positioning shift on Tuesday. We hedged Wednesday morning. By Thursday, the market was in full risk-off." This story becomes organizational mythology. It sells RecWM internally better than any presentation.

Design requirement

The early detection alert must be delivered with the right confidence calibration. Too many false positives destroy trust. Too few miss the bonding moment. The model must be tuned to a precision-recall tradeoff that favors rare, high-quality early detections over frequent, noisy ones. Better to alert 5 times a year and be right 4 times than to alert 50 times and be right 10 times.

Moment 2: "It Saved Me"

Design

The crisis interface is designed to enable this moment. When the PM executes a defensive playbook and the avoided loss becomes quantifiable, RecWM calculates and presents the "avoided loss" figure in the crisis debrief.

Product experience

"During the Q3 liquidity event, RecWM's Liquidity Vortex detection triggered 4 hours before the market selloff. The defensive playbook reduced portfolio drawdown from an estimated −3.2% to an actual −0.8%. Estimated value of early action: $12M."

This is the moment that makes RecWM un-cancellable. The PM now has a specific dollar figure attached to the tool. Every budget conversation is answered by: "It saved us $12M in Q3."

Moment 3: "It Knows Me"

Design

RecWM's adaptation layer learns the PM's preferences over time. Not just their positions — their cognitive style. Do they prefer narrative or quantitative briefings? Do they act on mean-reversion or momentum signals? Do they hedge early or late? Do they prefer gradual position adjustments or decisive shifts?

Product experience

After 6 months, the PM notices that the morning brief emphasizes exactly the things they would ask about. The action queue recommends trades that align with their style. The scenario tree highlights the branches they find most decision-relevant. The PM has the uncanny feeling that RecWM "gets" them — not in an artificial, chatbot-like way, but in the way that a well-trained assistant anticipates needs. This is the "cognitive symbiosis" moment.

Moment 4: "I Cannot Go Back"

Design

This moment is not engineered — it emerges naturally from the previous three. But it can be recognized and reinforced. When RecWM detects that it has been offline or unavailable (scheduled maintenance, technical issue), it generates a "reconnection brief" when it comes back online: "While you were disconnected, here is what happened and what you missed." This brief subtly reinforces the PM's awareness of what RecWM provides — by showing them the gap.

Product experience

The PM sits down on Monday morning after a weekend maintenance window. RecWM presents: "During the 36 hours offline, 7 fragments shifted state. Two compositions were activated that would have triggered amber alerts. Summary of missed signals follows." The PM reads this and thinks: "I was flying blind and didn't even know it." This is the moment of permanent dependency.

Part IX

The Social Layer

Design Principle: Shared Perception Creates Shared Identity

RecWM is not just a PM tool — it is an organizational nervous system. The social layer transforms individual cognitive extension into collective intelligence.

The CIO View

The CIO does not need to see individual fragments. They need to see the aggregate health of the portfolio team. The CIO view is a single screen showing:

  • PM Health Grid: Each PM's portfolio health score, displayed as a matrix. Color-coded. The CIO sees, at a glance, which PMs are in good shape and which are under stress.
  • Correlation Map: How correlated are the PM portfolios? Are they all exposed to the same fragments? The CIO can see crowding risk across the team.
  • Scenario Impact Matrix: Under each major scenario branch, what happens to total fund exposure? The CIO can identify: "If the Liquidity Vortex scenario materializes, PM A and PM C are both heavily impacted, but PM B is naturally hedged."
  • Aggregate Fragment Health: The fund-level world canvas — which fragments are most concerning for the fund as a whole?

PM-to-PM Communication

RecWM enables a new form of professional dialogue. Two PMs can "share canvases" — overlaying their fragment views to see where their perceptions agree and diverge. "My credit fragment is amber, yours is still teal — what are you seeing that I'm not?" This is a richer, more structured form of the hallway conversation.

Design — Share View: A "Share View" button on any fragment or composition opens a lightweight communication panel. The PM can send a fragment state to a colleague with a one-line annotation. The recipient sees the fragment in their own context — overlaid on their own canvas. This is not messaging. It is shared perception.

The Morning Meeting Transformation

RecWM transforms the morning meeting from a sequential briefing ("PM A reports, PM B reports...") into a collaborative situational assessment. The meeting room screen shows the aggregate world canvas. PMs add their own overlays. The CIO sees the synthesized picture.

The shared language makes this possible. When every PM speaks in fragments, compositions, and health scores, the meeting becomes faster, more precise, and more productive. The CIO asks: "Who is below 7?" Two PMs raise their hands. "What fragments?" "Credit for me, rates for me." "Are they connected?" RecWM shows the correlation. "Yes — both are driven by the Liquidity Stress composition." In three minutes, the fund has identified a concentrated risk that would have taken 30 minutes of discussion to surface in the old format.

Part X

Design Specifications and Rationale

Color System

The color palette is deliberate and grounded in research on color perception and emotional association:

ColorHex RangeRationale
Deep Blue #1a3a5c → #2d6ca2 Stability, depth, trust. Blue activates the parasympathetic nervous system — it is calming. Stable market states should feel calming.
Teal #2d8a8a → #4db8a4 Watchfulness without alarm. Teal is the transition color — it signals "something has changed" without triggering a stress response.
Amber #c4873b → #d4a24c Attention, warmth, urgency. Amber is the universal "caution" color — visible in peripheral vision, unambiguous in meaning.
Coral #c75c5c → #d44a4a Action, danger, criticality. Not pure red (which triggers panic and narrows attention) but coral (which demands attention while preserving cognitive breadth).
Background: Always dark (#0a0e14 to #141a24). This is not aesthetic preference — it is functional. Dark backgrounds reduce eye strain during extended viewing, improve the visibility of color-coded elements, and create the immersive, "cockpit" quality that supports cognitive extension. The PM should feel like they are inside the display, not looking at it.

Typography

The interface uses a single typeface family: a custom monospace variant for data (position names, numbers, fragment labels) and a proportional variant for narrative text (morning brief, scenario descriptions). Numbers use tabular figures exclusively — columns must align. The typeface is rendered at high contrast against the dark background, but at a size that discourages reading from across the room. RecWM is a personal cognitive instrument, not a wall display.

Animation Principles

All animations are continuous and organic — no sudden jumps, no step changes, no blinking. The world canvas evolves like a living organism: fragment nodes drift, connections flex, colors shift gradually. The animation speed is tuned to be fast enough to convey change but slow enough to avoid distraction. Target animation cycle: 2–4 seconds for any visual transition. This matches the natural rhythm of breathing and creates a meditative quality that supports sustained attention.

Sound Design

The ambient audio layer (optional) is designed by a sound designer, not an engineer. It must be:

  • Non-fatiguing over 10+ hours of continuous exposure
  • Distinguishable from office background noise
  • Emotionally neutral in the base state
  • Capable of conveying urgency without triggering startle responses
  • Processable by the auditory cortex in parallel with speech (so the PM can have a conversation while listening)

The reference model is the "room tone" used in film sound design — the barely perceptible ambience that tells you whether you are in a cathedral or a submarine. RecWM's audio tells the PM whether they are in a calm market or a stressed one, without them ever consciously listening.

Haptic Feedback

For mobile interactions, RecWM uses Apple's Taptic Engine (or equivalent) to provide haptic feedback that encodes urgency:

PatternMeaning
Single pulseInformational notification (morning brief is ready)
Double pulseAttention requested (fragment crossed threshold)
Continuous vibration (200ms)Action required (crisis mode activated)

The PM's phone becomes a peripheral awareness device — they feel the market through their pocket.

Conclusion: The Instrument, Not the Tool

The ultimate measure of RecWM's UX success is not whether PMs "like" it or find it "useful." It is whether, after 6 months of use, the PM's cognitive architecture has been permanently altered — whether they perceive markets differently, think about risk differently, and make decisions differently in ways they cannot fully articulate or reverse.

RecWM is not a dashboard. It is not an analytics platform. It is not a decision-support tool. It is a cognitive prosthetic — an artificial organ of financial perception that, once integrated, becomes indistinguishable from the PM's own intelligence.

The interface design decisions documented here — the ambient awareness layer, the progressive disclosure model, the morning ritual integration, the tribal language, the mastery progression, the crisis transformation, the bonding moments — are all in service of a single objective: making RecWM the instrument through which the PM perceives, comprehends, and projects the financial world. Not a window they look through, but an eye they see with.

Like the blind person's cane in Clark and Chalmers' formulation, RecWM must reach the point where the PM does not experience it as a separate object. They do not "check RecWM." They do not "look at RecWM." They see the world, and RecWM is how they see it. The cane is not where perception ends — it is where perception begins. RecWM must achieve the same status for financial perception.

That is the design target. Everything in this document serves it.
